As the Master prepared to respond, Wuzhuo struck him across the mouth, causing him to lose a tooth. Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment. He remained at Tianning. By...

This was a meeting of minds between teacher and disciple. He questioned him without interval, and later, having opened the Dharma for the Great Awakened One, he moved to Central India and subsequently relocated to Lingfeng.
Ascending the hall, he said: "More than half of the spring's ninety days have passed; the weather for blooming flowers is perfectly harmonious.
The warbling of the oriole upon the sea-blossom branches—do those who follow the worldly flow perceive this? Even so, though it is thus, first one must penetrate through sound."
A single phrase that pierces through: How would you say it? "The golden-reined horse neighs on the fragrant grass;
the jade-towered person is drunk beneath the apricot blossoms. Ascending the hall, he raised the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature, saying:

"A beauty of sixteen years embroiders slowly; beneath the purple *zhijing* flowers, the yellow oriole warbles. How pitiable, this boundless spring melancholy—it all lies in the needle being left unthreaded."
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the Jiawu year of the Chunxi era, Emperor Xiaozong summoned him to the inner palace and granted him a seat to preach the Dharma.

The Emperor cited the karmic occasion regarding "not being a companion to the myriad dharmas" and requested that he provide a *niantie* (critical commentary). Having finished his *niantie*, the Master offered this verse:
"A presser of oil squeezes out oil; Idle talk and long-winded speech are done with. With a hundred thousand strings of cash girding one's waist, One rides a crane up to Yangzhou. Jihai.
In the middle [of the hall], he ascended the dais, addressed the assembly, and passed away.
Chan Master Yuanjue of Mount Xiang’er in Pengshan, Meizhou, was the son of the Yuan clan of that prefecture; he left the household life and inherited the Lamp of the Dharma.

He passed the scriptural examinations and received ordination; his original name was Yuánjué (Yuánjué). When the Prefect filled out the temple registration form, he mistakenly wrote the character "Yuán" (Yuán) instead.

Suspecting that the Master might be displeased, the Prefect jokingly said to him, "Is it acceptable to have a name consisting of only one character? The Master laughed and replied, "One character is already too many. The Prefect marveled at this.
Having received full ordination, he left Sichuan to visit various eminent masters who possessed the Way. Later, he relied upon Dàguī Fóxìng and entered his room for instruction.
He recounted what he had seen. Xing said, "You are far off indeed; nevertheless, I know you to be a vessel for the Dharma. I shall appoint you as an attendant to manage guests.

Whenever the Master attended upon Xing, Xing would invariably cite the four characters of the *Lotus Sūtra*—*kai-shi-wu-ru* (opening, showing, awakening, and entering)—and command him to provide a response.
He further said, "Only when I nod my head vertically will you finally be correct. By chance, he was dismissed for failing in his duties. [End of excerpt].

Looking for it as if it were in front, it is neither orthodox nor biased; it cuts off the ten directions, its majesty subduing the great thousandfold world-system. Suddenly it is behind—what a leakage!

Chan Master Xian of Baohua in Suzhou Prefecture was a native of that same region. He ascended the hall and said: "The porridge has been eaten;

to place a head upon a head is to wash a bowl for a snake—drawing legs where there are none. If you ask further how it is, you will only bring about your own defeat. After a long silence, he called out loudly to the assembly.
When the assembly raised their heads, the Master said, "Return to the hall to drink tea. He then ascended the hall again and said: "Do not practice Chan. Do not speak of the Way."
Cease from study. Rest the mind and forget all artifice; it is ever vast and open. The ready-made koan is already full of complications;
this very "no-mind" is already a fabrication. Even if you were to sit and cut off the state prior to birth—after a long silence, he said: "Wrong! Wrong! Wrong!"
Chan Master Jue of Mount Dongshan in Shaoxing Prefecture later resided at Yingsheng. He ascended the hall;

after the three beats of the drum had ceased, he said, "Everyone has come forward, intending to investigate the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. Do you know that the sword has long since been lost?"
Even if one were to attain enlightenment directly and immediately, it would still be like cutting off one’s own head to seek life.

Dongshan had no choice but to press the matter from the perspective of the "second head. [He] struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall. Entering the hall: "The flowers are in full bloom; the scenery is warm and radiant."
Do not say that there is another heaven within a jar; if you can realize it at the tips of the hundred grasses—three *zhang* high in the east and eight *cun* wide in the west—I will ascend the hall.
Once, the butcher Guang’e went to where the Buddha was, cast down his butcher’s knife, and said, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas.
The World-Honored One said, "So it is, so it is. Nowadays, the monastic communities assume that this refers to the butcher Guang’e.
"In the past, there was a Buddha who manifested as a butcher by means of skillful means. To see it this way is like seeing Wide-Face; for now, let us say there is no connection. Again he said:
'Wide-Face was precisely a man who would not blink when killing people; he cast down his butcher’s blade and became a Buddha on the spot.

For now, let us say there is no connection. Furthermore, he said: 'When Wide-Face cast down his butcher’s blade, he declared: "I am one of the thousand Buddhas. For now, let us say there is no connection."
As for "counting," the number of Buddhas is clearly defined; for now, let us rejoice that there is no further involvement. Do you wish to recognize Wide Forehead?
After the winds and rains have passed over the peach trees by the roadside, where can a horse’s hoof avoid the remaining blossoms?
Master Fuzi Wen of Hongfu Temple in Taizhou Prefecture ascended the hall and, citing the story of Baizhang’s Wild Fox, offered this verse:
"Not obscured, not falling—how can you understand? If you understand, you will still fall as a wild fox before long. One night a cool wind arises from the painted horn."
The full moon fills the boat as it drifts upon the rivers and lakes.
Master Jue of Tianfeng at Taizhou Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "Within the realm of non-arising, there is no place for settled dwelling;
atop a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, how can one pause? For now, let us cast off our hands into the void and turn ourselves over directly—what is this one phrase?"
The Way. When a person encounters good fortune, their spirit becomes refreshed; entering fire, the true golden color becomes even more brilliant.
When the Head Seat Daozu of Chengdu’s Zhaojue Monastery first met Yuanwu, he attained enlightenment under the teaching "Mind itself is Buddha.
After some time, Yuanwu ordered him to share the seat [of the abbot]. One day, while leading the assembly into the inner quarters, there were about twenty people remaining. The Master...
Suddenly he asked, "When birth and death arrive, how can one avoid them? The monk had no reply. The Master threw down his whisk and passed away in an instant.
The assembly was all struck with astonishment and immediately informed Wuzu. Wuzu arrived and called out, "Head Seat Zuzhu! The Master opened his eyes and looked at him.
Wuzu said, "Rouse your spirit and pass through the barrier. The Master nodded his head and finally entered nirvana.
The Head Seat (Shouzuo) Yunju Zongzhen of Nankang Prefecture was a native of Danqiu.

While attending Yuanwu at Yunju, one day as he gazed up at the bell pavilion, he suddenly attained realization. When someone questioned him about this, the Head Seat responded with three verses, the last of which says: [Verse omitted per instructions]
I have a single pivot upon which I directly point it out to you: a thunderclap in the blue sky, as swift as a flash of lightning or a shooting star.

Even if Deshan and Linji were to apply their staffs and shouts in vain, what loss would this have to your own untransmitted wondrous function? Upon awakening, Wujian was greatly delighted; he once wrote on a wall:
"Dwelling atop the highest peak among a thousand crags, My years approach sixty, yet I remain carefree and relaxed. I need no longer let my name be hung upon the wall."
Regarding human teeth: [The Master] sweetly composed this for the hundred *shilu* monks this morning.
Xu Fu, styled Shichuan and titled the Layman of Donghu, served his late father, the Dragon Diagram Official (Longtu), whenever they visited Fachang and Lingyuan.
They would engage in discourse all day long, yet when the Duke heard of it, he regarded it with disdain. When Fachang passed away, [Xu Fu] was laughing.

During their conversation, the Duke was struck by his extraordinary nature and began to place profound faith in this Way. Later, while observing the mourning period for his father, he reflected that there was no way to repay his boundless debt of gratitude.
He therefore commanded Lingyuan to return to Xiaozhi Monastery to preach the Dharma. When Lingyuan ascended the seat and finished the exchange of questions and answers, he said:

"Gentlemen, consider the Dragon Diagram (Longtu) who, throughout his life, read ten thousand scrolls of books; like water being passed from one vessel to another, not a single drop was lost. Now tell me, where does he seek [the truth]?"
"Where have you always been attached? Now that you have cast off your consciousness, where will you place those ten thousand scrolls of books?
Upon hearing this, the Master was suddenly enlightened and said, "I have no regrets. Yuan then descended from his seat.
A scholar asked, "What did you just see that you speak in such a manner? Dongshan Gong said, "If I had seen anything, I would have left the Master at a loss.
Dayuan said, "In that case, I am not as good as you. Gong asked, "Master, what kind of mental activity is this? Dayuan laughed heartily.
During the Jingkang era of Emperor Qinzong's reign, he served as a Ministerial Secretary (Shangshu Waibang) and was a member of the court.
The fellow practitioner, who hung his alms bowl at Tianning and chose the Zhemu Hall to exert himself in the study of Yuanwu, was also pleased by the latter’s transcendent insight.
One day, he went to the Secretary’s Office and pointed to Yuanwu’s head, saying, “This old fellow has not yet touched the ground with his heels.
Yuanwu turned his face away and said, “How could a tortoise ever escape from inside a jar? The practitioner replied, “I am glad, Old Man...”
Han’s heels touched the ground. Wuzhuo said, "Do not slander him. The official then withdrew.
Zhao Lingjin, styled Biao zhi and known as the Layman Chaoran, served as the Governor of Nankang; his administration was equitable and his affairs were simple.
He frequently associated with Chan monks. In the intervals between public assemblies, he established a "room for Mazu" (a meditation hall). It happened that Yuanwu was residing at Mount Ou;

the Master went to him to undergo his rigorous training. Yuanwu would not grant him any concessions. When the Master earnestly requested instruction, Yuanwu said, "If you wish to attain realization in this matter, you must undergo a 'great death' once.
The Master attained silent understanding and once recorded it in a brief note, which read in part: "My house is poor..."
They encountered bandits. Who would have known that nothing remained? The house was empty and without a person; several times the thieves returned and even struck them.

Upon awakening, they perceived the truth and instructed [the others] to provide protection. In the winter of the Gengshen year of the Shaoxing era, the Duke, along with the Palace Secretary Wang Zao and the Vice President of the Council Li Bing...
When Minister Ceng Kai visited Mount Jing to pay his respects to Dahui, Dahui heard of his arrival and ordered the drum to be beaten for him to enter the room.
The Minister joyfully approached with incense tucked in his sleeve. Dahui asked, "Regarding the story of Zhaozhou washing the alms bowl, how do you, Layman, understand it?"
The Duke said, "What bowl are you looking for? and brushed out his sleeves to leave. Huì rose and grabbed him, saying, "The ancients attained enlightenment right here;
why do you not attain it? As the Duke was about to reply, Huì struck him and said, "What bowl are you looking for?"
The Duke said, "It is only now that this old man has finally recovered.
Li Mison, a Court Gentleman of the Second Class, was styled Layman Puxian. In his youth, he could read five lines of a book at once.

At the age of eighteen, he passed the provincial examination and attained the jinshi degree in the capital. He subsequently rose through various important positions; at twenty-eight, he became a Secretary of the Central Secretariat.

He entered the quarters of Yuanwu. One morning, returning from the early court audience, he reached Tianjin Bridge when his horse leaped; suddenly he attained realization, and sweat poured from his entire body.

He went straight to Tianning Monastery, where it happened that Yuanwu was coming out the door. Seeing him from afar, Yuanwu called out, "Zhongshu (Director of the Secretariat)! Congratulations, the great matter is finished!
The official shouted back fiercely, "Monk, why do you dazzle my eyes with such talk? Yuanwu gave a shout, and the official also shouted. Thereupon—

His spiritual acuity was swift and sharp; whenever he engaged in dialogue regarding awakening, he never yielded when the moment called for it. Later, he was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*).
He requested a clerical stipend and returned to Liánjiāng in Fúmián, where he built a hermitage to enjoy himself. One day, suddenly manifesting a slight illness, he urgently asked for a bath.
Having finished bathing, he sat in the lotus posture and wrote this verse: "In vain have I spoken of Mùhù since of old; today, it is clearly revealed. Space is pressed down flat."
"Xumi! Speak of the one path that points directly upward! Having said this, he threw down his brush and passed away.
Dao-ren Jue-an, surnamed Zu, was the niece of You Cha-yuan of Jian-ning. From her youth, she resolved not to marry and devoted herself to the ancestral Way.
Upon hearing the words from Yuanwu’s public discourse, she attained clear and thorough understanding. Yuanwu said, "You must still cast it all away."
Only upon seeing this did he first attain freedom. The Patriarch answered with a verse: “The pillar sprouts horizontal bones; Space brandishes its claws and fangs.
Even if you were to grasp this through the profound, It would still be sand in your eyes.”

Renling Benming was titled "Master of the Radiant Chamber. Having attained perfect enlightenment through his own karmic resonance, he traveled extensively to consult renowned masters and received their seals of approval from all.
On the full moon of the second month in the Gengshen year of the Xiangshi era, he personally wrote three verses and sent them to Qing of Caotang, subtly revealing his intention to pass away.

At the end of the month, he bid farewell to his relatives and passed away. Caotang appended a postscript to the verses, which were subsequently carved into woodblocks and circulated throughout the world. Great...
Huì once gave a teaching to bring this forth, in verse: "If you do not recognize afflictions as bodhi, To follow after afflictions is ignorance.
At the moment of their arising and ceasing, one must realize it: A hawk flies over Silla, yet people do not know.
If you do not recognize afflictions as bodhi, Pure flowers grow from the mud. When someone comes to ask me what to do, I eat my gruel."
Having finished eating, wash the bowl. Do not concern yourself with it; do not concern yourself with it. All day long you remain dull-witted, counting the sands of the ocean.
If you wish to recognize your original true face, this is the patriarch’s single liberation.
Those who cannot speak it die beneath the staff; those who can speak it also die beneath the staff. After all, what is it? "Do not travel at night; you must arrive by dawn."

Lady Fan of Fan County in Chengdu Prefecture was a widow who habitually sat and never lay down. Hearing that Yuanwu was residing at Zhaojue Temple, she went there to pay her respects and requested instruction on the causes and conditions for entering the Way.
Yuanwu instructed her to contemplate: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing—what is this?
For a long time, she found no point of realization. Lady Fan wept and said to Yuanwu, "Master, what skillful means do you have to enable me to..."
At a certain Chan assembly, Wuzu said, "There is indeed a skillful means. He then instructed [the student] to simply look into what this is.
Later, he had an awakening and said, "I never realized it was so close all along!"
Chan Master Wenshu Zhengdao of Chengde Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Taiping Qin.
He was the son of the Xu family of Danling in Meizhou. At the age of thirty, he received full ordination.

He went to Chengdu to study the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Consciousness-Only), believing that he had reached the ultimate understanding. A fellow student challenged him, saying, "The three realms are mind-only."
"All phenomena are but consciousness. Yet now, before my eyes, the myriad phenomena are vividly manifest; where, then, does the mind-consciousness reside?
The Master was at a loss and did not know how to respond. He subsequently left the mountain pass and wandered through the Jianghuai region.

Upon arriving at Taiping in Shu, he heard that during the night instruction at Foguan, the master raised the "Pine Tree" koan and, reaching the point where Jue Tiecuo said, "The former master did not say such a thing; do not slander the former master," [the Master suddenly attained realization]. Because of this—
He was in great doubt. After a long period of sustained mindfulness, one day there was a sudden breakthrough. He went to the master’s quarters to recount his realization.
As soon as Master Jian saw him coming, he closed the door. The Master said, "Preceptor, do not deceive me. Jian said, "The ten directions have no walls; why do you not come through the door?
The Master punched a hole in the window paper. Jian immediately opened the door, grabbed him, and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master—
Holding the mirror to his head with both hands, he spat upon it and departed. He then presented many verses: "Zhaozhou has a story about the cypress tree;
Zen practitioners have passed it down throughout the world. Most of them pluck at the leaves and search among the branches, unable to pull directly from the root source.
Master Jue said, "To say there is no such thing is precisely like reviling someone to their face with foul language. If a Zen practitioner...

Possessing the all-pervading eye, he excelled at discerning the true from the false within this [teaching]. Later, when the Mirror-like [Master] invited him to share his seat, Xiangshou requested that he open the Dharma at Tianning Monastery.
Not long after, he was promoted to the position of Wenshu at Dayue; ascending the hall, he let out a lion’s roar.
The Elephant King roars. Yunmen hides his body within the Big Dipper. Why did Baiyun call it a "hand"? The Buddhas of the three periods cannot know it;
the stray cat and the white ox, however, do know it exists. But tell me, what is this matter of their knowing it?
Rain beats upon the pear blossoms as butterflies fly; the wind blows the willow catkins as they roll away. [He ascended the hall.]
He held up his staff and pointed directly upward, saying, "Piercing through the heels of Kauśika. He struck once and said, "Shattering the skull of King Yama.
Then, pointing to the east, he said, "Penetrating the eyes of the carp in the Eastern Sea.
Pointing to the west, he said, "Stopping up the nostrils of the Queen Mother of the West. Now tell me: what is it like when none of this is so? This year...

The rains are frequent; everyone should dry their bedding and robes often. In the first year of the Xuanhua era, the Jihai year, an imperial edict was issued changing the title of monks to "Virtuous Practitioners" (Deshi).
The Master ascended the hall and said: "The matter of the Patriarch’s intent coming from the West is, this very day, exceptionally new.

Formerly I bore the appearance of a Bhikṣu; now I take the form of the Old Lord (Laojun). A crane-feather cloak over a silver-brown robe, with a banana-leaf turban wrapped around my head—I have no concerns regarding forest or spring."
Guest: "Twice I have received your grace. Therefore it is said: 'If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season.
Now tell me, what is the current season? Vairocana wears a jeweled crown to manifest the conventional within the absolute;
the old man Mañjuśrī dons a crane-feather robe to conform to the exigencies of the times. Since one person has already done so..."
It is so. It is the same for all people. When a great master establishes a monastic community (*saṅghārāma*), it is a joy to witness a gathering of immortals.

Together they sip the wine of the Immortal’s Delusion and sing the *Bùxū* verses in unison. Sometimes they read the *Língbǎo Dúrénjīng*; sometimes they discuss the elixirs of longevity and immortality.
Under the moon, lutes are played, their fingertips emitting the sounds of antiquity; by the eaves, chess pieces are laid out, their subtle moves producing divine wonders.
Beyond the pivot, take one step forward and you reach the heights of the Great Brahma Heaven; take one step back and you enter the city of the Nine Shades.

As for that phrase "neither advancing nor retreating," how would you speak of it? "Even if one transforms into an immortal on the path to the Three Purities, in the end it remains but a single illusory body in saṃsāra.
On the ninth day of the ninth month of the Gengzi year, he returned to the monastic order and ascended the hall. He said: "Unattached to fields..."

He donned feathered robes, which seemed quite suited to the physical appearance of the Old Lord (Laojun). For more than a year and a half, he reflected idly: "In general, prosperity and decline each have their own time.
Our Buddha knew that the Dharma would face difficulties; this is clearly recorded in the scriptures, and there is nothing I do not know of it.

Yet the Māra has seized the opportunity to confuse and disrupt the True Teaching. The sound of the gongs and cymbals has ceased; the begging bowl has been filled with extra legs. He employs many forms of deceit and fraud to mislead [the people]."
It is not that we lack a sagely sovereign; rather, it is because our Emperor’s sacred virtue and sagely brilliance have not forgotten the sacred entrustment.

He has graciously bestowed his imperial calligraphy and restored the monastic images, allowing them to be refurbished once more. This is truly like cold ashes catching fire again or withered wood flourishing anew. [I] am deluded by the divine nectar.
Nectar and jade broth are transformed; the *Buxu* hymns are turned into songs of returning home. Setting down the silver wooden tablet, he picks up the *niśīdana*.
"Yesterday I bowed with hands joined; today I offer greetings and inquire after your well-being.
Only the outward appearance has changed, not the person of old. I dare ask the assembly: who is this person of old? (He remained silent for a long while.)
He said: "The autumn wind dispels the suspicion of scattered disorder; it blows away the ashes of the Way from those years.
In the spring of the Jiyou year of the Jianyan era, he addressed the assembly. He cited the circumstances of Linji’s entry into extinction and his entrustment to Sansheng, saying:

"The treasury of the true Dharma eye was extinguished by a blind donkey—never did Linji speak such words. People of all times, past and present, have all spread this falsely. If you do not believe me, simply look at what follows."

In the third month, reaching the intercalary third month, Zhong Xiang rebelled. His followers wished to lead the Master southward into exile, but the Master said, "The purpose of studying the Way is to bring an end to birth and death;
why should there be any avoidance? When the rebels arrived, the Master was ultimately killed by them; his blood turned entirely into white milk.
The bandits were terrified and departed in regret. (The Master’s view of birth and death can truly be said to be like a dream or an illusion.
Chan Master Zhiyuan of Nanhua in Shaozhou Prefecture was a native of Yongkang in Shu.

Not long after he first set out on his travels (*xingjiao*), he heard that the monastery where he had received his precepts had been reduced to ashes overnight by a fire. Upon receiving the letter, the Master threw it to the ground and said, "In vain..."

This merely confuses people's minds. He was stern and cold; those from all quarters called him "Iron-Faced Ming. Entering the hall, he said: "This matter is most extraordinary; it speaks directly to the point without obstruction.
The old farmer from the eastern neighbor’s house has, according to custom, received a single piece of wood.

It not only penetrates sound and form, but also accords with the seasons. If you ask what school this belongs to, the eight characters do not apply to anyone. [He struck the meditation seat. *Jianchan* (Striking Meditation).
The seat, the lower seat, and ascending the hall—these are spoken of daily and raised at every moment. Like the earth upholding a mountain, what difference does it make?
A parrot from Longxi wins people’s affection; it is mostly because he can speak. Cease your reflections and keep company with him.
The wise, upon hearing this, should seize it with vigor. There is yet another matter, most extraordinary: the cat is uniquely adept at catching mice.
Descending from his seat, he ascended the hall and stirred the air with his staff, saying, "He stirs the long river into cream and curd;
yet the shrimp and crabs still have their eyes closed with rheum. He struck the ground once and said, "He transforms the great earth into gold;
yet the pauper remains, as before, bare-boned and destitute. Is it that one lacks one's own share? Or is it that one is unwilling to accept it? Among you, there must be someone who can do so.
"Carrying this burden, how many have lost their wealth and incurred calamity? He struck the floor once more and said, "Do you understand? When you reach the Jewel Mountain, you must open your eyes;
do not let it be that you return in a daze with empty hands. He ascended the hall and said: "The spring light is radiant and the flowers vie to bloom;
the cuckoo cries as the moon sets behind the western mountains. Gavāmpati sticks out his tongue in long astonishment—at what matter does this divide?"

"To whom do you speak? Ha! [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "Delusion does not delude itself; it is established in opposition to awakening. Awakening does not awaken itself; it is spoken of because of delusion.
Therefore, awakening is the essence of delusion, and delusion is the function of awakening. Both delusion and awakening are without source; within this, there is neither distinction nor commonality.
Since there is neither distinction nor commonality, they cannot be shifted. The Patriarch did not bring them here; the nostrils are a thousand [miles away]."

Chan Master Shangu of Gao’an at Yunju in Nankang Prefecture was the son of the Li family of Yangzhou. At the age of eleven, he left his home and secular life to receive ordination and study the sutras;

Xun received a prediction of his future enlightenment at Longmen. One day, a monk had his foot bitten by a snake.

The Eye-benefit Vessel (Yanyi) received this transmission. When it reached Zhaojue, he said, "Is there such a monk at Longmen? The Dharma-way of Dongshan has not yet fallen into desolation.
Later, after taking up residence, he ascended the hall and said: "Shao-lin’s wall-gazing conceals within it the East Land and the Western Heaven;
ascending the hall on Mount Ou fills the four quarters and the zenith and nadir, causing the mountains to stand majestic and the palms to be leveled as a foundation."

Peaceful. The water is murky yet ever naturally clear; the flowers are not brilliant yet bear fruits in the void. The wind does not stir, yet a single leaf falls. People have no dharma, yet they may seek instruction;
the Buddha has no mind, yet he can further achieve realization. With wild vegetables and plain rice, one prolongs the days;
letting go as circumstances arise, the Way manifests its own spiritual power. In the end, how is it? At midday, the third watch is struck.
Chan Master Wenlian of Xichan Monastery in Suining Prefecture was the son of the Zhang family of that district. He ascended the hall and said:

"If one proceeds exclusively in this manner, it results in the paths of ordinary people and sages being cut off, where water cannot flow through and iron snakes cannot burrow in; even an iron hammer cannot break it.
Reaching as far as thousands of miles, birds do not fly across. If one comes exclusively in this manner, one cannot avoid having a head covered in ash."
Above, they carry water and drag mud; they sing of nine but act as if ten; they point to a deer and call it a horse.
Not only do they betray the former sages, but they also bury their own spirits. I dare ask the assembly: tell me, is it the one who goes like this?
Or is it the one who comes like this? "The peony flower blooms on the Bodhisattva’s face; the palm leaves scatter upon the Yakṣa’s head. [Ascending the hall, he said: "All you..."

While they discuss the profound mysteries in a vast expanse, striking the bells and beating the drums every day, Xichan has no dharma to preach. He has thoroughly scrutinized the lanterns and the pillars;
he does not set up a mounting platform at his gate so as to avoid others coming to borrow the way. If one were to borrow the way— [The text ends here.]
You must look where you step. If you are off-center, it is like learning the gait of Tang at Handan. Entering the hall: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
the myriad phenomena of the universe spread out in all directions. Pick them up with your hand as they come and use them immediately. The sun is past midday—it is already the third watch."

When the mind ceases, the manifold phenomena cease; the paths of the four propositions and hundred negations are cut off. Even if Bodhidharma were to appear here, it would still be like placing grit in one’s eye.
Who is it that gives rise to the mind and who is it that extinguishes the mind? A wooden man joins hands with another and they return home together.

Yet, even upon returning to the fields of one’s native land, one still encounters a blow upon the crown of the head. Ascending the hall, he said: "In the first month of spring, it is still cold. He spoke directly.
Straight talk, straight talk! It seizes the nostrils of the monks and pierces through the very heart and liver of the patriarchs and Buddhas.

For those who know this, Bodhidharma never came to the Eastern Land and the Second Patriarch never went to the Western Heaven. For those who do not know this, who knows they have missed it right before their own faces?
"A distance of one hundred and eight thousand [yojanas]. I, this mountain monk, shall recite a verse for you once more. Great assembly, do not let it be in vain. It is still cold in the early spring.

Chan Master Huanglong Muchuan Fazhong of Nanchang Prefecture was the son of the Yao family of Siming. At nineteen, he underwent the scriptural examination and received ordination.

Having realized the principle of the three contemplations within one mind, he felt that he had not yet been able to obliterate all traces of his practice; thus, he traveled extensively to consult renowned masters.

Upon reaching Longmen, he observed a water mill turning and thereby attained enlightenment regarding the essential point of the mind. He composed a verse, saying: "The Great Dharma Wheel turns, enveloping all before one's eyes."
He asked again, "How is it? [Yunmen] replied, "Water pushes the stones along. He presented this to Foyan. Foyan asked, "What is the matter within that?
The Master said, "The water flows long in the mountain stream. Foyan said, "I have a final phrase; I shall wait to entrust it to you. The Master immediately covered his ears and departed.
Later, he went to Mount Lu and sat in meditation for three years at Kushi (Dried Tree) under Tong’an, abstaining from food. It was the Xuanhe era.

During this time, there was a great drought in Xiangtan. Although prayers were offered, no response came. The Master leaped into the Dragon Abyss and called out, "You unrighteous beast, it shall rain one chi!
and the rain arrived immediately. While residing at Mount Nanyue, he would often ride a tiger out for excursions; both Confucians and Buddhists would bow upon seeing his dust.
After residing [at the monastery], he ascended the hall and said: “Lord Zhang drinks the wine and Lord Li gets drunk; Consider this carefully—it is inconceivable.

He ascended the hall again and said: “Today is the fifteenth day of the first month. I have a matter for you to resolve: Be careful not to blink both eyes.”
He has been changed by the lamp-light. Entering the hall, he said: "I have a single phrase that does not borrow the mouths of the various sages, nor move my own tongue;
it is not sound, breath, or respiration, nor is it the discrimination of emotional consciousness.

Even if Vimalakīrti had remained silent in Vaiśālī and Śākyamuni had confined himself in his chamber in Magadha, it would be much like covering one's ears while stealing a bell—it would still fail to avoid the leakage of the celestial mechanism."
[This is] a leakage. Even if it were Deshan’s “stick upon entering the gate” or Linji’s “shout upon entering the gate,” if you approach Master Muguan’s school, you will receive only a single wedge.
Though there may be a thousand kinds of words and ten thousand ways of explaining, they all simply aim to make you rest within yourself.
Let the great earth and empty space be as they are—seven hollows and eight protrusions. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Do not look outward."

Nanming spoke thus: "Can you thereby escape being scrutinized and rebuked by others? After a long silence, he said:

The Hall. Where both phrase and meaning are excised, where there is not even a hair’s breadth or a speck of dust, it is like a mountain, like a peak.

Why did he instead go on to belch out the 'gruel and rice' of the monastery as if it were his life's work? Ascending the hall: "The黄梅 (Huangmei) rain."

Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised the case: Jueji asked a monk, "What is the meaning of Chan?

None of those who offered responses were in accord with the truth. Jueji provided his own substitute answer, saying, "To slander is its meaning. The Master said, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are slanders; the patriarchs of the seven schools are slanders..."
"The twenty-eight patriarchs of the heavens are slanderers. The six patriarchs of the Tang land are slanderers. The old monks of the world are slanderers.
All these people are slanderers. Even this mountain monk is a slanderer. Among them, is there anyone who does not slander?

Though those who discuss the profound and explain the wondrous are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, how can they compare to the intimacy of the slander of Shuangfeng? While he was manifesting illness, his disciple, the Professor Wang...

As Qiao reached an advanced age, the Master entrusted him with his final affairs, instructing him with a verse that said: "To recognize is for the mind to recognize its own source; to see is for the nature to see its own essence.
To recognize the source-mind and the original nature is precisely the great malady of the Zen school.

He added: "There is a thorn within the soft mud; do not say you have no doubts. At dawn, he bathed, changed his robes, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. The *jashè* (cremation) was performed.
Wherever the incense smoke reached, there were clusters of five-colored śarīra relics; his teeth and tongue remained uncorrupted. A stupa was erected to the west of the monastery.
Chan Master Fayun of Baiyang in Fuzhou Prefecture was the son of the Wen family of Mianzhou.

He relied upon Fuyan, and while listening to Fuyan’s general discourse (*pǔshuō*), Fuyan cited the *Heart-King Inscription* by the Great Being Fu (Bodhidharma): "The flavor of salt in water; glue and blue in color. It is certain..."
"It exists, yet its form is not seen. Upon these words, the Master attained realization. Later, while observing the rapid turning of the jewel-treasury, he suddenly clarified the Great Dharma.

He hurried to the master’s chamber, prostrated himself, and presented this verse: "The summit has a unique peak where clouds drift slowly; The source has no separate branches, and the water flows coolly.
If one wanders the mountains without reaching their ultimate end, One will forever be obstructed by the green mountains from seeing the eye. [The Master] laughed.
And he approved it. Later, while presiding in the Dharma Hall, he said: "Good things come piling up one after another; there is no need for fabrication or contrivance.

Yellow leaves falling in the forest are swept away by the water; white clouds drifting across the valley are rolled back by the wind. With a single cry from the cold wild geese, all sentimental thoughts are severed;
as soon as the frost-bell strikes, my mountain crumbles. The white poplar tree has yet another quality beyond others: throughout the night, its cold [endures]."
Stirring the dead ashes in the brazier, suddenly a monk comes forth and says, "Old man, you are showing off your wares; why do you act so wretched and beggar-like?
The mountain monk simply says to him, "I have been caught by you. Ascending the hall, he said: "What is my hand like? It is like a Buddha’s hand.
Up there are the Southern Star and the Northern Dipper. What is my foot like? It is like a donkey’s foot. All past matters are now forgotten."
Stop! Every person has their own karmic conditions; each one possesses a square base and a round top. Standing at the banks of Dayu Creek, the solitary moon’s reflection falls upon the deep bay.
If you do not understand this, it is difficult even to see. A single song from a fisherman passes over the distant rapids. To the assembly:

Conditions for defilement are easily met, but the work of the Way is difficult to accomplish. If you do not comprehend the myriad distinctions of conditions before your eyes, you will see only external objects.
The winds sweep vast and wide, withering the forest of merit; the fires of the mind blaze fiercely, consuming the seeds of Bodhi.
If one’s aspiration for the Way is as earnest as one’s concern for one's own life, and if one serves the multitude as if serving oneself, then both self and others will achieve their goals.

Seeing neither the faults of others nor one’s own righteousness, one naturally shows respect to superiors and humility to inferiors. Thus, the Buddha-dharma will manifest from time to time, and the dust of afflictions...
Liberation from the dust. Ascending the hall: The cock crows at the dawn moon; the dog barks at the withered post. It can only be realized in silence; it is difficult to enter through deliberation.
Where it cannot be seen, the earth trembles and light is emitted; where it cannot be expressed in words, heaven and earth are dark and yellow.
A six-foot-tall figure pats the city wall; the paper has originally come from Qingjiang. O assembly! This is clearly spoken, yet people find it hard to see. Yesterday...
The third watch of the night, the moon shines through the window. Entering the hall, he said: "The wind blows against the thatched roof, leaking from the ridge;
the rain beats upon you, O *kalyāṇamitra*, dampening your eyes. Though it is so clear, you do not know; thus you come here to stand with bowed head.

Addressing the assembly while ill, he said: "During my long illness, I have never once pushed aside my wooden pillow. When people come, they mostly ask, 'How is it? To their questions, I, this mountain monk, respond according to what is asked."
"Responding according to conditions: outside the window, the oriole has even more to say. As for this seven-foot frame—where exactly does one receive illness?
Let those among you who possess the eye try to point it out for me, monk! The assembly offered various remarks, but none were in accord.
The Master clapped his hands once, made a sound of retching, and said, "What a fine wooden pillow! The Master’s self-discipline was pure.
He suffered from illness. When he passed away, he walked alone with only his staff and umbrella. After his cremation, his relics were collected;
his eyes, teeth, tongue, and prayer beads were enshrined together with his sacred bones in a stupa to the west of the temple.
Chan Master Yunju Faru of Nankang Prefecture was the son of the Hu family of Danqiu. He relied upon Huguosi Monastery’s [Master] Rui to receive the tonsure and full ordination.
He traveled extensively to study under various elders. Later, he arrived at Longmen and reported his lifelong realizations to Foyan, who said:

"All of these are matters of intellectual study and understanding; they are not ultimate realities. If you wish to comprehend birth and death, you must seek wondrous enlightenment. The Master was struck with awe.

One day, he was appointed to oversee the Xiangji (Fragrant Accumulation) Hall, but he firmly declined on the grounds that his spiritual practice was not yet complete. Guanyan urged him, saying, "For now, take up the post. Among those there, there are many who will preach the Dharma for you.
Not long after, as he rose at dawn and opened the door to the kitchen, he caught sight of the Holy Monk (Śāriputra). Suddenly, he attained realization.
Zhengque addressed the Buddha Eye. The Buddha Eye said, “Do you see the Holy Monk here? The Master went before him, bowed in greeting, and stood with palms joined.
The Buddha Eye said, “I told you that there are many who will preach the Dharma for you. Later, while presiding over the assembly in the hall, he said:
“If there is even a single dharma, Vairocana falls into the rank of ordinary beings. If there are not even ten thousand dharmas, Samantabhadra loses his realm. He continued: “Toward...”

In this place, both existence and non-existence are cast aside; gain and loss are both forgotten. It reaches the point where the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are entirely unobtainable.
As for all the people here before you, tell me: throughout the twelve hours of the day, where do they establish their dwelling and sustain their lives?
"Donning the straw raincoat, standing askew beyond a thousand peaks; leading water to irrigate vegetables before the Five Elders. [He] ascends the hall. "Dry..."
Within the interior of Kun, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a single treasure, hidden within the mountain of form. Yunju, however, says it is not so:
"Within the interior of Qian and Kun, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a single treasure. He then throws down his staff and says, "The assembly must also recognize it!"
Chan Master Zhengxian Zhenmu of Guizong in Nankang Prefecture was a native of the Chen family of Tongchuan. His ancestors were renowned Confucian scholars.
In his youth, he followed Chong of Sansheng to become a bhikṣu and receive full ordination. He traveled to Chengdu, where he relied upon Daoci Xiu to study the sūtras and śāstras.
Upon merely glancing at it, he could recite it from memory; its meaning was also suddenly understood. Xiu called him "The Son of the Sūtra Treasury. He left Sichuan to seek out Foyan.

One day, upon entering the inner quarters, Foyan raised the phrase: "With diligent effort, one embraces the sandalwood tree. Before the sound of these words had even faded, the Master attained sudden awakening.
Foyan said, "Son of the Sūtra Treasury, you have let it slip! Thereupon, he personally wrote the two characters "Zhenmu" (True Herding) and bestowed them upon him. [Xin] Shaoxing Ji...
Having finished, he went to reside at Guizong. Ascending the hall, he said: "Now, how do you speak the first phrase?

If you could speak it when the world had not yet been formed, before your parents were born, before the Buddha appeared in the world, and before the Patriarch came from the West—that would already be the second phrase.

[He] attained it. Yet he could not avoid shifting from left to right. [Xuedou] struck his staff and descended from the seat. He ascended the hall;

Shengbian gave a shout. Foyan Ji held up the incense and said: "Lungmen Wushang is a profligate who does not believe in the Buddha-dharma and seeks to destroy Chan and the Way.
He has smashed through the barrier above Vairocana; a cat washing its face says it is doing well.
A single stick of agarwood incense burns upon the burner; changing hands and beating one’s breast is but empty vexation. He then shook his hand and said, "Stop this vexation!"
Placing his sitting mat over his shoulder, he performed a woman’s prostration and said, "Please do not be offended by this daughter-in-law from a humble room;
I have troubled you, Great Master. The Master questioned him from within the room, saying, "Why does a cat love to catch mice?
He asked again, "When the board sounds, why does the dog bark? The master's style was stern and cold; beginners were mostly daunted by it. There was Daomou...
The eulogy says: Before the Shengyuan Pavilion, one is full of shame; by the peaks of Luoyang, one acts with eccentricity. The transmission of "skin and marrow" has become a mere idle talk.
"A single shoe has no place to be buried. Were it not for this "one frost that penetrates to the bone," how could one obtain the fragrance of plum blossoms that strikes the nose?
Xuetang Xingjian remarked, "The former master still has such a person as this; this eulogy alone is sufficient to cut off the tongues of all people under heaven.
Consequently, monks flocked to him. At the end of his life, he ascended the seat, took up his staff, and—
He tapped once on the left side and said, "Among the thirty-two marks, this mark is missing.
He tapped once on the left side again and said, "Among the eighty minor characteristics, this characteristic is missing. Zhiyi drew it all in a single stroke; Zhitong laid bare the draft.
Again he tapped once and looked at the assembly, saying, "Do not be distressed. Accept it directly right now; there is no need to search further. He then descended from his seat and returned.

The Abbot sat cross-legged in a solemn and dignified manner and passed away. After the cremation, his remains and *śarīra* relics were collected and enshrined in a stupa built on what is called Xianren Mountain.
A monk asked Chan Master Fangguang Shen of Changsha Prefecture: "If there were even a single dharma, Vairocana would fall into the rank of an ordinary person."

"If the myriad dharmas did not exist, Samantabhadra would lose his realm. I do not yet understand the meaning of this; how should I interpret it? The Master said, "The wealthy lament that a thousand mouths are too few;
the poor resent that even one body is too many."

Shiji Shouzuo was a native of Chengdu. He studied extensively under various masters and later went to Longmen. One day, while sitting in meditation, he fell asleep. Suddenly, a chorus of frogs began to croak;
mistaking the sound for the clatter of a shaving board, he hurried toward it. Someone enlightened him, saying, "Those are the cries of frogs, not the sound of a board.
The Master was struck with sudden realization and went to the abbot’s quarters to disclose his experience. Foyan said, "Is it not so?"
When he saw Rāhula, the Master suddenly stopped him, saying, "Preceptor, there is no need to mention this; wait until you have left and seen for yourself.
Before long, he attained realization and composed a verse, saying: "In a dream I heard the sound of wooden boards; Upon waking, the frogs croaked. The frogs and the sound of the boards—"

The mountains and peaks were suddenly leveled. Thereupon, [the Master] attained even greater profundity. When [the Emperor] invited him to share his seat, the Master firmly declined, saying, "This is no trivial matter.
It is like piercing the eye with a golden needle; if there is a discrepancy of even a hair's breadth, the pupil will be destroyed.

I wish to remain in the stage of learning throughout successive lives, refining myself by my own effort. The Emperor then praised him with a verse, which said: "One who possesses the Way does so only because they frequently retreat."

Step by step, his humility and gentleness were naturally habitual as he turned the light back within; unaware that he was already atop the azure clouds, he still further concealed himself among the multitude.
In his later years, when scholars earnestly requested him to teach, he could not decline. Later, he spoke this verse: "Because all phenomena are empty, my mind is empty;
Because my mind is empty, all phenomena are the same. All phenomena and my mind have no separate essence; They exist only here."
"Now, within a single thought-moment—tell me, which one is that? The assembly was at a loss. The Master let out a shout and ended the session.
Chan Master Huiwen of Jingju Nunnery in Wenzhou Prefecture ascended the hall and said, citing Fayan’s instruction to the assembly:

"When the three beats of the drum have ceased, everyone comes forward in a throng; the Buddha-dharma and human affairs are all completed at once. The Master [Wenyi] said, "I, this mountain monk, say: Three..."
The communal drum ceased, and the assembly came forward in clusters. "The staff is not a broom handle; I shall give you thirty blows.
The official and lay practitioner Feng Jie, known as Jichuan, had sought instruction from various renowned masters since his youth, finally arriving at Longmen.
He stayed with Foyan for two years. One day, while walking in the Dharma Hall with Foyan, a temple boy happened to recite a verse as he hurried across the courtyard: "Ten thousand..."

Among the elephants, his body alone was revealed. [Zhao Mengfu] patted Gong’s back and said, “How wonderful! Thereupon, Gong attained realization. In the Ding-si year of the Shaoxing era, he was appointed as a Censor-in-Chief.
It happened that Dahui was about to ascend the hall at Mingqing Temple; when Dahui descended from the seat, Gong pulled him back and said:
The Master once said, "One who does not act is a mere insect. Today, for what reason are you here again?
Huai said, "The entire earth is this very Venerable Gaō; how then could it be otherwise? As the Master was about to respond, Huai struck him with his palm. The Master said:
"I have invited him myself. After the month had passed, he specifically requested to attend the summer retreat at Mount Jing. He named his quarters the "Immovable Pavilion" (Budong Xuan).

One day, when Huì took the high seat and finished citing the kōan concerning Yàoshān’s study under Shítóu and Mázǔ, the Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters and said, "Regarding the causal conditions just cited by the Worthy One, I have my own way of understanding them. Huì replied:
"How could you possibly do so? The Master said: "To act thus is not permitted. *Suru svāhā*.
Not to act thus is also not permitted. *Śiri svāhā*. To act thus and not to act thus—neither is permitted.
*Suru-śiri svāhā*. Huiyin then spoke in verse: "The Sanskrit and the Chinese are forged into one whole. Alas for the worldly man who has attained [this]."
Regarding this samādhi, he later learned that it was located in Qiongzhou. Wherever he went, he remained in tranquil seclusion without weariness. He once composed a verse of his own saying:

"In the intervals between public duties, I delight in sitting in meditation; rarely have I ever rested my side upon a bed. Although I manifest the appearance of a civil official, the name 'Elder' is proclaimed throughout the four seas.
In the autumn of the twenty-third year of the Xiangxing era (the Guiyou year), he requested leave from his administrative post and gave prior notice to his relatives.

He was informed that the date for his passing was set for the third day of the tenth month. When the appointed day arrived, he ordered that a high seat be prepared in the rear hall and that he receive guests as usual.
Between the hours of Chén and Sī, he descended the steps, faced the barrier with solemn reverence, and requested the Transport Commissioner to assume the affairs of Qióng.
Donning monastic robes and sandals, he sat upon the high seat and exhorted all officials, as well as the clergy and laity, each to turn toward the Way and support the gates of the Teaching.
He raised the banner of the Dharma. Then, taking up his staff and resting it upon his knee, he passed away with serene composure.

The Commissioner of the Circuit requested, saying, "Your movements regarding dwelling and departing are so free and easy; why not leave behind a verse to commemorate this rare occurrence? The Master opened his eyes and asked for a brush.

The inscription reads: "In the first month, on the third day; in the middle month, on the ninth; in the last month, on the seventh—the words of the Elder have ended, and the Turtle-Headed One’s eyes turn red as he finally departs for eternity.
Previously, following the Jianyan era, many collections of the Buddhist canon had been lost at famous mountains and great monasteries.

The Master repeatedly used his own salary to print and distribute a total of one hundred twenty-eight sets of the canon, praying for the longevity of the Sovereign and the well-being of the myriad people. His disciples...
Pu Dapin once recorded these events; his *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) and *Songgu* (Verses on Ancient Cases) were circulated in the world.

Chan Master Dayuan Shangua of Daping Monastery in Changsha Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Kaifu Ning. He was a native of the Yu family of Xingzhou. Once, he ascended the hall [to preach]. Xi Zhong...
He fashioned a chariot with a hundred spokes; he removed both ends and discarded the axle. Holding up his staff, he drew a circle and said, "Do not mistake the zero point on the scale.
He struck it once and descended from the seat. On the occasion of thanking the *gongtou* (officer of offerings), he ascended the hall and said:
"Untying the golden bell from the tiger’s neck startles the multitude and moves the masses; seizing the bright pearl from the dragon’s lair illuminates heaven and earth."
"I, this mountain monk, have arrived here today; I cannot praise it enough. How should you all proceed?
Raising his whisk, he said, "Blink your eyebrows and quickly realize it! He threw down the whisk and descended from his seat.

[He] ascended the hall and said: "When the mind arises, phenomena also arise; when the mind ceases, phenomena also cease. When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, one calls a tortoise a turtle. All.
"Zen virtue, have you spoken it yet? If you have spoken it, I shall give you my staff.
If not, return to the hall and drink tea. A monk asked, "What was the meaning of Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall? The Master said:

"When a fish swims, the water becomes turbid. [The student] asked, "The Second Patriarch performed three prostrations; why was it that he instead obtained the marrow? The Master said, "When the earth is fertile, the eggplants grow large.
[The student] asked, "'A single flower opens into five petals; when the fruit forms, it is naturally complete. What matter does this clarify?
The Master said, "A thief uses stolen goods as proof. [The student] said, "Sometimes riding upon a fine moon, one does not realize one has crossed the blue seas."
The Master said, "The Acharya has no share. [The student] asked, "When the 'phrase with meaning' and the 'phrase without meaning' are like a vine leaning against a tree, what then?
The Master said, "The man of the house has been thoroughly tested. [The student] said, "When the tree falls and the vine withers, where do the phrases return?
"How about that? The Master said, "Blown by the wind and scorched by the sun. [The student] said, "What about Lan’an’s great laughter? The Master said, "A Persian reading Sanskrit script."

The monk said, "Today I have clearly seen that the Master has reached mastery in every direction. The Master said, "Looking up, one weeps for the azure heavens. The monk bowed; the Master said, "Pass.
A monk asked, "What is it like when the lotus flower has not yet emerged from the water? The Master said, "Heaven and earth possess no different colors.
The monk asked, "And what is it like after it has emerged? The Master said, "Its fragrant scent pervades the entire world."

Chan Master Shitou Zihui of Huguo Monastery on Mount Diaoyu in Chongqing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Daisui Jing. He was a native of Hezhou in Dongchuan and was by family trade a stone mason.
Although he was illiterate, his mind aspired to the school of emptiness; he would frequently receive oral instruction on the *Lotus Sūtra* from others and was able to [recite it].

He recited it. He left his home and joined the community at Dàsui, where he performed the duties of sweeping and sprinkling water. Taking a rock from the cliffside, he never let his hammer and chisel leave his hands, yet he continued his recitation of the sutras without ceasing.

Dàsui saw him and took pity on him, instructing him to contemplate the kōan concerning Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman. After a long time, as he was chiseling a particularly hard spot in the stone, he struck with all his might.
Suddenly, he caught sight of a flash of fire like a bolt of lightning, and he attained sudden, thorough enlightenment. He rushed to the master’s quarters...
The Master prostrated himself and presented this verse: "Exhausting every effort, there is not a shred of clue; The sparks fly apart, yet it was always right here.
He then offered the verse on Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman: "The three armies do not stir, yet the banners flash; The old woman is truly the foot of the Demon King.
Zhaozhou’s handleless iron broom Sweeps away the dust and smoke until all is empty and stark. [He] followed with joy.
The Master approved him, saying, "You have penetrated it. He then bestowed upon him monastic robes. Because he had formerly been a stonecutter, people called him Huìshítóu (Stonehead).
He had a verse that said: "The Stonehead Monk—nothing can be chewed through; having shattered empty space, a few traces are revealed.
Subsequently, he returned to Mount Jiǎoyú and established the Huguo Chan Monastery, where his transformative influence became increasingly manifest. The Emperor...

In the hall, practicing Zen and studying the Way is much like calling out for thirst from the bottom of a well. Little do you realize that you are merely blocking your ears and eyes, unable to avoid it.
For instance, throughout the twelve periods of the day—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or in every movement and action—who is it?
If you cause them to see with the eyes and hear with the ears, where is there that is not the beginning of the path?

If you can recognize the beginning of the path, it is the very site of great liberation. Only then will you know that this old man, together with the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, shall bear witness for you. Therefore it is said:
"The Bhagavans of the ten directions share one single path to the gate of Nirvana. O virtuous ones, generally speaking, whenever a thing stands directly before you, you must...
To see the source of a single thing—to see that the source has no source. Since the source itself is not a source, where is it not perfect?
O practitioners of Zen! This old man has nothing that surpasses you; yet, what is there in you that does not equal this old man?
Do you understand? "The thirty-six thousand acres of Lake Tai—its moon speaks from the heart of the waves."
"To whom? "Descend from the seat. [The Master] had previously built a stone niche for himself using twenty-four slabs.
One day, he took leave of the assembly, entered the niche himself, closed the door, and passed away.
Chan Master Yujing of Husheng Monastery in Tongchuan Prefecture was the son of the Yang family of Chengdu. At the age of fourteen, he paid his respects...

Baima Anhui took Nan Tang as his teacher. Nan Tang brought up the koan of Xiangyan’s “Dragon Roaring in a Withered Tree,” and through their exchange and interrogation, the Master attained great enlightenment beneath the words.
One day, Tang asked: "Do not linger at the cold crag where the strange grasses turn green;
sitting amidst the white clouds, the essence of the school is not yet perfected. What do you say to this? The Master replied: "One must directly brandish the sword. If one does not..."
He brandished his sword. The fisherman perched upon his nest. Tang was startled and said, "You little fellow! The Master said, "Take care," and immediately departed.
He went out to reside at Dongyan. Entering the hall, he ascended the seat and said: "The moon gives birth to one. Dongyan has just settled in; my sorrow and solitude increase.

The dusty paths of the world have many twists and turns, Yet in the granaries there is not a single grain of rice or flour. The cliff is my companion, the spring is my mate. A cool breeze blows with a whistling sound.
Filling the room as they arrive, the mountain deities and local spirits are busy in the dark; the cloud-slabs, bells, and fish-shaped chimes shed tears in secret.

Do not say that in the human world one merely guards an empty cliff; there are also those who strike the western wall from the eastern fence. He once said to the assembly: "The most essential point of spiritual study is this."
Do not depart from the path of the Southern Hall; if you can penetrate the initial phrase and the final phrase, the affairs of a lifetime will be concluded.
Should this not yet be the case, I shall further divide it for you into ten gates, each to be used as a seal of verification for your own mind. Will you then attain stability?
First, you must believe that there is a separate transmission outside the teachings. Second, you must know that there is a separate transmission outside the teachings.
Third, one must realize that the preaching of the Dharma by insentient things is no different from the preaching of the Dharma by sentient beings.

Fourth, one must see one's nature as clearly as observing an object in the palm of one's hand, with every stage of realization being firm and secure. Fifth, one must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma.

Sixth, one must traverse the bird-path and the profound way. Seventh, one must be proficient in both civil and martial arts. Eighth, one must suppress the heterodox and manifest the orthodox. Ninth, one must...

With great capacity and great function, one must for ten reasons act among those of different kinds. If you wish to perpetuate the lineage of the Dharma, you must exhaustively fulfill these essential principles;
only then can you sit upon the curved wooden seat, receive the prostrations of all people under heaven, and dare to act as a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If you do not reach such a state, you will merely be engaged in empty pretension; at some future time, before the Lord of Yama...
Laozi has not yet let you go. Among the practitioners, each produced a verse from their respective gates to present to the Master. The Master showed them his own verse, saying:
"The essential points of the ten gates are placed within the palm; when the opportune moment arrives, action follows naturally. The author need not arrange a sequence of ranks;
for the most part, the beginning and the end constitute the foundation."
Chan Master Sheng of Nan Yan in Jianzhou, Chengdu Prefecture, ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "To protect life, one must kill;
only when all are killed does one dwell in peace. If you understand the meaning herein, you are clearly still halfway there.
But tell me, what about the phrase for reaching home? Śākyamuni and Maitreya have vast capacities, yet it appears they are still but his servants."
A monk asked, "I do not ask about letting go within the five ranks; as for holding fast at the three barriers, what is that like?

The Master said, "Holding the Mohe sword crosswise, I issue the full, correct command. [The monk] said, "I have received your instruction on holding fast at the three barriers. As for letting go within the five ranks, how is that?"
The Master said, "The universe is at peace; I shall execute the dull and stubborn. [The student] asked, "If that is so, then under Nan’an’s gate, the land is vast and the people are few.
The Master said, "A sharp and intelligent monk requires only a single spark. [The student] asked, "From antiquity to the present, when it comes to being born together and dying together, what then?
The Master said, "A house-thief is difficult to guard against. [The student] said, "Today this student has made a small excursion and encountered something great."

At Wanshou Monastery in the prefecture, Yuan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tiantai. Yuan asked, "Did you see Great Master Zhizhe?
The Master replied, "Even now, he is not lacking. Yuan asked, "Why then is he beneath your own feet? The Master replied, "I passed him by right before my face.
Yuan said, "The Senior Monk may truly be called one who is elegant without weeding and straight without support. He then went to Yuzhang to visit Dian.
Niu was traveling by way of Yunju when wind and snow blocked his path. He sat there for forty-two days. At the first hour of the day, the sound of the wooden board rang out sharply;
he attained great enlightenment all at once. Upon arriving at the gate, Niu alone pointed at the Master and said, "Where have you seen gods and ghosts come from?
The Master replied, "I heard the sound of the board at Yunju. Niu asked, "What is that? The Master said, "It has shattered empty space."

It was entirely without a handle or butt. The ox said, "The matter of the upward direction is not yet resolved. The Master said, "The eastern neighbor sits in the dark; the western neighbor shouts insults at each other.

The Master replied, "In studying the Way, one only fears lacking a foundation. If one has a foundation," [he continued].
He preached the Dharma to clay images, and his reputation also rose above all other regions. Yuan remarked, "Your capacity and discernment surpass those of ordinary men;
the 'dark wine' and 'great soup' are flavors that the common crowd cannot perceive. Upon returning to the East, he shared the teaching seat at Guoqing Monastery.
He emerged from seclusion to reside at Puzhai in Huangyan, followed by appointments at Taiping in Tai, Xiangfu in Ji, Dengci in Yue, and finally at Da...

"Let the wind carry the fragrance along the road as it pleases. As he was about to pass away, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly and instructed his disciples to offer a written memorial for him.

His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the foot of East Ridge.

Chan Master Yuantong Min was a successor of Chan Master Shouhui Miyin of Lushan Yuan Tong in Jiuyang Prefecture. He was born into the Chen family of Xinghua. Initially, he resided at...

Yuantong. He subsequently moved to the Great Maitreya Monastery in Tanzhou, where he ascended the hall and said: "One only knows today and tomorrow again; one does not realize the transition from the early autumn to the late autumn.

During the Zhenghe era, he entered the inner court three times to preach the Dharma. Emperor Huizong was greatly pleased and bestowed [upon him]—

"Inner Secretary," [Tong] said. The Master responded with an "Amen. Tong said, "How could there be any distance between us? The Master leaped up with joy and said, "I beg the Master to grant me further instruction.

"What is it? the Master asked. Tongdu said, "I have passed by you eight times, always keeping this thought in mind, yet I have not yet attained a sense of complete liberation.

The Master suddenly had an awakening and said, "Please grant me the final word. Tongdu then waved the fan twice. The Master said, "Intimate! Intimate!"
Qian Tong said, "The tongue of Ji Liao reaches three thousand li.

The Duke asked, "How is it that this is so? Tong quoted the entire sutra to show him. The Duke clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "Ha!
Tong said, "And yet you say it cannot be attained. The Duke prostrated himself.
While the Layman Minister of the Interior, Lu Hang, was warming himself by the hearth with Yuantong, he asked: "There is no need to laboriously bring up the various kōans of the various houses;
I ask the Master for a direct, single phrase of instruction. Yuantong gestured sharply and said in a stern voice, "Look at the fire!
The Minister hurriedly pulled back his robes and suddenly attained great enlightenment. He replied, "Clearly, the Buddha-dharma is not so very much. Yuantong shouted, "Put it down! The Minister—
"Very well, very well," [Master] Yuantong replied.
The Layman Zuoxidu Xiang asked, "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination; how should one approach it?
Yuan said, "Enter the mass of fire with your whole body. The Layman asked, "Ultimately, how does one comprehend it?"
Tong said, "Go straight ahead. The Master hesitated. Tong said, "Would you like some more tea? The Master replied, "There is no need. Tong asked, "Why do you not understand it in this way?
The Master attained the essential meaning and said, "I see now that it was all along too near. Tong said, "A hundred thousand eight thousand [li]."
Master Gong composed a verse, saying: "Inconceivable! This is a great mass of fire; thus one goes, without departing from this very place.
Master Tong said, "Eh! There is still this [remaining]. Gong said, "I beg the Master for further instruction.
Tong said, "Thus one goes; the cauldron is cast of iron. Gong bowed his head in gratitude.

Chan Master Yuan of Penglai on Mount Ningbo was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jiao of Tiantong. He resided on the mountain for thirty years without his feet ever crossing the threshold of his quarters; both monastics and laypeople revered him.
The Master had a verse that said: "A newly-sewn paper quilt, warmed by the fire, is cozy; A peaceful sleep lasts until the fifth watch."
I have heard that the bells and drums of the upper realm have sounded; thus, one more day has been added to this floating life.

Chan Master Xingdao Mo’an of Huiri Monastery in Suzhou Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "The crimson clouds are about to snow, yet have not yet snowed;

Chan Master Guangxiaoguomin of Guangde County was a native of Taoyuan, Changde. He ascended the hall and, citing the story of Nanquan’s beheading of the cat, said:

Even if both halls had been able to speak, blood would still have flowed through the streets."

Chan Master Xuefeng Qiutang Huizhong of Fuzhou Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Xuefeng Xu, ascended the hall and said: "All day long one is in a state of constant bustle, yet that matter remains unimpeded.
What is that matter? After a long silence, he said: "The mind does not betray others; the face shows no color of shame."

Chan Master Xuanmi Li of Shitai in Yangzhou Prefecture, successor of Chan Master Mingzhao Hui. A monk asked, "Are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as oneself, or are they different?
The Master said, "In the cool night at the long pavilion, the moon spreads its light mostly for the traveler. The monk said, "Thank you, Master, for your reply."

Startled, he ascended the hall. Upon reaching the front of the seat, the Master seized a monk and pulled him up onto the Dharma seat. The monk, terrified, attempted to flee.
The Master then pointed to the seat and said, "This platform—if one were to lead a donkey up here, it would surely defecate upon it as well.
Why, then, do you all refuse to accept it? He then drove them all away at once with his staff and looked back at his attendant.
It is said: "Dangerous!

Now tell me: how can the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye be revealed without being buried or betrayed? Is there anyone who can reveal it?
Come forth and reveal it! If there is none, take your poetry and books back to your old hermitage;

A monk asked Zen Master Lingyan Hui of Mount Emei, successor to Zen Master Zhen of Fushan: "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas;

Chan Master Daochuan of Zhiji in Yuzhou, a native of the Di clan of Kunshan, was originally a *gongji* (police officer) in his county.
Hearing that the head seat Qian of Dongzhai was expounding the Dharma for both monastics and laypeople, he went to follow him. He practiced seated meditation without weariness.

Qian. Qian named himself Daochuan (River of the Way). He said, "In the past you were called Disan; now your name is Daochuan. 'Chuan' is simply 'san.

At the beginning of the Jianyan era, he shaved his head and traveled to various regions. Upon reaching Tianfeng, he spoke with [the master].

When someone requested an explanation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Master composed a verse for it, which is now widely circulated in the world.

In the first year of the Longxing era, Zheng Qiao, a Palace Draftsman serving as Commissioner of the Huaisi Circuit, happened upon the vacancy at Yemuzi and invited the Master to open the Dharma there. Ascending the hall, he said: "The myriad shadows have been stripped away."
The first yang has arisen; the grasses, trees, gardens, and groves all send forth their sprouts. Only the bottomless bowl of the patch-robed monk remains as before, holding rice and holding soup.
He ascends the hall and says, citing Xuefeng’s one day ascending the seat and holding up his staff, looking eastward, and saying:

He struck the floor with his staff once and descended from the seat. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he gathered the assembly and said, "I have no dharma to transmit to you.

However, I have been ill for some time and have not been able to attend to you. Now, as I am departing this world, I shall speak a few words for you. He then recited a verse: "The mountain peaks are steep and the path is perilous; / The traveler’s feet stumble and falter. / If you wish to reach the place of ultimate peace, / You must first abandon the three poisons. Having finished the verse, he passed away. His disciples wished to cremate him, but the Master said, "Do not burn my body. Place me in a stone coffin and bury me in the mountain forest. After a hundred years, when the grasses and trees grow over it, then let it be burned. His disciples followed his instructions. One hundred years later, a local official named Wang Jian happened to visit the site. He saw the Master’s stone coffin still intact and, moved by his devotion, had him reinterred in a new stone chamber.

Subsequently, a monk named Zhixian came from afar to pay his respects. He opened the tomb and found the Master’s body perfectly preserved, sitting upright as if alive. He took the remains back to the monastery and enshrined them in a stupa. This is known as the "Stone Coffin" at Mount Shuangfeng. The Master was originally from Xingzhou. His secular surname was Chen, and his given name was Daoyuan. He was a man of profound character and great spiritual power. He traveled widely throughout the central lands, visiting many eminent masters. Later, he settled at Mount Shuangfeng, where he taught for thirty years. His disciples numbered in the thousands, and his influence spread far and wide. He passed away in the year of the Jiazi cycle at the age of eighty-four. His remains were interred on the mountain, and a memorial stele was erected. His legacy continues to inspire practitioners to this day.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is natural, brilliant clarity. If there were even a single thread, it would not be a single thread.
The Master said: "The moonlight last night was most excellent; today the autumn mountains possess boundless sentiment. He then ascended the hall for the discourse.
