In the Wuxu year of the Chunxi era, after retiring from Jingci Monastery, he composed a verse which said: "For six years I swept and cleaned the imperial capital."
The temple’s rubble has been transformed into a palace of Śakra and Brahmā; today, his work accomplished, he returns home.

From the tip of his staff, a pure breeze rises from all eight directions. On the day of the Buddha-bath in the year Jihai, he entered the Inner Contemplation Hall at Bao’en Temple in Jiahe to settle there for the remainder of his life.
Before long, he manifested illness and wrote a letter to bid farewell to the local officials. Sitting upright, he passed away. After his cremation, relics of five colors were obtained.

Beneficial. His teeth and fists remain unbroken. His verse upon departing this world says: "Throughout my life, I used what was necessary; at death, I am uniquely adept at playing with the living snake.
With a single punch, I shatter empty space; even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot find a crack or seam."
Chan Master Wuan Faquan of Daochang Monastery in Anji County, Huzhou Prefecture, was the son of the Chen family of Gusu.

He shaved his head under Master Chuan of Dongzhai and long relied upon Master Fozhi. Whenever he entered the inner quarters for instruction, Fozhi would question him on the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature.
The Master had no reply. One day, upon hearing a monk cite the verse of the Fifth Patriarch—“Zhaozhou’s sword with its blade bared”—he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
He composed a verse: “The drums and pipes thunder; he bares one shoulder. Incense mists the dragon towers as the boat of Yizhou sails forth.

Sometimes he goes barefoot, playing with the bright moon, Treading through the heavens beneath the waves of the Five Lakes. Later, while presiding over the assembly, he ascended the hall and said: “If you wish to manifest it before you...”

"Do not harbor notions of compliance or resistance. Holding up his staff, he said: "The Great Master of the Third Patriarch transformed himself into a horse-faced yakṣa and went to Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, Jambudvīpa in the south, and Uttarakuru in the north;
yet he has now returned, head and body, into this mountain monk’s hand. Originally, it was but a single black-lacquered staff. Do you see it? Even if you were to see it—"
"Entering hell will be like being struck by an arrow. [Zhaozhou] set down his staff and descended from the seat. He ascended the hall again, held up his staff, and said:

"All of you here, each one reaching for the heavens above and standing firm upon the earth, carry a *zhuli* staff slung over your shoulders, traveling on pilgrimage everywhere to test and examine the various quarters."
"Come here again! What are you looking for? As soon as you give it even the slightest pressure, you immediately say, 'Tiantai is on a work-assignment;
Nanyue is out hiking. But let me ask you: have you ever recovered the precious sword from the kingdom of Daśapura?
He planted his staff in the ground and said, "Be careful not to bite off a horn with your mouth. A monk asked, "What was it like before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch?"
The Master said, "There are no poor people under heaven. A monk asked, "What is it like after seeing this? The Master replied, "There are no wealthy men throughout the four seas.
On the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month in the Jichou year of the Qiandao era of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty, as he was about to enter nirvana, the assembly requested a verse.

The Master stared with wide eyes and looked down. When the assembly’s request became even more insistent, he then wrote the two characters "wu-wu" (no-no) and cast aside his brush, passing away. After the cremation...
His five-colored relics were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Jindou.
Chan Master Daosheng of Hanyan at Gushan in Fuzhou Prefecture was the son of the Wu family of Yan’an; he donned the monastic robes at the age of nineteen.

Fazhi (Buddhi) attained enlightenment while serving him; he then attended Fazhi at Lingyin Monastery and occupied the head seat. Later, he returned to his hometown and built a hermitage called Hanyan (Cold Rock).
When the Military Governor of Min inquired among the various mountains as to who was the most outstanding successor of Fazhi, everyone pointed to the Master.

Consequently, he went forth to preside over Zhití Monastery, subsequently moving to Chengtian, Huanglong, and Létán, before finally taking charge of Gǔshān. Ascending the hall, he let out a shout and said:
The entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions and the ten periods of time—past and present—are all contained within this very space; it is completely filled and packed to the brim.

Yet, were one to open up even a space the size of a needle’s point, then the great ocean would flow westward, the massive mountains would stand overturned, and the tortoises, crocodiles, fish, dragons, shrimp, crabs, and earthworms would all surge forth upon the level ground, leaping, frolicking, and dancing in waves.
Although it is thus, you must still take one further step from the top of a hundred-foot pole.

Only then will you tread at every step upon the inexhaustible wheel-treasury, and only then will you know that the nostrils rest upon the upper lip and the eyebrows are not beneath the eyes. Do you understand this thoroughly?
He then gave a shout and said: "Be careful not to let your throat touch what is taboo. This was on the day after the summer retreat had concluded.
Suddenly he asked his attendant, "What day is it today? The attendant replied, "The sixteenth. He asked again, "What is the lunar day and stem-branch?
The attendant replied, "Xinmao. He then entered his room and passed away while seated. He was sixty-nine years old; his stupa was erected at the foot of Mount Xianglu.
Chan Master Huitong Qingdan of Changsha Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Daowei Tai. He was the son of the Yan family from Pengzhou.

Initially, he left the mountain passes and arrived at Deshan, where he encountered Daowei ascending the hall and saying: "Zhaozhou said, 'The old woman of Mount Tai has already been thoroughly exposed for you. Furthermore—
"The Way—where does its meaning lie? After a long silence, he said, "Picking up yellow leaves from the ground, entering the mountains to push forth white clouds.
Upon hearing this, the Master was relieved. The next day, he entered the room. Baizhang asked, "Previously, at Baizhang, [you spoke of] 'not falling into cause and effect.'"
For what reason did he fall into the state of a wild fox? Later, when Baizhang did not obscure cause and effect, for what reason was he released from the wild fox body?

The Master said: "It would have been better to give him a clod of earth and bury him. Later, while presiding over the assembly, he said: "To speak of Buddhas and Patriarchs is like gouging a sore into healthy flesh;
to cite the ancients and the present is no different from serving up leftover soup and stale rice. To attain awakening upon hearing this once already falls into the secondary."
The Head. To act upon a single lift—this is already failing to hit the mark; you must know that this matter covers all like the sky and supports all like the earth.
A lion roams without seeking a companion; a strong man extends his arm without borrowing another’s strength. When Buddhas and Patriarchs pick it up, no patch-robed monk can stir it.

"What dharma have the sages of antiquity used to point it out to people? He gave a shout and said, "Do not engage in false conceptualization.
On the day of the Buddha-nature taboo, he ascended the hall: "A three-legged donkey prances on its hooves; step by step they follow one another, yet never meet.
From the treetops, a pair of fish are startled into flight; picked up, there is one old and one not old. Out of pity for the pines and bamboos, it draws in the pure breeze—what can be done about it?"
Stepping outside the door, one encounters weeds; thus, by calling out "husband," one recognizes him. Great capacity and great function are both cast down;

Now I am thus; is this not a joy? The external conditions of worldly toil have been swept away all at once. I am grateful for the grace of the various mountains visiting me; may you all be willing to bear witness. I humbly entreat you to take care of yourselves.
He set down his brush and looked toward Jian-tang, saying, "Which would you prefer for me: to sit or to lie down? Jian-tang replied, "Minister."

He departed immediately. What need was there to concern himself with sitting or reclining? The Master laughed and said, "Dharma brother, you must cherish yourself for the sake of the ancestral path," whereupon he closed his eyes and passed away.

The Elder is not like this. Today, at Phoenix Mountain, I have no leisure to turn the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths, nor do I have the strength to turn the staff.
I simply instruct everyone to walk with slow steps and speak in low voices. Why?
If you wish to avoid incurring karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the Tathāgata’s true Dharma wheel. [He ascended the hall.]

The Buddhas of the three periods of time take a single phrase and expound it as hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of phrases; they gather those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of phrases back into that very single phrase.
Yet, under the gate of the Patriarchs, there is not even half a phrase. If one simply remains thus, how many painful blows of the staff should one deserve?

"O worthy ones! Now, as for the Buddhas and the Patriarchs—if you say the Buddha is right and the Patriarch is wrong, or the Patriarch is right and the Buddha is wrong, you have not yet forgotten the duality of acceptance and rejection.

He remained in the Dharma Hall for seven days; his complexion was bright and lustrous, his hair grew long, and the crown of his head felt warm. After seven days had passed, he was buried on the western ridge of the hermitage.

Observe the conditions of time and season; when the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. He gave a shout and said:
"To speak in such a manner—those who benefit people are few, while those who ruin people are many."

To say 'is not' is also fine; the Elephant Path enters Penglai Island. Even to say "is" is irrelevant; even to say "is not"—treading upon a weightstone as hard as iron—is likewise irrelevant.
He steps forward. A vajra-jewel sword cuts him down right at the head. A-he-he! Do you understand? When one knows little, afflictions are few;

If you can realize it within this very moment, you will not fail to grasp it.

You may then eliminate the obstacle of delusion, pull out the arrow of hesitation, cut through the net of doubt, sever the river of ignorance and craving, clear away the dense forest of the mind, wash away the turbidity of mental defilements, straighten the crookedness of the mind, and cut off the cycle of birth and death within the mind.

Advancing further everywhere, open your mouth and utter a single word in a place where the explanations of Buddhas and patriarchs have failed to reach.

Call back Master Shandao and seek no other shortcut for cultivation. Otherwise, you will continue as before—abandoning your father and fleeing, wandering lost in foreign lands, bumping into this and that; how bitter it is, O Buddha!

Raising a fist and shouting is but a meager display; speaking of right and wrong is sinking into the mud. Cut off all manifold distinctions and cease pointing or directing.

The Duke said, "I have been studying and questioning for thirty years; how can you say I have not seen one? Haichao said, "See them in the place of joy; see them in the place of affliction."

Regarding the saying, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing," he attained sudden and thorough enlightenment. He composed a verse, which says: "Not mind, not Buddha, nor yet a thing;

The wild fox leaps into the golden-haired lion’s den. Wu’an approved of this and immediately sent a letter with the verse to present to Fohai. Fohai replied: "This..."
"The matter cannot be fully exhausted by paper and brush. If you, Layman, can come to see me, you shall surely have something to hear. He then went back to Tiger Hill.
Wumenhai came out to meet him and said, "Your realization, Layman, is sufficient only to enter the realm of the Buddhas; you have not yet even attained entry into the realm of the Māras.
The Layman continued to pay him profound respects, whereupon Wumenhai assumed a solemn expression and said, "Why do you not say: 'The golden-haired lion leaps into the wilds'?"
At the Fox Den (Hukū), the Master attained liberation. He once asked the various Chan masters: "If a husband and wife are fighting and their son acts as witness, tell me:
does he testify for the father, or does he testify for the mother? Huan’gan added a commentary, saying: "The small emerges and meets the great.
In the sixth year of the Chunxi era of Emperor Xiaozong, while serving as Governor of Linchuan, in the eighth year he was stricken by illness. One night, suddenly—
He took up his brush and wrote a verse, saying: "Beating the drum within the vast ocean, Hearing the bell atop Mount Sumeru.
The karma-mirror suddenly shatters; Turning over, one emerges into the void. He summoned his subordinates and showed it to them, saying:

"Life and death are like day and night; there is nothing strange about this. If one speaks in terms of the Way (*dharma*), how could there be life and death? If you conceptualize them as life and death,"
"Then one is far removed from the Way. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Huifang Chuan'an of Changsha Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Wenshu;
his secular surname was Xu, and he was a native of that prefecture. He went to visit Wenshu at Dayue.
Not long after, as the temple was being converted into a Shenxiao Palace, he happened to pass through Xiangnan on a merchant vessel.
Onboard, he heard a person on the bank shouting in his native dialect, "Jiàonà! At that moment, he attained a profound realization. He composed a verse, saying:

"A single cry from the heart of the Mian River— At this moment, I suddenly attain the harmony of my whole life. After many years of parting, we meet once more; All the sages return to the same source."
Traveling along the way, he ascended the hall after his appointment. Only in old age did he assume the title of abbot; he possesses not the slightest spark of profound mystery.
When he opens his mouth, nine out of ten words are perverse. Asked about the east, he answers with the west. To enter the world in such a manner—what efficacy or action can there be?
Sometimes he takes up three and lets go of two; sometimes he bestows them all at once.
Even so, only those on the same path can know it. But tell me, what is this matter that is known? "The nostrils have always hung downward. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The Patriarch Bodhidharma is under your feet. If you cannot step on him, you cannot lift him up. Look closely right before you and let him drop away—this is the illness."
At that time, who held it in their hands? Zhang Gonghui could examine the pulse; Li Gonghui could administer medicine.
The two vied with one another to treat him at once, yet they had no need for medicine as their approaches were incompatible. A mistake, a mistake!

Chan Master Wenshu Siye of Changde Prefecture was by trade a butcher. One day, while he was thrusting a pig with his spear, he suddenly attained a profound and penetrating realization of the source of the mind.
He immediately abandoned his profession and became a bhikṣu, composing a verse that said: "Yesterday was the heart of a yakṣa; today is the face of a bodhisattva.
Between the bodhisattva and the yakṣa, there is not even a single thread’s distance. He went to visit Wenshu, who said, "You are..."
"When you were slaughtering the pig, what did you see that led you to shave your head and travel as a monk? The Master then made the gesture of a butcher wielding a blade and shouted, "You butcher!
Go to the hall! The Master then went down to the hall. Later, when he succeeded Wenshu on the seat, he ascended the hall and, citing the story of Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the old woman, said:

They return to the One. All moon-reflections in water are encompassed within a single moon. When extended, they pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
when withdrawn, not even a hair’s breadth remains. Although these processes of expansion and contraction follow different paths, this matter fundamentally has no difference in its essence.
Only by being able to fix a single eye upon the root source can one see that all Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations have entirely manifested from within this.
The Three Piṭakas and the twelve divisions of the scriptures—all *sūtras* without exception—flow forth from within this.

Heaven and earth, the sun and moon, and the myriad phenomena of the universe are all established from within this. The three realms and nine stages, the seven destinies and four modes of birth, all emerge and submerge within this.
The hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates and immeasurable wondrous meanings, even including the various worldly arts and crafts—[all arise from here].
In the arts of performance, all manifest these deeds. Thus, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, Kāśyapa immediately smiled;
when Bodhidharma faced the wall, the Second Patriarch thereby attained peace of mind. When peach blossoms bloomed profusely, Lingyun’s doubts were completely purified;
when striking bamboo produced a sound, Xiangyan suddenly forgot all that he knew. This extended to Panshan awakening to the Way at a meat counter. Mi...
Le went into the fish market to meet people. Truly, it is said that even in moments of haste or distress, one must rely on this;
walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, he was always within it. Since there is such marvel, and furthermore such radiance;
since there is such vastness, and moreover such pervasiveness—why, then, do you all still have delusion and enlightenment? You must [understand this].
Do you understand? Fortunately, there is no place where light does not shine, yet there is still a moment of non-illumination.

Chan Master Lu’gan Huiwen of Langshan in Tongzhou, Yangzhou Prefecture, was born to the Zheng family of Fuzhou. He traveled extensively to study under various elders.

The eighteenth-generation successor of National Teacher Dajian (Baizhang) was Chan Master Xigan Daguan of Tiantong in Ningbo Prefecture,
a native of the Zhao family of Yiwu. Initially, he studied under Ying’an.
At Tiāntóng, he next met Wú’ān at Dàochǎng; later, within the quarters of Shuǐ’ān at Jìngcí, he clearly realized the point where these two elders extended their hands.
With a single phrase, he struck the mark, and upon returning to Lóngxiáng, Bǎitáng appointed him to the first seat.

Later, he opened Lingyan in Fayan Prefecture and presided over four monasteries. When he was appointed by imperial decree to ascend to Lingyin from Jinshan, he took the high seat and spoke on the kōan of the Second Patriarch asking Bodhidharma for peace of mind.
He offered this verse: The night in Chang’an is deep and the snow falls thick;
Seeking peace of mind, one becomes more restless. Even if one were to open the living eye before a word is spoken, How could one know that one has already been deceived by the Old Barbarian?
Chan Master Jian’an Sijing of Mount Yangshan in Yuanzhou Prefecture ascended the hall and said:
"Master Bodhidharma once said to his disciples, 'The time has come; you should each speak of what you have attained. Finally, Huike came forward, prostrated three times, and stood in his place.
Bodhidharma said, 'You have attained my marrow. The Master offered this verse: "Squeezing the eyes causes [visions] to appear..."
Huālì poses a question; having obtained another’s skin and marrow, he is deceived by him. Such blind fellows can cause much trouble—claiming it is cold even when there is no frost in the sixth month.
[This is the record of] Chan Master Dōchángquán, a successor in the lineage.
Chan Master Huizang I’an Youquan of Changzhou Prefecture was the son of the Qi family of Changle.
At the age of fourteen, he received full ordination; at eighteen, he went to Lingyin Temple to study under Fozhi. At that time, Wunan was serving as the First Seat (Dharma Seat).

In the meditation hall, Wunan posed the question: "How does one establish all dharmas from the ground of non-abiding? After a long time, the Master attained realization and replied: "Thread a needle in the dark."

The master Zhen blew air into [the disciple’s] ear; Anke accepted this, and he subsequently secretly transmitted the mind-seal (*citta-mudrā*) to him. Once, while sitting in meditation through the night until dawn, the one who distributed the gruel arrived;
the master forgot to open his alms bowl. A neighboring monk touched it with his hand, whereupon the master was awakened to realization.

He spoke a verse, saying: "A pitch-black K'un-lun man holds a fishing rod; The ancient sail is hoisted high as he descends the surging rapids. Amidst the shadows of reeds, he plays with the bright moon, Drawing forth..."
"The blind turtle on the fishing boat. Fozhi Chang asked, "When the mind encompasses the great void and its measure spans the sands of the world, what then?
The Master said, "The great ocean does not harbor a corpse. Zhi patted his seat and said, "This boy shall one day occupy this seat;
he will go about scolding the Buddhas and reviling the Patriarchs. The Master then further concealed himself and went to see Ying'an at Guizong, where he engaged in practice.
At Mount Jing, Dàhuì, as well as Wú’ān while residing at Dàochǎng, both appointed the Master to share the seat. Later, upon ascending the hall after his installation, he said:
"Today the mouth of the sack is tied shut; you with clear eyes, monks, do not wander about in confusion.
Where mental activity ceases, one turns the body around; even a sneeze becomes the lion’s roar. In the sandalwood forest, gallop as you please—raise your eyebrows to the very crown of your head!"
Born. Carving flesh to form a sore reveals the family’s shame. Entering the hall: "Chan, Chan! Without faction, without partiality.
When deluded, one is separated by a thousand miles; when awakened, it is right on the lips. Therefore, a monk asked Shitou, "What is Chan?
Shitou said, "A brick for a horse. Again, a monk asked Muzhou, "What is Chan? Muzhou said, "A fierce fire frying oil. Furthermore, a monk asked...
Shoushan was asked, "What is Chan? Shoushan replied, "A monkey climbing a tree, its tail trailing its head. "Great assembly, the Way has no crossroads; where one stands is solitary and perilous.
These three great elders traveled upon a living path before sound and employed a spiritual mechanism outside of time.

Yet, if viewed with the orthodox eye of a monk, there is no lack of distinction between them. One was like Zhang Liang entering the fray... [The text continues with the description of the other two masters.]
It was as if Xiang Yu were leading his troops while a single man possessed the strategic insight of Kongming in gauging the enemy.

If one can discern this clearly, they may stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Suddenly, a monk might come forth and say, "Elder, you have split the discourse into two parts. Just now you said:
The Way has no cross-paths; it is without faction and without partiality. Yet now, you further divide it into many degrees of superior and inferior. How will you respond to this? Do you understand?
"Holding hands while climbing the mountain, we exert our strength together; the breath escaping from the throat is known only by oneself.

In the autumn of the *gengzi* year of the Chunxi era during the reign of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty, he manifested a slight illness, wrote a verse, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away. [Tea.]
His teeth and tongue remained intact; he obtained countless relics of five colors, which were enshrined at Hengshan. His remaining bones were interred at the left side of the Wanian Temple.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Ti of Jiaoshan.
Chan Master Chidun Zhiying of Tiantong in Ningbo Prefecture cited the karmic occasion of Bodhidharma meeting Emperor Wu, and composed a verse:
"Raising the first hammer of Mount Sumeru— The jade pass and golden lock are difficult to strike open. To apply a heavy back-stomp again is but a labor spent in vain;

One should have regretted coming ten thousand miles from afar. (Zizan Yao: This should be included in this *Zengji*. It was recorded in Volume One, page twenty-seven, but as the printing blocks were lost, there is no way to include it here.)

Chan Master Tuigan Daoci of Jinshan in the Prefecture of Zhenjiang, Dharma successor of Chan Master Yinzhu of Mount Jing, was asked by a monk: "Xuefeng said, 'At the Wangzhou Pavilion, I have already seen you.
What is the meaning of this? The Master replied, "The left eye is half a catty. [The monk asked: "And at Wushan Ridge..."
"Have you seen each other yet? The Master said, "The right eye weighs eight *liang*. [The monk] said, "I have already met you before the Sangha Hall; how about now?
The Master said, "The nostrils point downward with their large ends.
[The monk] said, "What about when Ehu suddenly entered the abbot’s quarters, or Baofu entered the Sangha Hall? How was that? The Master said, "Water flows along the edge of the rocks."
Cold air comes out; the fragrance wafts from within the flowers. Entering the hall: This great matter is all-pervasive;
even before the new Jiaoshan left Dongxia, he had already met everyone. But tell me: what is this meeting?
"How many with their heads and horns have become dragons? The shrimp and crabs still glare with their eyes as before."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Ultimate Way is rooted in mindlessness; the dharma of mind is rooted in non-abiding. This essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous awareness that is never obscured.
Its nature and characteristics are profoundly still. Therefore it is said: 'When I beat the drum, the four great continents participate together.
When the staff is held horizontally, it spans the heavens and the earth; when the alms bowl is spread out, it covers the realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. To those who arrive...
Where the Elephant King walks, foxes and rabbits leave no trace. When the moon appears in the water, the wind and clouds naturally differ.
Neither past nor present can contain it; throughout kalpas its name remains unknown. A thousand sages fall before it; who dares speak against its head?
*Tu!* Within my royal treasury, there is no such blade.
At the Póng-ān of Mount Jìnshān in Zhènjiāng Prefecture, it was heard that Chan Master Yǒngcóng was the son of the Xu family of Yúqián in Hángzhōu.
In his youth, he relied upon Zīfú Monastery in his native district to leave the household life. At fifteen, he traveled to Jìngshān with his father;

admiring the sharp and incisive eloquence of Biéfēng, he informed his father of his wish to study under him. Biéfēng took him as a worthy vessel. Later, at Yùyù and Tiántóng, he encountered Mì’ān Quán.

During his prime, the Master traveled back and forth between the two dukes for over ten years. Later, he journeyed through Min and Yue, the regions east and west of the Yangtze, and north and south of Lake Dongting.
Whenever he encountered men of renown, he would engage them in repeated and extensive discussions, employing refined and elegant language until he had fully revealed his inner treasury.
He entered the monastic order at Jinghui Temple in Taizhou, then moved to Baoning and Jiangshan in Jinling, and finally spent his last days at Mount Jinshan. He lived to the age of sixty-five.
The fifty-seventh year of the lunar calendar.

On the occasion of the Dharma assembly at Shuanglin, Chan Master Jin of Sanfeng in Jinhua Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Yong, ascended the hall and cited the story of Baizhang and the wild fox. He offered this verse: "Not falling into [the two extremes]..."
Not obscured. To falsely accuse another of a crime is not obscured; it does not fall away, yet one binds oneself without a rope.
Piteous, like willow catkins dancing with the wind, sometimes they drift from the west back to the east.

Chan Master Meng’an Yuancong of Mount Jing in Hangzhou Prefecture was a dharma heir of Chan Master Guifeng Guang. A native of the Zhu family of Fuzhou, he attained the essential heart of the Dharma within the assembly of Huia Chan.
The community esteemed him as one of the preeminent disciples. In the Ding-si year of the Qingyuan era, he received an imperial decree while at Xuefeng in Fuzhou.
He moved to Mount Jingshan and ascended the hall. He raised the kōan concerning Yaoshan’s initial visit to Shitou and his subsequent realization under Mazu, saying:
"My case regarding my time at Shitou—like the kōan of the mosquito on the iron ox—is as follows. He then offered this verse:
"I have turned over my belly and poured out my guts to tell you, yet I do not know why you still hesitate. You should seize it right now with fierce resolve; do not wait for the break of day."

"Lost the Chicken. Entering the hall for instruction, he raised this story: One day, when Zhaozhou was on the latrine, he saw Wenyuan passing by. He suddenly called out, "Wenyuan! Wenyuan responded, "Yes?

Zhaozhou said, "On the latrine, I cannot speak the Buddha-dharma to you. He then offered this verse: On the latrine, I cannot speak the Dharma to you; The true meaning is right here before your eyes. If you seek it elsewhere, you will wander in confusion; Only when you realize its source can you be free from doubt.
Clearly and brightly the Way is not spoken; by whom can this principle be known? A gust of spring wind arrives, and flowers lie scattered and profuse across the ground.
The verse for those seeing off a monk says: Before the mountains the wheat ripens as the rain first clears; Mulberry and hazel trees are lush, their green merging with the fresh color of the willows.
Not a hair’s breadth remains, and the wind-bone is revealed; Every single thing is, in its very head, the body of a bhikṣu. [Fragmentary text] ... ten.
He passed away on the fourteenth day of the month; his stupa was at Mount Ben.

Chan Master Ziju Yuan of Deshan, a native of Tongchuan and a dharma successor of Chan Master Daomeng Xing of Dayue, ascended the hall and said: "When seeing the very act of seeing, that which is seen is not..."
"This is seeing. Seeing is itself free from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. He let out a shout and said: "The whale swallows the ocean until it is exhausted, revealing the coral branches.
If there were suddenly a monk among the assembly to come forward and say, "Elder, stop your drowsy talk," he would grant that such a person possesses one eye.
Ascending the hall, he held his staff crosswise and said: "One, two, three, four, five, six."
Seven, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Counting them backward and forward in rotation until the day of the future reaches its end:
because of the seven, one is seen; when one is seen, the seven vanish. One tramples through empty space; the iron ox breaks into a sweat.
Breath ceases and no trace remains. Throwing down his staff, he said: "You must let go of this as well before you can truly accomplish the work of study."
[The discourse] concluded. He ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said: "Sometimes the person is taken away but the environment is not;

the staff wanders freely in all directions. Sometimes the environment is taken away but the person is not; this mountain monk is in a state of utter confusion. Sometimes both person and environment are taken away;
the staff and the mountain monk leave no trace and swallow their voices. Sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away. [He struck the ground with the staff.]
Holding up his staff, he said: "This companion has traveled a thousand li with me; carrying you, it has crossed ten thousand mountains.

But when one suddenly encounters Linji, what then? He gave a shout and said: 'If you have not yet clarified the seal of the mind-ground, it will be difficult to pass through the barrier of the Patriarchs.'"
