The light shines forth, breaking through. Returning to the hall, he encounters the Holy Monk; he nearly lets him slip past right before his eyes. What is it that does not slip away?
"Extraordinary fifteen years ago; as before, it remains simply this. Hui presented him with a verse, saying:
"Casting off the body at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, rising up, one is once again clearly awake. Eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty, there is nothing else at all."
That master was not the same person as he had been in the past. Initially residing at Fuyan Hermitage in Lianjiang, his community of dependents was very large and he had no leisure time.
He posted a verse on the shrine of the local deity (galan): "A small hut, a small cottage, a small grove— Why does the Land Deity require eight or nine men?
If you understand how to take turns coming to offer incense, It will spare you from being ground into a heap of dust. That evening, the spirit...
To the Donor at Mount Chizhou: May you fulfill your vows as you have been exhorted. In the spring of the Jisi year of the Xiangshu era, [the Master] went forth to reside at Nengren Temple.
He ascended the hall and said: "Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell; treading upon a scale-weight, it is hard as iron.

Where there is no Buddha, pass by swiftly; the grass beneath one's feet is three feet deep. Three thousand miles away, do not mistakenly mention the North Star when meeting people. [He hung up his staff.]
“Sumeru! If it is so, then you do not go. With the staff-tip one picks out the sun and moon; one plucks the willow blossoms. The pupils in the eyes wear embroidered shoes.
He struck his staff and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: “The withered tree of Yanshan is the very marrow of Chan;
it does not lie in clever or novel phrases. If, turning your back, you suddenly can grasp it, it is like a great whale swallowing the moon amidst the waves.”
Flooded the heavens.
Chan Master Liaoxing of Dong’an at Lingyan Temple in Yizhen, Yangzhou Prefecture, ascended the hall and said: "He has been thoroughly exposed.
To let him off by one move is like a patchwork monk’s straw sandals. To manifest the form of an asura and perform a woman’s bow is the behavior of a wild fox."
A spirit-siren! He draws a circle and drops a dot in the void—this is but the trickery of a child. To slap the cheek and offer a palm, then brush the sleeves and depart;
this is precisely the state where karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no foundation to rely upon.
Even if one were to suddenly cut it off before the black bean has yet sprouted, there would still be no share of Yunyan’s staff to be had. I dare ask: [What is it?]
"Great assembly, tell me: where does the essential point for guiding others lie? Do you understand this thoroughly?
Since the spring colors first arrived at Songshao, the thirty-six peaks have remained green to this day. Ascending the hall, he said: "A single reed by the river, willows in spring;
in the heart of the waves, the person of old is not to be seen. If you, Snow-Court, would recognize the man of peace-of-mind, his nostrils remain as they were before."
[The Master] raised his upper lip and held up his whisk, saying, "The Patriarch has arrived! Do you see him? If you can see him, realize it this very moment.
If not, then from here to the West, the road is over one hundred thousand li. A monk asked, "When humans and devas meet, how do you instruct them?
The Master said, "The eight-sided staff in Vajrapāṇi’s hand. [The monk] said, "What if I am suddenly struck by a student?"
"When a person crosses through the mundane and the sagely and pierces through the profound barrier, what then? The Master said, "An iron pillar stands athwart the sea gate.
He asked, "What is the body revealed alone? The Master said, "A cat sleeping beneath a peony flower."
Chan Master Yichan Shanzhi of Mount Jiang in Jiankang Prefecture was a native of Yunmeng in Duan’an. He first went to visit Miaoxi, who asked him, “Where are you from?
The Master replied, “Anzhou. Miaoxi said, “I have heard that people from Anzhou are skilled at wrestling.”
"Is it so? The Master then assumed the posture of a wrestler. Xixi said, "The people of Hunan eat fish; why is it that the people of Hubei get a bone stuck in their throats?
The Master performed a somersault and exited. Xixi said, "Who would have known that within cold ashes there was a single bean ready to burst?
Later, he went to reside at Baoning. Entering the hall for a discourse, he said: "The Buddhas never appeared in this world; everyone’s nostrils reach up to the heavens. The Patriarchs..."
He never came from the West; each and every one stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. He bows high to Śākyamuni and does not prostrate before Maitreya.
It is only fitting that he should thus cut off the path of the thousand sages and stride alone through the great chiliocosm; this is no extra effort.

If you can understand him at the place where the Buddhas appear in the world and take up his mantle at the place where the Patriarch came from the West, you will realize that your own investigation has been incomplete for a lifetime.
"I am humiliated. Is there no true man (*mahāsattva*) capable of undertaking the work of a true man? Come forth and contend with Baoning!
If you have not yet reached this state, it would be better to tear [this robe] apart. He then descended from his seat.

One day, while Chancellor Chen Junqing, the Regional Commander-in-Chief, was hosting a tea gathering for the assembly, he raised the *kōan* concerning the "phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning, like a vine leaning against a tree."
He ordered the various masters of the mountains to offer critiques. All the masters praised him with extraordinary words. Finally, the Master said: "Zhang beats oil, Li beats oil;
they do not beat the body, but only beat the head. Chen was greatly delighted.
Master Wanshou Zihù of Yanping Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said, 'If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of ground in the great earth.
Wanshou is not like that. If a person recognizes their own mind, this is not yet the ultimate point.
But where, then, is the ultimate point? He raised his staff, struck it once, and said: "A sweet melon is sweet from stem to end; a bitter gourd..."
Root-and-branch Suffering.
Chan Master Liaoyuan Jingyun of Daming Mountain in Changsha Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "A single melody from Yunmen:

on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, auspicious snow falls from the void, piling up across the mountains and rivers. The mountain coves are steep and the ridges cold; the plum blossoms are just beginning to bloom. Grasping [the staff] in hand..."
With Mount Sumeru as his mallet, he laughs and strikes the drum of empty space, startling Kāla Brahmā until cold sweat breaks from his body like rain.
The wrathful Asura King clenches his fist against his chest and asks: "Ultimately, what is your fundamental principle? "Tsk! [he replies].
"At the peak of Shaoshi, I have also mistakenly raised this before."
Chan Master Shui-an Liaoyan of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was a native of Fuzhou. He ascended the hall and said:
"When the gateway of the face is crushed through, heaven and earth are as far apart; when the secure barrier is penetrated, white clouds stretch for ten thousand miles.

Even if one were to cut off both ends and find another way to turn, even after sixty kalpas across three lifetimes, one would still not have seen it in a dream. With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Chan Master Chizhao of Guangxiao Temple in Taizhou, Yangzhou Prefecture, ascended the hall. Having finished citing the story of the woman emerging from samādhi, he said:
"From of old, when beating the drum and playing the lute, it requires meeting two who understand each other.
When the jade pendants and phoenix bells have ceased their song and dance, the setting sun remains slanting as before at the gate."
*Continued Lamp of the Orthodox Lineage*, Scroll Nine;
*Continued Lamp of the Orthodox Lineage*, Scroll Ten.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir Śramaṇa Xingtong of Western Sichuan, a successor to the Patriarchs at Potalaka in the South Sea.
Dharma heir of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao, the seventeenth generation descendant of the Linji school under Dajian Huineng.
Chan Master Xuefeng Chongsheng Puci Yunwen of Fuzhou Prefecture was the son of the Shen family of Hongzhou. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"A sandalwood grove is surrounded by sandalwood; a lion grove is surrounded by lions; a grove of tigers and wolves [is surrounded by tigers and wolves]."
Surrounded by tigers and wolves; surrounded by thorny thickets.

O Great Assembly, among these four kinds of thickets, in which one would it be best to dwell for the summer retreat? If you can understand this, within ninety days you will surely each become a Buddha or a Patriarch.
If not, the forest of Prajñā will wither year after year, and the wild weeds of ignorance will grow ever thicker.
Nianchang (Nian Chang).
Chan Master Neng of Lianyun Dao in Chuzhou Prefecture was the son of the He family of Hanzhou in Chengdu.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of Jingqing’s 'Six Scrapings'? The Master said, "I have pierced through your nostrils. The monk said, "If I, your student, have nostrils..."
[The Master] said, "Piercing. But if there are no nostrils, what is there to pierce? The Master said, "To carry a stolen goods while crying out for injustice.
[The student] asked, "What is 'scraping the dust off the fur'? The Master said, "Jun, Yuan, Qian, and Ji; a pen stuck in one's head. [The student] asked, "What is 'scraping the fur off the skin'?
The Master said, "Shicheng and Qianhua; speaking and cursing each other. [The student] asked, "What is 'scraping the skin off the flesh'? The Master said—
[The student] said, "Jia, Mei, Guo, and Lang—there is a condition within my breast. [The student] asked, "What is 'scraping the flesh from the bone'?
The Master said, "Zhang, Quan, Fujian—their heads are as flat as fans. [The student] asked, "What is 'scraping the bone from the marrow'?
The Master said, "Yanglan, Zuoli—waves arise without wind. [The student] asked, "And how does one scrape the marrow? The Master said, "Eighteen, nineteen—a foolish person at night."

[Zou] said, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the 'Six Scrapings. What is the meaning of this direct statement? The Master said, "You will be left with nothing but a tongue-tied silence.
Chan Master Dao-yin of Zui-’an at Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was a native of Hanzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "At the foot of Mount Daxiong..."
The tiger, the mountain tortoise-nosed snake of the South—should you happen upon them by chance, embrace the prize and return home.
If you do not begrudge your skillful hand, then pull out their heavy fangs. Is there anyone? Is there anyone? Ascending the hall, he said: "Five times five is twenty-five.

The drum of empty space is shattered to pieces. The great earth does not admit even a needle; throughout the ten directions, there is not an inch of soil. What more need be said of spring’s growth and summer’s maturation?"

The sweet is sweet, and the bitter is bitter. On the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, the Master ascended the hall and recounted the dialogue between Great Master Mazu and Xitang, Baizhang, and Nanquan regarding the viewing of the moon.
The Master said: "Mazu let down his line a thousand feet; his intent lay in the deep pool. Xitang shook its mane, and Baizhang wagged its tail.
Although they surged through the waves and stirred up the billows, they could not avoid being caught on his hook and line. As for Nanquan—"

One may claim to have leaped over the Dragon Gate, yet who knows that one has merely fallen back into the great net? Is there anyone here now who can break free from the cage and emerge from the old mold?
It would be well for such a person to come forth and reveal some news, so that it may be known that [such a one] exists beneath the gate of Huazang.
It shall not be left desolate. Should this not yet be so, on this night the single orb is full; where is its pure radiance not present?
The Chan Master Zongyuan of Zhuyuan, in Jianning Prefecture, was a native of the Lin family of that same district. Having long relied upon Dahui, he shared the teaching seat at Xichan Monastery.
When Chancellor Zhang Jun governed the Three Mountains (Fuzhou), he invited him to head several monasteries, but he did not accept. He returned to his old village and established...
Mao’s studio was named Zhongmiao Garden (Garden of Myriad Wonders). Renowned monks and lay practitioners jointly requested him to open the Dharma for them. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"If you investigate this matter, it is like having lost a key; you simply keep searching and searching until, all of a sudden, you bump into it—*a!*—right here."
Open the padlock, and you will see your own storehouse; all provisions for use are fully present, requiring no seeking from others.
What else is there? To the assembly: Everywhere else, people pull out nails and extract wedges, untie adhesions and remove bonds;
here, I add more nails and wedges, apply more ropes and bindings, and send them off into the deep pool.
[He] left it to him to settle the matter himself. He addressed the assembly: "A person who presides over the Dharma must have a presence that swallows the universe, acting as a Great Dharma King.
Even if Śākyamuni Buddha or Master Bodhidharma were to appear, I would make them join their palms and stand behind me;
even if they were to stand there with the hairs on their bodies bristling with awe, it would not be considered excessive. One day, he raised this [case].
Regarding the World-Honored One’s initial statement upon his birth: “In heaven above and on earth below, I alone am the most honored,” the Master said:
“If you do not find it strange when it is strange, the strangeness will dissolve of itself. He added this further remark: “This small matter is just like bumping into a murderer.”
"If you do not kill him, he will kill you.
Chan Master Liao-ming of Mount Jing in Hangzhou Prefecture stood eight feet tall with a waist ten spans in circumference; wherever he went, people would inevitably gather to gaze upon him.
When Miaoxi was first exiled to Meizhou, the local prefectures and counties maintained extremely strict guard over his transport, and the Master carried his cangue for him.
He traveled on, enduring hardships and difficulties without ever slackening for even a moment. Once he arrived at his place of exile, several hundred monastics followed him to inquire about the Way.

Daoyuan, concerned that food would not suffice and fearing potential calamity, urged them to leave. The Master, however, refused to go, taking personal responsibility for providing the morning and evening meals.
He would often carry a *kaolao* (a woven basket) himself to beg for alms, and by evening, the various items for their consumption were prepared.

He returned in a formal procession. For seventeen years, he remained as if it were but a single day. When he received the imperial decree to resume his monastic robes and reside at the Yuyewa Temple, he never once departed from that place.
Within Miaoxi’s quarters, he did not permit his disciples to let out a shout. Whenever the Master entered the room, he would invariably give a loud shout before withdrawing.
Miaoxi posted a notice stating: "Those who let out a shout shall be fined one string of cash. The Master then secretly prepared...
He placed a thousand coins in his sleeve and, upon entering the hall, first set them down on the floor, let out a loud shout, and then departed.
He did this several times; Miaoxi could do nothing to stop him. Miaoxi again posted a notice stating: "One who shouts 'down' shall be fined one portion of the day’s communal meal.
The Master then went to the storehouse and said, "The Abbot requires ten taels of gold. The administrator, without suspicion, immediately gave it to him.
The Master took it into his sleeve and entered the abbot’s quarters. He then placed it on the ground and let out a loud shout. Xǐ was utterly startled.

After the session in the room concluded, the Master calmly questioned him and learned what had occurred; he gave a smile and said, "You fat fellow, with such an understanding of Chan, you will not have dreamed of it even in a donkey's lifetime.
After some time, he appointed him to succeed him at Tíuzǐ in Shūzhōu. Previously, Tíuzǐ...
In various manors, the cattle were struck by an epidemic and nearly all perished. By the power of his vows, the Master transformed two hundred oxen to fill their place.

For several consecutive years, the harvests were exceptionally bountiful, exceeding the norm; there were many such miraculous signs. He subsequently moved to reside at Changlu, where monks gathered like the spokes of a wheel.
When Miaoxi was residing at Jingshan, the Master came to visit him. Upon returning to Changlu, Miaoxi sent him a verse, which began: "Man..."
It is said that "a filial son emerges from the tip of the staff. I say: out of affection for one's child, one does not notice their ugliness.
When the Elder of Changlu came this way, Miaoxi wasted his breath in vain. Let it be that his false reputation spreads throughout the four seas;
even a jackal can make the lion’s roar. Who says there is nothing to present him as he departs? With a shout, Mount Iron Ring rolls backward. Later, by imperial decree, he resided at Jing.
Shan. Previously, Prince Yang had dreamed of an extraordinary monk who was tall and large-bellied, walking slowly and saying he wished to convert a village estate in Suzhou.
Upon waking, he found it strange. The following morning, the Master arrived; when the Prince went out to meet him, he was no different from the one in his dream.
He immediately called his kinsmen to come and see him. The kinsmen all lit incense and paid their respects. After the tea was finished, the Master spoke first: "Great..."
The Prince’s private estates were extremely numerous; he could have granted one estate in Suzhou to provide for the offerings to the Buddha and the feeding of monks at Mount Jing.

The Prince had not yet decided whether to grant them or not, so he instead ordered the preparation of a vegetarian feast. When the Master finished his meal, he departed immediately without uttering another word.

At that time, rumors spread both inside and outside the palace that the Prince of Huan had bestowed a Suzhou estate upon Mount Jing. Emperor Xiaozong heard of this, and when the Prince of Huan entered the court, the Emperor [questioned him].
The Emperor said, "I have heard that you, Great Minister, have donated a manor in Suzhou to Jing Mountain Monastery; I shall grant an exemption from its tax obligations.
Wang Hui bowed in thanks and departed. On the following day, he sent a letter to invite the Master, but the Master had already passed away two days prior. From that time on...
Whenever Wang He was at leisure, whether waking or sleeping, if he felt even slightly fatigued and his eyelids drooped, he would see the Master standing before him.

The Master said, "Among the six perfections, the perfection of giving is foremost. To begin well and end well—this is the ultimate goal. Thereupon, Wang He donated his male and female servants to the mountain monastery.
The Master had great karmic affinity with the place; monastics gathered there from all quarters, and the Buddhist services were exceptionally sublime throughout Jiangzhe.
The two lakes were thus named, and he was hailed as the reincarnation of the Bagua Monk.
Recently, there was the attendant San-shan, who had long served Da-hui; he once silently investigated the "Bamboo Cudgel" kōan but made no progress.
One day, after finishing his period of seclusion in the room, he requested instruction. Huì said, "You are a man from Fuzhou. I shall give you a metaphor:
it is like taking a fine grade of lychee and peeling off the skin and shell all at once, placing it directly into your mouth with your hand;
yet you do not know how to swallow it. The Master could not help but laugh and said, "If the Master swallows it, that would be a disaster!"
Later, Huì asked the Master, "Regarding the lychees you swallowed the other day, it was simply that you did not know their flavor.
The Master said, "If one were to know their flavor, it would only lead to further calamity."
Chan Master Miaodao of Jingju Nunnery in Wenzhou was the daughter of Huang Shang, the Minister of Shangshu in Yanping.

Having finished the exchange of questions and answers during her ascent to the hall, she said: "Let the questioning cease for a moment; even if one possessed the eloquence that overturns the ocean and the spiritual mechanism that topples the mountains."
Within the school of the patch-robed monks (*śramaṇa*), not even a single point is of any use. Moreover, before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was nothing at all.

Since our Patriarch came from the West, many institutions have been established, which have continued down to us, his descendants. Before this assembly of gods and men, I, this mountain monk, stir up waves where there is no wind;
that which neither speech nor silence can fully encompass pervades the great expanse, yet it cannot be expressed through words or explanations.
Pervading all places throughout the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, his entire body is eyes; confronting the student directly, he is like lightning rolling and stars racing—how can one find a foothold?
At times, a single shout possesses the full authority of life and death; at times, a single shout leaves even Buddhas and Patriarchs unable to discern it;
at times, a single shout leaves him vulnerable on all eight sides; at times, a single shout leaves him unable to save himself. He then let out a shout and said: "For now—"
The Way is a single shout. Is it the full majesty of life and death? Is it that which neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs can discern?
Is it being beset from all eight directions? Is it being unable to save oneself? If you can discern within this, you are fit to repay the unrepayable debt of gratitude.
If, however, you have not yet reached this realization, I, this mountain monk, shall speak a dream while dreaming. Raising his whisk, he said: "Do you see?"
"Ma! If you see it, you are obstructed by the thorn of seeing. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and said, "Do you hear it? If you hear it, you are deluded by the sensory object of sound.
Even if you were to transcend both seeing and hearing, that would merely be the small fruit of the Two Vehicles.

To take a step beyond this—to cover form while riding upon sound, to fully release and fully gather, and for host and guest to interchange—is why it is said: "If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe..."
"Regarding the conditions of time and season, I venture to ask the assembly: what kind of season is it now? The vast wind of benevolence supports the sacred transformation;
the joyful breath of harmony aids in the prosperity of peace. [He] threw down his whisk and descended from the seat. He then asked: "What is the Buddha?"
The Master said, "Not Buddha. [The monk] asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Bones and old trinkets.

[The monk] asked, "When words cannot express the matter and speech does not meet the occasion, what then? The Master said, "Before you have even defecated, you have already fallen into a pit and a ditch."
Chan Master Wuzhuo Miaozong of Zishou Nunnery in Suzhou was the granddaughter of Chancellor Su Song.
At about thirty years of age, she grew weary of the world’s fleeting nature and cast off her worldly finery. Having consulted various senior masters, she attained right faith.
While observing the summer retreat at Mount Jing, Dahuai ascended the hall and cited the karmic conditions of Yaoshan’s initial meeting with Shitou and his subsequent encounter with Mazu.
The Master attained sudden enlightenment. Huì descended from his seat. Fēng Jìchuān provided a commentary on each section, saying:
"It is not permissible to act thus. *Sūla svāhā*. It is not permissible not to act thus. *Śīrī svāhā*.
It is not permissible to act thus or not to act thus at all. *Sūla-śīrī svāhā*. Huì presented this to the Master, who said, "I have seen it before."

Guo Xiang annotated the *Zhuangzi*. Those who discerned the truth remarked, "It is actually Zhuangzi annotating Guo Xiang. Hui, perceiving that his words were extraordinary, again raised the story of the Rockhead Monk and the Old Woman to question him.
The Master replied with a verse: "A single-leaf skiff floats upon the vast and boundless; The moon shines clearly upon the water’s surface."

Paddling the oars and dancing the sweeps, they depart from the registers of *gong* and *shang*. Clouds, mountains, sea, and moon are all cast aside; thus one wins the long dream of Zhuang Zhou’s butterfly. Huixiu departed.
Feng suspected that his realization was not rooted in the fundamental. Later, when Huixiu passed through Wuxi, Feng invited him onto his boat and asked:
"A woman gave birth to seven sons; six did not meet with a true connoisseur. This one remaining—does he not even deserve it? Then [he struck him].
He threw it into the water. Master Dahui said, "A man of the Way understands this; how do you understand it?
The Master replied, "What has been presented above is entirely the truth. Feng was greatly startled. When it was Dahui’s turn to hang up the plaque, the Master entered the room. Dahui asked him:
"The ancients did not leave their quarters; why then did they go to the manor to eat oil-cakes?
The Master said, "If you, Reverend, let Miaozong pass, only then will I dare to deliver a message. Huairang said, "I let you pass; try to say something.
The Master said, "Miaozong also lets the Reverend pass. Huairang said, "What about the oil-cakes? The Master gave a shout.

With a single shout he departed. Thereupon his fame spread in all directions. In the *guwei* year of the Longxing era of Emperor Xiaozong (1173), Zhang Xiaoxiang, a Palace Attendant, came to govern this prefecture and invited Zishou to take up the Dharma.
Upon entering the monastery and ascending the hall for the formal address, he proclaimed the essence of the Patriarchal Vehicle.

The Tripitaka transcends all verbal expression; the Patriarch’s command is now being enacted. The ten directions are cut off at their very source. When the followers of the Two Vehicles hear this, they flee in terror;
even those on the Ten Stages still harbor doubts upon reaching this point. If one belongs to the ranks of the eminent, they understand without a word being spoken.

Even if one were to employ such maneuvers as shifting the stars and changing the constellations, or apply such mechanisms as seizing the banner and plundering the drum, these would still be but empty fists—how could they possess any real meaning? Beyond this...
The One Path has not been transmitted by the thousand sages; scholars exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections.
At Mount Ling, the entrustment was given in accordance with the needs of the times, proclaiming the Three Vehicles according to the various capacities of beings.

Today, I, this mountain monk, together with those of this world and other realms, the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests, and the fourfold assembly present here—each shall turn the Great Dharma Wheel.

Their lights intermingle and entwine like a net of precious threads. If even a single blade of grass or a single tree did not turn the wheel of Dharma, it could not be called turning the Great Wheel of Dharma.
Thus it is said: "Upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests a jeweled-king realm; sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Wheel of Dharma.
Seizing the opportune moment therein, one performs immeasurable, boundless, and vast Buddha-activities.
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, the one becomes the immeasurable, and the immeasurable becomes the one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears.
Without moving a step, one travels to Maitreya’s pavilion; without turning back to hear, one enters Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate. Sentient and insentient beings—
The nature and its characteristics are equal; this is neither the wondrous function of spiritual powers nor the mere natural course of things.

To be bold and clear regarding this is to fully repay the imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace all at once. But tell me: what is the phrase for repaying this grace? "The heavens are high and the myriad forms are upright;
the seas are vast and the hundred rivers flow toward them. [He] ascended the hall and cited Yunmen’s address to the assembly on the fifteenth day.
"I do not ask about what was before. After the fifteenth day, bring me a single phrase.
[The Master] provided his own substitute response: "Every day is a good day. The Master said: "Every day is a good day. Buddhist Dharma and worldly dharma are both fully encompassed therein;

there is no need to seek out something mysterious or profound elsewhere. Simply continue until the alms bowl has been wetted twice. [The student] asked: "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the circumstances'?"

[The student asked about] the "environment. The Master said, "Wild flowers bloom along the road; everywhere there is fragrant incense. [The student asked: "What is 'seizing the environment but not seizing the person'?
The Master said, "In the vast universe there are countless people; how many among them are true men? [The student asked:
"What is 'neither seizing the person nor seizing the environment'? The Master said, "At every place, green willows are fit for tethering horses; at every household's gate..."
Tou reached Chang’an and asked, “What is it for both the person and the environment to be simultaneously snatched away? The Master said, “Snow covers the reeds; a boat lies across the broken bank.
Tou said, “I have already received your instruction regarding the field of human activity; as for the ultimate vehicle of the ancestral teaching, what is it like? The Master then struck him.

When the Court Gentleman and Layman Wugou Zhang Jiucheng was not yet a successful candidate for the imperial examinations, he heard a guest discuss how renowned scholars such as Yang Wenyong and Lü Weizhong had attained such profound and subtle realization through the study of Chan. He then came to admire this path.
Upon hearing that Baoyin Ming resided at Jingci Monastery, he went there to inquire about the essentials of entering the Way. Ming said, "In this matter, it is simply a matter of not..."

He set it aside. After a long time of pure cultivation, when the moment arrived, he naturally entered realization. He then brought up Zhaozhou’s “Cypress Tree” koan and was instructed to keep it in mind at all times.
For a long while, the Master had no realization. He took his leave to visit Shanquan Qing, asking:
"This matter is within the lot of every person; each one can achieve perfection. Is this so? Qing replied, "Yes. [The Master] asked: "Why is it that nine out of ten people have nothing at all?"

Master Qing produced a rosary from his sleeve and showed it to him, asking, "Whose is this? The official looked up and down, unable to respond. Qing put it back in his sleeve and said, "If it is yours, then take it.

As soon as there was even a trace of deliberation, it was no longer yours. The official was struck with awe. One night, while using the toilet, he heard the croaking of frogs and attained sudden enlightenment. He composed a verse: The great matter is right here; Why seek it elsewhere?

When the sound of the frog is heard, The mind is naturally at ease. The myriad dharmas are all empty; There is not a single thing to grasp. I have now realized my original face; How could it ever be sought from others?
A single frog’s croak on a spring night: it shatters the universe, and all share one family. At such a moment, who can truly understand?
Xuefeng suffered aching feet at Lingtou; Xuansha had his own story. On the following day, he visited Fayan Yi; their words and spirit were deeply in accord.

It happened to be the anniversary of his father’s death, so he went to the Mingjing Hermitage to offer provisions for the traveling monks. The abbot, Weishang, saw him and extended his hands; the Master (Fenyang) immediately—
"Hai! The Master struck the Official on the cheek. The Official stepped forward, and the Master said, "Mr. Zhang, Registrar, how can you slander the Great Prajñā?
The Official replied, "My own realization is simply like this; what about you, Master? The Master then cited the story of Mazu ascending the hall and Baizhang rolling up his mat to interrogate him.
Before the official had finished recounting the words, he pushed over the table. The Master shouted, "Mr. Zhang!"
[The Master] recorded the killing. He sprang up and asked a monk standing nearby, "What about you? The monk was at a loss. The Master struck him.

Turning to Chang, he said, "When the ancestors do not settle their affairs, the calamity falls upon their descendants. Chang laughed heartily. The Master offered this verse: "The circumstances of rolling up the mat are truly marvelous;
When heard by those in all quarters, they all knit their brows. The table and tray are kicked over, and people scatter like stars."
"Zhi Han has never been deceived from the start. Shang replied, "From the start, I have not yielded to him at a high price.
Striking out two brows amidst the hundred-battlefield, you must understand how he seized the horns and charged through the pass. In the monastic groves, who would dare deceive him further?
In the *Guichou* year of the Xiangxing era, after winning the highest honors among the scholars, [Zhao] again visited Shang at Dong’an. Shang said, "Fushan Yuanjian said: 'Yield...'"
"You have entered the chamber of Fenyang; you have now reached the gate of Fushan, yet you have still not seen the old monk. The Master asked, "How is it with you?
The Master rebuked an attendant monk, saying, "Why do you not answer him? The monk was at a loss. The Master struck the monk with his palm and said, "Indeed, there are no dragons in a toad's den.
In the autumn of the year Dingsi, when Dahui presided over Mount Jing, the Master read his *Yuyao* (Essential Sayings).
He sighed and said, "I know there are people in the Chan school who uphold its teachings; it is a regret that I have not yet met one.

Later, when he served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, he happened to invite Master Hui to preach the Dharma at Tianzhu Monastery. Although the Master went three times, he did not meet him.

When Master Hui finally returned his visit, the official greeted him with only the customary inquiries of greeting and well-being. Master Hui, however, silently recognized him. Subsequently, [the official] received a temple stipend and returned to his hometown. Upon arriving...
At Jingshan, [Zhao] Hui discussed the principle of "investigating things" (gewu) with Official Feng and several other gentlemen.

Hui said, "Gentlemen, you know only of 'investigating things,' but you do not know of 'things being investigated' (wuge). The gentlemen were at a loss. Hui laughed loudly. One of them asked, "Can you provide an explanation? Hui replied:
I have not seen it recorded in any fictional tales that there was a man among the people of the Tang who conspired with An Lushan to rebel.

This man had previously served as the Governor of Langzhou, and a portrait of him was kept there. When the Emperor Minghuang visited Shu, he saw it and, in a fit of rage, ordered his attendants to strike the image with a sword.

At that time, the Governor of Langzhou was residing in Shaanxi; suddenly, the head [of the statue] fell to the ground. You, Master, upon hearing this, immediately grasped its profound meaning and inscribed the poem "The Immovable" (Budong).

Xuēnbì said: "Zisháo [taught that] one must 'investigate things' (gewu), while Miaoxi [taught that] 'things are mastered' (wuge). If you wish to know the 'single thread' (yiguàn), it is simply two times five hundred. Huìshǐ approved this.

Later, while serving as the Magistrate of Shàoyáng, he encountered the calamity of his father's death. While passing through Jìngshān to provide a vegetarian feast for the monks, the person holding the reins of government intended to have Huì discuss current state affairs;
consequently, Huì was exiled to Héngháng. The Duke remained at home observing the mourning period. Once the mourning was over, he was sent into internal exile.
In the spring of the *bingzi* year, while returning north from Nán'ān under imperial grace, I passed through Xīngàn. It was then that Huì arrived;

we traveled together by boat and engaged in an intense discussion on the essentials of the School, never once mentioning past events. Subsequently, he governed Yǒngjiā. In the autumn of the *dingchou* year, having requested leave to retire, he took a detour to visit Huì at Yùwáng.
The following year, Huì received an imperial decree to once again take charge of Jìngshān, and went to pay his respects to the Master at Qìng.
At Sennyū-ji, the Lord said, "In my dreams, I always recite the *Yǔ* and the *Alì*; what do you think of this? Hui cited the *Yuánjué jīng*:
"Because of stillness and tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear therein, like images in a mirror."
The Duke said, "Were it not for you, Master, one would never have heard such a discourse. He then offered a verse on the Three Barriers of Huanglong:
"What is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? All the patch-robed monks under heaven have no mouths. Even if one were to suddenly lift them up and walk away, It is still running within a ghost cave;
it cannot be denied. What is my foot like a donkey’s foot? One is again stuck by sticky glue. Turning over, straight—”
Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven, he has already encountered the "rat-poison" of another; it cannot be vomited up. Every person has their own place of karmic affinity.
For several thousand years beneath the Iron Ring Mountains, even when the three calamities reach as far as the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven, this donkey still remains right by one's side.
One must exert diligent effort.
The lay practitioner Li Bing, a government official (Zhenzheng), whose courtesy name was Hanlao, had devoted his heart to the ancestral Way for many years.

When he heard that Dahui categorized "silent illumination" as heterodox Chan, he felt a mixture of doubt and indignation. However, upon seeing Dahui address the assembly and cite Zhaozhou’s famous koan regarding the courtyard cypress—saying, "Zhaozhou’s cypress tree:
today I raise it up once more; break through Zhaozhou’s barrier, do not seek words in vain"—[his doubts were resolved].
[The Master] spoke: "I venture to ask the great assembly: since you have already broken through Zhaozhou’s barrier, why do you instead go out of your way to seek words?
After a long silence, he said: "At first I only spoke of the length of the thatch; it was only after burning it that I knew the ground was uneven. The official attained realization and said to Huì:
"Had it not been for the Master’s later words, I would have nearly missed it. Later, he sent a letter seeking resolution, saying: "I, [Name], recently..."

I have received your instruction and reply, and I fully comprehend its profound intent. I myself have experienced three things: first, regarding matters, whether favorable or adverse, they respond according to conditions without remaining within my breast.
Second, my past habitual tendencies, though once thick and heavy, have spontaneously become light and subtle without the need for deliberate expulsion.

Third, regarding the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients, which I previously found utterly bewildered by, I now occasionally experience a sudden flash of insight; this is not something I am concealing from myself. As for the Great Dharma mentioned in your previous letter—
These unclear words likely stem from a fear that one might be content with a mere fragment; they should instead be expanded and fulfilled. How could one seek a superior understanding elsewhere?
As for the manifestation of the pure and sublime stream, it is certainly not non-existent in principle; how could I fail to wear this upon my heart as a cherished lesson?
The lay practitioner Liu Yanxiu, courtesy name Ziyu, was a student of the Jewel (Baoyue). Having been appointed as the Prefect of Yongjia, he went to seek the Way from Dahui.
Dahui said, "When a monk asked Zhaozhou, 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou replied, 'No. Just look at it like this.
After a long time, the official attained clear realization and composed a verse, which says: "Zhaozhou’s cypress tree is truly groundless; One pursues it upon the objective realm."
It is indeed a great difficulty. At every place, green willows are fit for tethering horses; at every household’s door, one penetrates to Chang’an.
Layman Wu Weiming, whose courtesy name was Yuanshao, had long studied under Zhenxie and attained the samādhi of self-enjoyment as his ultimate realization.
Later, he visited Dahui at Yangyu and joined the assembly for the private interview. Dahui brought up the koan: “The dog has no Buddha-nature.”
Xinghua asked a question. As the Master (Zhaozhou) was about to answer, Huai struck him with his bamboo staff; the Master had no reply and remained there to seek instruction.
One day, Huai said to him, "There is no need to display your cleverness; you must simply 'crack' and 'break through'—only then can you confront birth and death.
If you merely display your cleverness, what end will there ever be? Zhaozhou then took his leave. While traveling along the Yanping River, he suddenly—
However, having attained realization, he wrote several verses in succession and sent them to Huì, all concerning what had been asked in his room. One said:
"Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing; throughout the body, a single set of golden chain-bones. Zhaozhou personally saw Old Nanquan."
Jiedao said, "Zhengzhou produces radishes. Hui immediately spoke a verse to certify this, saying:
"A whole body of golden chain-bones, Fit to serve as a model for devas and humans. If you wish to recognize Linji’s little page, He is none other than the white-handed thief of old."
The layman Huang Yanjie of Monsi, whose courtesy name was Jiefu and pen-name Miaode, had his doubts suddenly severed beneath Dahui’s single shout.

Dahui certified him with the seal of realization. Once, while discussing the story of Shoushan’s bamboo switch, he reached the point where Yexian snatched it away, broke it, and threw it down the steps, asking, "What is this?
Shoushan replied, "Blind! The Master said, "When Miaode reaches this point, in a hundred ways..."
I am incapable [of composing such]. However, I recall having once written a poem on wax plum (*líméi*). It says: "I imagine chewing the wax upon the branches;
Startled by the fragrance, it resembles orchid. Deep within the heavy snows of the village ahead, Do not mistake it for the mountain plum."
Lady Ji Fazhen of the Qin state had lived as a widow since her youth. She cast aside worldly splendor and often subsisted on vegetarian fare, practicing conditioned dharmas.
Consequently, when Dahui sent Chan Master Qian to deliver greetings to her son, Duke Wei, the Duke retained Qian to instruct him in the ancestral Way.
One day, Fazen asked Qian, "How does the Abbot of Jingshan usually guide people? Qian replied:
The Master only taught people to contemplate the kōan of the dog having no Buddha-nature, as well as the kōan of the bamboo whisk.

It simply means that one must not utter a word, must not engage in deliberation, must not seek understanding at the moment the question is raised, and must not take responsibility at the moment the mouth opens.
"Does the dog have Buddha-nature? No. He only taught people to contemplate in this manner, and thus [the student] came to believe it with utmost sincerity.
Thereupon, he sat in meditation through the night and investigated with all his might; suddenly, everything became transparently clear and unimpeded. He returned home with humble words.

Zhen personally wrote a brief account of his entry into the Way and composed several verses to present to Hui. The last of them says: "Reading the scriptural texts day by day is like meeting an old acquaintance."
Do not say there are frequent obstacles; with every lift, there is a new turn.
This is the Dharma heir of Chan Master Miaoguang Jiaozhong, the eighteenth generation under Great Mirror (Dajian).
Chan Master Zhong’an Huikong of Fashi Monastery in Quanzhou, a native of the Cai family of Ganzhou, ascended the hall on the first day of spring.
Holding up his staff, he struck it once and said, “First, strike the head of the spring ox. He struck it again and said, “Afterward, strike the tail of the spring ox.
Startled, the void enters the eye of a lotus fiber; Śākyamuni has no way to hide his tracks, and Maitreya is in haste.
He traveled a thousand *li*. Mañjuśrī, however, knew where he was heading; he clapped his hands and laughed with joy. But tell me, what was there to be joyful about?
"Last night the spring breeze entered the gate; immediately one sees a thousand flowers blooming upon the pestle. Ascending the hall, [he said]:
"A thousand houses of pavilions, a momentary autumn wind—one only knows that coolness arises in the sleeves, unaware that leaves have fallen from the groves. At this—

This offering is attained; at every point, the whole is true. Should this not yet be so, let us meet with formal greetings of cold and warmth. Entering the hall, [the Master] said: "The Elder Śākyamuni said: 'In all those lands, however many kinds of minds there may be among sentient beings, the Tathāgata knows them all. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata says that all these minds are non-minds; it is precisely for this reason they are called "minds. You must understand this."* *Note: This passage is a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. "Ma! When one’s ambitions are fulfilled by the spring breeze, the horse’s hooves gallop swiftly; in a single day, one views all the flowers of Chang’an.

A monk asked, "The Buddhas of the past have established precedents for the *kaṭhina* ceremony and the summer retreat (*an-gu*). I wonder, what is their fundamental principle? The Master said, "Mount Sumeru is cast into a lapis lazuli bowl.
The monk then gave a shout. The Master then struck him.
Chan Master Tanyu of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Lu family of Tiantai. He left home to become a monk under Daorong of Zifu Monastery.
At the age of sixteen, he received full ordination and studied the teachings of the Tiantai school. Later, he abandoned that path to visit Dahui at Mount Jing;
he subsequently called upon Xuechao Yi and Ciyuan of Ci'an. Having failed to gain realization while staying at Dongxi Chan Monastery in Min, he traveled to Quannan to study under Jiaozhong.

Upon hearing the account of Xiangyan’s karmic conditions regarding the striking of the bamboo, he attained sudden and clear realization. He composed a verse and presented it to Zhong, who tested him with the words, "Xuansha did not yet reach the ultimate.
[Xiangyan] responded without impediment. Zhong said, "You may now go see Miaoxi," and Xiangyan immediately took his leave for Mei Yang.

Having served with diligence for four years, he ascended the hall after his stay. "The Buddhas appearing in the world commit robbery and murder; the Patriarchs coming from the West blow wind and set fires.
The good spiritual friends of past and present have the mouth of a Buddha but the heart of a snake; the monks of the world throw themselves into cages and traps.
Is there not a man of natural magnanimity, a truly outstanding hero, who will lend a hand for the sake of the ancestral school? The Master presided.
"What is it that propagates the Buddha-dharma? After a long silence, he said, "Even if there were such a thing, it must be cut into three pieces.

He ascended the hall for a small lecture (*xiao can*). "De Shan does not answer questions; for a thousand ages this has become a topic of talk in the monastic communities. Those who come to question him receive thirty blows—those who are accustomed to speaking of 'refutation' and 'bluster.
At that time, a monk stepped forward—one truly capable of breaking through. De Shan struck him immediately. What a refined scholar!"
Ya! Before you have even asked a question, you already have a cangue upon your head and shackles upon your feet.
"Where are you from? "I am a man from Silla. Holding hands, they laugh heartily—yet before you have even stepped onto the ship's railing, thirty blows would have been well-deserved.
Yun Yuan, as before, continues to deceive one another; today, such a critique and reprimand are truly appropriate. How excellent!
"Thirty blows! Now tell me: was this a reward or a punishment? Those who possess the eye of a student of the Way should try to discern this.
Ascending the hall, he cited the anecdote of Yunmen asking a monk about the karmic cause regarding "The luminous, tranquil illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges," and offered this verse:
"Fishing for shrimp and crabs on level ground; Shooting a soaring falcon across the vast heavens. The old, limping Yunmen— A thousand mistakes and ten thousand errors. Later, he passed away.
The stupa was erected at his home mountain.
Chan Master Weiyin of Xingan An in Qingyuan, Jixian Prefecture, was the son of the Li family of Changle, Fuzhou.

In his youth, he left the Min region and relied upon Guang of Xunjiang Chan-yue, where he received the monastic precepts. One day, Guang [addressed him] with fifty-three [verses] regarding the Buddha-land.
The *Zhishi Song* (Verses on Knowledge). He entrusted it to various *vina* (administrators). His teacher attended by his side heard the lines:

"When staying in the forest, there is a time one must see the Buddhas of the ten directions; idly observing with nothing to do, a single piece of mind. Upon hearing this, he immediately grasped the essential point. The teachers were greatly amazed.
He returned to Min to pay respects to the elders Gushan Fuxin Cai, Dongchan Yue'an Guo, and Xichan Lan'an Xu. At that time...
When Huì'ān was residing at Guīshān, the Master went there to seek instruction. One night at the hour of the rat, while searching for a clean towel, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.
At dawn, he hurried to the abbot’s quarters and presented this verse: "Vast and boundless is the consciousness of karma, Originally having no basis to rely upon.

Last night at the third watch, I turned my head and took a look. A single flash of numinous light— The original nature, revealed in its entirety. Huì'ān nodded in approval. Thereupon, the Master departed the ridge and went on to see [Dàoxuān].
At Jianfu Temple, Yan Wan’an was quick-witted in his responses during the private interview.
Yan [Zhaojue] said in a stern voice, "This man from Fuzhou has been corrupted by others. Not long after, he went to Meiyan to see Dahui.
Dahui asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "Meeting face-to-face; there is nothing else. Dahui asked, "How do you maintain this? The Master replied, "Hunger..."
"Come and eat rice; when weary, come and sleep. Subsequently, he returned north with Huì and resided at Yùwáng Monastery. He later moved to Jìngshān.
One day, Huì asked, "So many people have entered the room; how many have spoken to the point, and how many have not? The Master replied:
Wuye Zhiyan simply watched. Suddenly, Huì opened his hands and asked, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? Wuye said, "The weather is cold;
please, Master, let us roll up your sleeves. Huì suddenly struck him with a bamboo staff and asked, "Tell me, was that a reward for you or a punishment?"
The Master then presented ten or so verses on the karmic encounters between Buddhas and patriarchs to Hui. Regarding the verse on the World-Honored One’s first birth, he said:
"Coming forth with his head already constitutes an error; How much more so when opening his mouth to claim supremacy? Had he known how to deeply conceal his tongue at that time,"
"Huiwei struck the rhythm [in approval], saying: 'To avoid letting idle worries reach one's descendants.

Later, Huaihai propagated the Dharma at Tiantai Zhenru, then moved to Ba'en, Shanglan in Yuzhang, and Qingyuan in Jizhou. A monk asked: 'The Third Sage said, "Whenever I encounter a person, I emerge."'"
"When he goes out, he does not act as a person. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "When the flowers move, the butterflies follow.
[The student] asked, "Xinghua said, 'I do not go out when I meet people; if I go out, I am acting as a person. How about that?

The Master said, "Buying a stone, one gains more clouds. He ascended the hall and raised an example: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall? Yunmen said, "The substance."
Lujin asked, "Master, Yunmen strikes at the collar from within his sleeves and digs out the lapel from beneath his armpits; he is indeed a skilled hand.
Yet, if one examines him closely, he cannot avoid leaving behind threads and strands. Someone then asked, "When the tree withers and the leaves fall at Baen Temple, what then?"
He simply said to him: "Next year there will be new branches; the spring wind’s disturbance shall not cease until the end. Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said:
"Within the lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna-dharma*). He pointed and asked, "This here is Master Hengquan’s staff;
which one is the Single Vehicle Dharma? He struck the floor once with the staff and said: "The thousand peaks’ momentum ceases at the edge of the mountain."
"The sounds of ten thousand streams vanish upon returning to the sea. On the sixth month of the *Renzi* year of the Shaoxi era of Emperor Guangzong of the Song dynasty, he manifested illness.
On the nineteenth day, he wrote a verse: "The final word is entrusted face-to-face; to deliberate or reflect is to propagate worldly conventions.
He then passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Luo Hu Ying Zhongwen composed a biography of his conduct.
Chan Master Duan’an Zu Zhu of Gong’an, Jingzhou Prefecture, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Yan of Donglin, was a native of Nanping. He ascended the hall and said:

"It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. The drool of the wild fox has been squeezed dry; the lair of the mountain ghost has been kicked over. Amidst the level fields and shallow grass..."
Strike up the tawny-tailed tiger! From within the vast expanse of the great void, let loose the magnificent falcon soaring through the high heavens.
A-he-he! Its wind-bone is revealed. Casually brought forth before the multitude—after all, what exactly is this thing? *Du-du!*
Ascending the hall, he said: "Jade dew hangs upon the green grass; the golden wind stirs the white water lilies. A single cry from a cold wild goose awakens those who have not yet awakened.
Chan Master Fayuan of Baoen Temple in Tingzhou Prefecture was a native of Guozhou. Ascending the hall, he cited the story of the cause regarding Juzhi’s pointing of the finger.
On this occasion, the verse says: A beautiful woman rises from sleep, too weary to comb her hair; She takes up a golden hairpin and inserts it, then leaves it at that.
In truth, her physical form is naturally excellent; Even without applying rouge or powder, she remains elegant and graceful.
Chan Master Kengtang Yanchong of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Sheng family of Yuqian.

In his youth, he left home to become a monk at Mingkong Monastery. He first studied under several venerable elders, including Dayu Hongzhi, Zhengtang, and Danyuan. Later, he heard Donglin address the assembly, saying:
"In this place of mine, there is nothing else mysterious or subtle; there is only gruel made of wood shavings and rice with iron nails for you to chew."
[The Master] chewed [the words]. The Teacher secretly rejoiced in this and went directly to him. He set forth what he had perceived.
Lin said, "According to your point of view, you are sitting right within the realm of reflective awareness. Thereupon, the Teacher cast away everything he had previously acquired all at once.
One day, hearing a monk cite Nanquan’s saying, "People of the present age see this single flower as if it were a dream," he silently experienced a realization.
He said, "Striking the grass is only intended to startle the snake. The next day, he entered the room. Lin asked, "Where was it that Yantou secretly conveyed his meaning?
The Master said, "Today I have caught this old thief red-handed. Lin said, "The life of Master Bodhidharma."
"It is in your hands. As the Master was about to open his mouth, Lin struck him a blow across the chest. The Master attained great enlightenment; he was so overcome that sweat poured down his back.
Nodding his head, he said to himself, "Linji said, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much.
Was this not empty talk? He then presented a verse: "To act for others, one must act to the end; To kill a person, one must see the blood. Deshan and Yantou..."

"A single line of iron ten thousand miles long. Linran, after taking up residence, ascended the hall for a discourse. "The World-Honored One spoke where there was no speaking; Kāśyapa heard what was unheard. He struck his staff and said:
"Where do the flowing waters and yellow leaves come from? An ox, trailing crows of the cold season, passes through a distant village.
Ascending the hall again, he cited Xuefeng’s instruction to the assembly: "The entire earth is this gate of liberation. Why then..."
He pulled with his hands, but it would not go in. The Master said, "Great Xuefeng, you have split the talk into two pieces.
Since the entire earth is this gate of liberation, why use force to pull? Ascending the hall, he said: "If you go on in this way all the time, the grass before the Dharma Hall will be a fathom deep.
If you come back in this way all the time, the mud beneath your feet will be three feet deep. Tell me, what then is the right way?"
