Dharma heir of the Chan Master of the Tiantong lineage,
the nineteenth generation under Dajian (Daokai) in the Linji school.
Chan Master Wujing Che of Tiantong Monastery in Ningbo Prefecture cited the story of a monk asking Yantou: "In the midst of vast confusion, how does one distinguish the host?
Yantou replied: "A copper oil-ladle filled with oil. He then offered this verse: A million brave soldiers enter the Han Pass;
Their majesty is like a fierce tiger, their formation like a mountain. With a single blade he directly takes Yan Liang’s head— This was not Lord Guan.
It is indeed a great difficulty.
Chan Master Ding of Jinnao Peak in Fuzhou Prefecture inscribed this upon the portrait of Xuansha: "A green raincoat was not exchanged for a golden seal;
For a thousand ages, such refined elegance belongs to Master Xie. Having caught the scaled dragon, no one recommended him; On a cold night, he listened upon the sands."
*Miángláng*.
Chan Master Fǎzhōu of Biépǔ at Dàochǎng Monastery in Húzōu Prefecture—a dharma heir of Chan Master Yùwáng Yìn—once composed a eulogy for Guanyin Carrying a Fish Basket, which begins: "The moon..."
The slanted brow seals the solitary sea gate; chasing waves and following currents is no mark of a true man.
With both hands he lifts it up for others, exchanging fish eyes for a bright pearl.
Chan Master Wujie Guan inscribed this on a portrait of the World-Honored One leaving the palace: "Not staying in the royal palace, what a foolish fellow!

Climbing over the city wall at midnight—truly strange indeed! Having practiced austerities for six years, who would care for you? When his stratagems were exhausted, he had no choice but to come out of the mountains."
Chan Master Wuliang Chongshou of Ruiyan in Ningbo Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Ruyi Yuwang, recounted the following:
When Minister Bai asked Niaoke, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Niaoke replied, "Commit no evil; practice all good. The Minister said, "Even a three-year-old child..."
"Child," [the Master] said, "you even know how to speak like this. Guo said, "Though a three-year-old child may be able to speak thus, an eighty-year-old man cannot act accordingly.
He then offered this verse: Evil has no appearance; goodness has no form. Both are nurtured and grown from the field of the mind. Without revealing a sharp edge, I lightly pierce through:
Bodhi and afflictions are equal, as empty and level as space. [The Master] cited the World-Honored One beholding the morning star at night.
The Circumstances of Awakening to the Way. A verse says: When the morning star appears, the eyelids are pierced; Chinese words and barbarian tongues, tens of thousands upon ten thousands.
Beggar, who became rich overnight—stop talking in your dreams! In whose hearth is there no smoke from the fire?

Chan Master Xing of Beishan at Xuefeng Monastery in Fuzhou Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master He Shanqing, recounted the karmic occasion of the World-Honored One’s enlightenment upon beholding the stars. The verse says:
Six years of freezing left his eyes devoid of light; A single glimpse of the morning star was like frost after snow. Carrying water out of the mountains, he emerged again and again.
Calling out to sell it, one knows not that the rivers and seas are vast and white.
Chan Master Wumen Can of Jianfu Temple in Raoyou Prefecture was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Yuyang Kan; he was a native of Liutang in Taihe County, Jixian. He followed Yuyang...
He attained the Dharma. In the sixth month of the Dinghai year of the Baoqing era of the Lizong reign, he accepted an invitation to reside at Jianfu Temple.
Subsequently, he moved to Kaixian. In the Jichou year of the Shaoding era, he again presided over Jianfu. Entering the hall, the mountain monk says today:

"I open the gates of hell and universally summon all people throughout the great earth to create the karma of hell and realize the fruit of hell. If there should be even one person who attains Buddhahood or becomes an ancestral patriarch, I—"

"I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment. Having ascended the hall and finished offering incense, he said: "The heavens are high and the earth is deep; the sun reaches its zenith and the moon declines.
To fully uphold [the Dharma] and to partially uphold it are worlds apart. Chan Master Can has, throughout his life, known only how to put on clothes and eat meals."
When I heard others speak the two words "Buddha-dharma," it was like the wind passing over the tops of trees or water poured upon a stubborn stone.

Today, my face has been split open and I am called an "Elder. I wished to discuss the matter with you all, yet for no reason, having braved the great heat of the fifth and sixth months and traveled two thousand li on a long road, I have lost everything at once. Nevertheless, thank heaven there is still...
The staff-holder is here. Holding up the staff, he said: "Staff-holder, try to speak! He struck it once and said:

"In this world of peace and clarity, one must strictly avoid false words. That evening, he gave a small discourse: "Paddling the oars and raising the sails, I steer a bottomless boat, sailing crosswise across the sea.
With a divine head and a ghostly face, I employ the Unwritten Seal to examine those from all quarters who have come from as far as two thousand li."
Dwelling in the mountains, he single-mindedly upheld this matter. Raising his whisk, he said, "Look! Look! The seal-pattern has already been revealed.
He drew a line and said, "The seam of the brocade has already opened. Whether Buddhas or Patriarchs, whether sages or ordinary people, all are sealed within this very place by a single seal.
It reaches such a state that the entire world and its vast lands are filled with a whistling wind. Suddenly, among the assembly, there was one who...
The assembly came forward and said, "Venerable One, please do not be so alarmed or startled. I realized this samādhi back in the era of Bhagavān Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja Buddha.
[The Master] asked, "And what then? He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat. He then ascended the hall for the formal discourse.

Yunmen administered three blows of the staff to Dongshan; Huangbo struck Linji with three blows of the staff. This is like reducing the hearth while adding more soldiers; it is a waste of salt and sauce.
One does not suffice as a single entity, nor do two suffice as a pair. How much reed flowers there are facing the red smartweed!
People only look at the fishing line. [He] ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma-gates of all Buddhas, the essential mystery of the Patriarchs... [He continued: "Last night, four..."
"Rain on the eaves. This expresses being as impermeable as a vessel filled to the brim. You all, if you can take responsibility here and maintain this assurance—[the Master] waves his hand and says:
"Picking it up! Picking it up! Opening the furnace, he thanks the elders for treading upon the field and ascends the hall.
Regarding Zhaozhou’s “Guest and Host” koan: for one whose ground is stable and secure, words come forth the moment the mouth opens; they simply walk with confidence.
He stepped right upon it. If one cannot distinguish east from west or north from south, one cannot avoid having one’s boundaries encroached upon by others.
Under the gate of Jianfu, all are people whose fields and lands are secure and well-defined. Picking up the incense spoon and setting down the fire tongs—each and every thing is perfectly authentic.
Why is this so? The public evidence is clear. [He] ascended the hall; at Linji, half...
A ladle. Half a ladle where the mountain rests. Jade is originally without flaw, yet one vainly carves it. Having years but no virtue—Old Muzhou. For no reason, he squeezed and broke Yunmen’s leg.
On the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascended the hall and said: "No talismans are written; no medicines are gathered. To raise the dead and ward off misfortune.
He took up his staff and said, "Fortunately, there is this one here. He struck once and said, "The entire monastery is permeated with its fragrance."
The days are long during the summer breeze. People dwell in the world of the fragrance of lotus flowers. On the eve of opening the summer retreat, I offer this small private instruction:
The great Flower Treasury Ocean is vast and boundless; rivers, streams, brooks, and gullies flow into it, all losing their original names.
Fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs swim within it, all losing their original natures. The Buddhas of the three periods attain equal and perfect enlightenment therein.
"All sentient beings wander within this [reality] through birth and death; the great assembly present here has achieved effortless cultivation within it.
He took up his staff, struck once, and said: "Kaixian’s staff has sucked it all dry in a single gulp!"
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time, all sentient beings, and this great assembly before us—where, ultimately, do they tread?
After a long silence, he said: "The waves at Caoxi are just like those elsewhere; countless ordinary people are submerged beneath the surface. At the Winter Solstice small *chan* session:
"When a drop of water turns to ice, you must not yet cease your efforts; when the cliffs collapse and the rocks shatter, it is precisely the right time to advance. Even if...

One may understand that "a single thread is long," yet one has not yet understood that "the single thread is long. Even if one were to understand that "the single thread is long," one still has not understood that "the single thread is long.
Therefore, while the local dialects may be similar, the prefectures and counties differ. Kaixian, however, is not like this:
in a state of constant bustle and haste, with the cock crowing at dawn and the bell tolling at dusk, one calls winter summer and calls summer winter—yet the single thread is short.
Who can control the long night? Where the snow and frost have ended, there is the spring breeze. While re-residing at Jianfu, he gave a small *chan* talk that evening:
"Going, going—yet truly not going; this is the Dharma abiding in its own station. Coming, coming—yet truly not coming; the marks of the world are eternally abiding."

This mountain monk has counted the years on his fingers; it is now five years since I returned to Donghu. The lotuses are gone, their rain-bearing canopies no more; yet the spring breeze still lingers at the tips of the willow branches.
There is not a single hair’s breadth of the mark of coming or going; there is not a single hair’s breadth of the mark of new or old.
If you see, you see together with all people; if you hear, you hear together with all people. Suddenly, if someone were to come forth from within this and say:
"Muwen is taking property that should remain permanent and making it his own to use; he is truly being excessive, excessively so!
*Sha!* (A sound of realization) — it turns out there was someone among the assembly! Again, he raised the case:

When Deshan gave a small-scale sermon (*xiaocan*) and refused to answer questions, hooking [the monks] in a place of non-doubt, a monk stepped forward and said, "I have finished. Deshan struck him. The monk then said, "Indeed, I have a question."
[The monk] had not yet asked [a question], yet [Shishuang] struck him immediately. "You ignorant fellow who does not recognize pain or itch! Shishuang said, "Where are you from?

This was the second time he brought down the iron hammer. The monk replied, "A person from Silla. As soon as these words were spoken, Shishuang sent him out. Shishuang said, "[You have been sent away] before you even stepped onto the ship's railing."
I would give him thirty blows. The thunder was immense, yet there were no raindrops at all. O assembly, both the elder and younger De-shan failed to follow through;
they led this monk to thrash about like a dragon with a snake’s tail, emerging and submerging his head within a thicket of weeds.
At that moment, had he waited for the monk to say, "I have not even asked a question, so why do you strike me? he should have struck him thirty times right on the instep of his foot. Why? Because...
"One must be thorough in what one does for others. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "The wind whistles, the rain whistles. Heaven is high, earth is thick;
the waters are wide, the mountains are distant. Great Master Bodhidharma traveled pointlessly from Liang to Yin.

Great Master the Second Patriarch lost his arm for nothing. Monk Shuilao was not right to eat [the rice]. Great Master Mazu’s single kick brought down the great Chan Buddhas of the world—what a waste!"
Having personally been struck with four canes of rattan, speaking of it makes one’s resentment impossible to extinguish. Entering the hall, [the Master] said:

"Before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had yet arisen, there was a naturally occurring phrase—neither east nor west, neither horizontal nor vertical. Yet the patch-robed monks gnaw at the east and chew on the west;
from morning until evening, they are helpless before the horizontal and helpless before the vertical. He struck his knee once and said:
If you can take a single step forward into this very place, the voice will naturally issue forth and both hands will deliver it.

If you merely learn it from the pages of a book or copy it from a printing block, then though the mountains have no end and the waters have no limit, when you ascend the hall for the summer retreat, you will know nothing and understand nothing; you will simply eat your fill and sleep soundly. If you wish to attain it—
"To realize the goal within a fixed period, one must realize such a samādhi. The Master once wrote in a letter to his friend Zhimuwen:
"What is there to say about holding a monastic post? In recent years, how many have been appointed to positions in the halls by imperial decree?

How many among them can even be mentioned in passing? If I were to have a mouth capable of swallowing the Buddhas of the three periods, then [the teaching on] the curved wooden seat would ultimately..."

If one does not even sit on a seat, what cause for regret is there? How can it be that one remains without learning? I, [Name], formerly entered the assembly and observed that those who could read and write often failed to cultivate refined conduct;
consequently, I resolved never to serve as a secretary. As for the elders who occupy positions and claim the title of "Teacher,"...
Furthermore, he often looked down upon others and consequently had no intention of entering the world [of monastic life]. Now, all his initial aspirations have failed to materialize.

Having resided at the monastery for ten years, he is known as an Elder (Changlao), yet he remains simply the former Chan-zuo Càn. In his diet, clothing, and daily conduct, he is no different from the monks of the hall.

The disciples who follow him number no fewer than one hundred to one hundred and ten per year. On the fifth day of each month, when the drum is beaten and he ascends the hall, he conducts himself in this manner.

In my ordinary interactions among the elders, I have spoken various subtle and great Dharma-gates according to my own capacity, neither daring to deceive students with empty, deceptive talk, nor daring to mislead them with hyperbolic, over-the-top words.
When I reach a point where there is no handle to grasp and no flavor to savor, I laugh joyfully to myself; though those listening may not understand why I laugh.
Scholars and officials know me well; yet those who do so know me merely as one who reads books, composes essays, restores neglected works, and possesses a stubborn backbone.
For those who know that I have even a few hairs of courage are rare indeed.
The twentieth-generation successor of National Teacher Dajian, Chan Master Ming of Jingci, had as a dharma heir Chan Master Liangyi of Kuku in Taiyuan.
When Master Yi visited Jingci, Jingci asked, "Where have you recently departed from? The Master replied:
Shuiguang asked, "At this very moment, where is the light? The Master let out a shout. Shuiguang said, "Stop for a moment;
tell me, how deep is the water in West Lake? The Master hesitated, and Shuiguang struck him and drove him out. After a long time, he attained awakening.

He offered this verse on seizing the opportune moment: "A single phrase for the occasion leaves not even a thread of hair exposed; as soon as the 'blow-off-brush' is unfurled, the entire great earth is encompassed.
Cizong said: "The mind-seal of the ancestors—you have now attained it. You should dwell in a deep valley and wait for the right time to go forth and transform beings.

In the *xiyou* year of the Xianchun era (1273), he left [seclusion] to take up residence at Lingju Monastery in Zhongshan. Upon ascending the hall, he said: "Linji and Deshan were like clouds rising to form clouds; Zhao..."
In the two prefectures of Muzhou, they mixed water and mud to patch the eastern fence with the western wall; their eyes looked toward the southeast, yet their intent lay in the northwest.
Each one possessed only the heart to love the walls, but lacked the will to dismantle the city.

This led later on to certain elders who were utterly devoid of substance, who drew analogies and matched precedents to smooth over edges and join seams, speaking of the yellow while [ignoring] the black.
Yellow! To discuss the black base while discussing the black—on a plain white ground, a heap here and a load there; looking at it, it is truly laughable.
If one had any breath left in their throat, they would certainly not follow such a path. At that time, several monks came forward in competition.
The Master took up his staff and struck them all down at once.
Chan Master Xuan’ou Xingduan of Mount Jingshan in Hangzhou Prefecture was a descendant of the He family of Linhai; his mother was Chen. His family’s occupation was hereditary.
Rushi was naturally gifted and outstanding from birth. At the age of twelve, he received the tonsure under his paternal cousin Maoyu at Huacheng Monastery in Yuhang.
At eighteen, he received full ordination. Regarding all forms of literature, he did not rely on instruction from a teacher. Initially, he visited Zangsou at Mount Jing.
The old man asked, "Where are you from? The Master said, "Taizhou. The old man gave a shout. The Master spread his sitting cloth. The old man shouted again. The Master withdrew his sitting cloth.
The old man said, "I let you off thirty blows. Go to the hall for study. At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
Later, he served as the First Seat at Mount Jing. In the year *gengzi* of the Yuan Dade era, by imperial decree, he took up residence at Zifu Temple in Huzhou.
He was bestowed the title Chan Master Huíwén Zhèngbiàn. Subsequently, he presided over Zhōngzhú. In the *rénzǐ* year of Huángqǐng (1312), he moved to Línghǐn.

By imperial decree, a *shuǐlù* assembly was established at Jīnshān, and the Master was commanded to preach the Dharma. Upon completion of the rites, he entered the presence of the Emperor at the Beidiàn Hall;

the Emperor further bestowed upon him the title Fó rì pǔ zhào, and he took his leave to return south. He retired to raise his parents at Xīqiū on the west side of Liángzhǔ. In the *rénxū* year of Zhìzhì (1322).
The seat at Mount Jing was vacant, and the Master was invited to fill it. A monk asked, "What is the Eye of the True Dharma?
The Master said, "The Stone Gannang at the crossroads. The monk asked, "Is this it right here? The Master said, "The moon is like a drawn bow;
little rain, much wind. He ascended the hall and, citing a case, said: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: [Mu].
[He said: "No. Furthermore, a monk asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, "It has.
A teacher remarked, "If 'no' is taken as the ultimate, why did he later say 'it has'? If 'it has' is taken as the truth, why did he previously say 'no'?
If you can catch Zhaozhou here, I will grant you dominion over all under heaven and above. He ascended the hall and said: "The mind is not the Buddha."
"Rabbits and horses have horns; wisdom is not the Way. Cows and sheep have no horns. [He] suddenly seized his staff, drew a line, and said: "One night, a rain of falling flowers;

the flowing water in the stream is full of fragrance. [He] ascended the hall and said: "The autumn wind is cool, the autumn nights are long; travelers who have not yet returned yearn for their hometowns.
[He] struck the meditation seat and said: "From this point on, one will not return; yet if one were to return, it would be attained—such are the misty landscapes of the Five Lakes."
"Who is there to contend? He ascended the hall and said: "At the frontier garrisons, the horns blare at dawn; in the empty mountains, the night bell answers.

Everyone hears them together; where is there not perfect penetration? On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, he ascended the hall to express his gratitude to the Supervisor of Revenues, the Master of the Bathhouse, and the Rector (Karmadāna).
He said: "A thousand grains, ten thousand grains—all arise from a single grain. From what place does this single grain itself arise? A thousand lamps, ten thousand lamps..."
It arises from a single lamp. From what place does this single lamp arise? Once you recognize one lamp, there are a thousand lamps, ten thousand lamps; lamp after lamp, there is no doubt.
Once you recognize one grain, there are a thousand grains, ten thousand grains; grain after grain, there is no obstruction.
A three-legged donkey trots on its hooves, trampling through the boundless seas of fragrant water. [The Master] picks up his staff, strikes once, and says: "At the crown of the head."
He also gave the junior monk a single blow; he could not avoid it. He asked, "Where have you come from, newcomer? Where are you from, Venerable One? The monk replied, "From Linzhen.
The Master said, "Monks who fabricate Zen are as numerous as hemp and millet. Go to the hall! Then he questioned a resident monk:
"The Chessboard Rock shall split open your forehead; the Almsbowl Pond shall soak rotten your soles. As the monk was about to answer, [the Master struck him].
The Master then gave a shout. He asked a monk, "Setting aside for a moment the words: 'He splits apart the Hua-yue Mountains, their beauty reaching to the heavens;
he releases the Yellow River, its clarity through to the bottom,' tell me, on the ground of plain reality, bring forth a single phrase! As the monk was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him.
The Master took scolding, rebuking, and angry invective as compassionate instruction; he practiced the way of great public righteousness by acting contrary to common human sentiment.
Whenever there was anything that benefited sentient beings, he performed it secretly and never spoke of it until his death. He was born in the year of Yimao of Baoyou during the Song dynasty.

On the fourth day of the eighth month of the Xin-si year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested a slight illness. Having bathed and changed his robes, he wrote a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying:

"Fundamentally there is neither birth nor death; how could there be going or coming? A flaming fire erupts from an icy river; flowers bloom upon an iron tree. He set down his brush, extended one foot, and passed away.
His remains were kept in the shrine for seven days, during which his countenance remained as if alive. His worldly age was eighty-seven, and his years of monastic seniority were seven.
16. On the eleventh day of this month, his entire remains were enshrined and interred in the Jizhao Pagoda Courtyard. His fingernails and hair were divided and used to construct pagodas at Huacheng.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Ying of Jingci.
Chan Master Liaowan of Mount Jiangxin in Wenzhou Prefecture was the son of the Jin family of Linchuan. He was thin and frail in appearance.
At the age of fifteen, he gained renown for his proficiency in the examination-style essays.

He subsequently left home to receive the tonsure at Changle Monastery in Jinxī and traveled to study under various masters, including Yǎnxī Wén, Jīngsǒu Jué, and Jiǎnwēng Jìng; he found complete accord with all these elders. Later, Dōngsǒu took charge of Nánpíng.
He instructed his master to record this. By chance, while passing a shrine, he saw paper ashes swirling upward; he was suddenly liberated, forgetting all that he had previously realized.

He immediately reported this to the elder, who questioned him thoroughly and granted his seal of approval (*kengyō*). Later, while traveling to Tiantai, the assembly requested that he open a Dharma hall at Han’an.
After three years had passed, he moved to Xianju Zitan. Ten years later, he moved to Shushan. On one occasion, he struck the drum for his own dismissal.

The General Superintendent of Jianghuai assembled the leaders of various mountains to welcome him to Kaixian. Upon the Master’s arrival, the monastic community was completely renewed. Another ten years passed.

He moved his residence to Jiangxin. Whenever he encountered even the slightest displeasure, he would immediately abandon the place and depart. It happened that Yuejian Ming of Mount Lu invited the Master to return to Dongxi.

When Ming passed away, the assembly again requested him to take charge of Kaixian. The Master declined with all his might, but being unable to refuse, he finally accepted the request. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly.

Silent and still, yet bustling and noisy; it has no connection whatsoever to the rungs of a ladder. Having already trodden the path that transcends the ordinary, there is not an inch of grass for ten thousand miles.
Yet, as soon as one steps out the door, it is all grass. One encounters the wood-seller, who is none other than the old man who plants the pines.

In the crystal palace, the moon is full and round; upon the coral branches, the sun shines bright and clear. Entering the hall: when meeting Yao or Shun, one presents the *Dianmu* (the "Canons and Proclamations").
One must establish one's lifelong course. When encountering tyrants like Jie or Zhou, one employs the sword and the axe to utterly sweep away all old nests and tracks.
For people like us—dried up by the sun and wind, firm and resilient, pure and naked, bright and unadorned—how could there ever have been so many complications?
It is truly strange that when Chan Master Chen Muzhou saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately say, "This is a ready-made case; I grant you thirty blows. Look closely at this!
This too is a desperate calculation for survival. Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said:

"As for this staff—[the lineage of] the four sevens in the Western Heaven and the two threes in this land—none of the old monks throughout the world have been able to handle it. Today it has fallen into the hands of Kaixian;
it has neither head nor tail, yet it can be extended and withdrawn; it is free from form and name, and it can both grant and seize. Nevertheless..."
"This is merely for those of middling and inferior capacity. But what of it when a person of the highest caliber arrives?
With his staff, he drew a line and said, "I let this one pass. On the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month of the Renzi year of Huangqing, he fell ill and sat upright.
After seven days had passed, he ordered his bath and changed his robes, then wrote his final instructions to the assembly. He remained serene...
He passed away. His body was cremated, and countless five-colored *śarīra* relics, like beans, were collected; his eyeballs, teeth, and cranial bone remained entirely unburnt.

At that time, the *Ucchā-stūpa* of Yuzhang was renovated. By order of the Imperial Preceptor (Imperial Preceptor *Qianchi*), the Chancellor of the Jiangxi Provincial Administration, the *śarīra* of the World-Honored One formerly enshrined therein were placed within it.
He then dispatched an envoy to divide the *śarīra* from the Master’s eyeballs and enshrine them in silver.
[His] remains were enshrined in a casket and interred there; the remainder was divided and buried at Dongxi.
Chan Master Yizhang of Yue-lin, Fenghua County, Ningbo Prefecture, was a native of Wenzhou.

He first established the Dharma at Tianning in Wuyuan, then moved to Jianfu in Raozhou. Later, he presided over Taitang in Mingzhou, subsequently ascending to Changsheng, and finally resided at Yue-lin in his later years.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ancients said, 'In this place, I have no Dharma to give to people; I simply settle the case according to the facts.
In the realm of manifesting the holy, I likewise have no Dharma to give to people, nor do I settle the case according to the facts. He raised his staff and asked: "What is the Buddha?
A bare foot treading upon a lotus flower. "What is the matter beyond the Buddha? Carved beams and painted rafters. He then cast down the staff.
Taking up his staff, he returned to the abbot’s quarters. On the fifteenth day of the second month, he ascended the hall and struck his whisk, saying:
"Today, Zhangsheng shall take that black bean that burst forth from the cold ashes thirty years ago and exchange it for the eyes of the Old Barbarian.
He let out a shout and said: "Even if there were a dharma superior to Nirvana, this one shout of mine would not constitute one [such dharma]."
[The Master] raised his staff and ascended the hall. "Lu Zu faced the wall; Ma Gu closed his door.
Although these two great elders lived several hundred years apart from Tianning, today I must give each of them twenty blows of my staff.
Why? It is like making a lamp from oil and wax: unless it is lit with fire, it will never shine. He addressed the assembly: "All you venerable seniors, come forth and cease [your idle talk]."
Maintain the inhalation. Throughout the two periods of six hours [of the day], do not by any means employ your body and mind for other purposes.
Even if you wave your arms about, it is still the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. Even from the tip of your toe, a venerable ancient Buddha emerges.
It is better to have no affairs than to strive for such things. Ascending the hall, he raised the story of Huanglong’s Three Barriers. The Master said: "Old man Huanglong has a flat head."

Therefore it is said that the dialects of Zhangzhou, Quanzhou, and Fujian are so authentic they can deceive everyone in the world, yet cannot deceive the people of Zhangzhou, Quanzhou, and Fujian themselves.
Entering the hall, he pointed to his left and said, "This is the incense burner. Pointing to his right, he said, "This is the flower vase.
One is able to take a single meaning and make it into immeasurable meanings; one takes immeasurable meanings and treats them as a single meaning.
The Venerable Master Chen weaves straw sandals; Master Deng Shibai beats a clay drum. Entering the hall, he said:
"Venerable elders, every step is a place where you yourselves bear witness. You must attain self-conviction before you can return home and sit in peace. If it is not so," [he continued].

The *niddhūpaka* worm is the belly of the crab; the *siphonophore* is the eye of the shrimp. Entering the hall: "The five thousand and four hundred and eighty volumes can be expressed in a single phrase.
He then rose and said, "Stand here and wait for everyone to grasp it," and immediately descended from the seat. Entering the hall again.
All things that exist within all worlds are, in their entirety, the wondrously luminous, primordial mind of Bodhi.
When *shípí* enters water, it becomes dry; when it emerges from water, it becomes moist. *Dúhuó* remains unmoved by the wind, yet sways of its own accord when there is no wind.
At the end of his life, he wrote a verse: "Eighty-three years—what sort of thing is this? The cypress tree attains Buddhahood; empty space falls to the ground. He was then cremated.
The śarīra was crystalline and clear; his teeth and rosary remained unimpaired.
Chan Master Ziyuan of Yunwu in Jinhua Prefecture was the son of the Ye family of Kuocang and the ninth-generation descendant of Wugu Xing.
Initially, he studied under Jingcou Jue at Lingyin Temple, and subsequently visited Dongcou Ying at Jingci Temple, where he served as the temple administrator.

The Secretary (Jishi) was once compiling a commentary on the Buddha’s Enlightenment when he said, "One awakens the essence of vision at midnight. The Old Man (Baizhang) replied, "Why not say that one extinguishes the essence of vision at midnight?
The Master was so startled that his thighs trembled and sweat poured from him, as if a thick veil had been lifted from his eyes.

He clearly perceived the place where the Old Man acted for the benefit of others with hands hanging down in ease. From then on, he remained deeply concealed and steadfast; even after Zhizhe succeeded him at Shuanglin, the two...

"Tiemo’s axe was merely forced upon him by others. On the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month of the Renzi year of Huangqing, while conversing and laughing with guests, he suddenly ordered his attendant monk to fetch a brush. He wrote a verse and passed away.

Chan Master Kumu Rong, a successor of Chan Master Wufang An, offered this eulogy for the Third Patriarch: "Wind and illness entwine his life; the world can offer no cure. His family is poor and he suffers robbery—how even more pitiable!
Who would have known that when seeking the culprit, there is nowhere to be found? This is precisely the moment the thief returns to an empty house."
Chan Master Fohui Huiji Yuanxi of Mount Jing in Hangzhou Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuyang Guanzhi. He was the son of the Tang family of Yuzhang.

Both the Master and his elder brother, Yuanling, studied for the civil service examinations. Once Yuanling had passed the examinations, the Master then went to Mount Shaming in the Western Hills to receive the tonsure.
He was about to travel abroad when his mother provided him with silver to serve as travel funds. The Master said, "Sufficient wealth leads to the loss of one's resolve," and he declined it.

He then stayed with Wuchu at Yujing. Wuchu was struck with wonder and admiration upon conversing with him. Later, he visited Dongsou Ying at Nanping, where he served as the Director of the Record Office (*dian jishi*).

During the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, Yang Lianzhenjia was commissioned by imperial decree to retrieve the *śarīra* relics from Yuyang Monastery. He personally came to the Master to request a commemorative inscription, and consequently invited him [to join the project].
They were traveling together. The Master declined, saying, "I have an elderly mother; her survival or demise following the war is unknown. He then took his leave and returned to Jiangxi.

When Yuanling died in the line of duty, only the Master’s mother remained in the hall; he supported her, and his filial piety became renowned. In the *Bingshen* year of the Yuanzhen era, he took up the abbacy at Baizhang.
At the beginning of the Zhida era, he succeeded to the seat at Jingci. Entering the hall, he said: "Yunmen spoke of this single character 'Universal' (*pu*); it exhausts [all things]."
The people of the great earth could do nothing about it; they did not realize that Yunmen was treading upon the four corners of the ground.

Had he, at that time, let out a thunderous shout to rouse his majesty and wait for the other’s anger to flare, then slowly offered a greeting, saying, "Do not take offense at my intrusion," he would not only have saved this old man, but ensured his words would circulate throughout the world.
Ascending the hall, [he said]: "In the Three Realms there is no dharma; where [is it]?"
Seeking the mind: white clouds serve as a canopy, flowing water acts as a lute. There is no interval between past and present;

who is the one who knows this music? Striking the whisk, he said: "One tune, two tunes—no one understands them. After the rain has passed, the autumn waters in the pond are deep. Ascending the hall, he said:
Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak, cold ashes cannot be stirred to red. A single firefly emerges; a solitary crane flies over Liaodong.
Ascending the hall for the commencement of the retreat, he made the gesture of tying the mouth of a cloth bag and said: "Today, Nanshan has tied the mouth of the cloth bag shut.
You all, each and every one, shall dwell in peace within it—body and mind at rest—in the wisdom of universal equality."
Suddenly there is one who breaks through the azure void and knocks down Mount Sumeru. Do not say that the knot was not tied securely. After a long silence, he said:
"A net covering the heavens, hundreds of thousands of layers thick. He then cited the story of Fú of Táiyuán, who awakened to the Way upon hearing the sound of a horn.

The verse says: Qinseng entered the vast ocean; Taishi traveled to famous mountains. From then on, along the road outside the city of Yangzhou, strict orders were issued that the gates were not permitted to open early.
In the year Jiayin of the Yanyou era, he moved again to Mount Jing. Shortly thereafter, he returned to Nanping with his staff in hand.
Baizhang and Dayang vied with one another to welcome and invite him; unable to refuse, the Master eventually returned to Mount Yang and resided there.
In his third year [of retirement], as he was about to manifest his passing into nirvana, he wrote by hand a letter of farewell to those with whom he had associated.

He further composed a verse of parting for the assembly, cast aside his brush, and passed away on the seventeenth day of the intercalary eighth month of the Jiwu year of the Renzong Yuanwu era (1319). He was eighty-two years of age.
His entire body was interred beneath the Golden Cock Stone. Furthermore, his nails and hair were divided and enshrined in stupas at Jingci and Xiyin.

Chan Master Wén of Jìngshān was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yúnfēng Miàogāo of Jìngshān in Hángzhōu Prefecture. Fú was a native of Chángxī; his family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. His mother...

Wǎn once dreamed that an infant was sitting upon the heart of a lotus flower by a pond with his palms joined; he reached down and took hold of it. Upon waking, he gave birth to his teacher, who was thus named Mèngchí (Dream-Pond).
His spiritual brilliance was exquisite and penetrating; he was fond of books and studied with diligence, especially delighting in the Buddhist scriptures. He settled at Yúnmèng泽 (the Yunmeng Marsh).
Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he first visited Chijue, then saw Wuzhun, and later went to Yuyang, where he met Yancui and was entrusted with the keys of the library.
One day, Yancui raised the analogy: "It is like an ox passing through a window frame; its head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through."
Because his tail could not pass through, the Master had a sudden realization. He immediately said, "The whale swallows the ocean water until it is exhausted, revealing the coral branches.
Xuexi said, "You have only managed to say half of it. Later, when Xuexi moved to Nanping, the Master went with him.

Later, he left the world and resided at Dalu in Yixing. He subsequently moved to Quanzhong in Jiangyin, then to Heshan in Hexian. By imperial decree, he took up residence at Jiangshan for thirteen years.
In the year of Yihai during the Deyou era, the monastery was beset by military forces. Among the soldiers were those who coerced the Master for gold; one pointed a blade at him and threatened him.
The Master extended his neck and said, "If you wish to kill me, then kill me. My head is not for you to sharpen your blade upon."
Shi’s words and expression were entirely devoid of fear. The soldiers were moved by his transformation; they cast away their blades and departed.
In the *wuchen* year of the Yuan *zhizhi* era (1280), he moved to Mount Jing. Previously, the temple had suffered from a fire, and only one-tenth remained in its original state.

Within a few years, it was restored to its former splendor. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The preceding thought is ordinary; the succeeding thought is sacred. Cut them with a single stroke—do not hesitate another moment."

Therefore, at the assembly of the Nirvana Sutra, the butcher Guang'e cast down his butcher’s blade and immediately declared, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas. Nevertheless, as the saying goes:
"Without the strength to lift a cauldron and pull a mountain, a black steed from a thousand li is not easily ridden.

To the assembly: Distinguish the essential meaning before words; clarify the fundamental principle beneath the phrase. Mount Dongji blazes with fire; the preaching of the Dharma is like the tranquil, deep waters. Be single-minded.
Those who merely strive for the circulation [of the teachings] are trapped within their own efforts; they cannot avoid mutually obstructing one another.
If there are still those who linger in the realm of viewing and listening, they will be caught in a state of frantic bustle—morning cocks and evening bells.

To ascend the hall and treat sounds and forms as the poison of non-arising, or to regard sensation and perception as the pitfall of humanity—such talk, who does not know? Yet coarse food is easily satiated, while fine...

"Chewing on the difficulty of hunger. He ascended the hall and said: "Before the world had taken form, heaven and earth were in profound stillness. Before the sentient and the Buddha were fully manifested, the entire body was completely true.
Without cause, the Great Being Jiaorong leaped forth from the eagle’s nest; having split open his own face-skin, he was already being sketched by others.
Furthermore, the old barbarian with missing teeth did not rely on his own fundamental nature, but gazed afar toward the land of China, where there was a..."
Riding upon the capacity of their faculties, they have traveled ten thousand miles from afar. Their intention in coming was to jostle for position and seize the market;

yet now, the drums resound at the Phoenix Pavilion and the bells toll at the Azure Tower. Every turn of the throat strikes a taboo, and there is no door for them to set foot through. The entire nation finds it difficult to pursue them, and they are once again exposed.
The new Jingshan, having no choice but to act, has boarded another’s vessel and entered another’s domain. The new official does not take charge.
Regarding past matters: ultimately, how is it? [The Master] struck the meditation seat and said: "The watchtower is silent, storing the moonlight of a thousand peaks;

the frontier grass lies idle, spreading the autumn of ten thousand miles. Entering the hall, he said: "The five peaks stand steeply; those who reach them must be such people. A single mirror hangs in the sky;
there is nothing that does not receive its illumination. The ancestral heritage remains as it was; what is the livelihood of a patch-robed monk?"

When all has undergone transformation, there is no place where one can lay hold; this is precisely when one should be alert and mindful. When there is no door through which to set foot, only then is it fit for practice.
Until the mountain clouds grow serene and the stream waters flow murmuring, until the single melody is impartial and the myriad realms enjoy their work—when it is thus, to whom does the merit belong?
From of old, the chariots and books shared a common script and track; today, the four seas are united as one.

In the spring of the Wuzi year of the Zhizong era (1268), the Monastic Registrar Yang Nianzhenjia was commissioned by imperial decree to assemble the virtuous masters of both the Teaching and Chan schools from Jiangnan for an audience to discuss the Way.
The Emperor asked, "What is the fundamental principle of Chan? The Master stepped forward and replied, "As for Chan, it is pure wisdom, wondrously perfect;
its essence is fundamentally empty and still. It cannot be known through seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, nor can it be reached through thought."
"It can be understood through the discernment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The Master further asked, "May you recount the lineage of the Chan school?

The Teacher replied, "The lineage of Chan began with the World-Honored One Śākyamuni. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a golden *pātra* flower and showed it universally to the great multitude;
only Kāśyapa alone smiled. The World-Honored One said, 'I possess the True Dharma Eye...'"
The treasury of the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* was entrusted to you. Kāśyapa received this charge, and from him it was passed down through successive generations until it reached Bodhidharma.
Anticipating that the land of Eastern Zhendan possessed the capacity for the Mahāyāna, Bodhidharma traveled by sea and stayed at Shaolin for nine years.
There he found Huìkě, who did not rely on written words but directly pointed to the human mind to see [one's nature].

"By realizing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha; this is the essence of the Chan school. The Emperor praised him highly. The Master then spoke with composure, saying: "Chan and the Teachings (Jiao) are fundamentally of one body.
It is like hundreds of thousands of different streams that all converge into the sea, where there is no difference in their flavor.

Or it is like Your Majesty sitting in command of the mountains and rivers, with the empire unified; the four barbarian tribes and the hundred蛮 peoples arrive from every direction, yet they must all follow [the same path]."
One enters through the Shuncheng Gate; only upon reaching the Golden Hall and beholding the Dragon’s Countenance in person can one be said to have arrived home.
If one belongs to the School of Teachings, merely relying on words and letters without attaining the profound essence, one remains outside the Shuncheng Gate.
If one belongs to the School of Chan, even if one has worn out six or seven meditation cushions, as long as one has not attained realization, one likewise remains outside.
"To call those who merely follow the gates of the teachings 'those who have reached home' is entirely unacceptable.
Thus, those who practice the teachings must thoroughly comprehend the profound intent, while those who practice meditation must achieve sudden awakening to their own minds.

Only those like your servants today, who have personally ascended the golden hall and beheld the Emperor's countenance, may truly be called 'those who have reached home. " The Emperor was pleased and granted them food.

He then withdrew and took his leave of the Emperor to return south. At that time, Mount Jing was again threatened by the planet Mars (Venus), and the Master exerted all his efforts to rebuild it until it was resplendently renewed.
On the seventeenth day of the sixth month in the year of Gui-si, he wrote a verse and passed away.

The Master was born on the seventeenth day of the second month in the year of Ji-mao of the Jia-ding era; his worldly age was seventy-five, and his monastic seniority was fifty-nine. His stupa is located at the temple.
On the western slope [of Mount Tianzhu]:
Iron Mirror Zhi Ming, Chan Master of Heshan in Huzhou Prefecture, was the son of the Huang family of Changxi in Fudang.
He first visited Yao-sou Mi at Tianning Monastery in Jiahe, and later met Yanxi at Jingci Monastery; after a long time, he received certification of his realization.

He visited Qingxi Yuan at Tiger Hill; Zangsou Zhen was his successor at Double Peak (Shuangjing). In the *Xinsi* year of the *Zhiyuan* era, he appeared in the world at He Mountain and later moved to Damei.
In the *Gengzi* year of the *Dade* era, he returned once more to He Mountain. Ascending the hall, he said:

"If you strive with intent, it will be like a donkey’s years before you see my face. If you let go completely, it appears in an instant. When Xiangyan heard the sound of the bamboo being struck, he saw through to the root."
I do not ask about the face you bring with you; tell me, in such heat, where can one seek refuge? Return to the hall for tea. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"The wilds are shrouded in autumn gloom; the crickets all sing. Maple leaves fall from the forest, each a piece of naked heart.
Bodhidharma’s crown has no bone; his descendants search for a needle at the bottom of the sea. What is it like when you suddenly find it?"
"Who says the palace of the Dragon King is deep? Entering the Hall: If Bodhidharma had not come to the Eastern Land, the imperial highway would have few travelers;
if the Second Patriarch had not gone to the Western Heaven, many would have been drinking private wine. Before which mountain is there this one great road?"
"Coming from the south and going to the north—how many are there? It is merely a single stone in the middle that no one has ever stepped upon.
Is there anyone among you who can step upon it? He threw down his staff and said, "Look underfoot! Ascending the hall, he said:
"Today is the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month. I remember Dongshan leaving Cha-du; he fell into Yunmen’s net."
Among his disciples, there was one who had been wronged and, until now, had nowhere to appeal. [The Master] raised his whisk and said, "Master Yunmen is coming!
Tell me, which mountain’s staff should he receive? But tell me, where does his fault lie? It lies in improperly playing with people’s sons and daughters.
On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of the Yimao year of the Renzong reign (1315), he called his disciples together to entrust them with his final instructions.
He took paper and wrote in large characters: "The net is severed; there is no room for evasion. The waves of the great ocean are stilled; empty space is revealed alone.
He threw down his brush and passed away with a sigh, at the age of eighty-six.
Chan Master Zhihong Jian of Tiantong, Ningbo Prefecture, first resided at Zhenru in Xinzhou and later moved his seat to Tiantong.
He ascended the hall and said: “The Buddhas are not real; they preach the Dharma to deliver all sentient beings. The Bodhisattvas possess wisdom, yet their vision of nature is not clear.
White clouds have no mind or intention, yet they pour down as rain upon the world. The great earth has no feelings, yet it can cause all things to grow.”
"Grasses and trees. The ancient masters' proclamations such as these were skillful enough to open the way for humans and devas within the Dharma of the Four Truths;
yet, from the perspective of a monk, they are not merely ten thousand miles away amidst the white clouds. [He] ascended the hall and, holding up his staff, said:
One may have many aspects, yet there are not two kinds. The withered mulberry tree knows the wind from heaven; the sea water knows the cold of heaven.
Hearing this said, the staff-bearer could not help but laugh heartily and say: "To leave one's body may still be easy, but to speak from the very essence must be difficult.
He threw down his staff, descended from his seat, and cited Yangxuan’s question to Liangshan: "What is the path of formlessness?"
At the site, Shanshan pointed to a hanging scroll of a Bodhisattva and said, "This was painted by the Recluse Wu.
Xuán attempted to offer a word in response, but Shanshan hurriedly asked, "This one has form; which one is without form? Xuán then attained realization and immediately prostrated himself.
Shanshan said, "Why do you not utter a single phrase? Xuán replied, "I would not decline to speak, but I fear it would be recorded on paper and brush. Shanshan—
He laughed and said, "These words shall be inscribed upon a stele. He then offered this verse: True emptiness is formless and beyond all models;
The essence of emptiness is subtle, while the painted image is coarse. If asked to speak, I do not decline to ascend the paper; Yet the bearded man from the Western Heaven has no beard at all.

Chan Master Xuexi Yi of Yuan Tong on Mount Lu in Jiuzhou Prefecture, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Tian Tong Qian, inscribed this upon the portrait of Xinghua: "A precious treasure from the Central Plains has its origins;
it pressed the King to draw back his head-wrap. Reaching this point, if one lacks the 'blue and white eyes,' how can one respond to the critical moment?"
Who would dare to treat this lightly?

Chan Master Yuetai Zuyun of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Penglun of Shuanglin, was the son of the Zhou family of Nanchang. [He passed away] in the Jiawu year of the Duanping era.
He was born on the first day of the eighth month. At the age of thirteen, he went to rely upon the monk Sengyan of Jia Rui in the commandery, where he shaved his head and received full ordination.
One day, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all atoms.
Suddenly, he had an awakening. He immediately went to see Zhixu of Bieshan at Jiangshan. When Zhishan asked, "Where have you recently come from? the Master replied, "Jiangxi. Zhishan said, "Horse..."
"Is the Great Master at ease? The Master joined his palms and stepped forward, saying, "I prostrate to the Abbot.
Not long after, he went to Hangzhou and met Duànqiáo Lún at Jìngcí Temple. Jìngcí asked, "Is it true that Linjì received three severe blows from Huangbo? The Master replied:

Cizhou said, "For what reason did you strike me three times under the ribs with your fist? The Master replied, "I received an ox from one person; I return a horse to another. Cizhou nodded in approval.
After Cizhou passed away, Boshan Jieshi filled his position. One day, while in the stone chamber, Jieshi raised the koan of the "Pine Tree in Front of the Courtyard.
As the Master hesitated, Jieshi raised his voice and said, "Why do you not say: 'Before the Yellow Crane Tower'?"

At Parrot Isle (Yingwu Zhou), the Master attained sudden enlightenment upon hearing the words of the teacher. He was immediately appointed as the attendant for the incense. After some time, he returned to Mount Lu.

Dongyan invited him to reside at Yuan Tong and requested him to share the seat [of the abbot]. The Governor of Jiujiang then commissioned the Master to take charge of Xilin. This occurred in the year Jiawu of the Zhizhen era.
He moved to Kaixian, and later to Donglin. At the beginning of the Yuanzhen era, he was summoned by imperial decree to have an audience with the Emperor;

his responses pleased the Emperor, who bestowed upon him the title of Chan Master Tonghui via an imperial edict, along with a golden-embroidered Dharma robe. In the Yisi year of the Dade era, he moved to reside at Lingyin.
He once interrogated a monk, saying: "The myriad Buddhas of the fine dust are upon your tongue; the holy teachings of the Tripitaka are beneath your heels."
"Why do you not have a sudden flash of realization? The monk was at a loss. The Master then gave a shout. He asked another monk, "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his servants;
who is he? The monk prepared to respond, and the Master struck him. He asked a newly arrived monk, "Where have you come from? [The monk] replied, "From Min.
The Master said, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained there? [The monk] replied, "When hungry, one eats; when tired, one sleeps. The Master—
Cuo Seng asked, "I do not yet understand: how do you, Master, conduct the affairs of the monastery here? The Master shook his sleeves and returned to his quarters.
In the year of Dajiyou (1089), one day he gathered the assembly for a final farewell and spoke this verse: "Coming through the meeting of conditions, Going away when conditions disperse.
The Mount Sumeru is toppled, And empty space alone is revealed. Thereupon, he passed away peacefully. His age was seventy-six. His years as a monk...
At fifty-three years of age.
Zen Master Lai of Shimen at Tiantong, in Ningbo Prefecture, a successor of Zen Master Ji of Lingyin, once composed a verse on scissors which says: "Forged from solid steel."
Cold light floats; two blades clash, refusing to cease. In the direct and immediate way of acting for others, how has he ever moved so much as a single thread?
Master Bingtong Chanshi, the Wild Old Man of Xuedou in Ningbo Prefecture, was a native of the Zhang family of Xinchang. He studied under Dachuan. One—

One day, as he entered the room for his turn, Chuán raised the story of the mountain being burned by fire in the twelfth lunar month. As the Master was about to open his mouth, Chuán suddenly brandished his bamboo staff and struck him.
The Master attained sudden enlightenment regarding the essential meaning. Later, he thatched a hut and leaned on his staff atop a peak, where he shut his door daily to transcribe the *Lotus Sūtra*.

There was once a verse by an old man who did not disdain guests, expressing his desire to transcribe a scripture in a moment of stillness: "Late in life, responding to Xuedou’s invitation, I see a monk departing for Huading Peak.
Beholding the stream to the west, he composed this gāthā: 'The lofty peak stands firm amidst the clouds; The eighty-year-old river elder’s field of vision is empty.
When we meet, do not speak of traveling on pilgrimage, Lest it cause his pair of ears to grow even more deaf. —From the *Chengzong Da* (Great Collection of the Chengzong Era).

On the Mid-Autumn Day of the Gengyin year, Chan Master Chang of Guankxi in Yuezhou Prefecture, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Cheshan Tianning, ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly and passed away.
His verse on mountain dwelling says: "When at leisure, I gaze upon the green pines upon the rocks; a hundred..."
The patched Zen robe is worn out and mended again; today one need not worry about tomorrow’s provisions. One’s entire life is contained within the alms bowl.

Chan Master Liaohan Zhiwu of Daqing Nunnery in Shaoxing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xuefeng Xin. She was born into the Wang family of Fuzhou. In her youth, she paid respects to Master Xiang...

Shan Pusheng attained liberation while reciting the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "The lands of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty," he experienced a sudden and profound awakening.
At that time, Shan was staying at the Southern Courtyard of Tuiyang on Beishan; he lived in seclusion at West Hermitage on Gushan, where the Master went to pay his respects and seek instruction.
Shan asked, "Where do you, Elder, reside? The Master replied, "I do not reside by the banks of the South Terrace River.

Shan asked, "Ultimately, where do you reside? The Master said, "Excuse me," and immediately departed. Shan shouted after him, "Why are you running away? You deserve a blow from this mountain monk's staff!
The Master’s face flushed with heat and he broke into a sweat. The following day, he went back again to seek further instruction, saying, "Yesterday, I—"
"I have come only to pay my respects to the Abbot; what fault could there be? Shan said in a stern voice, "If you come here again, I shall find your faults!
The Master was relieved and said, "The bright moon clearly illuminates the traveler at night. Shan looked at a monk standing nearby and said, "Look!
