He toppled the five Sumeru mountains; at midnight, the sun rose.
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
*Xùdēng zhèngtǒng*, Scroll 14 and Scroll 15.
Compiled by the Chan monk Xingtong of Western Sichuan, a successor to the Patriarchs at Potalaka in the South Sea,
of the Linji school under the twenty-second generation of Dajian.
Chan Master Yiyan Daoxian of Xiangguo Monastery in Luojing was a successor of Chan Master Baidu Cishi.
A native of Yanmen, he was precocious from birth, possessing exceptional intelligence and outstanding character.
At the age of twelve, he expressed his desire to leave the household life; his parents hesitated, but the Master said, "My son’s resolve is firm; it cannot yet be changed."

He was detained by force and subsequently entered the Western Mountains of the prefecture. Upon hearing the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* reach the chapter on "Knowing that Illusions are Immediately Departed," he attained sudden and profound realization, as if meeting an old acquaintance.
He then took his leave of his teacher, who said, "Since your aspiration lies in the Gate of the Patriarchs, now is precisely the time for you."
While traveling through Fenzhou, he visited Faduo. Upon seeing him for the first time, Faduo recognized his potential and ordered him to serve in the attendants' quarters.
One day, as Faduo held up a bamboo staff, he asked, "Ultimately, what would you call this? Just as the Master was about to offer a reply, Faduo struck him across the head.
Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. He then prostrated and said, "Stop, Preceptor! What the ancients said—that 'the Buddha-dharma is not much'—is no empty boast."
Yanguan said, "Do you now finally understand my meaning? The Master replied, "The Great Kindness of the Abbot is such that even if I were to shatter my body, it would be difficult to repay.
Yanguan instructed him, saying, "Your years are still young; when the time comes, the principle will manifest. The Master served in labor under him for seventeen years.
In the *Bingchen* year of the Hongwu era, he went to reside at Fengxue in Ruzhou. Entering the hall, he said: "Linji burned Huangbo’s Zen..."
Calamity arises from within the inner gates; Xiangyan wept for Miaoshan. A staff hooks a thief—there are some fellows who ruin their own homes.
Hearing Fengxue speak thus, he was darkened by his own confusion and arranged it himself, saying, "This old fellow disgraces the former sages. He broke his cauldron and sank his boat.
"A monk such as this—how could he be fit for conversation? I, too, possess that which was entrusted to me by my late teacher;
I am about to bring it forth for you all to take up. He picked up his staff and said, "Look! Look! Tell me, how does this differ from the ancients? He then threw down the staff.
On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of the Gui-si year of the Yongle era, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "I am about to depart."
He entrusted his final instructions to his disciples—all matters of great importance for the Dharma—and passed away in serene composure.
He was eighty-five years old by secular reckoning and seventy-seven years of monastic seniority. His stupa was erected on the southern mound of Bianjing.

Chan Master Xibai Lijin of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jingshan Ming. He was the son of the Yao family of Suzhou. In his youth, he relied upon Baoji Monastery to leave the household life.
He traveled to Mount Jing to see Guding Ming. When Ming raised the karmic cause concerning Deshan seeing Longtan, he showed [the story] to him.

The Master studied the *Yì* (Book of Changes) and after a long time attained realization. In the *Dīngyǒu* year of the Zhìzhèng era, he entered the world at Ruìguāng Monastery. At the beginning of the Hóngwǔ era, he was transferred to Jìngcí Monastery.

In the spring of the *Xīnhài* year, by imperial decree, he resided at Tiānjiè Monastery. In the winter of the *Rénzǐ* year, an imperial edict established a Great Unrestricted Assembly (*Wúzhē Dàhuì*), and the Master was commanded to ascend the seat.
The Emperor’s carriage visited him in person. One day, manifesting a slight illness, he passed away. His stupa was erected to the west of the city of Jiāxīng.
In the Gengxu year of the Hongwu era,
Chan Master Kongsou Wuzhi, a Dharma heir of Chan Master [Deshan] Jingshan, resided at Chongning for eight years.
He was transferred to Zhongzhu to preside over Huilingyin Monastery, where the vacant seat had been waiting for him to fill.

Not long after his arrival, due to past affairs concerning his former residence, he reached the capital and passed away on the road. At the moment of death, he wrote a verse: "At fifty-five years of age, I have attempted to patch the void;
Having severed the barrier of birth and death, Midnight is now high noon. His disciples, including Duanjing and others, performed the funeral rites according to the Dharma.
Vibhūti’s tongue and his rosary remained intact. His remains were enshrined and buried on the eastern ridge of Lingyin Temple.
Furthermore, his remaining bones were divided and interred at the source of the Nine Bends in West Creek. This was on the third day of the fifth month in the year of Xinsi during the Hongwu era.
Chan Master Tianlong Sidao Daoyan of Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Yao family of Changzhou. His name was Guangxiao, and he styled himself Taoxu (Fleeing Emptiness).

At the age of fourteen, he left the household life at Miaozhi Hermitage. During the military chaos at the end of the Yuan dynasty, he traveled extensively throughout the Jianghu region, deeply concealing his talents.
He studied under Yuan’an of Mount Jing, from whom he fully realized the essence of the Dharma. He served as the head of the inner records for three years.
He brought universal joy to the world beyond and was promoted to the rank of a celestial dragon. He once inscribed his own portrait, saying:

"Having seen through the plantain tree and the staff, I casually reveal my wind-and-flow elegance. Sometimes I brandish the whisk made of tortoise-hair, until even empty space smiles and nods its head.
During the Hongwu era, he was selected as a eminent monk and attended upon the Emperor Wen at the Yan residence. During the Yongle era, he served as an assistant...
The Emperor wished to appoint him to an official post, but he would not accept. One day, when summoned for an audience, the Emperor secretly had someone drape him in official robes and cap.
He was then promoted to the rank of Junior Master of the Heir Apparent (Taizi Shaoshi) and urgently ordered to issue a formal expression of thanks.

Having no choice, he accepted the appointment; thus, everyone began to address him as "Shaoshi. Nevertheless, he never grew his hair out and remained exceptionally strict in his moral conduct. When offered a wife and concubines, he resolutely declined them. Once...
There is a poem on his life in seclusion that says: "The spring swallows have raised their young and left the old nests; at noon the rooster crows. Having ceased pecking, I read by the shaded steps.

This allows one to imagine the Master’s state when he was halfway through his life. Later, when his illness became grave, the Emperor visited his residence and inquired about his final affairs. He replied:
The renunciant, moreover, had nothing he was attached to that could compel him [to speak]. In the end, he remained silent and passed away peacefully. His worldly age was eighty-five.

The Emperor posthumously conferred upon him the title of Duke of Rongguo and the posthumous name Gongjing (Venerable and Tranquil). He authored one scroll titled *Daoyulu* (Record of the Remnants of the Way), which circulates in the world.

[There is a eulogy for Linggu Dingyan, which says regarding his shadow of the precepts: "By this view, Dingyan points to a locust tree as a willow; by not viewing it thus, Dingyan mistakes the morning star for the Big Dipper. But how then does one see? Dingyan expands the vast void..."

He took the autumn waters of profound stillness as his spirit. In his preaching, he preached without preaching; in his hearing, he heard without hearing. His conduct was as pure as frost, yet his appearance was as warm and flourishing as spring. Governing a great monastery of extraordinary scale, he reverently received the most magnificent imperial grace.
His fame reached everywhere, far and near, and his virtue was never solitary but always had its companions. Truly, he may be called the rightful grandson of the Great Master Xianlongxiang.
Chan Master Nan-shi Wen-xiu of Jing-shan in Hangzhou Prefecture was a dharma heir of Chan Master Wan-shou Ren. He was the son of the Li family of Kun-shan.

He left home life at Shao-long Hermitage and took Master Zhi-xing as his preceptor. When Master Xing-zhong Ren resided at Yun-zheng, the Master went to follow him; their minds met like a needle and its eye.
He first resided at Pumen Monastery in Suzhou, then moved to Lingyan, and thirdly presided over Wanshou Monastery.

At the beginning of the Yongle era, an imperial edict was issued summoning those among the Confucian, Buddhist, and Daoist traditions who were profoundly versed in literary meaning to compile the Yongle Dadian. The Master responded to this summons.

Having completed his formal leave-taking, he returned south to his seat at Mount Jingshan. Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "The Dharma assembly has already commenced and the Dharma drum has sounded;

the fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds. We pray that the Master will offer a prayer for the Emperor. The Master said: "The sun and moon are the celestial eyes; Mount Sumeru is the mountain of longevity. The monk asked:
"When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, the heavens rained down the four kinds of flowers. When the Master appears in the world, what auspicious signs are there? The Master—

[The monk] said, "A single ox drinks water; five horses do not neigh. [The Master] said, "If that is so, then the meaning of joyful serenity has been transmitted for a thousand ages, and the ancestral wind of silent illumination has spread in all four directions.
The Master said, "Better that good things never happen at all. Then he said, "The Tathāgata appearing in the world is a dung-carrier;
the Patriarch coming from the West is a fortune-teller. As for the rest—Deshan, Linji, Dongshan..."

Yunmen, Guishan, Xuefeng, Xuansha, Nanquan, Zhaozhou, and their ilk—each displaying their own sharp mental acuity and alternating between illumination and function—were all nothing but smugglers of private salt.
Here in the New Pumen, I shall sweep them all away at once. Why?
Because having fortunately encountered the era of Yao and Shun, one ought naturally to rejoice in non-action. He further raised the case: A monk asked Yangqi, "What is the Buddha?"
Qiyuan said, "A three-legged donkey trots on its hooves. [The monk] asked, "Is it not simply this? Qiyuan said, "Old Teacher Chang of Hunan.
[The monk] said, "Master Yangqi, great as you are, having been questioned by this monk, could not avoid revealing both your hands and feet."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The ten directions have no divergent paths; why then do some seek Mount Tiantai to the south and others seek Mount Wutai to the north?

Before one's eyes there is no different grass; why then is the peach blossom red and the plum blossom white? After a long silence, he said: "Break through the barrier of the Patriarchs, and everything is your own.
Lingyan ascended the hall and said: "The entire great earth is oneself; so too are the myriad phenomena of the forested world."

From what source could there be a realization that does not reach the bottom? To those who do realize it, I give thirty blows of the staff; to those who do not, I likewise give thirty blows of the staff.
Everywhere else, this is "after the gruel," ascending the hall for formal teaching; at Lingyan Temple, it is "after the session," ascending the hall for tea. Ascending the hall.
This morning, on the first day of the seventh month, before the gate, the golden wind rustles. Suddenly, the drum is beaten and we ascend the hall in a single file;
yet even this cannot be spoken by the pillar. We prostrate before Śākyamuni and the lanterns, and inquire after his well-being. Only Zhijī possesses the state of non-action.
The patch-robed monk remains as he was: eyes askance and nose straight. I dare ask the assembly: which of these is "having no affairs"?
The patch-robed monk remained silent for a long while and said: "This bundle is three feet long. Wanshou [Temple] thanked the head officers and offered a Dharma talk on praying for rain.

A clever patch-robed monk rolls about like a wheel; when facing guests, he stands with his body turned slightly to one side. He binds together the conditions of the community, transforming [offerings] into charcoal and provisions. Listen!
The rooster flaps its wings and crows; the tea ladle leaps from the ground. He plants his staff upright and says:
"The rain that fell upon the river last night has divided into ten thousand household streams. Ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat, he says:

"Perfect Enlightenment can give rise to all phenomena, yet all phenomena have never departed from Perfect Enlightenment. Even ants know the coming rain and seal their burrows; the cicada sheds its skin in response to the seasonal change."
Flowers. How many times do they stick to the hands and the soles of the feet? How many times do they appear in the vertical and horizontal strokes of the character "十" (ten)?

In ascending to the hall [to teach], he cited an ancient worthy who said: "When the sun rises, the light of the mind shines upon heaven; when the earth is shrouded in darkness, the nature of the ground is obscured. Those who do not know heaven and earth are merely rigid."
The Way possesses heaven and earth. Speaking thus, those who have attained thorough enlightenment throughout the past and present are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds;
those who misunderstand it are likewise as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds. [With the whisk, he draws a line and says: "The Anavatapta Lake is forty *zhang* deep and forty *zhang* wide.
On New Year’s Eve, during the small *chan* session: Nāgārjuna filled his alms bowl to the brim with water; Kātyāyana threw it away.
The needle for embroidery is lowered. Deshan waves his hand from across the river; Gaoting strides away crosswise. Morning bells ring and evening drums beat;
the wind moves and dust rises; magpies screech and cranes cry. There is not a single place that is not this.
At such a time as this—now, on the thirtieth night of the twelfth month—I dare ask: do you all understand? Only when there are clouds and billows reaching the heavens...
It can accommodate fish that swallow ships; there must be winds of ninety thousand *li* before one can bear wings that reach the heavens.
When the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, he ascended the hall and said: "Śākyamuni, from the Tuṣita Heaven, took birth by entrusting himself to a womb.

While still within the great vessel of the womb, he already had the power to cure the grave illness of birth and death. Upon his descent into the world, he immediately pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth."
It can be seen that this is something that cannot be grasped or accumulated. When the morning star appeared, he suddenly awakened to the Way;

this was precisely like a diseased eye seeing floating flowers in the sky. Throughout forty-nine years and over three hundred assemblies, whether speaking extensively or briefly, directly or circuitously, openly or secretly—was this not merely the delirious chatter of one in a deep sleep? Upon reaching the end, he finally rubbed his chest.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "You all should carefully contemplate my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold. Behold it with full satisfaction, lest you later regret it.
If you say that my parinirvāṇa means I am no longer your disciple, you are not my disciples; if you say that I do not enter parinirvāṇa, you likewise are not my disciples.
My illness has reached the vital organs and the diaphragm; it can no longer be cured. Not only would worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness, but even Jīvaka himself could do nothing."
Even the Divine Physician would have to retreat three stations. Today, a distant descendant of the Northern Mountain must treat him.
If he cannot be treated, future generations will forever lose their reliance and protection.
If he can be treated, then the body of purple-golden hue—lofty, majestic, and brilliantly radiant—will manifest everywhere. (He strikes the whisk.)
He said: "The willow color is tender as fresh gold; the pear blossoms are fragrant as falling snow. At Jingshan, he ascended the hall and said:
"The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by the One Dharma. Before you is Bowu Peak; behind you is Lingxiao Peak;
in between is the Buddha Hall. What do you call 'the One Dharma'? After a long silence, he said: "The National Teacher Yizhu was originally from Kunshan."
The Master entered the hall. Master Ma said: "Since the period of chaos, for thirty years, there has been no lack of salt and sauce.
Here there is not even two ounces of gold; the common man buys three pints of wine. He entered the hall and said:
"But study the living word, do not study the dead word. To manifest objects upon the head is the dead word; to step and tread upon the Southern Dipper is the living word."
Turning around, he overturned the Big Dipper. This is a "dead word. What is a "living word"? After the rain has passed through the streets of Suzhou, one puts on embroidered shoes.
When the assembly hesitated, he threw down his whisk and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent lies right before the eyes.
It is not a dharma of the present moment, nor is it something reached by the ears or eyes. At the head of the inkstone-washing pool, the clouds drift slowly."
Grass grows lushly upon the tomb where the rooster was buried. From within his room, he uttered these words: "The source of the Way is not far off; where is it?

For what purpose did the Patriarch come from the West? There is no tree of Bodhi; who gave it its name? A monk asked: *Note: This passage is a famous excerpt from the *Record of Linji* (Linjilu), containing the final instructions of Master Linji Yixuan.*
"What is the guest within the guest? The Master said, "Supporting a staff, one stands beside another's gate.

"What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "Leaning against a dew-pillar in front of the hall. "What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "One's life and destiny belong to another.
"What is the host within the host? The Master said, "Holding a vajra scepter in one's hand. [This occurred] when he saw a monk in the courtyard.
[The monk] passed by. The Master said in a stern voice, "The eaves of the roof are collapsing! The monk looked up. The Master said, "A hawk has flown to Silla.
Seeing the monk enter the gate, he immediately said, "You fellow who treads upon prefectures and counties—you deserve thirty blows right under your heels.
[The monk] said, "I have not even asked a question, yet you have already granted me these blows. The Master said, "Wait until you open your mouth; then you will be fit for them."

"What are you doing? the Master asked. As the monk hesitated, the Master shouted him out. When the monk entered for an interview and unfolded his sitting cloth, the Master said, "In my place, there is no leftover gruel or stale rice;
there is no need to use up your worn-out cooking cloth. The monk replied, "Out of compassion, Preceptor. The Master said, "The green stone pillar before the gate has laughed itself to pieces.
Throughout his life, the Master occupied four monastic seats (*daochang*), each of which produced noteworthy achievements. In his later years...

He selected a site for his retirement to the left of Jizhao Pagoda and built a thatched hut to dwell there. At the age of over seventy, he passed away. (His *Zengji xù chuándēng* [Supplementary Collection of the Continued Lamp Record] circulates in the world.)

Chan Master Jueyuan Huitan of Tianjie Monastery in Jiangning Prefecture was a dharma heir of Chan Master Longxiang Xin. He was the son of the Yang family of Tiantai. His mother dreamed that a bright moon fell into her lap;

she swallowed it and subsequently conceived. At birth, his countenance was dignified and striking. Upon reaching a slight age, he relied upon Dajun of Faguo Monastery in Yue to leave the household life.

He was from a family of the [Zhu] clan. At the age of sixteen, he became a monk of the Great Sangha. Hearing that Xiaoyin presided over Zhongzhu, he went there to visit and inquire, fully expressing the intensity of his quest for the Way.
Xiaoyin rebuked him, saying: "That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure. The Way resides within oneself; why seek it from another?
The Master withdrew and attained realization. One day, upon hearing the story of Baizhang’s wild fox, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
[Zhaozhou] said, "The Buddha-dharma has fallen into my hands. Yunyan asked, "What principle have you seen?
The Master spread his two hands and said, "Not worth half a coin. Yunyan nodded in approval. One day, as the Master entered the gate, Yunyan asked, "Where have you come from?

The Master said, "I have come from traveling the mountains. Yunyan asked, "As for that which was 'pressed through' at Luopo during your travels to consult various masters—what is it? The Master said, "Not yet."
Upon entering, he presented himself to the Master. Yunyan said, "Why do you not bring it forth right now?

The Master hesitated; Yunyan then gave a shout. From that moment, the Master was suddenly liberated. On another day, Yunyan spread out both hands and said, "I have opened my eight characters wide for you.
Why are you unwilling to accept it? The Master said, "Do not try to obstruct me. Yunyan said, "Come forward."
"I shall come to speak for you. The Master covered his ears and departed. Later, when the Abbot [of] Longxiang retired, he appointed the Master to share the seat with him.
In the *Renchen* year of the Zhizheng era, he took up residence at the Patriarch’s Hall of Niushou for three years, after which he moved to Qingliang Guanghui.

He ascended the hall and said: "A single phrase is pitch-black ink; it has no handle, yet it possesses a standard. After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? The pestle pounds toward the southeast; the millstone..."
Turning toward the northwest, he ascended the hall. "The Sutras have masters of the Sutras; the Shastras have masters of the Shastras.

Today at Longhe, we shall let loose a single thread of the Way to divide the sections and arrange the segments. He took up his staff, struck it once, and said, "Tell me, what chapter and verse is this?
Ascending the hall is a ready-made public case; although many throughout past and present have understood it, there are many who have misunderstood it.
"It is not for lack of them that gold and brass cannot be distinguished, nor jade and stone separated.
Everything is like the single teaching of today’s Bodhidharma—what kind of person could possibly shoulder this? Here at Longhe, I shall distinguish them directly:
Upādhyāya Zhang and Upādhyāya Li—one has long arms, the other has large eyes. After a long silence, he let out a single sigh and descended.
[The Master] took his seat and addressed the assembly: "The spring breeze blows vast and wide; the spring days linger on slowly. The yellow oriole sings upon the branches of a hundred flowers.
Within this, there is boundless meaning—whose message can it be known by? A monk asked, "When the mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot be suppressed or restrained, what then?
The Master gave a sharp shout and said, "Who is it that suppresses them? In his private quarters, he said to a monk, "Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day..."
There is no portion for you to peck and devour; there is no portion for you to pursue. Do you understand? The monk was at a loss.

The Master said, "If you have not yet clarified three, eight, and nine, it will be difficult to avoid self-muttering. In the year of Yiwei, the Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Jingjue Miaobian.
In the year of Bingshen, when the imperial army settled Jianye, the Master went to pay his respects at the military headquarters. Upon seeing him, [the Emperor] sighed in admiration.

It was said: "He is a monk of true merit and virtue. He was appointed as the abbot of Jiangshan; after more than a year, it was renamed Longxiang and established as the Great Tianning Temple. By imperial decree, the Master was appointed to preside over it.

A grand memorial service for the deceased was convened, and the Master was commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. The Emperor’s carriage visited in person, and the honors bestowed were most generous.
The Emperor personally inscribed the characters "The World's Foremost Zen Grove" (Tiānxià dìyī chánlín). In the Wushen year of the Hongwu era, he was granted purple robes and gold.

A square-collared robe with a hem was presented, accompanied by an imperial edict appointing him as the Great Chan Master Yanfan Shanshe Liguo Chongjiao, to serve as the abbot of the Great Tianjie Monastery and preside over the Buddhist affairs of all the mountain monasteries.
At that time, the selection process was orderly and the evaluation was impartial.

The imperial altars and ancestral shrines were served with supreme impartiality. Among those of noble ambition and the recluses dwelling in the mountains and forests who embraced the Way, many rose up together like horses yoked side by side.

In the sixth month of the summer of the Gengxu year, during a court deliberation on the Western Regions that had not yet submitted, the Emperor—recognizing that the people of that land highly esteemed the Buddha-vehicle—issued a special edict for the Master to go there.
Receiving this command, the Master set out on his journey that very day. From Yang in Min, through all the kingdoms and cities he passed, there was no one who did not hear of it.
The wind came and returned. In the seventh month of autumn in the year Xinhai, he arrived at the kingdom of Hala and proclaimed the majesty and virtue of the Son of Heaven.

He was lodged at the Foshan Monastery, where its king treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher. In the ninth month, the Master manifested slight illness; the king and his ministers all came to offer their condolences.
After bathing and changing his robes for a brief moment, he said to those around him, "My karmic conditions have come to an end;
I cannot return to life. He sat upright in the *paryaṅka* posture at midnight. The Master asked, "Is the sun about to rise? He replied, "Not yet.
The Master questioned him again and again, until finally he said, "The sun has risen. The Master passed away with a serene expression. His secular age was sixty-eight; [his monastic seniority was...]
Fifty-three days passed, yet his complexion remained as if he were alive. The King carved fragrant wood into a shrine and constructed an altar for his cremation.
When the firewood was consumed and the flames extinguished, there were countless *śarīra* relics; his tongue, jawbone, and teeth remained uncorrupted.

He collected the *śarīra*, the sacred bones, and the uncorrupted remains and interred them within the Pratyekabuddha stupa in that kingdom. On the Jia-yin day, in the ninth month, he returned to the capital with his companions.

He reported these matters to the Emperor, who expressed deep lamentation. An imperial decree was issued for Zongle and others, the abbots of Tianjie and Jiangshan Monasteries, to enshrine the Master’s robes to the left of the Yu Hua Terrace.
His *Dharma Words from the Five Assemblies* were circulated throughout the world.
Chan Master Quan-shi Zong-le, whose courtesy name was Ji-tan, resided at Tianjie Shanshi Monastery in Jiangning Prefecture. He was the son of the Zhou family of Linhai in Taizhou.

He was born on the seventeenth day of the seventh month in the Wuma year of the Renzong era of the Yuan dynasty (1318). At the age of eight, he followed Xiao-yin at Zhongzhu Monastery to receive his initial training;
at fourteen, he shaved his head; and at twenty, he received full ordination. One day, Yin asked him: "The National Teacher [Tianyi Yihuai] said..."
He called for his attendant. The attendant responded three times. "What do you think of this? the Master asked. Yunyan said, "How can you carve out flesh to create a wound?

Xuedou said, "I took you for someone extraordinary, but it turns out you have nothing at all. The Master gave a shout. Yunyan prepared to take up his staff, but the Master shook his sleeves and departed.
Yunyan subsequently went to Mount Jing to study under Yuansou, who appointed him as the head of the secretarial office (*jishi*). Later, he emerged from seclusion to serve as abbot at Xuan.

To the west of Zhishui, in the year Wushen of the Hongwu era, he moved to Zhongzhu. On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, he entered the temple and ascended the Dharma hall to address the assembly:
"The sword of the Vajra King, brandished horizontally, causes a thousand demons to vanish; the eye of Śakara, piercingly illuminating, causes the myriad existences to hide their forms."
"Having arrived here, expansion and contraction depend on me; killing and giving life are applied according to the occasion.

It reaches the point where, within Thousand-Year Rock, the heavens leap with coins, and the waters of the pond flow back against the current of the Eastern Sea. Do you all know this or not? Raising his whisk, he said:
"The stone shoot before the courtyard has put forth its branches; look and see the phoenixes roosting in the high boughs. He then cited: When Nanquan first entered the monastery...
The assembly escorted him into the abbot’s quarters. A monk asked, "Dwelling at ease in the abbot's room, with what do you instruct people?
Nanquan said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox; when I rose at dawn, I had lost the fire. The Master [Zhaozhou] said, "Great Nanquan!
Not only did he deceive others, but he deceived himself as well. This is the function of the new Tianzhu; I want everyone to know it. Suddenly, if someone..."

Question: "Dwelling upright in a small room, what will you point out to people? [The Master] struck him across the back with his staff and said, "Tell me, are you the same as the ancients, or are you different?
He then planted his staff and descended from the seat. In the *Xinhai* year, he moved to Mount Shuangjing.

That winter, an imperial edict summoned ten Buddhist monks of realized virtue from the Jiangnan region to the capital. At Taiping Xingguo Temple, they established a grand memorial service for the Dharma.
The assembly convened. The Master was seated at the head of the ranks. Having fasted and purified himself, the Emperor composed a memorial and petition. The imperial carriage arrived in person;

the Emperor donned the *píbiàn* cap and robe, tucked in his jade tablet (*yùguī*), and faced north to pay homage to the Buddha. The various ministers each wore their dharma robes to follow in attendance. Prior to this, the Emperor had commanded the Master.

A musical composition for offering to the Buddha was presented. The Emperor inscribed eight chapters for the work, titled: *Shanshi* (Benefiting the World), *Zhaoxin* (Manifesting Faith), *Yanci* (Extending Compassion), *Faxi* (Dharma Joy), *Chan Yue* (Zen Rapture), *Bianying* (Universal Response), *Miaoji* (Sublime Salvation), and *Shancheng* (Wholesome Accomplishment).
He commanded the Grand Court Music Bureau to provide the rhythmic accompaniment through song and dance.

At that time, he obtained the "Cypress Tree" (Jingchuan) hermitage. First, there was the merit arising from Yihuai; second, there was the power of his friends' rigorous polishing.

One day, as the hermitage was being established, the hermit raised the koan: "The phrase with no phrase is like a vine leaning against a tree. He asked the Master about it. As the Master hesitated, the hermit struck him across the back.
The Master was indignant and did not sleep all night. At dawn, hearing the sound of a fire-stick being struck, he attained sudden, thorough penetration. He then said to the hermit...
Dongshan said, "Regarding last night’s koan, today I must settle it for you. Dongshan gripped his staff and asked, "Where does the phrase return?
Before the words were finished, the Master snatched the staff from Dongshan's hand, snapped it into two pieces, and tossed them out the window, saying:
At another time, he burned a path elsewhere and entered the hall to lie down. Hearing this, Huan-sheng asked specifically, "I am glad that Elder Xing has completed his great matter.
The Master shouted, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor. One day he asked An, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?
An said, "Autumn trees shed yellow leaves; on a cold day, one digs a hearth in the ground. The Master said, "For now, I shall..."

He questioned another. Later, he visited Zen Master Tianshi Quan, who brought up this story and asked: "In years past, I once asked a master and friend whether the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings are the same or different.
He said: 'Autumn trees shed yellow leaves; on a cold day, one digs a fire-pit in the ground.
Today, I ask the Venerable Master to provide a definitive judgment. Quan said: "This old man’s wrists have lost their strength in recent years; he can only lean on his staff by his bed."
He leaned his head against the wall. The Master said, "There is someone who does not approve of the Master speaking in this way.

The Patriarch picked up his staff and struck him, saying, "Wait until the eyes of the pillar open of themselves; then I shall hurl an iron caltrop right in your face. The Master then prostrated himself.
Later, he appeared in the world at Puguangming in Li. In the Ding-si year of the Hongwu era, he moved to Yongqing in Changzhou. By imperial selection, he resided at Fu.

Chou Shushan was again commanded by imperial decree to serve as the abbot of Tiantong. A monk asked, "When an ox passes through a window frame, its head, horns, and all four hooves have already passed through;
why is it that its tail cannot pass? The Master said, "The bowl slipped from the shoulder.

The monk said, "If that is so, then the Great Huì of old is the Fo Lang of today. The Master said, "Do not mistake the City of the Six Dragons for your maternal uncle's house. The monk said: [silence].
The Master was asked about the instructions he had given for his return journey. The Master said, "One must urgently spit it out.
He ascended the hall and said: "One is three; three is one. Whether saintly or ordinary, the distinction does not go beyond the wooden man wearing brocade robes or the stone woman’s sudden elegance.
She is accustomed to playing the stringless lute and can blow the holeless flute. She walks at the bottom of the deepest sea and stands upon the highest peak."
Standing atop the pinnacle, the incense pillar comes to prostrate; empty space joins in clapping its hands; the ten thousand phenomena listen with bated breath.

Everyone laughs at this one throw. But tell me, what is it they laugh at? To starve to death inside a grain basket—people refuse to accept their own situation. Opening their mouths, they eat for free.
Even if you reach the Thirty-three Heavens, how could you ever exhaust your original hunger and suffering? (He strikes the meditation staff and says: HŪṂ!
"Hūṃ! He then descended from his seat. Entering the hall, he said: "This morning is the first day of the tenth month; the patch-robed monks prepare for winter.
Stir the flames of the hearth, and do not ask further about firewood or charcoal. When thirsty, drink the soup of molten copper; when hungry, eat rice mixed with iron nails.
Great assembly, do you know that the sack has no thread to bind even an ant? The kitchen lacks even a grain of flour to attract a fly? To reach such a state as this—this must not be overlooked."
Avoiding idleness. Zhuo strikes his staff and descends from the seat. To thank the head officers, he ascends the hall.

As soon as the whisk of hair is blown, the boundless Flower Treasury World (Avataṃsaka-lokadhātu) is manifested. With the golden mallet held in hand, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are summoned or released at will.

The tea bowl is smashed to pieces across the ground; its golden resonance and jade-like vibration shake the leaking lamp. Wherever the cup touches, it illuminates past and present; the hare’s horn and the staff wielded like a staff.
He lifts up the sun and moon of the great trichiliocosm; with a whisk made of tortoise hair, he turns the Dharma wheel through kalpas as numerous as dust motes.
Does he still see the mountains of the Buddha-land? With a leap, he strikes and breaks through the nostrils of you all; does he blind the eyes of you all? He lets out a shout and says:
"The spring breeze and summer rain arrive in their season; white peaches and red apricots bloom in succession. Entering the hall, [he said]: "On this day last year..."
Dwelling on Mount Laṅkā, that assembly of four groups rejoiced because one person was missing from their place.

This year, on this very day, dwelling on Mount Buddhakṣetra, this assembly of four groups rejoices because one person is missing from their place. Striking the whisk, he said: "A single body becomes infinite bodies."
The immeasurable body becomes a single body. When walking, it walks throughout heaven and earth; when sitting, it sits pervading all places.
What need is there to speak of east, west, south, north, other directions, or this world? Nevertheless, this is still but a conjured city. But tell me: where does one truly arrive?
"How is it with the single phrase 'the place of jewels'? He then descended from his seat. He ascended the hall and said: "Greed, anger, and delusion are precept, concentration, and wisdom;
precept, concentration, and wisdom are greed, anger, and delusion. Ignorance is the knowledge and vision of liberation; the knowledge and vision of liberation is ignorance.
All sentient beings are the Buddhas; the Buddhas are all sentient beings. When the moon sets, the mountain has no shadow; when the wind comes, the trees have sound. Great!

"A thousand non-obstructions. Waiting for the pillar, the clamor spreads across and down. He gave a shout and descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "Today is the first day of the tenth month.
A monk has prepared the charcoal and opened the furnace. You know well the time and the season; I do not concern myself with 'it is,' 'it is not,' 'that,' or 'this.
Before the birth of Buddhas, the thatch-roofed hut’s command allows the pure breeze to flow freely through the imperial capital. One day there was one..."
A few monks arrived from Xuefeng. The Master asked, "Are you the disciples of Master Ning?
They replied, "Yes. The Master said, "May I ask about your family affairs? They replied, "We may. The Master said, "Wrong.
He asked again, "Before Mount Fushan, the three grasses and two trees roar like lions day and night; is this the speech of One Peak? They replied, "It is. The Master said again, "Wrong."

The monks remained silent. The Master said, "How is it that you have not maintained even the five precepts? In his later years, he retired to Puguang Temple, intending to spend the remainder of his life there.
Chan Master Wuchude of Dafui in Chengdu Prefecture was the son of Shin of Shinsu in Japan; he was intelligent from childhood.
When Xing encountered groups of children at play, he would invariably lead them away; upon seeing monks, his countenance would brighten with joy.
He followed [the master] to Tianning Monastery in the prefecture, where he left home and received full ordination. He read extensively across all branches of learning.

Subsequently, mindful of Jue’a’s character, he requested permission from the king to accompany a national envoy to the imperial court to spread the teachings. When the envoy returned, the Master wished to remain in the Middle Kingdom (Huaxia), and the Emperor granted his request. First...
He attended Quan-shi, serving as his internal secretary for a long time until he fully mastered the essence of his Way.

When Shi [Quan-shi] was on a journey to the Western Regions, the Master traveled to the ancient capital of Youdu and stayed at Qingshou Monastery. It was the Renxu year of the Hongwu era. At that time, Du’an Yan arrived and took charge of the monastery’s affairs;
he regarded the Master as a younger son, and together they vigorously propagated the fundamental tenets of Linji, finding great mutual affinity. This was the Gengwu year.

The Master was instructed to depart. He paid homage to Emperor Xian of the Emei [dynasty] and was commissioned to ascend the throne at Daisui Temple in Pengzhou, where he offered the fragrant incense for Quanshi.
He resided there for seven years, during which his Dharma assembly flourished greatly. In the Renchen year of the Yongle era, by special imperial decree, he was appointed to lead Longquan Temple.
Holding high the seal of the patriarchs, he examined and discerned those who came before him; his every word transcended the realm of forms and signs. He had always delighted in...
He provided relief to the poor and distressed, diminished his own needs while enriching others, and was skilled at guiding sentient beings.

In the ninth month of the Wushen year of the Xuande era, he sat upright without illness and passed away in silence within the Vajra Chamber of the Tuiqu (Retreat) Cloister. After cremation, more than a hundred śarīras were obtained;
his disciples then erected a stupa to enshrine them.
Chan Master Zufa Liang Liaoduan of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jianyan Yue Tangyan. He was a native of the Lu clan from Ning County in Siming.

At the age of fourteen, he received the tonsure under Yue Tangyan at Jianshan Monastery in Kunshan. He received the full precepts at Wutai in Ning County and subsequently returned to serve [his master].
Wu Xianyi attained a high level of mastery in the art of ritual offerings and adornments.

In the *bingchen* year of the Hongwu era, he served as the secretary (*jishi*) to Fuxin while the latter resided at Linggu and Tianjie monasteries. Mu’an Kang Shuzhong and Mukan Cong were both his friends beyond their years.
Later, he emerged from seclusion to serve as abbot at Guangxiao in Tiantai, followed by appointments at Zituo, Mayu, Jingshan, and Putuo in Mingzhou.

In the late era of the Nengren Monastery in Yue, he presided over Jingci. During the Ren-shen year, when Jingci was afflicted by the planet Venus (Mars), the Master was presented with a new set of *kāṣāya* robes and an alms bowl by the newly installed Prince of Shu.
In the Bing-xu year of the Yongle era, the imperial court summoned the Master to serve as the General Director of the Buddhist Teachings.

Upon his return, he built a residence by the lakeshore called the Lotus Flower Dwelling (*Liánhuājū*). In the Ding-hai year, he traveled to the capital at the summons for official business; the Emperor ordered him to reside there.
At Wuguosi on Mount Wutai, before he had even ascended the steps of the hall, he suddenly said to those around him, "My worldly karmic ties have nearly come to an end.
Three days later, he bathed, changed his robes, sat in the full lotus position, and passed away. This was on the third day of the seventh month in the year of Jichou (1629).

He was buried at the foot of the Lotus Flower Abode (Ōkua-kyo). His secular age was sixty-four, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was fifty. His *Yi-yu-lu* (Record of Unrestrained Sayings) exists in circulation.
The World-Honored One.
Chan Master Wuben Wenkeng of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Daode of Daochang. He was the son of the Xie family of Dinghai in Siming. At the age of ten...
4. He left his home village for Wutai Temple, where he shaved his head, donned the dyed robes, and studied the Vinaya.
Hearing that Gufeng was flourishing in his teachings at Baoning, he went there to pay his respects. Gufeng asked, "I have heard you have composed verses on the 'Ten Oxherding Pictures' of Liangshan;
try reciting them. As the Master prepared to respond, Gufeng suddenly covered his mouth and said, "Where is the ox? The Master replied, "I have already trampled upon your Reverence's crops."

Feng said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master covered his ears and departed. Feng marveled at this and appointed him as an attendant. At that time, Zhongfang Lun was living in retirement at the New Hermitage to the right of the temple.
The Master went back and forth there to resolve his doubts and refine his understanding. In the *bingwu* year of the Zhengtong era (1356), he began teaching the Dharma at Jueyan in Gusu.
During the Hongwu period, the Jingle Yuan in Yixing requested that the Master change his method from lecture-style teaching to Chan practice. Not long after, an imperial edict arrived.

He relocated Jingshan to the east of Xiaoling and bestowed upon it the name Linggu. By imperial decree, Wuwai Xi was appointed as the abbot, and the Master was ordered to occupy the first seat to serve as a model for the assembly.
In the year Yihai, he succeeded to the abbacy of Lingyin, where he resided for five years.

In the spring of the Ji-mao year of the Jianwen era, he manifested a slight illness; when Hong Hou visited him at his chamber, the Master was experiencing labored breathing. Hong remarked, "Zhaozhou..."
"The Way. While all people are driven by the twelve double-hours, this old monk makes use of the twelve double-hours.
How about you, Master? The Master straightened his body and said, "What do you call the 'twelve double-hours'? Hong said, "But what can one do about the urgency of the breath?
The Master let out a thunderous shout. He asked those nearby, "What is today's date? They replied, "The twenty-seventh day of the second month."
He then sought out a brush and wrote a verse, saying: "I am seventy-five years old; regarding nirvana and birth-and-death, I do not fall into empty space.

Turning over on my back, I lean against that which flies hither. He then cast the brush aside and passed away peacefully. At his cremation, his cranial bone remained indestructible, and the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting.
His disciples, including Zongyan and others, collected the remains that had not been consumed by fire and enshrined them in a stupa at Shuanggui Monastery.
The distribution of nails and hair; interred at Jingle.
*Xudeng Zhengtong*, Volume Fifteen;
*Xudeng Zhengtong*, Volume Sixteen.
Compiled by the Chan monk Xingtong of Western Sichuan, a successor in the lineage of Nanhua Putuo,
of the twenty-fourth generation under Dajian of the Linji school.

Chan Master Yuanqin of Erang, a successor of Chan Master Miaoxian of Xia'an, was a native of Xiushui in Heshui. He traveled extensively to consult various masters but attained no realization whatsoever.
Upon entering the Western Capital, he visited Xia'an at a lodging house. Xia'an asked him, "There is a clever person in Zhejiang; have you seen him?"
The Master said, "Yuanqin is a dull-witted fellow. Yuan'an said, "I want a dull-witted fellow to serve as my supervisor and storekeeper; do you understand? The Master was at a loss.
Yuan'an said, "It is a pity that you have come from thousands of miles away only to miss this opportunity. Thereupon, the Master began to practice with intense diligence.
One day, seeing a rat pass over a shelf and overturn an oil jar, he suddenly attained full realization. He rushed to see Yuan'an and said, "I have already..."
"He has been caught! Master An grabbed him and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master replied, "A single pellet of mouse droppings has defiled the soup in the cauldron.
Master An said, "You blind fellow! Go to the meditation hall. From the Jia-wu year of the Chenghua era, the Master resided at Eyang for over forty years.

His feet never crossed the threshold of his quarters. The venerable masters of the four directions held his conduct in high esteem. The Master single-mindedly rejected all worldly affairs, striving to emulate the character of Fenzhou and Fengguo.
Finally, when Zhiyou came to seek instruction, the Master applied the authentic hammer and tongs of his lineage to him.
Only after ensuring that [the student] had deeply penetrated the innermost recesses did he first transmit the Great Dharma.
Chan Master Jie’an Zhengying of Linggu Monastery in Jinling was a successor of Chan Master Xiang of Linggu; he was a native of Jinxī and succeeded to the vacant seat at Kaiyuan Monastery in Quanzhou.

Tanhua received the appointment as abbot. Following the imperial decree, he entered the monastery on the sixth day of the sixth month of the Wuyin year and ascended the hall to open the dharma assembly.

A monk asked about the commencement of the dharma feast and the presence of the fourfold assembly: "How does one repay the Imperial Grace and the Buddha’s Grace? The Master said: "The spring of ambrosia opens up and flows across the great earth.

Regarding the Master's single phrase for repaying his own debt of gratitude, [the monk] asked: "The Master has pointed out the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West; how shall it be proclaimed? The Master said: [He remained silent.]
"A stone pagoda before the courtyard soars into the cold void. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then the entire world has never been hidden.
The Master asked, "What do you see? He replied, "I truly do not dare to deceive myself. The Master said, "Your eyesight is quite dim.
[The monk] asked, "What is the Master’s one phrase for benefiting others? The Master said, "A rabbit-horn staff picks up the moon in the heavens; a tortoise-hair whisk..."
He dispersed the clouds along the seashore and said, "If that is so, then humans and devas shall all rejoice, and the four seas will return to benevolence. The Master said, "First, shut your mouths!
He then continued, "Recently, I was honored by the Imperial Decree with the four characters 'Pure Mind and Clean Self,' by which I was commanded to reside at this monastery.
Do you all understand the Sage’s intent? These very four characters are the transmission of the Buddha’s mind-seal; they are the seal of stabilization."

The Bright Pearl of the Ocean. This mountain monk has come from the south specifically to bring this forth and bestow it universally upon the great assembly. You must know that worldly dharmas and Buddha-dharmas are one:
the setting clouds and the solitary wild goose fly together; the Buddhas of antiquity and the Buddhas of today share the same hue as the autumn waters and the vast expanse of heaven.

The mind of Heaven is unfathomable; as the mountains grow ever higher, the ocean grows ever deeper. The words of the Sage are inexhaustible; Heaven spreads its vast canopy and Earth spreads its broad support for all people.
Do you understand? Is it not that one remains unstained by the dust of the world? Is it not that one does not crave the flavor of the Dharma?
"Mo! Is it not that you do not drink the wine of non-action, nor sit upon the bed of Nirvana? If you understand it in this way, it is not that what is not is not; rather, what is is not.
Today, I dare not keep this hidden for long, but shall point it out directly before you for all of you.
He then took up his staff, struck the ground once, and said: "The wooden man dances out before the Dharma Hall; let it be as it may."

In the Yantian era, white snow flew; when the Master arrived, all that had fallen into ruin was restored. In the Renwu year of the Yongle period, upon his return from the imperial court, the various mountain monasteries unanimously appointed him to reside at Xuefeng in Fuzhou.
The flourishing of his Dharma path was no less than that of Zhenguang (Zhenjue). In the Jiachen year of the Hongxi period, by imperial decree, he resided at Linggu Monastery in Nanjing.
He passed away in the first year of the Xuande period. His recorded sayings exist, and his name is inscribed in the *Gujing* (The Ancient Mirror), volume three.
[He] practiced in the world.
Chan Master Liming Lizhong Cheng of Puming Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Jingci Lian;
he was the son of the Sun family of Qiantang. At the age of thirteen, he entered the service of [Master Jingci].
Guangruo left home to become a monk and first visited Zu Fang. Inside Fang’s quarters, Fang raised the koan regarding the story of the mountain being burned by fire in the twelfth lunar month.
The Master presented a verse, saying: "The white clouds obscure his former tracks; In the twelfth month, the mountain-burning fire is bright red.
Suddenly, the breeze of compassion fans it forth; Where it was cold and icy, it is now warm and glowing. Fang held him in high esteem. Later, at Beiguo, he established Puguang Temple.
Ming Temple. In order to receive those coming from afar, he did not remain long before requesting to return to Ciguang.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of the *Xinyou* year of the *Zhengtong* era, he ascended the hall. "This year I am eighty-one years old; old and ill, I follow conditions and pass the days.
This year I shall record the events of next year; next year I shall record the events of this very morning. When the *Guihai* year arrived, he passed away as scheduled at the age of eighty.
13. His cremated relics were beyond counting, and a stupa was erected at Puming.
Chan Master Zhaoyuan Zongjing of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou Prefecture was styled the Elder Tianxuan; he was the son of the Gao family of the prefecture.
Having tonsured himself at his home mountain from childhood, the Master remained there for a long time under the leadership of the late Zufa, by whom he was granted the imperial decree.
He subsequently took charge of the library keys. In the *Xinmao* year of the Yongle era, he was selected by appointment to reside at Huguo Temple; he later moved to Xuedou.

In the *Yichou* year of the Zhengtong era, the Director of Monks (Senglü) nominated him to fill the vacant seat at Jingci Temple. In the *Dingmao* year, the Imperial Court bestowed upon him the title of "Da... [Great...].

Master Zang went to the palace to express his gratitude for the imperial favor and resided at Mida Temple. There he manifested a slight illness and said to those around him, "My karmic conditions have come to an end.
He bathed, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away peacefully. His secular age was seventy-six and his monastic seniority sixty years.
He was interred in a stupa on the ancestral mound of Ouhua.
Chan Master Wunian Zhiyou of Shouzhou, the twenty-fifth generation successor under Dajian and the dharma heir of Chan Master Eryang Qin,
was a native of Hanzhou in Shu. Setting out for the south, he traveled to Siming.

He ascended Mount Tianmu. Later, he studied under Xuefeng Yicun and Nanquan Puyuan. Nanquan asked him, "Where have you been traveling? The Master replied, "The South. Nanquan asked, "How are the Buddha-dharma there?
The Master said, "The mountains and rivers are no different. Nanquan asked, "What is my hand like compared to the Buddha’s hand?"

The Master remained silent for a long while, then looked up and said, "Do not say there is no difference. Later, upon examining the karmic occasion of Xinghua striking the *vīnā* (chant leader), he attained a vast and great awakening.
He composed a verse, saying: Xinghua strikes the *vīnā*; On level ground, one meets calamity.

Last night, the clouds of South Mountain Flew toward the peaks of North Mountain. Yang saw this and expressed his joy on his behalf, saying, "You have not come here in vain. This was during the Jiajing era.
First: Chan Master Wunian You, the twenty-sixth generation successor under Dajian, propagated the teachings in Shouzhou for thirteen years before passing away.
He was a dharma heir of [the aforementioned master].
Chan Master Jingshan Huibao was a native of Zhugong. While traveling through Shouzhou, he went to visit Wunian. Wunian asked, "You have bypassed the counties to travel to the prefectures;
for what purpose, ultimately, do you come? The Master replied, "Regarding the great matter of birth and death, I seek the Master’s guidance to deliver me.
Wunian asked, "Are you a person from Jingzhou? The Master said, "I am. Wunian asked, "Where is the *ācārya* right now? The Master was about to—
Dajian Huaihai replied, "Yes. Guishan Yuanian said, "If it were simply like that, there would still be some slight difference. The Buddha-dharma is not something to be reached through deliberation;
go to the meditation hall. From then on, Huaihai applied himself deeply under his guidance. One day, Yuanian called out, "Disciple! Huaihai responded. Yuanian asked, "Where are you?
At these words, Huaihai attained realization of the fundamental meaning. He then said, "The Master’s great compassion is truly that of a teacher of devas and humans."
Reflecting on his passing into *nirvāṇa*: in the thirty-seventh year of the Jiajing era, the Master entrusted the Dharma to the Venerable Tierniu Yuan, who retired to Zhongnan Mountain;
he was the twenty-seventh generation descendant of Dajian.
Chan Master Tien-niu De-yuan of Qinling was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jing-shan Bao.
Having realized the seal of his mind under Jing-shan, he later lived as a hermit in the Qinling Mountains.
One day, wearing red cloth trousers and a bamboo hat, he was wielding a hoe in the earth when Chao-yang came to visit him and said, "This fellow..."
He appeared like a soldier. The Master said, "Watch the arrow! Yang made a gesture as if dodging the arrow, and the Master approached him, took his hand, and walked with him.
Upon reaching a hermitage, the Master said, "I am a descendant of Jing-shan; I have been waiting for you here for several decades.
Now that you have come, you must seek out someone to revitalize the ancestral Way. He stayed there for three months and was given this verse: "Follow..."
The body can strike and plunder; splitting the arrowhead, one skillfully seizes the nest. The Three Mysteries emerge from this; the Three Essentials are not many.
With the probing pole and shadow-grass, host and guest are distinguished; when the lion loses its tracks, what can be done about me?
Chan Master Lianchi of Chaoyang, of Xizhou Prefecture, a successor in the twenty-eighth generation under National Teacher Daquan,
was the son of the Fan family of that prefecture; he was a descendant of the former Prefect Fan.
This is the "Afterword to Ma. When he was young, he lived beneath the trees. One day, a monk visited but did not meet him; consequently, he inscribed a couplet on the wall that read:
"Amitābha Buddha is idle; Recitation is busy. In every thought one attains Buddhahood; Without thought, there is nothing.
Without even 'nothing,' there is no twisting of the nostrils. The Supreme Vehicle of Chan: Meditate in the morning, meditate in the evening. Meditate until you reach Chan."

"Stillness is also stillness; inquiry is also stillness; even stillness itself is stillness. When the Master saw this monk split open the gateway of his face, he was suddenly weary of the world and went forth to shave his head and join him.

However, that monk had already departed. Thereupon, the Master took up his staff and alms bowl and traveled south, undergoing myriad forms of hardship and toil, taking only this couplet as his theme for constant mindfulness.
After a long time, on the road at Luojia, the Master encountered a monk of magnificent bearing and extraordinary appearance. The Master...
Previously, when he slipped and uttered one recitation of the Buddha’s name, the monk said, "This is a door-knocking tile;

what use is it to him? The Master then asked, "What is it like after it has been cast away? The monk replied, "Leaves fall and return to the root; when they come back, there are no words. Only then did the Master achieve sudden enlightenment.

He subsequently traveled to the assembly at Shaolin, where he attained a profound realization through wordless silence. Nevertheless, the Master harbored a deep longing for the dharma-lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Carrying this burden was no easy task; he ultimately would not consent [to remain]. He eventually entered Guanzhong and crossed the Qinling Mountains, where he received the instruction of Tianniu (the words of which are recorded in the "Chapter on Tianniu").
Returning from Emei to Xizhou, he resided at Chaoyang Cave on Mount Zhuti in that prefecture for twenty years.
When Juyun came to attend upon him, he asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? Yun immediately folded his hands and said, "Please..."
The Master [Yunmen] was held in high esteem. Again, someone asked, "If one does not use voice or physical form, what shall one call the person of original nature?
Yunmen immediately stepped out and ordered a monk to go and investigate the one right there. The monk said, "As for the one right there, what is it that he investigates?
The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows. Furthermore, he accepted an invitation from a presiding seat-master; upon arriving at the sacrificial altar, he pointed to the altar and asked, "This..."
"What place is this? The master replied, "The Northern Altar. The Master said, "I have long heard that the Northern Altar is originally located here," at which the host was at a loss for words.
On the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month of the eleventh year of the Chongzhen era, he passed away while sitting upright.
The Master was sixty-six years of age; his entire body was enshrined in a stupa beside the cave.

Chan Master Chungju Chuyun Chwi-man Kwang-jin, the twenty-ninth generation successor under National Teacher Cho-yang Chi of the lineage of Da-gan, was a native of Yi-bin in Sungju. His secular surname was Li. His ancestors...
For three lifetimes he was a brāhmaṇa. His father had no heir; he prayed to the Buddha, and [the boy] was born. On the day the spirit descended, eight great beings visited his house.
One of them pointed and said to the father, "These are the Eight Precious Arhats appearing in the world.
The mother immediately renounced meat and ate only vegetarian food. After three years she weaned him. When he reached the age of fifteen, he sat by the window reading with his fellow students.
Record: While casually gazing at chrysanthemums, I sighed and said: "These flowers wither this year and will bloom again next spring.

I have often heard that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift. Even one who studies the classics cannot avoid birth and death. Ultimately, I abandoned my studies and went to Mount Shaoye to attend upon Master Hao.
After a long time, I returned to my hometown, where I obtained the records of Dahui and acquired the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; it was as if I were encountering old possessions once more.

Second: He gave forty-three formal sermons. Birth and death are but a fleeting moment; there is nothing with which to compare them.

Coming and going—what relevance do they have? This old monk speaks with direct sincerity: let those who doubt, doubt; let those who believe, believe; let those who practice, practice. Even so, one must not let this pass unexamined.
*Ei!* With these words, he cast down his brush and passed away peacefully. During the cremation, his teeth and jaw remained intact.

Chan Master Gaodeng of San Kong Temple on Liangshan was the son of the Zheng family from Pengzhou.

He entrusted [his body] to the waterside, and having finished speaking, he passed away.

Fully releasing and fully gathering, one accords with the Sole Honored One. At sunrise in the hour of the Rabbit, who cares whether others are ugly or beautiful? Facing the current, one flows freely and expansively, transcending high and low.
Leaning on a staff, one wanders at ease, following whatever is clumsy or clever. There is neither sorrow nor vexation; from the beginning, it has been just one old man and one [old woman].
Ageless. If someone asks me about the school from the West, when hungry I eat my meal; when cold, I add a layer of clothing.

At the hour of eating, I seek neither comfort nor satiety, nor do I seek glory. Letting go of all conditions, there is not a single thing remaining. The great earth, mountains, and rivers are swallowed in a single gulp.
Quelling the weariness of poverty; green waters and blue mountains enter the eye as mere dust. Ten fingers on two hands—look at him, he is no ordinary man.
At the hour of Youzhong (9–11 a.m.), touching his own nose, there is nothing to do.

Hindering frequent play, the Great Garuda enters the sea and the old dragon is startled; silently and without cause, he beats his two wings.
At noon in the southland, after the third watch has struck, the moonlight pours forth. A red wheel encircles the earth as it emerges from the South Sea, startling Master Caoshan awake.

it is like Xie Sanlang on his fishing boat. This was originally that tiger of Xuansha. Before noon has passed, the wine of Cao Shan never intoxicates;
having drunk three cups or two goblets, he breaks through the city of sorrow and sleeps soundly with legs outstretched. He stands out from his kind and rises above his peers. Thus is the Way.
The person is neither base nor noble; they win the spring light as they pass every fleeting moment. From the beginning, all the Sages have had no fixed station.
At the hour of *shen* (the seventh watch), an old man from the smokeless fields comes carrying firewood. Upon arriving home, he does not inquire about the price of rice in Linling.
There is no tea in the pot, yet there is resentment in his mouth. Having understood the treasure beneath the robe, the pupils of the eyes are the people before one. Facing the bustling marketplace...
His reputation for being a great recluse flows far and wide; at the tip of his fishing pole, he is accustomed to catching red-scaled fish.

When the sun enters the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), do you know the path down the slope? What will happen when the sun rises tomorrow? As before, three times three is still nine. The Elephant King roars the lion’s roar;
foxes, wolves, and jackals have nowhere to run. Today, as he stands face-to-face, he lets it all slip out: the tongue was originally not...

Exiting at dusk during the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m.). Sitting alone in a thatched hut, it is superior to a stone chamber; quietly contemplating the lame Sumeru Mountain, one laughs at Changfang’s art of traveling a thousand li.
Forgetting the year and not recording the day, I know only that from a single dung-stick, a thousand sages emerge.

Too lazy to descend from my meditation seat, I am scolded by others; even Mañjuśrī once suffered censure and rebuke. At nightfall during the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.), though the wooden gate is set, [it remains open].
There is neither internal nor external. Calling out to a servant for fire, he used the moon as a lamp. Its light shone through clearly before his single mat, where there was no bedding or cover.

Joy turns to sorrow; is misfortune turned to prosperity? Bamboo and trees strike one another, giving rise to ten thousand sounds. On the path of Caoxi, few people travel. If you are a connoisseur of sound, you still will not understand.
At the hour of Zi in the middle of the night, he attained enlightenment upon seeing the morning star and established the fundamental principle. How vexing that Yunmen’s staff fell [upon him]!
Come! To this day, what benefit has been gained from your failures? The mountain is the mountain; the water is the water. Meeting the straight, encountering the curved—there is no "this" or "that.
The Dharma robes have been transmitted through three dynasties and six generations; who dares to compare them to the five petals of a single flower?
Chan Master Banya Dengeu of the Bamboo Hermitage in Yusam, Chungju, was the son of the Ro clan of that district. In his youth, he enrolled in the local school.
Later, when Cheongchung began to propagate the teachings at Yusam, the Master attended him for many years. Not long after, his wife passed away, and he too shaved his head.
One day, while [Master] Chung was ascending the hall at Chongseong, the Master stepped forward and asked: "What is this 'nine-layered iron drum'?"
A single arrow pierced through it. Zhong said, "The drum, eh? The Master made a gesture as if presenting something. Zhong said, "Pierced! Pierced! The Master then prostrated himself.
He subsequently built a hermitage to the south of Mount Yushan; after several years, he further established the Nine Peaks Monastery.
Chan Master Yeunbeon Dyeongyeong of Niusu Unyeon in Chungju was the son of the Ran family of Pyeongneung.

At fifteen, while reading the *Record of Grand Master Dahui*, he reached the koan of the bamboo stick and gave rise to doubt.

In the year Jia-wu, he went to visit Master Sanshan at Chongsheng Temple to investigate the koan "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? along with the koan of the bamboo stick, from the springtime onward.

During the summer retreat, he was as if intoxicated and then as if awakened. When Fenzhou Zhong went south of the Yangtze River, the Master was able to attend upon him morning and evening for consultation.
One mid-autumn evening, while serving tea with two monks, the lid of the teapot happened to fall to the ground; suddenly, the continuity between past and future was severed. He ran to see Zhong.

Zhong questioned him regarding the story of the old woman who burned the hermitage. The Master’s response was slightly delayed. Zhong said, "Not yet. Although you have attained something here, you are still unable to let it go.

The Master attained sudden enlightenment; everything he had previously acquired was instantly purified and exhausted. He went to consult Zhong, who presented several cryptic and erroneous cases;
