There, Jing requested that Yu compose an inscription for his master’s stupa. Yu asked, "Did the Master first see the iron ox, or did he first see the cow?
Jing replied, "My late master personally saw Yangshan come. Yu laughed and said, "I shall try to sketch this out for you."
Chan Master Xiling of the West White Void Valley at Mount Jing in Hangzhou Prefecture was a native of the He family of Yiwu.
At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head at Zishou Monastery in Dongyang. After receiving the full precepts, he went to Shuanglin to visit Xuzhou Yuan.

Subsequently, he relied upon Dongsou Ying at Jingci Monastery, where he served as the head of the inner records (*neiji*). When Shilin took over the abbacy, the Master served as the attendant (*shizhe*). One day...
He went to visit Xueyan at Beijian. Xueyan brought up the karmic cause and condition of Huanglong seeing Ciming to interrogate him;
his responses were perfectly in accord with the truth, and Xueyan approved. When Xueyan moved to Dayang, he invited the Master to occupy the First Seat. One day, Xueyan asked:
"When Linji was at Huangbo, he received sixty blows of the staff three times. Why did he go to Daoyu’s ribs [to seek the meaning]?"
He clenched his fists. The Master said, "You are killing people with your dullness. Yunyan then struck him. The Master shook out his sleeves and departed.
In the *Ciyuan* year (1266), as Yunyan was about to pass away, he patted the Master's shoulder and said, "I entrust this burden to you.

The Master replied, "In the end, I shall not be buried alive here. Not long after, Yunyan passed away. The assembly followed by requesting the Master to succeed him on the seat. He frequently offered three phrases for instruction.
Yan Lai-xue said: "Set aside the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings for a moment; bring forth a single phrase from within the mouth of a shrimp.
When the dog hears the sound of 'wa,' why does it bite through the pillar in front of the Dharma Hall?
When the otter at Jing Bridge swallows Jiyun Peak, what is this? What level of capacity is this? While traveling on pilgrimage, Tieguan Shu once questioned the Master. It happened that...
A small-scale *sanhui* (sermon) on the Winter Solstice. The Master cited the anecdote concerning Yunmen’s “millet cake. Guankuan presented four verses as an offering.
The Master asked, “Who are you? Guankuan replied, “I am Upāsaka Shu. The Master asked, “Where have you come from? Guankuan replied, “From Yunmen. The Master said:
"You are demented; you are mad," [Zhao]guan said. Guanyou replied, "Where are the eyes of the Master? The Master then shouted. Guan also shouted. The Master struck out a fist.
Guan stepped forward, met him, and said, "Setting aside the blow for a moment, what is the meaning of the 'Yunmen cake'?
The Master flung his hand and snatched away Guan's hat. Guan said, "Wrong. The Master struck several more punches. Guan said, "Fists!"

"His head has no eyes; later he will be scrutinized by others. The Master went to the gate, stepped on the seven-fold robe (kaṣāya) so it fell to the ground, and struck him across the waist with several blows, saying, "I shall let you know my methods. Guan said, "An unjust blow! An unjust blow!
The Master called out loudly, "Head cook, lock this fellow up and send him to the storehouse! During a year of famine, the Master always shared his food with the assembly.
One day, while conversing with a guest, it passed the middle of the night. Overcome by hunger, the attendant requested that he take a spoonful of grain to make a meal.
The Master said, "It must not be so. How could the permanent property of the monastery be used privately by its abbot?

In the year *Bingchen* of the *Yanyou* era, the provincial government submitted a petition to the imperial court, inviting the Master to preside over Mount Jing. A monk asked: "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended."
"The future mind cannot be apprehended. What does this mean? The Master said, "One does not give a gift to one's own kin.

In his youth, the Master once dreamed of wandering through the Arhat Hall of Jingci Monastery. Upon reaching the southeastern corner, he suddenly saw a venerable elder pointing to a poem between the lintels and beams, which read:
"A single chamber, vast and silent, opens at the summit; Several peaks are like paintings, their blue hue mingling with the moss. In ordinary moments, [the wind] turns..."
He discarded the *pātra* leaves and personally tailored his own hundred-seam *kāṣāya*. Initially, the Master did not understand this;

however, when he moved from Mount Yangshan to Mount Shuangjing, it was only then that he realized Mount Yangshan possessed the *pātra* leaf sutras and Mount Jing possessed the Yangqi robe. That one appeared at one place and the other at another was entirely predetermined.
Previously, the Emperor Shizu had summoned him for an audience to preach the Dharma, and as his discourse met with the Emperor's approval, he was granted the title "Fujian" (Buddha-Mirror).
During the Dade era, the Chan Master was further bestowed with the title Dayuan. Upon becoming the abbot of Mount Jing, Emperor Renzong conferred upon him the honorary title Huizhao Dabian.
On the twelfth day of the fourth month in the Renxu year of the Zhizhi era (1322), he wrote a final testament by hand to entrust his protection to lay patrons and exhorted his disciples.
He spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly and passed away in the Budong Xuan Hall. His entire body was interred in the Chángpú Field. He was seventy-six years of age at the time of his death.
He was fifty-seven years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*). His *Baoyan ji* (Collected Works on Waterfall Rock) and his *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) were circulated in the world.

Chan Master Tianyin Muchuan Yuanzhi of Nengren Monastery in Jianchang Prefecture was a native of the Yao family of Gaoyang. Both his father and elder brother were former advanced scholars (*qianjinshi*).
The Master aspired to the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). In the year Jiayu of the Xianchun era, at the age of nineteen, he entered the community under Hui... of Yangshan.
Langshan served [his teacher] diligently for several years. During the Yuanyuanzhen era, he went to reside at Nengren Temple; after two years, he departed.
His collected works, the *Mushen ji* (Collection of Pastoral Seclusion), contains a preface to the departure of Master Miaozhi for Zhejiang, which states in brief:

"In the past, when Master Yue of Longan was already leading the assembly at Dongshan, he still considered his own realization of the Way to be incomplete. He further concealed his name and went out into seclusion."
He sought him out amidst meals, drinks, laughter, and conversation;

upon hearing a single extraordinary word from Master Su, he humbled himself and lowered his status, approaching with the decorum of one seeking counsel, not begrudging the slight to his own reputation, and was ultimately able, within the span of a brief discussion, to...
Thus he obtained all that he desired for the rest of his life. It was not merely that the Way of Yun’an relied on him so as not to fall into decline;
had Master Su not relied on Yue to manifest himself to the world, the world would likewise have never known what kind of person he was.
For fame is the outward manifestation of the Way. In antiquity, when people possessed its manifestation, they sought its reality to respond to it; yet nowadays—
Scholars, on the contrary, use outward appearances to harm the reality. Once they occupy a certain name, the power of their exalted status becomes so haughty that it can no longer be bent.
Even if they inwardly measure themselves and find it unsatisfactory, how could they possibly debase their minds to seek what they have not yet attained? Alas!
This is why the present differs from the past, and why the Way has declined. And so forth. He passed away in the Great Virtue year of Wuxu.
At Mount Lu, his worldly lifespan was forty-three years.
In the twenty-fourth year of the Zhiyuan era, Iron Mountain Qiong, the Chan Master of Cihua in Yuanzhou, left home at the age of eighteen. He first studied under Xueyan at Dayang.
One day, in the meditation hall, Xueyan raised the karmic cause-and-effect story of Prince Yeta, who offered his bones back to his father and his flesh back to his mother.
Having attained realization, he composed a verse: "A single blade of grass manifests a jade tower; I have discerned the idle topic of past and present.
Lifting up the moon atop Mount Jiyun, I toss it before people like a hundred-flower ball.
Upon the passing of Zhizhi, he went to visit Dongyan. Dongyan asked, "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. How do you understand this? The Master replied, "Embracing..."

He cried out in indignation. Dong said, "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not an object. What is it? The Master replied, "A falcon bursting forth from between the brows, soaring toward the vast heavens.
He then visited Mount Meng, where the Master of the mountain invited him to share the seat. Entering the hall, he said, "Winter is at the beginning of the month."
Selling the quilt to buy the ox; at the end of the winter month, selling the ox to buy the quilt. [The Master] strikes his staff: "Here there is no tail and no head;
midway, all is brought to rest. Walking, rest and rest; sitting, rest and rest; staying, rest and rest; lying down, rest and rest.
When the eyes of sleep are opened wide, the five clouds manifest their auspiciousness. Radiant wind and clear moon pervade everywhere. The plum blossoms on the withered branch."
At the ancient ferry crossing, the faint fragrance occasionally drifts before the wind. Although one has reached this point, the path that goes beyond is ten thousand *li* from Yaizhou.
How can this be seen? Leaning on my staff, I say: "Enough, enough. Later, he passed away and was interred in a stupa behind the Avalokiteśvara Pavilion (Qiong succeeded Dianshan Yi;
this entry was mistakenly listed here).
One day, Chan Master Fangshan Bao of Ruiyan in Taizhou Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Lun of Jingci, hung up the notice for a private interview with the assembly. He posed this koan:
"When Nanquan slew the cat, what was it like? The assembly offered various responses, but none were in accord with the truth. At that moment, there happened to be a servant present.
A bystander remarked, “The rat has become the master. The Master said, “What a clever turn of phrase! It is simply that it ought not to have come from your mouth.
He then presented the verse on Non-seeing: “When a man of the Way succeeds in leaving the mountains, He opens his entire heart and mind to me.
It is level and even like the surface of a mirror, Clear, profound, and utterly free of even a speck of dust. Suddenly, he attains this...”
A phrase for turning back: Rolling up his patchwork robe through the cold clouds, he returns at once. At the Eighty-thousand-fathom Flower-Crested Peak, a single laugh shatters the iron mask.
Once he has reached his home mountain, all discursive thought ceases; he snaps a withered vine to prop open the bamboo gate.
Within the hearth of dung-fire, the news is good: the fragrance of the taro is the very fragrance of the Way.
Master Juexiangjian of □□ Prefecture cites the story of Dongshan’s illness and offers this verse: "The path to Dongshan leads through Yunyan;
At the point of severance, it is difficult for those to reach it who must pass through. Only when the living eye opens at the tip of the staff Can one proceed."
Only then do you know there is not a single hair’s breadth of separation. Addressing the assembly, he raised the case of Touzi asking a monk:
"It has rained well for several days; tell me, from where does the rain come? The monk had no reply. Later, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he attained realization and composed this verse:

"Travelers on the road vie with one another to gather the fragrant blossoms, Unaware that beneath their eyes the springtime passes by. Last night, a sudden shower of falling petals— One [verse missing]."
The flowing waters of the hundred and ten cities are fragrant.
[Regarding] the case of Master Yongzong Ben of Fu[zhou] citing the story of Jia Shan’s study under Chuanzi, he offered this verse:
"Laughing, he abandoned Zhulin Temple; I thought there was so much at Huating. He exhausted his very life beneath the oar."
Regarding the funeral: it appears that success or failure rests with Xiao He.
[The Master] cites the karmic conditions concerning Elder Fu’s “Sacred Arrow” from the [Xuanhe] Shengfu Bamboo-Hut Chan Master. The verse says:
"Green braids double-rein the jade-colored steed as it neighs; A pale white spring robe is girdled by a green sash.

Returning at midnight beneath the blossoming moon, The golden whip strikes down a flight of scattered red petals. It is also said: "The nine-layered city is not far at all; Arrows shot through its many walls are more than enough.
Suddenly encountering the place surrounded by three armies, There is clearly a path leading straight to the heavens. [He] raised [the verse].
The Case of Linji Visiting Pingtian. The Verse says: "The path before one's eyes is as level as a whetstone;
Why not stride along with dignified ease? Provoking the old woman, her ox-nature flares up; To stand bare-chested and receive blows—how pitiable!"

Chan Master Dongyan Jingri of Tiantong in Ningbo Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Tiantong Hui. He was the son of the Liao family from Duchang in Nankang. From childhood, he abstained from meat and pungent roots.
At fifteen, he received the tonsure at Xianglin on Mount Lu. He first visited Changyang and Shishuang, and subsequently traveled to Zhejiang to seek instruction.
Chijue did not find accord [with his teacher]. He went to Mount Jing to see Wuzhun, who held him in high esteem. Later, he visited Xiyuan Hui at Tiantong;

the latter’s instructions were entirely based on those of Wuzhun, and Chijue subsequently attained a secret realization of their essential meaning. Wuzhun appointed him as the Keeper of the Storehouse (Librarian).
Subsequently, he served as the First Seat under Wuwen Can of Kaixian, from which point his reputation grew daily more prominent. During the Jingding era, he went forth to preside over Yuan Tong.
He succeeded to the abbacy of Donglin. In the *Renchen* year of the Zhizhi era (1292), he was transferred to Yuyang. Not long after, he retired to live in seclusion at Xuedou.

In the *Gengzi* year of the Dade era (1300), he presided over Tiantong. The Master was born in the *Xinsi* year of the Jiaoding era of the Song dynasty (1221) and passed away in the *Wushen* year of the Zhida era of the Yuan dynasty (1308).
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he wrote a verse, saying: "Heaven is the canopy and earth is the casket; what need have I for a stupa or a lid? I shall reduce my body to ashes..."
"His bones shall become mountains and rivers; once my words have been spoken as arrows, do not engrave them further. Two days later, he bathed, sat upright, and passed away.
Upon his cremation, the roots of his teeth remained uncorrupted. He was interred in Qingfengwu on the western cliff. He was eighty-eight years of age and seventy-one years since his ordination.

Chan Master Yuetting Chung of Mount Jiangshan in Jiangning Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Yuan of Wuxue, recounted a monk’s question to Baiyun: "The old year has passed and the new year has arrived;
what is the meaning of non-transmigration? Baiyun replied, "The eyebrows are above the eyes. The verse says: Fallen leaves...
Already followed the flowing water away; the spring breeze has not yet released the hundred flowers into bloom.

The face of the green mountain remains as it was, spread out all day long facing the setting sun. Regarding Mañjuśrī’s three instances of spending the summer retreat and Kāśyapa’s striking the gavel to propose his expulsion, the verse says:
The young lord in brocade robes is accustomed to wandering in spring; The beautiful lady with white hair harbors much resentment. He is wealthy...

Even a thousand mouths are still too few; being poor oneself, what can one do for this single body? [The Master] raised the story of Ciming’s winter notice posted for the assembly and offered this verse:
Above the painting, below the painting; shortening it, lengthening it. Clearly revealed, broadly deliberated.
How does this compare to the "Great Yellow" (rhubarb) produced in the capital?
Chan Master Dingsheng Deming of Yuyang in Ningbo Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuyang Michan. He was the son of the Liu family from Yongdong.
At the age of sixteen, he relied upon Master Cheng of Yuetai to receive the tonsure and dye his robes. He first visited Master Xisou Tan at Xuedou and subsequently studied under Master Wanji Mi.
Miji remarked, "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi, while Wǎngmíng was able to do so?

The Master said, "In the spring colors there is no high or low; the flower branches are simply short or long. Miji held this in high regard and appointed him to manage the treasury. He later appeared in the world at Yùwáng Monastery, where he was granted the title Fó rì pǔ guāng (Sunlight of the Buddha).

[He then offered a verse on the kōan of Chuánzǐ’s capsizing boat: The boat has turned over; The fisherman is gone. The sky is vast and empty; The water is deep and clear. If you wish to see the old man, Look at the moon reflected in the stream.
It is said: "In this vast and tranquil world, he occupies the essential ford; his single oar is a livelihood that weighs as much as a thousand *qun*. On the path of Zhu Jing, travelers are few;
the depths of the blue sea cannot match the profundity of his heart. Later, he entered nirvana and was interred in Dongyun Pagoda. He was eighty-four years old.
He was sixty-seven years old at the time of his death.

Chan Master Zhimei of Sita on Lake Hu in Jiaxing Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Chuan of Jingci. He was the son of the Bi family of Jinling; from birth, he was exceptionally brilliant and refined.
Having no intention to serve the secular world, he left home to venerate Mokuin. During the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty, he received the *pravrajyā* and full ordination (*upasampadā*).
With a keen resolve, he traveled extensively to visit various masters; at Yujian Ying, Yunfeng Gao, and Yuepo Ming, he all sat at their feet and was acclaimed as a preeminent disciple.
Finally, he met Wumen at Jingci Monastery. Regarding Wumen as one possessed of the Way, the Master devoted himself to him with all his heart, fully revealing the source.
Di. In the *dinghai* year of the Zhizhi era of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty, he emerged at the Double Pagoda Temple in Wu.
Not long after, he moved to the Three Pagodas Temple in Hezhou. Within a few years, all the great monasteries were fully established under his leadership.
Subsequently, he received an imperial decree to reside at Lingyan in Pingjiang, and later moved to Yongfu in Poyang and Yuyang in Siming. This was in the *xinwei* year of the Zishun era.
Master Jingci was diligent in all his endeavors, taking it as his primary responsibility to propagate the Way and establish its foundations, never for a moment relaxing his efforts.

One day, he suddenly summoned his assembly to entrust them with his final affairs. He took the Huanyou Hermitage, which had been built to the east of the previous three pagodas, and renamed it Sichen (Four Dhyānas).
He instructed that those whose names and reality corresponded should dwell there. Sitting upright, he passed away peacefully at midnight at the age of... [years].
Seventy-fourth [in the lineage].
The Dharma successor of Chan Master Jianyan Daoci,
the twenty-third generation under Dajian [Huineng].
Chan Master Shuzhong Wuyun of the Empty Chamber at Ruiyan in Taizhou Prefecture was a native of the Chen family of Linhai in his home prefecture.
He received the tonsure under Jizhao of Mount Jing. After traveling to visit various masters, he first called upon Lingshi at Jingci Monastery, and subsequently studied under Yiyuan Ling.

After more than a year had passed, he returned to pay his respects to Jizhao, who appointed him to reside in the Zemo Liao (Hall for Selecting Wood). Later, he traveled to Siming, where he met Taibai Di.
The Master was in the collection hall one day when he went with Mudan Cong and Dazong Xing to Zhituo in Taizhou to visit Zhuyuan Dao.
He intended to ask about the "Mu" (No) phrase, but as soon as he opened his mouth, Yuan gave him a shout. The Master attained a sudden and great awakening;
it was as if sweat poured down from his entire body. He presented this verse: "The dog has no Buddha-nature. Spring colors fill the imperial capital. Zhaozhou’s eastern..."
In the courtyard, a gourd was hanging on the wall. Yuan laughed and said, "Even if you understand it this way, how can that suffice? The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
From this point on, he was deeply moved and spoke to his fellow practitioners, saying: "This matter is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, one knows for oneself."
It is by no means found within words or letters. Had we not encountered this old fellow, we would have been buried for a lifetime by mere intellectual understanding.

Should you one day take up a thatch roof to dwell under, you must not forget your origins. Later, Guding Mingzhu succeeded to the abbacy of Jing Mountain and invited the Master to return to the Meng Hall.
There he daily delved into the profound mysteries and became a model for students. There was none who did not...
For what reason did he avoid the military conflict and return to Siming? Initially, he went forth to reside at Lingyan on Mount Xiang; subsequently, he presided over Ruiyan in Huangyan.
At that time, Mengtang E was residing at Rulong, hoping that the Master would become the successor to Jizhao. The Master said, "My original vow lies elsewhere; it cannot be diverted.
On the day of opening the hall, he held up the incense and said, "When the ancients appeared in the world, they offered incense to repay the milk of the Dharma."
Furthermore, when people of today offer incense upon leaving the world, they do so to repay their worldly debts of gratitude. Master Yun, however, does not agree with this at all.
In years past, while traveling on pilgrimage, I went to Mount Zituo to visit an old monk clad in coarse cotton robes. He had no dharma to bestow, and I had no dharma to receive.
It was solely from within this state of neither bestowing nor receiving that I produced [this offering] to provide for my late master, who resided at Jianyan Chan Monastery in Kunshan.
The Venerable Master Zhu Yuandao of the Temple did not seek to calculate merit or repay his debt of gratitude; he simply wished for everyone to understand.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of Ruiyan? The Master said, "The wind cannot enter. The monk asked, "Who is the person within the realm? The Master said, "Water cannot wet them.
The monk asked, "I have already received your instruction regarding the person and the realm; as for the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage, what is it like?"

The Master said, "The true does not conceal the false. [The monk] asked, "The *dharmas* have the characteristic of quiescent extinction; why then do the shore move when the boat travels, and the moon shift when the clouds race?
The Master said, "What a fine message! I only fear you will misunderstand it. [The monk] said, "A double case.
The Master said, "The waters of the sea do not produce ice. [The monk] asked, "In Vimalakīrti’s chamber, the sun and moon were not used for illumination. As for the Master’s chamber—"

"What constitutes clarity? The Master said, "The object sees the master; the eyes stand bolt upright. [The student] asked, "When Mahākāśyapa closed his room and Vimalakīrti remained silent, how far apart were these two?

The Master said, "They are buried together in a single pit. [The student] asked, "When Deshan entered the gate and immediately struck with his staff, and Linji entered the gate and immediately shouted—after all, what matter of clarity did they clarify?
The Master said, "A thousand tents in the north of the desert; the south of the Yangtze River..."
A ten-thousand-bushel ship. [A monk] asked, "What is the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth? The Master said, "A live sparrow in the mouth of a fierce tiger.
[The monk] asked, "What is the phrase that cuts off all streams? The Master said, "An eight-sided staff in the hand of Vajrapāṇi."
[The student] asked, "What is the phrase of 'following the waves and chasing the currents'? The Master said, "Li Bai grasping the moon; Zhang Qian riding the raft. Small Assembly (Xiaocan):

The Lingyan Peak is steep and precipitous; those who reach it must find it difficult. Those who have already reached it enjoy peace and happiness, while those who have not yet reached it remain solitary and exposed.
For those who are solitary and exposed, it is precisely right to step forward; for those who are enjoying themselves, they must surely take a step back.
Regarding oneself, it is said: "Matters do not have a single direction. Sometimes the head is taken as the tail; sometimes the tail is taken as the head.

In gathering and releasing, advancing and retreating, how could there be fixed rules? When Mahākāśyapa closed his room and Vimalakīrti remained silent, although these were called the full manifestation of the true command, they still had not reached the ultimate point.
This mountain monk, at the very beginning of entering the gate tonight, as we gather together—
First, I establish three articles of law for you all: First, you must not give rise to the view of a Buddha. Second, you must not give rise to the view of the Dharma.
Third, you must not say that you do not give rise to the views of a Buddha or the Dharma. If you follow and practice according to these, [you shall attain liberation].
"Take it for granted that his eyebrows will become entangled. [The Master] suddenly took up his staff and said: "An eye of clarity has no fixed patterns.

Looking down from the highest point, there is insufficiency; leveling out from the lowest point, there is abundance. He struck the ground with the staff and said: "The iron ox does not eat grass by the fence;
he goes straight to sleep atop the summit of Mount Sumeru. [He then] ascended the hall to thank the special messenger. "The Great Master Bodhidharma... [Ten times].
Coming ten thousand *li* from the West, he intended to be a man who could deliver a letter and convey his message; yet when he faced King Liang, he could only say with all his might, "I do not know.
Holding up his staff, he said: "There is guest and there is host; there is ritual and there is music.
With hands and face clearly distinguished, the full moon is revealed; at the crown of the head, the golden bell is shaken. He ascended the hall and said: "The bright moon shines upon the high crags."

The sound of water cascading over the ridge ahead—how clear and pure are the ears and eyes! In profound stillness, one understands the nature of the mind. Alas, Avalokiteśvara! You carry snow to fill the well.
[The Master] descends from his seat. [The Master] ascends the hall: "The meaning of the Patriarchs is not some separate dharma.
When walking on the ground, the shoes are worn through; when lying on the bed, the socks are pulled off. To act just like this is too much of a riddle; not to act like this leaves nothing to fit."
Shuilu of Mt. Gui was like a wild ox; Baizhang was like a wild duck. Carrying water and dragging mud is not worth looking at;

the halo behind the head is most brilliant. (He let out a shout. Entering the hall for instruction, he said: "The wind does not come, so the tree does not move; the mind does not arise, so objects do not reach it."
A monk asked Yunmen, “What is the Buddha? Yunmen said, “A dried-up shit-stick. A monk asked Yangqi, “What is the Buddha?
Yangqi said, “A three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves. Listen well, assembly! When I tell you it is a dragon, you stubbornly refuse to believe.
As expected, he has won the prize and returned. Entering the hall, [the Master] said: "Monks of the Zen school say, 'There is nothing we do not know; there is nothing we do not understand.
Yet when suddenly asked, 'What is the matter of traveling on pilgrimage? their mouths hang down like a flat carrying pole. Wherein lies the sickness?
The sickness lies in having too much knowledge and too many explanations. To study in such a manner is not as good as being a farmer in a village of three households."
Someone asked, "How was the harvest this year? [The Master] recounted it point by point, like pouring water from one vessel into another.

This was because he lacked conceptual understanding and had no discrimination. The autumn air was bitterly cold; everyone returned to their respective halls. Take care. Ascending the hall, [the Master said:
"Leaving behind kin, severing attachments, shaving your hair, and donning the dyed robes—having entered this gate, what should you do? If you possess a sense of shame..."
Shame! This is true renunciation: first, leaving the home of worldly dust and affectionate attachment; second, leaving the home of the burning house of the three realms;

third, leaving the home of coarse delusions and afflictions; fourth, leaving the home of subtle delusions and ignorance. Only when one has emerged from these four kinds of homes may one truly be called a member of the family of patch-robed monks (*śramaṇa*).
But tell me, what is this family of patch-robed monks? It is where one encounters an enemy and meets with foul-mouthed, petty folk.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all atoms. Holding up his staff, he said:
"Śākyamuni the Old Man has arrived! His three hundred and sixty bones and joints, and eighty-four thousand pores, each and every one radiate great light."
It shines through and penetrates lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Within them, whether saintly or ordinary, sentient or insentient—among all those touched by its light, there are none who do not realize Great Nirvana, attain Great Peace and Bliss, and obtain Great Enjoyment. Leaning on his staff, he said:
If you do not investigate the source at this very moment, you must wait until the future to question Maitreya.

Addressing the assembly: In the deep spring of this mountain monastery, the grasses and trees flourish; several times I have intentionally opened the wooden gate. The traveler remains only beyond the green mountains;
the cuckoo calls out again and again, yet none returns. Entering the hall: Upon this mass of bare flesh there is a thing—vivid, numinous, and radiant.
Vague and indistinct, it shifts and transforms according to circumstances, entirely free from restriction. One must know its place of origin with clarity;

Shortly thereafter, a rumor spread among the common people that the authorities were selecting young boys and girls. Master [Fengxue] asked [Zhaozhou]:
"Suppose someone suddenly comes and asks the Abbot, 'How do you deal when they come to seek a boy or a girl? Fengxue said, 'I simply hand him a bamboo comb.

At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment, penetrating to the very source of the Dharma. Fengxue then wrote a portrait eulogy (zhenzan) and gave it to the Master, saying: 'My appearance is inconceivable.'"
[This] is a matter for deliberation. Neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs can recognize it; I alone permit this unworthy son to see half of its nose.

Someone once asked about the relative strengths and weaknesses among the various disciples of Gao Feng. Gao Feng said, "As for the former head monk and the others, it is not that they have no knowledge or partial understanding at all."
Yi-shou, the Head Seat, was certainly a sturdy old bamboo stalk, though it may have been bent seven or eight times;

yet Wenben, the Rector, was truly a tree of *lin*, *zi*, or *nan* timber upon that stalk—his future growth as a vessel of great utility will be difficult to measure. When Feng passed away, the Master took charge of the monastery affairs.
Finding the constant inquiries from kings and ministers a distraction, he resigned his post and traveled through the rivers and lakes, dwelling sometimes on boats and sometimes in hermitages.
He had no fixed dwelling place and styled all his residences "Huanchu" (Abiding in Illusion). Although Emperor Renzong issued summons to invite him, he did not go.

The Emperor bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* robe and the title of Chan Master Foci Yuanzhao Guanghui. Furthermore, by imperial decree, Shizi Chan Monastery was renamed Shizi Zhengzong Chan Temple.
At that time, the Xuanzheng Yuan offered him the positions of abbot at Lingyin and Jingshan, but the Master declined them both. Previously...
The Prince of Shen, Wang Zhang—the Prince Consort and Grand Marshal—sent someone to inquire about the Dharma;

finding this insufficient, he again requested an imperial edict to personally carry the Imperial Incense into the mountains to pay his respects. The Master ascended the seat for a general discourse. Emperor Yingzong specially issued an edict to bestow incense.
He was granted a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*. The Master frequently rebuked his students, saying that they merely valued verbal proficiency while failing to seek actual realization.
He once addressed the assembly, saying: "The reason why Chan practice today lacks efficacy is threefold: first, a lack of the genuine resolve of the ancients;
second, failing to treat birth-and-death and impermanence as a matter of supreme importance; and third, not being willing to sacrifice [one's life] for eons..."
What you have practiced and what you hold dear does not descend [into the depths]. Furthermore, you do not possess the long-enduring body and mind of non-retrogression.
Ultimately, where does the illness lie? It is truly because you do not recognize the root of birth and death. Now, as for that root:

its nature is truly perfect and luminous, fundamentally devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, or coming and going. It is simply because of a lack of awareness that a fleeting deluded mind suddenly arises, causing one to lose sight of the source.

The source is the void that receives the cycle of transmigration; for this reason, the Way is such that delusion therein begins birth and death, while awakening thereto causes the cycle of rebirth to cease.

This is rooted in delusion and fundamentally based on falsehood. One should know that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; light and darkness, form and emptiness; the five aggregates and the four elements;
and even all phenomena, whether moving or unmoving—all these are the very root of birth and death. If one has not yet turned toward the Truth...

Having attained a sudden, transcendent awakening within the reality of dharmas, if one were to establish a separate life beyond that awakening and maintain a distinct conceptual framework, how could such a person ever plant their feet upon the shore of birth and death?
If even the slightest hair’s breadth remains unexhausted, they will inevitably be drawn back once more by superior and wondrous sensory conditions.
Delusion lies right there. One gives rise to various divergent conceptions; though one may claim to have attained clear understanding, in reality this is not yet the case.
Only those who take the great matter of birth and death as their own paramount responsibility can exhaust all thieving minds and thus be fit for true integration with the Way.

Should even a hair’s breadth of views regarding good and evil, acceptance and rejection, or love and hatred, continuity and interruption, remain, then branches and leaves will sprout. How can one not be cautious?
"Ha! Addressing the assembly: Looking ahead, he is right there; turning back, he is suddenly behind. The bamboo pheasant cries by day; the flower-dragon bell roars at night.
Before you have finished listening to a single word, who among you now moves their mouth? Alas!
Students take such phrases as these and deliberate upon them as if they were some kind of conceptual principle, thereby adding such wild weeds to their own naturally pure field."

This is like fox saliva and foam; it has already defiled you. Yet you fail to reflect upon the opening of the ancients' mouths, which is like a great mass of fire, like a great whirlwind—there is no place for you to settle therein.
It is also like a "blow-to-the-hair" sword; when casually drawn forth, its sole purpose is to sever the life-root of men.
How could this be grasped through the calculations of mind, intellect, or consciousness? If it were so, then [even] Ānanda...
Ānanda did not need to undergo further cultivation, and the Second Patriarch did not need to trouble himself by cutting off his arm. Why is this?
Those Ānanda and the Second Patriarch possessed wisdom surpassing that of others and their consciousness was clear and lucid; as for what you understand, had they not heard it?

It is simply because when the mind does not achieve wondrous awakening, one’s ground of vision is not liberated. If the ground of vision is not liberated, then every movement is the functioning of the emotional consciousness, rolling it into action.
A mere mob, everywhere clinging to grass and leaning on wood, merely echoing what is hollow and responding to empty sounds.
This causes the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (the clarified butter) to remain within an impure vessel, where it turns into a poisonous drug. At all times, they are like a ghost that knows no liberation.
When seeing someone speak of mind or nature, they immediately lean on a fence or grope along a wall, trying to latch onto it and carry it away.

As soon as they see someone raise [the topic], finding no handle to grasp, they turn their faces away; yet when the place where teeth and claws emerge appears, they cannot avoid the functioning of consciousness and so swallow the dates whole.
Such people as these have two masters within their daily single mind, constantly contending with one another.

As they arise and cease, at times they take *prajñā* as their object, thereby forgetting the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); at other times they take the conventional truth as their object, thereby forgetting *prajñā*.
Unaware that they have stumbled right beneath their own heels, they instead claim, "My practice is not yet mature; my cultivation is not yet pure.

Thus, they diligently cultivate virtuous deeds and create tainted causes (*sāsrava-hetu*) as a means of support. Furthermore, there is another class who treat Buddha-nature with superficiality and negligence.
Those who are crude and reckless regarding True Suchness (Tathatā) encounter all objective conditions and treat them as a single, uniform principle;

they stubbornly attempt to dismiss them, even to the point of violating the rules of discipline and transgressing the prohibitive precepts without any sense of restraint. When it comes to dealing with the realm of differentiated phenomena, they are utterly at a loss.
To dismiss the fact that one cannot practice is to be ignorant of one's own face-to-face deception;

yet one instead claims, "My capacity has not yet overcome [the obstacles] and my learning is not broad," and thus proceeds to seek out ancient teachings to broaden one's knowledge and experience. Or again, one may forget the physical form and die the death of the mind.

They cease their practice and still their thoughts, merely using them to fuel their wild intellects. As for these two types of practitioners mentioned above, they lack right mindfulness within themselves;
moreover, from the very beginning, they have never encountered a true master who can "bite like a pig-dog" to thoroughly cleanse them.
Remaining mired in their own delusions, they fail to recognize their own illness. All day long, they speak recklessly and debate with unrestrained tongues—altogether...
This is merely scratching an itch with a leather shield. Studying in this manner requires a single moment of resonance at the very brink of birth and death;
it is like blowing into a net to try to fill it—it would be either foolish or mad. Among those who act as teachers in recent times, many are unable to exhaustively reach the source.

Desiring only that students quickly attain understanding and reach the "Warmth" and "Heat" stages of realization, many teachers roll themselves along with others, frequently employing such phrases as "The Lord of Ruiyan," "Linji’s Person of No-Rank," "Mind is Buddha," or "Who is he?
They do so regardless of whether the student has yet established a firm footing, fearing only that they might fail to grasp the meaning. Furthermore, they tell them: "Investigate! (Chán).
Who is it that studies? Who is it that seeks to see one's original nature?

It is simply because they wish to recognize a mere shadow and light within this very place—that they clench their fists, point their fingers, advance, and retreat, never departing from the present moment.
This is precisely the Great Meaning of the West. Yet students fail to distinguish between good and evil; they fall into his conceptual traps, like oil soaking into flour, never to be extracted.

To emerge from this state is truly pitiable. This is fundamentally because one does not know that within the minds of sentient beings there is perfect purity and profound stillness, originally free from defilement.

It is merely because the arising of emotional attachments creates a barrier to wisdom, and the transformation of appearances causes the essence to become alienated. Once a single delusion flickers into being, ten thousand conditions are established individually.
Thus, externally one falsely perceives mountains, rivers, the great earth, light, darkness, form, and space; internally, one falsely perceives the four elements and the five aggregates.

The aggregates, seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, up to the eighty-four thousand afflictions, as well as the characteristics of bodhi, true thusness, nirvana, and the buddha-nature—all these do not exist apart from this single delusion.

However, if one wishes to eliminate this deluded thought, it requires that one’s practice be fully matured, that one sever the root and stem, cut off the distinction between the holy and the ordinary, and achieve a sudden, decisive awakening. Not...
However, even if you surpass the Second Patriarch in realization and exceed Ānanda in wisdom, you remain seated within the eighth consciousness.

To use consciousness to eliminate consciousness, or to use delusion to dispel delusion, is like trying to avoid one's own shadow by standing in the sun, or attempting to extinguish eye-flies in empty space;
it is merely a waste of effort that results in further differentiation. This is why the venerable masters of old could do nothing with this state, and thus they brought it forth [as a teaching].
A single-handled folding knife is thrust into the very life-root of this being. Waiting until it reaches a point where it can no longer turn back, one exerts all one's strength to push through;
suddenly it is severed, and with a crack, it snaps. Delusive thoughts vanish and perceptions cease; seeing falls away and attachments are forgotten.

Thereupon, the myriad phenomena of the universe appear vast and profoundly serene; hearing, seeing, sensing, and knowing are liberated in their own place—ten thousand myriad things are unified as one.
The world melts back into the one mind; naturally, dharma after dharma is entirely true, and every single thing is manifest.
Even so, if you wish to open your mouth and breathe before a monk, you must still receive three thousand blows in the morning and eight hundred in the evening.
Only when the living eyes reopen upon his dead skull will you have a share in speech. Small Assembly Sermon. Great.

The Way is present before one’s eyes: mountains are mountains, waters are waters. The profound mechanism transcends all things; the sage is not merely a sage, and the ordinary person is not merely ordinary.

In a single thought, all is clear and penetrating; ten thousand functions are vast and open. In the Crystal Palace, the autumnal colors are serene; the myriad phenomena of the universe swallow and spit forth the bright moon-jewel.
In the Snow-Pine Studio, the浩然 (haoran) spirit is profound and deep; the six windows of the screen and desk interpenetrate like precious silk threads.
The Net: there is not a single thing that does not manifest ultimate transformation, nor a single event that does not expound the True Vehicle.

Although Zhuang Zhou’s dream of being a butterfly occurred by his pillow, how could one dare guarantee he was at a loss for a timely response? Although Zishao heard the frog under the moon, it was not permitted that he could present himself face-to-face.
This one move cannot be named and cannot be described; even at the very point where it is known, one has already fallen into the deep pit.
The event is thus, and the principle is thus. When you understand it in this way, you have already sunk into the ocean of consciousness.
Therefore it is said: "Divine light shines alone; its glorious traces endure for ten thousand ages. Having entered this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.
But as for this phrase of "not harboring intellectual understanding," how can it be pointed out? The jade palace is high in autumn with no boundaries; the golden garden is in full bloom in spring.
Addressing the assembly: "The sword of wisdom is held aloof in daily life; naturally, it has never required sharpening.
Gods cry out and ghosts wail with terror, yet corpses lie scattered across the wilds without its blade being revealed. When the ancients spoke thus, they had already wounded their own lives.
Little did they realize that within the armory of the True King, there is no such sword. Addressing the assembly on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month (the Buddha's Enlightenment Day):

Profoundly profound and beyond dependence; wondrously wondrous and without reliance. Solely revealing the true permanence, fully manifesting the ultimate essence. It cannot be named and cannot be described; it is like snow and ice withered away.

In principle there is no obstruction, and in phenomena there is no obstruction. The heavens are vast and the earth is remote; ten thousand miles of clouds have gathered, yet at the fifth watch they clear.
The four directions reveal the stars shimmering in the long expanse of the sky. Having peeled back the forehead behind the limit of Vipaśyin, it is a perfectly round, radiant light.
Brilliantly! It pierces the eye-sight behind the skull, leaving it pure, naked, and starkly clear.

It restrains the divine mechanism of thirty thousand kalpas—swift as wind and fierce as thunder—and brings forth the drowsy chatter of five thousand scrolls, surging like the ocean and massing like clouds.
"Great assembly! Śākyamuni the Old Man has arrived. He is right now within the eyes of everyone.
Beholding the morning star, he attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment upon the crown of his head. Do you all perceive even the movement of his eyebrows? If you have not yet understood this,"

"Each of you, please return to the hall. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Longya said: 'Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real, simply because they have been identifying with the spirit since time immemorial.
This is the root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas; the deluded call it the 'original person. Today, this Old Seat-Bearer shall overturn their case for them.

Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real—what need is there to identify anything at all?"* *Note: The original text contains a play on words between "shen" (spirit) and "shi" (to know/recognize). The commentary suggests that practitioners mistake the conscious mind for the ultimate reality, thereby perpetuating the cycle of suffering. The Master's response challenges this very act of identification.*

It is simply because one has recognized the Buddha from of old; it is not that there is much more to it. Since the very source of birth and death is not even questioned, what is the person of original nature?
He gave a shout and said: "Be careful not to misinterpret this. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the Guihai year of Zhizhi (1323), he spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying:
"I have one phrase to entrust to the great assembly. If you ask further how it is, there is no basis."
He could sit upright; placing his writing brush down, he sat peacefully and passed away. His secular age was sixty-one, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇerī-vassa) was thirty-seven.

His entire body was enshrined in a stūpa on the western ridge of his native mountain. In the year Jisi of the Tianli era, Emperor Wen bestowed upon him the posthumous title Zhijue and named the stūpa Fayun.
In the year Jiashu of the Yuantong era, thirty fascicles of his collected works were granted for inclusion in the canon, and he was posthumously titled National Teacher Puying.
Chan Master Duanya Liaoyi of the Tianmu Zhengzong lineage in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Yang family of Deqing.

At the age of seventeen, upon hearing the recorded words of Peak (Gaofeng) delivered during a formal assembly, he went to pay his respects and attend him. He served Peak at the "Deadlock Gate" (Sigan), where Peak instructed him to contemplate the koan:
"All dharmas return to One; to what does the One return? Consequently, he was named Congyi. On another occasion, Peak raised the story of the Ox for the assembly.

The Master had heard the "Conversations by the Window Lattice" and harbored doubts, investigating them day and night. One evening, while passing by Bowanyu Pond, he saw snow falling from the branches of a pine tree and attained realization.
He went to Feng to present a verse, saying: "I ask not of south or north, east or west; the great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one expanse of snow.
Before his voice had even ceased, Feng struck him with a heavy blow and drove him out. Unconsciously, he fell to the bottom of a cliff. Others thought that...
He was certain to die. His fellow students climbed through the vines to rescue him, but he was uninjured. He then vowed that within seven days he would attain realization.
Before the period had even ended, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He rushed back to Siguan (Dead Gate) and cried out, "Old Monk, today you cannot deceive me!
He then spoke a verse, saying: "The mountains and rivers of the great earth are a single expanse of snow; once the sun shines upon them, they vanish."
From this point on, he no longer harbored doubts regarding the Buddhas and Patriarchs; there was no longer any distinction between north, south, east, or west. Feng then ascended the hall and said:
"For over twenty years, I have spread a net that covers the heavens to capture phoenixes and ensnare dragons, yet I have never encountered so much as a shrimp or a crab.
Today, however, a tiny gnat has flown into the net. Though it is truly not fit to be looked upon, [I shall deal with it]."
"Thirty years later, he went to the summit of a solitary peak and raised his voice in a great shout. But tell me, what did he shout?
He raised his whisk and said: 'The mountains and rivers of the great earth are a single expanse of snow.

The Master said to his fellow students, "If there is one person in the entire world who awakens to the true source and returns to the origin, everyone will know it from the very beginning. Feng sighed in admiration of his brilliance and speed, and soon returned to seek instruction.
His parents then escorted his mother to Upper Baitong in Wukang, where they lived in a thatched hut. Once his filial duties were completed, he returned to the mountain to see Feng.
Feng said, "Many people see you as one who drags mud and carries water. The Master replied, "Two eyes facing two eyes.
Thereupon, Feng shaved his head for him and changed his name to Liaoyi. After Feng passed away, the Master became even more reclusive, remaining in a humble position with a low-spirited demeanor.
After the fourfold assembly had repeatedly requested him to remain, he finally consented to dwell at Shizi Zhengzong (The Lion’s Orthodox Lineage). He addressed the assembly:

"If you wish to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, to be forever liberated from worldly toil, you must strip away the skin and replace the bones, severing your past existence so that you may be revived anew—like cold ashes suddenly bursting into flame."
That withered wood has flourished again—how can this be taken lightly?
I have been at the old master’s place for many years, and every time I was struck by his great staff, it penetrated to my very marrow; yet I never once harbored a thought of leaving.
Even now, as soon as I am touched upon that painful spot, tears flow involuntarily. How could I be like you, who leap for joy at the mere taste of a little bitterness?
Upon tasting it, he immediately shook his head and turned away, failing to realize that the bitter taste can eliminate a hundred ailments.
Generally speaking, when one's practice reaches the point where effort is effortless—like a boat sailing with the current—the helmsman must hold the rudder firmly;
should even a hair’s breadth of a divergent thought arise, one may be certain of losing one’s life. When reaching the state of absolute oneness, not a single [thought] should be stirred.
Maintain a mind of diligent effort. Do not give rise to even a single thought of laziness.
Do not give rise to even a single thought of seeking enlightenment. Do not give rise to even a single thought of gain or loss.

As soon as a thought arises, all manner of demons will enter your heart and armpits, causing you to become deranged and to speak nonsense and confused words, forever becoming a member of the demonic family; even a Buddha would find it difficult to save you.
"Be careful, be careful," he said. On the final day of the year in the *Guiyou* year of Emperor Dianshun’s *Yuansheng* era, he addressed his attendant, saying:
"There is one matter as vast as heaven; do you understand it thoroughly? After a long silence, he said: "Tomorrow is the New Year's festival.
On the sixth day of the first month, go to the west of the Fayun Pagoda and point to a vacant space, saying: 'It would be even better to erect a seamless pagoda here. That evening...

He conversed and laughed with the practitioner as if it were his usual routine. When night fell, he said, "The old monk is going to Tiantai tomorrow. The practitioner replied, "I shall follow my teacher.
The Master said, "Even if you were to run like a galloping horse, you could not catch up to me. At dawn the following day, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
His secular age was seventy-two, and his monastic seniority was forty-nine. His entire body was enshrined in a lion-shaped stupa.

On the day of Master Shenshan’s passing at Yanhou, thunder crashed and rain lashed down, plunging the midday into darkness. At his funeral, snowflakes fell in profusion, and the forest trees were draped in white.

Several thousand people attended the burial. Initially, while at the assembly for the funeral feast at Zhongfeng, the Master had said to the assembly, "Twelve years from now, we shall gather once more for an assembly for this old monk.
The assembly did not believe him deeply at first; it was only now that they began to do so.

Verification: In the seventh month of the *wuchen* year of the Zhizhi era (1316), the imperial court, in admiration of the Master’s conduct and realization, issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title of "Great Master Fohui Yuanming Zhengjue Pudu" (Buddha-Wisdom, Perfectly Enlightened, Rightly Awakened, Universal Deliverance).
He was the Great-Awakened (Dajue) Bunan, Chan Master Zu'ong of Hangzhou Prefecture, a native of Ninghai County in Mingzhou. He served under Gaofeng with the utmost devotion.

For a long time, he personally attended to the tasks of pounding grain and cooking. His appearance was very dark and emaciated; he was blunt and possessed little literary refinement. Initially, he served as the head of the monastery, and later he became the leader of the assembly. His expositions of the Dharma were exceptionally outstanding.
In the year Xinmao, Qu, the Director of the Office of Imperial Sacrifices of Heqia, offered a large estate to High Peak (Foguo Yuan) to provide for the community.

High Peak declined the offer with great earnestness, whereupon Qu separately established Da Jue Temple and invited the Master to take charge of its affairs. When High Peak approached his final passing, he entrusted the Master with the responsibility.
He attended to his final affairs. He once composed a verse on dwelling in the mountains, which says: "Taking shelter under trees, I bind thatch to form a house;
Gathering thorns, I weave a fence by the stream. It is because this lazy Zan lacks spiritual efficacy That the Celestial Edict has come thrice.
His lofty character and distant resonance can generally be imagined from this. Later, at the Guizitang Hall in Zhongzhu, he wrote a verse and passed away while seated.
Zhongkong, who had received the essential instructions from Chan Master Gaofeng at Chanzhi Temple on Mount Baiyun in Chuzhou Prefecture, later settled there in retirement.
Zen practitioners from all directions heard of his reputation and came to visit him, until shoes were piled outside his door.

One day in the summer of the *bingzi* year of the Zhizheng era (1336), he took up his brush and wrote this verse: "Earth, water, fire, and wind—this was the prediction of the Buddhas of the past. Dig deep into the earth and bury me."

There are two points: first, to spare the donor from having to gather more firewood; second, to avoid the criticism that there were no relics. He threw down his brush, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Lingyun Ding.
Chan Master Shicheng of the Banruo Juexue Temple in Nanchang Prefecture addressed the assembly:

"Those of resolute will, taking advantage of the dry firewood and convenient water within the community, and the warmth of the Sangha hall, should remain outside the gate for three years; they will certainly attain great realization.

There are some who, as soon as they begin their practice, feel a sense of lightness and ease in their hearts and perceive purity before them, whereupon they immediately abandon their efforts all at once."
If you compose verses and stanzas with a quick tongue and facile speech, thinking you have achieved something great, you will surely waste a lifetime.
It is a pity that all the mental effort exerted thus far will be abandoned midway; when the three-inch breath is severed, what will you have to rely upon?
Brothers, if you wish to transcend birth and death, you must practice authentically and realize authentically. King Yama does not...
Fearing that you might be able to speak and discourse [on the Dharma],

here is the record of Chan Master Shaodai of Tongjiang at Baolin Temple in Jinhua Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Ling of Jingshan. He was a native of the Wu clan from Yanzhou and his family had resided for generations in Tongjiang.
He took this as his monastic name. In his youth, he entered Fengshan in his home village to shave his head and receive the full precepts.

He visited Xugou at Jingshan, where he received the seal of mind-to-mind transmission. Having traveled extensively to attend various masters, one day he said, "From this day forward, I know that the Dharma has no differing flavors.
Thereupon, he ceased his formal study of the masters and read through the Tripitaka three times. He became thoroughly proficient in the principles of both Buddhist and secular learning.

He resided at Jingci Temple on Dongyu Island and was appointed to keep the treasury keys. In the *Renshen* year of the Zhishun era, he emerged from seclusion at Wulong in his hometown, and later moved to Baolin on Mount Yunhuang.
His Dharma assemblies were renowned for their extreme grandeur. One day, manifesting a slight illness, he struck the drum to assemble the congregation to express his gratitude.
When the assembly requested a verse, the Master took up his brush, threw it to the ground, and said: "Even if I were to write until Maitreya’s descent into the world, how could I ever depart?"
Having finished these words, he passed away. His worldly age was seventy-four, and his years of monastic seniority were fifty-eight. Upon cremation, his relics were like deep blue pearls;
his teeth and jawbone remained unbroken. He left behind three collections of recorded discourses.
Chan Master Zhuyuan Zhengyuan of Jingshan in Hangzhou Prefecture was a descendant of the Duke Ou Yang Wenzhong. His family had resided in Nankang for generations.
At the age of twenty-seven, he left home to shave his head and receive the precepts; thereafter, he traveled to visit various masters.

He first called upon Xugu, who posed the koan of Longtan extinguishing a paper candle with his breath, asking, "What is the meaning of this? The Master replied, "A scorched stone can shatter thick ice."
Tang said, "What is it like after it has been broken? The Master said, "One knows it through searching. Tang asked, "What is that which is known?

As the Master was about to respond, Tang struck him across the back with his staff. The Master was startled and realized the essential meaning. Later, he appeared in the world at Guanyin Xingsheng Monastery, followed by serving as the abbot of Daochang Lingyin.
He subsequently moved to Jingshan, where he was granted the title Chan Master Fohui Cizhao Puying. Thus...
In the sixth month of the Xinchou year of the Zhi Zheng era, he demonstrated his entry into nirvana. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Mount Jing.

His disciples divided his fingernails, hair, and *śarīra* relics, which they enshrined at Daochang Monastery. His secular age was seventy-three, and his monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-vaṣa*) was forty-five.

Chan Master Shiwu Qinggong of Fuyuan, in Huzhou Prefecture, was a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Xinxin of Daochang. He was a son of the Wen family of Changshu and was born at the beginning of the Xiachun era.
In his youth, he relied upon Chongfu Temple to receive the tonsure and later received full ordination. He first visited Fengge, who instructed him that "all dharmas return to one."
"Where does 'one' return? he asked, instructing him to investigate this. He served [Feng] diligently for three years without achieving any realization.
He took his leave of Feng, who said, "There is a blind donkey in Wên; there is Jiān in Huái. You should go see them. Consequently, he went to Jiān in Jiānyáng.
Jiān asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Tiānmù. Jiān asked, "What instruction did you receive? The Master replied, "'The myriad dharmas return to one; where does one return...'"
“Where? Nanquan asked. “How do you understand this? The Master was speechless. Nanquan said, “This is a dead word. What is wrong with you?
Why did I have to speak to you like that? The Master bowed and requested further instruction. Nanquan said, “Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell;
where there is no Buddha, pass by quickly. The Master did not attain realization. Nanquan said, “This too is a dead word.”
The Master was so startled that he broke into a cold sweat. One day, while in the inner quarters, Yuan’an brought up the previous conversation again.
The Master said, "When one mounts a horse, one sees the road. Yuan’an rebuked him, saying, "You have been here for six years and still hold such a view!
The Master left in a fit of indignation. On the way back, he suddenly looked up and saw a pavilion in the wind; he attained a sudden realization and returned to tell Yuan’an: "I..."
Jiawu said, "Today I have finally understood the 'live word' (huoju). Yun'an asked, "How do you understand it?

The Master replied, "On this clear and bright season, when the rain has just cleared, the yellow oriole sings clearly upon the branch. Yun'an nodded his head in approval. Consequently, the Master remained to study under him closely for some time before taking his leave.
As Yun'an saw him off at the gate, he said, "In the future, we shall share the same reliquary stupa. Not long after, Yun'an moved to another monastery, and the Master [followed him].
He again relied upon him. [The Master] held the keys to the treasury of the Dharma. Yue Tang Yin became the abbot of Lingyin, and the Master served as his second seat.

After concluding his formal studies, he built a hermitage on Mount Xiawu by Lake Hong. He delighted in poetry and composed various verses on mountain life. In the fourth month of the Xinwei year of the Zhishun era (1351), he went forth to reside at Fuyuan in Danghu.

Perpendicular and horizontal lines intersect; meeting in the depths of water and clouds, yet atop a thousand peaks.

Chan Master Zhigang of Lushan Zhengjue in Jinhua Prefecture was a native of the mountain foothills; having received the Dharma, he traveled abroad.

Nothing is more noble than virtue. Awakening is the cause of *prajñā*; following [the Way] is the Buddha of *bodhi*. One should know that planting beans does not produce hemp;
cause and effect are naturally clear and distinct. Even so, tell me: how can this be seen?

it is like a skilled archer, whose aim is off by no more than a hair’s breadth. Naturally, one encounters the source at every turn and accords with the path at every headland.
There is no need for cultivation or realization, for it is primordially perfected. The entire earth is the field of supreme, wondrous enlightenment, pervading the entire dharma-realm.

This is the ground of true suchness (*tathatā*). Every person has their share in awakening to it; every individual knows it to be without deficiency. When not a single thought arises, one enters *samādhi*;

with the whole body cast down, all attain total freedom. Reaching this point, what need is there to speak of nirvana, birth-and-death, or true suchness?
Buddha-nature: there is not a single dharma that accords with the mind; one directly cuts off the ten directions.

He scattered celestial incense. On his deathbed, he addressed the assembly with a verse, saying: "Seventy-six years have passed; all is clear and vast.
I have pressed through the void until Mount Sumeru stands overturned."
Chan Master Chulin of Mount Pingshan at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of Wang Shi of the Renhe clan in that same prefecture.
At birth, there were extraordinary omens. When he was twelve years old, his parents sent him to Guangyan Monastery to enter the monastic order. At seventeen, he received full ordination.

When the Master was traveling to visit various teachers, his mother prepared his travel gear and sent him to pay his respects to Wuye at Jinhua. Wuye invited him to reside in the position of Attendant.

Chan Master Tianzhen Weize of Haimen, Hangzhou Prefecture, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Kuangshan Yuan. His courtesy name was Bingbo Laoren (Elder Ice and Gall). He was the son of the Fei family of Wuxing.

Chan Master Wujian Xiandǔ of Huading Peak in Taizhou Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ruoyan Bao. He was a native of the Ye clan of Xianju and was born during the Xianchun era.
He received the tonsure at Gutian Hou. Initially, he visited Zangshi Zhen at Tianfeng; subsequently, he paid his respects to Fangshan Bao at Ruiyan.
He built a hermitage on Huading Peak, where he applied himself with diligence day and night. One day, while engaged in manual labor, he attained a sudden and profound realization;

the doubts that had plagued him throughout his life were instantly dissolved like melting ice. He hastened to inform Fangshan, who bestowed a verse upon him as a seal of approval. He then returned once more to Huading.
Sitting for forty summers on a single seat, his feet never crossed the threshold. He opened the *śāla* pavilion to guide those who came to study.
Addressing the assembly: "The wind is cool and crisp; the sun is bright and clear. The *campaka* flowers bloom, filling the road with fragrance.

You worthy ones, when hungry, eat; when weary, sleep; when hot..."
Seeking coolness when it is hot and turning toward the fire when it is cold—each moment is true and natural, each moment is clear and wondrous.

Chan Master Yuanzhan of Qiujiang at Songyan in Ningbo Prefecture had long associated with eminent masters (dragons and elephants).

Later, he studied under Fangshan and attained the essential meaning [of the teachings]. While traveling, he happened upon Songyan; captivated by its purity and excellence, he could not bear to leave. He then sat cross-legged upon a rock, when suddenly—
Two tigers crouched beside him as if in a posture of protection. The Master ordered them to lie down and slept soundly with his back against theirs.

The local mountain folk marveled at this and immediately established a monastery on that very spot. The Master resided there, remaining aloof from worldly affairs; beyond the giving of the Dharma, he was as tranquil as still water.

Sitting cross-legged in meditative repose, he entered his burial niche. A flower bloomed upon an iron tree; a clay ox bellowed. For a month, a long radiance shone, illuminating heaven and earth.
He further told the assembly, "Fifteen years hence, this temple shall be consumed by fire. If you open my niche, the fire may be extinguished.
When the time arrived, it was indeed so. The assembly hurriedly opened the niche; the Master’s countenance was as if alive, and his nails and hair had grown long.

Chan Master Yiyuan Ling of Fengshan in Hangzhou Prefecture was a native of Ninghai. He received the precepts under Yunfeng at Mount Jing and studied under Fangshan at Ruiyan, where he served as the head of the administrative offices.
One day, while in the master’s room, he requested instruction on the story of Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman.
Mount [Shan] said, "Venerable one, try and offer a single phrase. The Master said, "All the people in the great earth are at a loss as to what to do with this old woman.
Mount Shan said, "I, this mountain monk, am not like that; all the people in the great earth are at a loss as to what to do with Zhaozhou.

At these words, the Master was like one who has broken out in a sweat after an illness. Later, while presiding over Fengshan, he ascended the hall and cited the occasion when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and Mañjuśrī addressed him.
The Master struck the meditation case (kōan) and said: "The World-Honored One has already spoken erroneously; Mañjuśrī has already transmitted erroneously;
today at Xinfengshan, I have already raised it erroneously. Do you understand? When a written character is transcribed three times, the 'crow' (wū) becomes a 'horse' (mǎ).

One day, seeing a monk throw a "Chart for Selecting Buddhas" (xuǎnfútú), the Master presented this verse: "The hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and sentient beings— Do not seek them within the chart."
A forceful contest: cast the Heart-Seal (cittamudrā) forth with lightness toward the front. Dignified and majestic, sit at ease within the field of quiescent radiance (*śāntaprabhā*).

He spoke again: "The ancients had no leisure even to trim their nails; yet you, the younger generation, can you bear to let this time pass in vain? For now, cast aside your diagrams and choose the Buddha!"
When the moment of the ultimate convergence of the *śāntika* and *abhicāruka* rites arrived, he cast forth a single seal and exclaimed with joy, "I have attained Buddhahood!
Little did he know that at all times and in all places, these are precisely the sites where you attain Buddhahood; yet you remain unaware of it.
The acupuncturist Ding was a native of Tiantai. He studied under Fǎngshān of Ruìyán and once received his seal of approval.
He composed a verse on lapis lazuli which says: "Let go, let go; Take up, take up. A single point of numinous light Shines upon heaven and earth."
A verse by Chan Master Pingshi Di of Tiantong, in the lineage of Chan Master Rujing of Tiantong, sending off Attendant Yun to visit Master Zhenke of Jing Mountain:

Sitting before the Hall of the Bright Moon in the deep night, a lingering ray of light reaches even to the Long-geng star.
National Teacher Nanzan Musō Jūshō of Japan was a dharma successor of Zen Master Gao Feng Rujing.
He was a descendant of the Genji clan from the province of Settsu in his native land, a ninth-generation descendant of Emperor Uda.
He entered the monastic life at the age of nine and became a full monk at eighteen. He frequently dreamed of traveling to Shushan in China.

At the beginning of his second journey, an elderly monk presented him with an image of Bodhidharma, whereupon he named himself Shushi (Sparse Stone). He then resolved to travel to visit various masters.
First, he called upon Wuyin Fan; next, he saw Yishan Ning. He fully expressed his sincerity in seeking the Dharma.

Yishan said, "In our school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma to be given to others. The Master asked, "Is there not some expedient means? Yishan replied, "The original state..."
"It is vast and empty; this is the Great Expedient. The Master remained in a state of doubt and frustration without ceasing.

He visited Gao Feng again, who asked, "What instructions did Yishan give you? The Master recounted his previous words. Gao Feng shouted in a stern voice, "Why do you not say that the Master has let slip no small amount?
At these words, the Master attained realization. He redoubled his efforts with even greater vigor. One night, after sitting for a long time, he suddenly leaned against the wall and collapsed.

He attained a sudden and great enlightenment and composed a verse containing the line, "Casually striking through the very bones of space. He presented it to Master Feng, who granted him his seal of approval (*inka*).

Thereupon, he emerged from seclusion to follow the profound source of Master Wuxue Yuan. Later, he widely propagated the teachings of the school in his own country and was bestowed the title of National Preceptor Pujie.
The Master’s will was set upon the mists and clouds; leaving the world was not his primary desire, yet he was invited to come forth.

He declined all these honors with great earnestness. When the ruler of that country raised an army to campaign against Nanchan, he entered the presence [of the Master] and, after being invited to sit, requested his retirement.

The King said, "It is not for any other reason; I merely wish to seek the Way from you morning and evening. He again insisted that the Master enter Tianlong Monastery and bestowed upon him a title and a handwritten edict.
Later, he manifested his passing in the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven. His secular age was seventy-nine, and his monastic seniority was sixty. Complete.
His reliquary stupa was located behind the monastery. As for the nails and hair he had cut during his lifetime, which were interred at Yunju, they produced numerous śarīras from within the hair.
