He followed Tian Tong Zu’an Shanjian for a long time, but did not attain realization. He went traveling to visit Liaotang at Tianning Monastery.
Tang asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tiantong. Tang said, "Braving the rain and piercing the cold, what such desperate urgency do you have?
The Master said, "Precisely because the matter of birth and death is urgent. Tang asked, "What is this matter of birth and death? The Master made a striking gesture with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*).
The Abbot said, "Dare you come here to pull a tiger's whiskers? Go to the Hall! One day, while in the meditation hall, the Abbot brought up the story of the cypress tree in the courtyard.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, the Abbot struck him across the face with his palm. From this, he attained awakening.

Initially, he took up residence at Beichen Monastery in Fuzhou; later, he moved to Yunju. In the *Guiyou* year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict summoned eminent monks from throughout the land. The Master...

He responded to the imperial summons, and his eloquent exposition pleased the Emperor. That autumn, he was commissioned to perform sacrifices at Mount Lu. When the rites were completed, an imperial edict appointed him as the abbot of Mount Jing.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of Yunju? The Master said, "The road turns, the stream winds back; the empty courtyard is still.

The monk asked, "What is one who dwells within that realm? The Master said, "In an age of Great Peace, one has a body of freedom. The monk said, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding both the person and the realm."
[The Master] said, "I wish to hear a single phrase for those at the beginning stage. The Master replied, "A hairless hawk flies close to the sky. A question was asked:
"When one encounters a person who has realized the Way on the road, and does not respond with either speech or silence, what then? The Master said, "Only one who has realized the Way knows.
The questioner said, "How can you, Master, meet me with such weapons of war? The Master said, "Catching a thief is not as good as scaring him off. The questioner said, "For one with clear eyes..."
"One cannot deceive him in the slightest. The Master said, "I knew from the start that you did not have good intentions.

He asked a newly arrived monk, "In this place of mine, tigers and wolves block the path and thorns reach the heavens. What urgent business brings you here, O Honored Guest? The monk replied, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master.
The Master said, "I shall not ask about the phrase you uttered upon entering the gate; however, as for the sandals beneath your feet, what..."
[The Master] asked where he had come from. The monk hesitated; the Master then gave a shout. He asked again, "Where did you leave yesterday? [The monk] replied, "Lushan.

The Master said, "No need for further examination. The Master once examined a monk, saying, "I have recently received an official document ordering that you, Venerable Sir, must be 'tidied up' (examined)."
The monk said, "I am no spy. The Master said, "Even so, you must first undergo interrogation. The monk said, "Master, do not use your position to bully others.
The Master extended his hand and said, "Bring me your credentials. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him with his palm.
Another monk said, "I have long heard that the Master possesses such a vital pivot of teaching. The Master said, "This mountain monk has lost face. A monk asked, "I have received..."
[The monk] said, "I have heard that the Master has a device for 'straightening things out. Is this true or not? The Master stared at him intently and said, "Are you coming forward to confess?
The monk replied, "This student has already overturned the meditation seat! The Master asked, "Where are you from? The monk said, "Keep your eyes open!
The Master said, "You are a spirit clinging to the grass and leaning on the trees. Later, while clearing away weeds, a monk asked, "How many [years] has this plot of land been here?"
At that time, he had cleared the ground completely. The Master raised his hoe and said, "I wonder, Elder, what do you call this? The monk was speechless.
The Master threw down the hoe and said, "When will this patch of ground ever be cleared? He asked: Question: [What is this?]
"Riding the tiger's head and gathering its tail—what about the matter in between? The Master said, "He has attained freedom.
[The monk] asked, "As for the ancient saying, 'I too cannot bring it forth'—what is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Entering the water and seeing the tall man.
On the day of the discourse at Jingshan, a monk asked, "Receiving the grace from the nine-layered heavens, atop the Five-Crested Peak..."
Holding fast at the ancestral pass, the Chan practitioners of the four seas all lean their ears, wishing to hear a single song of ten-thousand-year joy.
This student has come forward; I pray that the Master will raise the chant. The Master said: "Strike the golden bell atop the summit of Mount Sumeru. [The student] said:

"In that case, a man of transcendent measure clarifies matters of transcendent measure; during a time of Great Peace, one sings a song of Great Peace. The Master said: "A difference of a hair’s breadth, and heaven and earth [are divided]."
[The monk] said, "A vast distance separates us. You, Master, have come from afar from the capital and have recently arrived at Mount Jing.

What is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said, "Wait until the Bowel Peak leaps up, and then I shall tell you. [The monk] said, "I have just heard it said in the preface: 'A withered tree of a thousand years meets the spring;
a single generation of *tánhuā* flowers manifests as an auspicious omen. This may truly be called sincere speech. The Master said, "Do you believe this?"
"What is the use of the many mental consciousnesses calculating? The monk said, "On this day when the feast for dragons and elephants is spread, one casually pulls back the silken banner and returns.
The Master said, "If you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, take care not to suffer the 'dotted forehead' (failure). The monk requested further instruction. The Master said:

"What is lacking in your own portion? Yet you come to request further instruction. As the monk prepared to respond, the Master said, "You know only how to hurry along the road, but you do not realize you have missed the way.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The mouth of the alms bowl faces the sky. The monk said, "That was used by an ancient master. The Master said, "I use it most appropriately. The monk asked, "How so?"

"This is a most extraordinary matter. The Master said, "A field of a thousand years has eight hundred owners. The student said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "To this day it cannot be taken away;
it is left for the old farmer to plow. Question: "What is the Way? The Master said: "When the trees fall, the cliffs and rocks appear. The student asked:
"As for what the former worthies said—that there are carp on the mountain peaks and duckweed in the bottom of the well—what is the meaning of this?"
"How is it? The Master said, "If you see it and do not seize it, it will be a thousand miles away when you think of it.
He ascended the hall and cited Yunmen, who said: "On level ground there are countless dead people; he who can emerge from the thorn-brake forest is a masterful hand.
At that time, a monk said, "In that case, the Head Seat in the hall has a point of excellence. Yunmen said, "Sulū sulū. The Master said, "Yunmen was like this..."
As for the Way, Yunju was not like this. On level ground, he brought countless people to life; to enter the thicket of thorns is to be a master hand.
Suddenly, if someone comes forth to speak of long and short, he takes up his staff and strikes them across the back.
Why? Water wets what is moist; fire seeks what is dry. Calamity and fortune have no gate; they are summoned only by oneself. He addressed the assembly: "In the house of a patriarch..."
Having attained even a single word or half-phrase, there is nothing that does not serve to extract nails and pull out wedges for the student, to untangle adhesions and remove fetters.
It is like skillfully wielding the Great Black Sword (Tāo Ā); naturally, one does not injure one's own hand.

Nowadays, those who occupy the seat of the Master and instruct their disciples merely memorize texts and adorn their speech with flowery language to boast to later generations, thereby increasing evil habits and remaining unaware of their own true nature.
The path of the body is like wearing tattered rags while walking through a thicket of thorns; one cannot move with ease.
At this point, the school of the Direct Pointing of Shaolin falls to the ground, which is truly a cause for lamentation. You who travel as itinerant monks must each carry your own eyes;
do not allow yourselves to fall into the nets of others from which you can never emerge. As the ancients said: "Having entered this gate, do not harbor conceptual understanding. If...

According to this mountain monk’s perspective, even if you were to suddenly forget all intellectual understanding, you would still be a person outside the gate. Upon reaching this point, you must distinguish between the black and the white;
take care. [Ascending the hall: "When what meets the eye is not understood as the Way, how can one know the path when setting foot upon it?"
The ancients spoke thus; it was much like laboring without merit. Where this mountain monk sees it, I wish for all of you to know it together.
He suddenly took up his staff, struck once, and said: "If only the snow could melt away completely, spring would naturally arrive."
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: The true Buddha has no form; what is there to bathe? To see empty flowers in the air at the Lumbinī Garden is a false perception.
Yunmen’s command has not reached its full effect until this day. Suddenly grasping his staff, he called to the assembly, saying:
"How do you handle the matter of today? One lost the sword in Kunming Lake; on the banks of the Qujiang River, one found a saw. He struck the ground with the staff and descended from the seat.
The Master ascended the hall and said: "When this old monk was clearing the wilderness, I dug up a single polished axe-head upon the foundations of this Dharma Hall.
For a long time I have gathered you, my brothers; if there is anyone among you who can make use of it, I shall entrust it to you with both hands.
But if you cannot bear its weight, then let the old monk take it back. Why such a desperate hurry? It would be better to cast it onto the rubbish heap and let it be."

[The Master] said, "Master Shen can say such things and get away with it, but I cannot say such things and get away with it.
Sandou said, "I have attained it; you have not. The Master said, "Xuansha and Gushan were a difficult elder brother and a difficult younger brother.
If one wishes to emerge from this, both are still lacking in awakening. Xuedou said, "He only knows how to greedily gaze at the white waves, unaware that he has lost his hand."
“Oar! Where are the eyes of the clergy and the laity? He suddenly picked up his staff, drew a line, and said:

“A tangle of willow threads cannot be gathered; they are draped with mist upon the jade balustrade. On the occasion of the Buddha-Bathing ceremony, he ascended the hall and raised the case concerning Yueshan’s dialogue with Nun Zun regarding the bathing of the Buddha.
The Master said: “Yueshan could let go but could not take back; Nun Zun could take back but could not let go. Altogether...”
"The eye that transcends the school has not yet appeared. Huanglong Nan said, "As for these two venerable masters, one coming out and one going in, I have not yet seen who wins or loses.
Thirty years from now, do not misrepresent this; you have already made a mistaken use of names and phrases.
My own realization at Jingshan is something I wish all of you to know together. Today, in the hall, we are invited to bathe the Buddha. As for 'this one' and 'that one,' they must not be moved."
[He] attained [enlightenment]. When the handle of the ladle reaches the hand, do not be negligent or coarse. Striking the whisk, he said: "Offer this profound mind to the dust-motes and lands;
this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. On the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the Guiwei year of the Yongle era, he passed away at Budong Xuan (The Immovable Pavilion).
His worldly age was fifty-eight, and his monastic seniority was forty-five. After his cremation, wherever the smoke and flames reached, [relics] remained.
His virtues were like pearls strung together. His stupa was erected on the southern slope of Mount Lingxiao.
Chan Master Yuanliang Yueming of Tiantong, in Ningbo Prefecture, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shouchang Yuan. He was the son of the Zhou family of Ninghai. Initially, he resided at Ruiyan.
Later, he moved to Tiantong. He offered this inscription for the stupa of his predecessor, Master Hongzhi: "Alas! A mountain does not refuse the dust, and thus it can achieve its height;
the ocean does not refuse the flowing waters, and thus it can achieve its depth.

Had the Master not previously prepared the wheel of vows for the six perfections and ten thousand practices, how could he have established the merit of this Great Dharma throughout past and present? When a Sage appears in the world, he acts as..."
A teacher for a hundred generations, a peer appearing but once in a thousand years—only you, Master, have attained this. Your towering stupa shall forever stabilize this eastern valley;

the true regulations of our school’s tradition shall thus be restored. These humble words of proclamation are deeply engraved upon the cliffs and gullies, praying that you may return once more to serve as a model for the Dharma.
Chan Master Jingxi Lai Fu of Dingshui Monastery in Cixi, Ningbo Prefecture, was a dharma heir of Chan Master Yue of Mount Jing. He was the son of the Wang family of Fengcheng in Nanchang.
In the Renwu year of the Zhizheng era, he received the tonsure at Xifang Temple in his native county. He then traveled to Shuangjing to pay respects to Nan Chu, remaining there for a long time.
He then attained realization and entered [the path]. Avoiding the military conflict, he eventually took charge of Dingshui Monastery in Cixi.

All that had fallen into ruin was restored to a brilliant new state. Because the war had obstructed his travels, he was unable to visit his mother; he therefore built a cottage east of the stream named Puan (Reed Hermitage).
I adopt the interpretation of the Venerable Master Chen. Later, he moved to Tianting Monastery in Ningbo and Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou.

He raised the story of Mazu sending someone with a *yuanxiang* (circle) to Jingshan, with the verse: "Sealing it back and returning it, I thank you for your special kindness; The sea moon and mountain clouds are manifest to those who see them intimately.
Do not blame Nanyang for being too talkative; Who in the universe is a person free from doubt? He raised [this case].
A monk asked Mazu about the saying, "Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations. The verse says: "A single scroll of ice-silk, five colors fresh;
The jade shuttle skillfully weaves the spring of the Phoenix Pond. The embroidered mandarin ducks are displayed for you to view, Yet the golden needle is not passed on to others.
He then raised the dialogue between Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti regarding the teaching of the non-dual Dharma-gate. The verse says: "In the realm of Wondrous Joy..."

Regarding the "Inquiry into Sickness" chapter: Before the occasion even arose, he had already scrutinized and penetrated the old Vimalakīrti. Within the atoms of all lands he constantly speaks, while empty space listens;
a single silence in response was already far more than enough. Concerning the dialogue where Mañjuśrī instructs Sudhana to gather medicinal herbs, the verse says:

"Do you understand when this medicine is brought forth? This divine prescription need not be asked of Jīvaka. If one says its skill in killing and reviving is complete, Then the multitudes of beings across the great earth..."
Illnesses increased considerably. [The Master] raised the dialogue concerning Lingyun seeing the peach blossoms and Xuansha’s remark that he had not yet reached the ultimate.

He offered this verse: All head toward Chang’an to tread the early spring; Purple steeds follow the fragrant dust wherever they go. Year after year, amidst the songs and pipes of the east wind— How many are there who truly recognize the peach blossoms?
In the *wushen* year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned to the capital. He was granted a meal in the inner court and received the Emperor’s personal consolation.
He was treated with great generosity. Just as the Great Assembly at Mount Zhong was being established, the Emperor issued an edict for the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma.

He further commanded Prince Chun of Shu to follow the Master to inquire about the Way. There exists a letter of over one thousand words titled "Reply to the Questions of Prince of Shu on the Essential Methods of Chan Meditation," as well as a letter of over five hundred words titled "Reply to the Questions of Prince Jin on the Essentials of Chan.
Among his writings are the *Puanji* (Collected Works of Puan) and the *Puan Waiji* (Supplementary Collected Works of Puan).
He traveled through the world.
Chan Master Xiūān Wúzhìkě of Jìngcí Monastery in Hángzhōu Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Língyǐn Míng; he was the son of the Lí family from Línghǎi in Tàizhōu.
At the age of twelve, he entered Shimen Temple under his uncle, the śramaṇa Zhongzhi. At nineteen, he received full ordination and became a bhikṣu. He visited Pujue at Lingyin Monastery;

during their brief exchange of questions and answers, his doubts were suddenly dispelled. In the *bingxu* year of the Zhizheng era, he emerged from seclusion to serve as abbot of Ansheng Monastery in Taizhou.
After five years there, he was transferred to Long’en. Two years later, he succeeded to Zhenru. The following year, he traveled...

The Xuanzheng Yuan selected him to preside over Longhua Temple, where he sat for thirteen summer retreats. In the *guichou* year of the Hongwu era, the Prefect of Hangzhou ordered him to take charge of Zhongzhu Temple.
Upon his arrival, the veteran monks of Jingci Temple all strove together to oppose him, repeatedly refusing to yield;

having no other choice, he was forced to reside there for two years before retiring to lie in seclusion at Zhuyuan. One day, manifesting illness, he summoned those around him and said, "I am about to depart."
His attendants stepped forward with a cup and writing brushes, but the Master waved them away, saying, "In our school, there is fundamentally no speech; it is simply tranquil and still.

He passed away at the age of sixty-nine, with fifty years of monastic seniority. After his body was cremated, his teeth and jawbone were found intact like strung pearls, and his *śarīra* relics were brilliant and lustrous.
His remains were like golden crystal; his disciples collected all that was indestructible, along with his skeletal remains, and returned them to the Longhua Pagoda to be enshrined there.
Chan Master Hui'en Juechu of Jiangxin Temple in Wenzhou Prefecture, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Xin of Tianjie, had long relied upon Xin while Xin resided at Hulong.
On the banks of the river, the Master once shared the teaching seat with [his predecessor]. Later, when Xìn entered nirvana, the Master took up residence at Shèngquán in Jiànyè.
He subsequently moved to Yǎshān in Yǒngjiā. Not long after, the position at Jiāngxīn became vacant, and the local governor invited him to preside over it.
His writings include the *Recorded Sayings of the Three Assemblies*.
Chan Master Wuming Qianyan Yuanzhang of Fulong Monastery in Yiwu, Jinhua Prefecture, was a successor of Chan Master Tianmu Ben. He was the son of the Dong family of Xiaoshan.
At the age of seven, he followed his paternal uncle, the bhikṣu Tanfang, at the Famen Monastery in Fuyang. At nineteen, he received the tonsure.

He received full ordination and studied the Vinaya at Lingzhi Monastery. Later, while attending a meal for the monastic community hosted by the Chancellor at the Prime Minister’s residence, Zhongfeng happened to be seated there.
Seeing the Master from afar, he called out to him and asked, “How do you spend your daily life? The Master replied, “I practice the Buddha-recitation. Zhongfeng asked, “Where is the Buddha now?

As the Master hesitated, Zhongfeng rebuked him with a stern voice. The Master prostrated himself and requested instruction on the essential points of the Dharma. Zhongfeng [responded] with the word “Dog.”
He was given the "The Son Has No Buddha-Nature" discourse. He lived in a thatched hut at Lingyin for three years without his side even touching the mat.
One day, upon hearing the sound of sparrows, he attained realization. He hurried to see Feng, who again rebuked him. The Master returned in indignation.

At night, when all was quiet, a rat overturned a cat’s food bowl; as it fell to the ground, it made a noise. Suddenly, he attained full awakening. He went back once more to question Feng, who said: "Zhao..."
Zhaozhou asked, "Why do you say there are none? The Master said, "The mouse eats the cat's food. Feng said, "Not yet. The Master said, "The food vessel is broken.
Feng asked, "What is it like after it is broken? The Master said, "The square bricks have been crushed to pieces. Feng then smiled and instructed him, saying, "Guard and maintain this well yourself.
When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. Having received these instructions, the Master went into seclusion at the Eastern Hermitage of Tianlong.
Xiaoyin presided over Zhongzhu and earnestly recommended his reinstatement. The Xuanzheng Yuan’s Tuo-huan also dispatched messengers to urge him, but the Master declined them both.
Before long, various monasteries vied with one another to invite him; however, realizing he would not be tolerated by the times, the Master took up his staff and crossed the Tāo River.
He traveled east to Fulong Mountain in Yiwu, where the mountain resembled a blue lotus flower, and there he established his hermitage.
Pointing toward the edge of a cliff, he said, "There is water on this mountain; I shall dwell there. Suddenly, a mountain spring overflowed, appearing the color of white milk.

The Master then took up residence beneath a large tree. This was in the tenth month of the Dingmao year of the Taiding era. Previously, there had been a Chan temple on the mountain named Shengshou, which had long been abandoned and in ruins.
When the Master entered the mountains, the local villagers all dreamed that a strange monk had arrived, and they subsequently joined together to [rebuild it].
He felled timber to construct a refined hermitage, which, following its original name, was developed into a great monastery (*mahā-vihāra*).

The imperial court thrice dispatched high-ranking ministers to bestow incense and confer upon him the title "Chan Master Fohui Yuanjian Puzhi" (Buddha-Wisdom, Perfect Mirror, Universal Salvation), along with a golden-embroidered dharma robe.

A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "A wild horse enters an ox pen. The monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A wild horse enters an ox pen."
The Master said, "It is raining well today. [A monk] asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "It is not far from here to Yiwu. [Another] asked, "What is the guest within the guest?
The Master said, "Placing your hands together at your chest and asking another person. [Another] asked, "What is the host within the guest?
The Master said, "Sitting upon the hall at noon on the coming day. [Another] asked, "What is the guest within the host? The Master said—
[The monk] said, "At times he is joyful, at times he is angry. [The monk] asked, "What is the Lord among lords? The Master said, "Transversely grasping the Mohe sword—no Buddhas, no Patriarchs.
[The monk] asked, "What is the white ox on the open ground? The Master said, "Lying down in the grass. [The monk] asked, "Who can ride it?
The Master said, "One who has no beard or mustache. [The monk] asked, "Among the three bodies, which body preaches the Dharma? The Master said...
[A monk] asked, "The oil-selling woman combs her hair with water; 'Deshan’s staff, Linji’s shout'—what is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "An evil person takes precedence. [Another] asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Lacking the strength to raise my fist.
[Another] asked, "What is the meaning of Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing? The Master said, "I have a mouth, but it cannot be opened."
Question: "In the midst of the vast and turbulent dust, how does one distinguish the master? The Master raised his fist and showed it to him. Question: "After distinguishing him, what then?
The Master said: "Where is your master? Question: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his servants;
I wonder, who is he? The Master said: "A broken broom on a heap of refuse. Question: "I do not understand, Master. The Master said: "Ask."
He took his seat on the meditation platform. A monk asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "To have a mouth like one who is mute.
The monk asked, "What is the second phrase? The Master said, "To have eyes like one who is blind. The monk asked, "What is the third phrase?"
The Master said, "Even if the staff were broken, I would still not let you go. He then threw down his whisk and said, "This is the old monk’s second phrase.
What is the first phrase? He then descended from the seat. On another occasion, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'?
The Master said, "The sun shines upon the mountains and rivers; their reflections quiver. The monk asked, "What is 'taking away the environment but not... [The text here is incomplete].

"Seizing both man and environment. The Master said, "When the battle array is set against the water, one’s courage and strength increase. [The student] asked, "What is it like when both man and environment are seized?

The Master said, "Even before a sharp blade, one remains ever level; even with the most virulent poison, one remains at ease. [The student] asked, "What is it like when neither man nor environment is seized?
The Master said, "The rustic elder knows nothing of the labors of Yao and Shun; he beats the drum loudly to sacrifice to the River God."
The monks prostrated. The Master said, "A musk deer naturally has fragrance; why stand against the wind?

He then said, "It is easy to turn mountains, rivers, and the lands back into oneself, but it is difficult to turn oneself back into mountains, rivers, and the lands. Having brought this forth, he concluded.
"Before your parents were born, bring forth a single phrase. [He] addressed the assembly. "Today is the first day of the month; the ascent to the hall has been completed.
*Hraḍana*. The sun rises in the west. [He] addressed the assembly. He cited the karmic conditions concerning Deshan’s carrying of the alms bowl and added:
"As for this final phrase, Deshan, Yantou, and Xuefeng—none of them could leap out of it. Thereupon, he let out a shout.
"A great man should become a true king; why rely on a borrowed one? He addressed the assembly, and after a long silence, said:
"Does the assembly understand? If you understand, all matters are as one family; if you do not understand, there are ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences.
Linji said: "When I was at Huangbo, I received sixty severe blows of the staff; it was like being brushed with a bundle of mugwort. Now I wish to reflect upon another beating—who would give it?"
As he was about to strike, a monk stepped forward and said, "I will strike first. Jie Du handed his staff to the monk.
As the monk reached out to take it, Jie Du struck him immediately. Observe how he directly reveals this: there is not even a hair's breadth of room for you to approach;
how could this be fathomed by ordinary sentiments? Usually, I scold you bitterly and beat you with a heavy staff, yet you do not give rise to ignorance.
[The assembly] assembled, yet they merely held a Dharma-assembly; when have they ever dreamed of the ancestral style of my predecessors?
Therefore, the ancients said: "The Way of Linji is about to fall to the ground—how painful! At such a time as this, what should be done?
To transcend the multitudes, one must be a man of heroic spirit; to match the victor, one must be a lion’s cub. [To the assembly: Master Fu Daoshi said:

Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning, one rises together with him. Whether rising or sitting, he is always in attendance; whether speaking or remaining silent, we dwell together.
Not separated by even a hair’s breadth, they are like form and its shadow. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this sound of your voice.
Xuansha said, "Great as Master Fu Dashi was, he recognized nothing more than that which is bright and lucid.
Dongshan Cong said, "Tell me, do monks ever sleep during the day? Baoning Yong said, "When one wishes to sleep, one sleeps;
when one wishes to rise, one rises. Washing the face makes the skin glow; drinking tea moistens the beard. The great ocean is but red dust."
Birth. Waves arise upon level ground. Hehe, ahehe. Lili lila. O three venerable elders, you are much like Xu Liu carrying planks.
Master Fu Dashi still has not rid himself of his worldly airs; if one speaks of the supreme vehicle of the patriarchal lineage, you all lack awakening.
Now tell me: what kind of eyes does ignorance possess? Have you not heard it said: "One must truly brandish the sword"? If...
Without brandishing the sword, the fishing father perches in his nest and addresses the assembly: "Today is the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month. Yunmen’s single melody has never had a score.
How could it compare to the Unobstructed (Wuming) tune, which rises ever higher? Spontaneously sung forth, the ten thousand mountains dance.
With the great earth as the lute and empty space as the drum, every beat follows one another and every sound assists the next. You people must listen well!"

How can the "White Snow" and "Spring Sun" be counted? Who among you knows the true meaning within this? Through the long, silent night, the wind passes through the pines. [The Master] addressed the assembly:

He cited the case where Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra gave rise to views of the Buddha and views of the Dharma, and were consequently cast by the World-Honored One’s majestic power into the two Iron Ring Mountains.
The Master said: "O Great Assembly, if you do not give rise to views of the Buddha or views of the Dharma, will you still avoid being cast away?"
"Are the two Iron Ring Mountains small? The World-Honored One, too, was like one who loves his child so much that he does not notice their ugliness.
He addressed the assembly, citing Langye Huijue: "A phrase and no-phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree; when the tree falls, the vine withers—a fine pile of rotten firewood.
Dahui said, "The heart of a thief is always fearful. Although it is thus, the kindness is great and hard to repay. The Master said, "One person becomes a Buddha."
Regarding the deliberation on the Dharma: one person may propagate it according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet when examined closely, it is found that all are lacking in awakening.
As for the place where ignorance is seen, it must also be known by everyone. Whether there is a phrase or no phrase, it is like a vine leaning against a tree; when the tree falls, the vine withers.
Xiang addressed the assembly: "The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. On every side, the green mountains spread their smiling brows.
The Sutras have Sutra masters; the Shastras have Shastra masters. Do not take umbrage that this old monk has no Dharma to preach; it merely tires you all to stand here for a short while."

Addressing the assembly: "A single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function proceed simultaneously. To understand the meaning within this, it is like striking the third watch at noon.
"All you Zen adepts," he said, "speaking thus, the four corners have already fallen flat to the ground. Thereupon, he let out a shout.
Now tell me: which is the guest and which is the host? Which is the illumination and which is the function? Again, he lets out a shout and says:
"This very one is the guest; this very one is the host; this very one is the illumination; this very one is the function. Again, he lets out a shout and says: "And yet, it is not the guest."
"It is not the master; it is not the illuminator; it is not the function. What is it? He then gave a shout and said:
"To step forward seeking understanding is to deliberately strike down one's own spirit. To the assembly he said: "The waters at Dragon Gate are swift; a single phrase cuts across the current.
The wind atop the thatched hut is high; waves rise from a thousand mountains. The Buddhas of the three periods hold their tongues in awe; the six patriarchs..."
"The Patriarch had his share of 'cutting off the forehead'; the old monks of the world look up at him in admiration, unable to reach his level.
As for you all here, how will you meet with Wuming? [He suddenly picks up his staff and says: 'In this way, in this way—man and environment are both snatched away.
Not in this way, not in this way—illumination and function are simultaneous. [He strikes the ground once and says: A dragon gives birth to gold."
Phoenix! Breaking through the azure lapis lazuli. (He lets out a shout. To the assembly: When the World-Honored One held up the flower, he was scattering sand in people's eyes.
Kāśyapa’s smile was his whole body falling into the weeds. Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing was a grievous injustice to Heaven.

The Second Patriarch’s “seeking peace of mind” was like a rat dwelling in gold. Deshan’s striking with the staff was wild and reckless; Linji’s shouting below was like trying to stop thirst by eating salt.
Thirsty! A mountain ox feigning to drink from a stream; washing earth with mud. Yangshan thrusts in his spade—his very life cannot escape it.
Jueyi points a finger—what kind of principle is this? Xuefeng rolls a ball—an old man who knows no shame. Shigong draws his bow—deceiving the blind and the deaf.
Zhaozhou interrogates the old woman—a great deal of confusion. Xuansha has not yet reached the end—the story is split into two pieces. This whole crew!
"You wretched, decrepit old fellow! In life you were reckless; in death you are callous. Your offenses fill the heavens; your skulls litter the wilds.
Ignorance could not restrain itself and has buried you in the same pit as him.
Holding up his staff, he struck it once and said, "It makes the wind shiver through the worlds of the ten directions. Before the Dharma Hall, the weeds are more than ten feet deep!"
"Where do you all go to vent your breath? After a long silence, he said: "If you intend to direct your mind toward it, the two Iron Ring Mountains will close in.
Let it be natural, and it will be permeated through and through. He then struck once. When a guest arrived, he ascended the Dharma seat after donning his robes.
"One might think this Way-man is a high monk of many wonders," [the guest thought]. "In truth, he can do nothing at all. The west wind blows.
A fine rain falls; fallen leaves fill the empty courtyard. A guest comes to visit; the green mountains naturally welcome and see him off.

[The Master] ascends the hall at the request of the Japanese nation for the sake of the Dharma robes. He cites Shimen Cong, who said: "Of the twenty-eight patriarchs in the Western Heaven, all received the transmission of the robe and the Dharma.
After the Sixth Patriarch in this land, those who attained the Way were many; yet they transmitted only the Dharma, not the robe."
As for robes: ignorance is not like this. A robe is used to represent the Dharma; therefore, it is called the "Dharma-robe.
Because people can broaden the Way, it is called the "Dharma-body. Because it is omnipresent and nowhere obscured, it is called the "Dharma-eye.
Today, I request before the assembly this single Dharma-robe of the Great Ancestor of High Peak, to be offered in worship at Mount Geumgang in the Kingdom of Goryeo.
Furthermore, this single Dharma robe of my late master Huanzhu has been in my possession for thirty years.
Now, Chief Seat Dazhuo wishes to request it back for his own offerings.

Striking the whisk, he descended from his seat. On the fourteenth day of the sixth month of the Dingyou year of the Zhizheng era of Emperor Yuan.
Manifesting a slight illness, he bathed and changed his robes. Gathering the assembly, he spoke a verse, saying: "Throughout my life I have been loquacious; today, I have failed.
One phrase roars through the heavens—the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished. He passed away suddenly. His secular age was seventy-four, and his monastic seniority was fifty-six.
His disciples used a ceramic sarcophagus to enshrine his entire body and interred him at Qingsong Monastery. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Fohuijian.
The Master:
Chan Master Lintu Wize of Shizi Forest Monastery in Suzhou Prefecture, a native of the Tan family of Julong, Jixian.

He received his monastic training at Heshan and attained the Dharma under Zhongfeng. After he took up residence [at the monastery], a monk asked: "Buddha after Buddha hands it down; patriarch after patriarch transmits it. At this point, the text ends.
"In the end, what have you transmitted? The Master said, "Before your feet had even crossed the threshold, I gave you thirty blows.
A monk asked, "If Bodhidharma did not come to this eastern land and the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven, is there still a way to benefit others?
The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is this way of benefiting others? The Master said, "The lanterns in the bathhouse laugh until one side is split."
The monk said, "Is it not this very point where the student turns himself around? The Master said, "There is no road to ascend to heaven; there is no gate to enter the earth.
The monk said, "Today I am most fortunate to have heard the lion’s roar. The Master then gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master said:
"If you wish to prostrate, go ahead and prostrate. This one shout has never once fallen to the ground.

A monk asked, "The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma with a single sound, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind. I wonder, Master, how do you guide people? The Master said, "A frog leaps up into the sky;
an earthworm dashes across the Eastern Sea. The monk said, "If that is so, then one transcends both Buddhas and Patriarchs."

The Master said, "Where did you see this? The monk replied, "Throughout ancient times and the present, it has never fallen; it is clearly right before one's eyes. The Master said, "You fabricated Chan practitioner!

[The monk] said, "A horse has a bloated belly. [The Master] said, "Ten generations of past and present—beginning and end do not depart from the present moment of thought.

[The monk] asked, "Since there is a beginning and an end, how can they not depart? The Master said, "Throughout the world, one seeks a physician to apply moxibustion to the left shoulder-blade of a pig.

"What excellence does he possess? The Master said, "A small fish bites through the leg of a cormorant; a white heron takes flight and perches atop the branch of a tree.

[The student] said, "The mind of nirvāṇa is easy to understand, but the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify. I pray that you, Master, will provide instruction on the similarities and differences among the five schools."
The Master said, "Stepping back three paces, I show you all this: Zhaozhou spoke the word 'wu' (no). Opening one's mouth reveals the heart and liver;
why then do you all create obstacles for yourselves? A monk requested instruction, saying, "All sentient beings, down to the smallest insect, possess Buddha-nature.
Why is it that only the dog has none? The Master said, "Forget about the dog; even if you were to ask Śākyamuni himself..."
"Does Maitreya still possess Buddha-nature? The monk also said, "He does not. The monk asked, "Zhaozhou’s Chan is on the tips of his lips;
why can he only say the word 'no'? The Master said, "Zhaozhou’s insight only reached this point.
The monk asked, "Does the Master not approve of Zhaozhou? The Master said, "Yes. The monk asked, "Zhaozhou was an ancient Buddha; why..."
He would not consent. The Master said, "Where is Zhaozhou? and immediately after, he gave a shout. He addressed the assembly:
"In other quarters, there is 'sea-shell Zen,' 'oyster-shell Zen,' and 'iron-spade Zen. Here in my place, it is like a gourd on the water:
as soon as it is touched it moves, and as soon as it is pressed down it rolls; it is lively and slippery, leaving you with no way to deal with it. Yesterday was the beginning of Yang."
"Returning. See how he has spoken and brought forth the roots of birth. "All of you, try to pick it up for me and look!
He addressed the assembly: "Sometimes he extends the Buddha-hand; sometimes he lets out the donkey's hoof—wrong! Sometimes he slaps the meditation seat; sometimes he strikes the incense table—wrong!
Sometimes his tongue grows hair and his lips grow mold; his staff leans against the wall corner for years. —Linji Yixuan.

"The nostrils of the mountain have all been pierced at once. "Wrong! "All you Zen practitioners, if you can recognize this old monk in those three places where he was wrong, I will invite you to eat noodles made without flour.
To the assembly, he said: "The Great Master Linji said, 'In my place here, this is the living meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West.
Whatever is needed for the occasion, it is used immediately. He then picked up his whisk and waved it."
He said, "In my place here, it is also alive. When you need it, you use it; everything is as the occasion demands.
Now tell me, is this the same as Linji’s, or is it different? He struck once, threw down [the staff], and said, "Master Linji still lacks this one move.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not reached, take a step forward. Where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not spoken..."
At that place, he spoke of taking up a single phrase and addressed the assembly, saying: "One *pu* is nine *li*; three *pu* are twenty-seven *li*.
This is a place where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not traveled; yet this old monk has traveled there. Today is the third, tomorrow is the fourth, and the day after is the fifth.
This is a place where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not spoken; yet this old monk has spoken here. He let out a shout and said:
"It is better to engage in mutual abuse with a person of wisdom than to converse with one who lacks it. Addressing the assembly, he raised an analogy:
"It is like a cow passing through a window lattice; its head, horns, and four hooves all pass through, yet only its tail cannot get through. The Master said:
"This is where the Patriarch Dongshan left his affairs unfinished. For thirty years I have traveled among the teachers, and I too have two matters that remain unresolved.
What are these two matters? When hungry, one wants to eat; when weary, one wants to sleep. He addressed the assembly: "The lame rely on their staff for their lives;
those crossing the water rely on their boats for their lives. There is a reason for this; there is no other way."
Because one body gives rise to the sorrow of another body. In the school of the patch-robed monks, they snatch away food and drive off the oxen.
If you intend to look with your eyes, they immediately shut the doors and windows; if you intend to open your mouth to speak, they immediately block your throat.
When there is no moon on the night corridor, they do not light a lamp; let the pillar continue until its head is smashed. To the assembly: Compassion is not the Buddha; wrath is [the Buddha].
"It is not a demon. In Mingzhou,布袋 (Pudeng) drags it horizontally and vertically; everyone is soiled by their own excrement yet remains unaware of the stench.
On clean ground, it is precisely the right place to defecate. How far apart are the golden nest and the grassy nest? When the cold season comes and the leaves fall, no one sweeps them up;
let them pile up as much as they will before the gate. He addressed the assembly: "The old fellow Tianru is but a single dull-witted monk. What [dispute]..."
Yet people fail to recognize him for what he is. When they say he is towering and majestic, he is actually quite humble and unassuming;
when they say he is humble and unassuming, he is again towering and majestic. At times he assumes the guise of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), discoursing on the profound and the wondrous;
at other times he manifests three heads and six arms, exhibiting anger and malice. In each of these instances...
"You try to recognize him but fail to grasp him. Little do you realize that this old man is not within your eyes;
he is, rather, within your nostrils. If you do not believe me, reach out and feel for him. Even if you fail to find him, you will at least find your own nostrils.
He addressed the assembly, citing Linji: "I was at the place of my late master Huangbo, where I ate six..."
The Ten Sticks of Pain. They are like a broom made of thistle branches. The Master said: "What a coarse fellow with stubborn skin and leathery bones, one who knows nothing of pain or itching!
How does he compare to the descendants of recent times? Every one of them has blood beneath their skin;
you cannot move them even by a hair’s breadth. How extraordinary! He addressed the assembly, citing the story of Baizhang and the Wild Fox. The Master said: "It was previously stated—"
"Not falling. Later he said, "Not being obscured. This drew in the wild fox, who followed the pack and joined the ranks. *Hè!* (A shout).

Had he been able to let out this one shout at that time, five hundred lifetimes—past and future—would have been ground to dust all at once. To the assembly: Śākyamuni the Old Man cannot push him open;
Bodhidharma the Great Master cannot drive him out. He has drawn in a single mu of field where three snakes and nine rats dwell, exhausting them all.
It is easy to call out a snake; it is difficult to send it away. [The Master] struck his knee and said, "What difficulty is there?

If one has the *Bai Ze* (White Deer) diagram at home, such monsters will certainly not exist. He addressed the assembly: "When a daughter is about to be married off, she must request instruction from her parents on every method for managing the household and making a living.
Only in the matter of giving birth to and raising children does she possess these abilities naturally, without waiting for instruction."
As a secular proverb says: "There has never been one who learned how to raise children before she married. How true! Yet, the monastics of the Chan school in recent times have not been so;
they first learn how to preach the Dharma, and only then learn how to become Buddhas. They would rather fail to become Buddhas than do otherwise.

It is impossible that he would not preach the Dharma. How extraordinary! Although the Master did not take charge of monastic affairs, he constantly provided guidance according to the capacity of his listeners.

The Provincial Chancellor and other high officials all prostrated themselves before him, observing the etiquette of disciples. He was repeatedly invited to prominent mountains throughout Zhejiang, yet he firmly declined to go.
He sought seclusion among the marshes of Wusong, where his disciples established a site in the Wu region and constructed buildings for him according to the regulations of a great monastic community.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the name Shizi Lin (Lion Forest). He resided there for thirteen years, and his reputation for the Way grew daily.
In the year Jiamu of the Yuan Zhizheng era, the Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title Chan Master Foxin Pujie Wenhui Dabian, and additionally granted him a golden-embroidered dharma robe.
After his passing, he was interred in a stupa at Suisi-en.
Zen Master Kosen Ingen of Japan’s Kenchō-ji Temple was a native of the Fuji clan in the province of Sagami. The Fuji were a noble lineage within the nation;
the Master was born with extraordinary signs. At the age of thirteen, his parents suddenly relinquished him to the monastic life, and he set out by sea.
He traveled south in search of instruction. Initially, he visited Wujian at Tiantai, who directed him to consult Zhongfeng. Zhongfeng ordered him to serve as an attendant.

The Master repeatedly presented his insights, but Zhongfeng rebuked him, saying, "If you do not sever the roots and sense-objects, how can you be free from entanglement? The Master withdrew and wept in sorrow.
He neglected both eating and sleeping. Lingfeng took pity on his sincerity and said to him: "This mind encompasses all phenomena;
when deluded, it is birth and death; when awakened, it is nirvana. The delusion of birth and death is indeed not easily cast off, yet the awakening to nirvana—"
It is like a speck of gold dust entering the eye; you should know that Prajñā is like a great mass of fire—approaching it will scorch your head and blister your forehead.
Only by maintaining a single thought of non-retrogression, living together with all who live and dying together with all who die, will you naturally accord with the Way.
Should you still fail to awaken, even if a thousand Śākyamunis and ten thousand Maitreyas were to pour out the waters of the four great oceans and enter into you...
"The faculty of hearing is entirely a delusive affliction; none of these are ultimate. Upon hearing this, the Master was struck with awe and broke into a cold sweat.

One day he attained realization and hurried to tell Feng, saying, "Yuanzhen has crashed headlong into a silver mountain and an iron wall! Feng asked, "Since you have entered the silver mountain and the iron wall, why have you come here?
The Master was relieved and fully understood. Feng then instructed him, saying, "Take good care of yourself."
He studied under Jichin, as well as the masters Xugu Ling, Gulin Mao, Dongyu Hai, and Yuejiang Yin, all of whom called him a "lion cub.
When Qingzhuo Cheng returned to his home country, he accompanied the master back; he was revered by those both near and far.

Initially, he took charge of Huilin Temple in Jia Prefecture and successively presided over eight monasteries. Later, he resided at Jianchang Temple in Xiang Prefecture, where one day he gave a final instruction.
While ill, he said to his attendant, "The time has come; you may bring me a brush and inkstone. He then said, "My stupa is already completed, yet its plaque remains unwritten.
He then boldly inscribed the two characters "Xinyin" (Mind-Seal) and passed away while sitting upright. This was the first month of spring in the year Jiayin.
Initially, when a disciple wished to paint a portrait of the Master, he requested a eulogy in advance. The Master drew a perfect circle and inscribed upon it:
"The wondrous marks are perfectly luminous; suchness is unmoving. Meeting [it] at every encounter—what face is this? His worldly lifespan was eighty years.
His monastic seniority was sixty-seven years.
Chan Master Gumei Zhengyou of Gaoyang Mountain in Jianning Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Cheng of Prajna. He was the son of the Ding family of Guixi and relied upon Mount Moshan.

Originally receiving his monastic precepts, he later studied under masters of the "absolute learning" (wuxue) and clarified the fundamental tenets of the school. He wandered through the Jianghuai region for nearly thirty years before entering Min.

Initially, he presided over Tianxin Monastery in Nanpu. In the Jiazi year of the Taiding era, the Jianyang District Magistrate Jiang Demao and the elder Chen Yizong donated their garden to establish a hermitage and invited the Master to be its founding abbot.
The imperial plaque bestowed upon it read "Dajue Miaozhi. Within his quarters...
Every time he raised the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature, he used his tongs and hammer to test and examine [his disciples], never showing the slightest leniency.

At the opening of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall: "Mount Yang’s opening of the retreat is his ordinary livelihood. His eyes emit light; his nostrils breathe the air. When hungry, he eats; when weary, he sleeps.
While others everywhere scatter earth and raise dust, Mount Yang has attained the 'Heart Empty' degree. Thus concluded the summer retreat.
Ascending the hall: For ninety days the feet are restrained; this is, in itself, a mistake. For three months one dwells in retreat;
it is to bind oneself without a rope. When the sack is untied, heaven and earth are vast and empty. Letting go is like tortoise-hair; gathering it back is like hanging a hare’s horn.
Try hanging both eyes in the void; a gust of cool wind arises at the corner of the hall. Ascending the hall: Another ninety days of restraining the feet have passed.
Half [the path remains]. The ground of the mind is not yet clear; it is like pulling a fire-drill—the light has not yet emerged.

Do not let your time and energy be spent in vain. Settle this idle koan. On level ground, you have unexpectedly caught a thief. The old monk comes forth to settle it for you. Small Assembly (Xiaocan):

The moon sets behind the mountain peak, somber; clouds span the valley mouth, dark. If you wish to clarify the matter of birth and death, you must directly see the person of original nature. Is there anyone who understands?
"Is it the person as they originally are? After a long silence, he said: "When the night is still, there is no need to borrow the moon again; the jade hare always hangs in the vast void.
He was born in the *yǐyǒu* year of the Zhìyuán era of the Yuan dynasty and passed away in the *rénchén* year of the Zhìzhèng era.
He taught the Dharma for twenty-nine summers and lived in this world for sixty-eight autumns. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the mountain where he resided.

Chan Master Zhizhe Yichan was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jingci De-yin Puren of Hangzhou Prefecture. He was the son of the Zhao family of Lanxi. At the age of ten, he took up his studies under Qiutan at Baoshi Temple;
at fourteen, he received the tonsure; and at twenty, he began traveling to visit various masters. At that time, Liao Ran was propagating the Way.
The Master went to visit Zhizhe Temple, where his spiritual faculties were ignited by a sudden encounter. He was immediately appointed to attend to the incense.
Later, he met Nan Chu at Shuangjing, where he shared the teaching seat and expounded the Dharma. In the year of Yiwu of the Zhengtong era (1395), he took charge of the West Peak Pure Land Monastery.

In the year of Wuxu (1398), the Ming Emperor Taizu personally led the six armies to Wuzhou and visited Zhizhe Temple, issuing an imperial decree for the Master to preside over it. In the year of Jiachen (1404), he was transferred to Jingci Monastery.
One day, he manifested a slight illness and, counting on his fingers, said, "It is now the fifth month of summer. His attendants replied, "Indeed.
The Master said, "The eighth day of the eighth month is most auspicious; I shall pass away then. When that time arrived, he adjusted his robes, sat upright, and passed away.
His secular age was sixty-four, and his monastic seniority was fifty. His *Mountain Dwelling Poems* and the records of his teachings from three assemblies were circulated in the world.
Chan Master Zhizhan Dexiang of Hangzhou Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Jingci Lin.
A native of his own province, he and Tong’an were both successors of Pingshan.
