The Master questioned him further and again asked, "The Buddhas have not spoken it; the Patriarchs have not transmitted it.

Setting aside the flapping of lips and beating of tongues, or the twinkling of eyes and raising of eyebrows—bring me that one phrase for reaching home! Zhuzi remained silent. The Master said, "The time since the Sage has passed far away; yet..."
"Have this son well-guarded and sustained.
Zen Master Ning of Yifeng presented his realization to Xizhu, who examined him and showed him a verse, saying: "Lush green mountains, layered deep;
rain falls in a misty veil. The lion’s golden mane is not loosened by pulling. I myself know that the time has not yet come—ten times..."
He released nine arrows into the void.

Chan Master Kong'an of White Lotus was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jinglong of Empty Valley at Biyuan in Huzhou Prefecture. He was the son of the Chen family on Turtle Mountain in Dongting, Gusu.
When he first met Lanyun, he later went to Tiger Hill (Húqiū) to pay his respects to Shì’ān and receive the tonsure. When Shì’ān moved to Línghyìn, the Master followed him for seven years.
Subsequently, he traveled to Tiānmù to pay homage at the ancestral pagoda, where he stayed with his staff for over a year. Suddenly, he attained a profound realization.
Upon returning to Lanyun, Lanyun expressed his joy for him. Later, while residing at Bìyán, a monk asked: "What is the great Dharma of the Buddhas?"
The Master said, "This question is most intimate. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when one stands face-to-face in full exposure?

The Master said, "The journey is not yet the truth. [The monk] said, "If a man from the South were to ask about snow, I would say it is willow catkins. The Master said, "How can you call a bell a jar?
In his later years, at West Lake, he selected a site on Xiuji Mountain for his burial vault and built a dwelling there.
The residence was named Zhengzhuan (Orthodox Transmission) Pagoda Courtyard. He further composed an inscription for the pagoda, the gist of which read:

"Alas! Life and death are but a single dream; what need is there for a bone pagoda? It is merely to manifest the fragrant flow of the Buddha-dharma and ensure that the traces of its spiritual power remain unbroken.

By clarifying the truth through illusion, the life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is secured, so that its source is distant and its current flows long. Though this illusory body perishes, the Buddha-nature does not migrate. Hereafter...
The visitor beheld the towering stūpa, its peaks lush and verdant; birds sang among the lofty trees, and springs cascaded from secluded crags.
Without pursuing external objects and without clinging to the internal mind, all likes and dislikes were utterly forgotten, and he was immersed in a state of serene harmony.

Only then did he realize that the Dharma-realm is his body, empty space is his mouth, and the myriad phenomena are his tongue—preaching the Dharma day and night without ever ceasing. Herein he saw it.

Attaining clarity and penetration, as if suddenly sobering from a drunken stupor, one attains a vast realization: that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have never entered nirvana, and this old monk has never passed into parinirvāṇa.
Within the great perfect mirror, we face one another directly; the intent of the Patriarch who came from the West is handed over with both hands.
It is like the ancient masters: Yunmen’s successor was Qingyuan, and Qingyuan’s successor was Dayang; there is no before or after, no coming or going.

Within the sands of the great trichiliocosm, self and other are not separated by even the tip of a hair; throughout the ten ages of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from this very moment of thought.
Master Lanyun was the preceptor of my own preceptor, Jinglong; such is the mind-dharma of Jinglong.
He received the seal of approval from Lan-yun, who was the Chan Master Nan-ji An. He attained the direct lineage of Linji for twenty generations.
Tracing his lineage upward to Tian-zhen, it reaches back to Wu-ji Yuan and Xue-yan Qin; thus, there was no fixed rule regarding his succession of the Dharma, whether preceding or following them.
The principle penetrates past and present, reaching the ultimate reality. The inscription says: Vastly encompassing the Dharma-realm, empty and boundless;

the ascent and descent of all spirits never cease. The Buddhas and Patriarchs manifest their responses as guides and teachers. Having fortunately encountered this transformative ritual in my past lives, though I am not skilled at propagating the Way, I have acted according to what was appropriate for my capacity.
He passed away in Wulin; his remains were interred on a mountain cliff in a *stūpa*.

He was laid to rest in peace. His life span was equal to the mountains; returning from the illusory back to the illusory, he passed from the conditioned to the unconditioned, through the cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.

This Way is level and easy to traverse. In the spring of the eighth year of the Zhengtong era (the Guihai year), at the age of fifty-two, Jinglong composed the *Konggu ji* (Collected Works of the Empty Valley) and the *Shangzhi Shangli bian* (Compilation on Honoring Rectitude and Honoring Principle).

Chan Master Guji Jun of Tianjie Monastery in Jiangning Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fulin Du. A native of Songling in Gusu, he entered the monastic life at the age of thirteen at Rizhou Temple in Yuezhou.
At fifteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He first visited Shiwu Yonggong and subsequently met...
Sanqu Lanmu attained proficiency in the practice of *dhyāna*. He then went to visit Gumei at Gao’ang; upon rising from his prostrations, he reported his realization as it truly was.

Gumei struck him and drove him out. This happened three times. Consequently, he returned to his native village with companions and established a limit for himself to practice "wall-contemplation" (*bi-guan*) for nine years.
Every three years, he would burn one finger; after burning three fingers in succession, one day, suddenly—*pieh*!—he had a flash of insight.

Later, Daishi went to visit Folin, where they reached a profound accord through their dharma-contests. Consequently, he remained there as the head of the assembly; at that time, he was twenty-eight years old.

When the community urged him to emerge from seclusion, the Master fled his traces and left the mountain, leaving behind this verse: "For half a year we relied on one another, chanting the patriarch’s pivot;
Several times we discussed the Way, honoring your majestic authority. Now that I leave the mountain, I shall speak of the path back home; This is yet another brow added upon the eyes."

For over thirty years, he had concealed his brilliance within the crags and gullies. He possessed a lifelong fondness for secluding himself in mountain valleys, and for three decades there had been no verse regarding his reluctance to welcome or bid farewell to visitors.
During the Hongwu era, by imperial decree, he ordained a thousand monks. Upon arriving at Fanchang, the assembly requested that he open the hall on Mount Donglu.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The very word 'Chan' (Zen) is but a provisional designation. What, then, is meant by 'investigating' (can)? It lies..."
It is simply a matter of faith. To deliberate upon it is to deviate; to open one's mouth is to err.
If one’s resolve to awaken is not sincere and one’s aspiration is not fierce and sharp, one will spend winter on this side and summer on that side; advancing today and retreating tomorrow.
After searching for a long time without finding anything, one then says that the Buddha-dharma has no efficacy, and instead turns outward to memorize a bellyful of it and transcribe a whole volume.
It is like a stinking vat of dregs; such a wild fox spirit has nothing to do with it, even if Maitreya were to descend to be born.
A true practitioner of the Way who wishes to escape birth and death must pass through the barrier of the Patriarchs.
To pass this barrier and escape birth and death is not a matter of merely speaking of it and then stopping there. One must take the various Patriarchs of the past as a model. Zhao—
For forty years, Master Zhou did not allow his mind to be distracted—what was he doing? Changqing sat until seven cushions were worn through—what was he doing?
Xianglin spent forty years before finally becoming a single whole—what was he doing?
Even down to those of successive generations who truly practiced, exerting themselves with bitter diligence—what were they doing? As for me, this mountain monk, today my mouth is chattering away.
The Ground. Drawing from the past to verify the present—for what purpose? O practitioners of Zen:

since there exists a model of those from of old who, not sparing their own bodies or lives, accumulated merit and virtue to achieve wondrous awakening and personal realization, why do you not summon great courage and exert great diligence?
Before the Triple Gem, make deep and solemn vows, swearing that as long as birth-and-death remains unclarified and the Patriarchal Barrier remains unpierced, you shall never [desist].
Descend from the mountain. Thus set out; cut off the myriad divergent paths and do not consort with the ten thousand dharmas.
Before the seven-foot single mat on the long couch, hang your alms-bowl bag high and stand as upright as a cliff a thousand fathoms high. Set a firm limit for yourself and act with urgency.
Spend this entire life practicing until you have reached thorough penetration. If you resolve upon this mind, you will certainly not be deceived. I—
I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never prove false. In the Dinghai year of the Yongle era, he again received imperial edict to spend the remainder of his life at Tianjie Monastery.
He was the twenty-sixth generation descendant of Dajian (Nanyue Huairang).

The verse of entrustment from Wànfēng to Chánmāster Bǎozàng Pǔchí of Dèngwù Mountain in Sūzhōu Prefecture, successor to Chánmāster Wèi of Dèngwù, says: "The fist strikes back at the ribs where it was pained by Dàyú;
The Three Essentials and Three Mysteries transcend both the orthodox and the biased. A lion cub within the lair of Línjì— From lamp to lamp."
Xu Yan inherited the lineage of ancient and modern traditions. Later, Xuefeng Chengyuan succeeded him on the seat as the second patriarch.
When Xu Yan asked Xubai, "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. How do you understand this? Xubai stepped forward to pay his respects and stood with his hands joined.
Xu Yan rebuked him, saying, "After all this time you have been here, are you still harboring such a view? Xubai was then filled with indignation and reached the second [level of realization].
He attained great enlightenment during the night. After the Master passed away, he was interred in a stupa beside Wanfeng Peak.

Chan Master Wunian Shengxue of Jiufeng, in Wuchang Prefecture, was the son of the Chen family of Yingshan in Suizhou. At the age of nine, he received his formal training under Yuan at Baolin Temple in that same prefecture.
He first visited Wumen, who instructed him with the words: "Where does the one return? (referring to the *Gao Feng* [Peak] verse).

While staying there, he entered Mount Song and studied with great diligence. One day, he attained a realization and composed a verse containing the line: "The myriad phenomena are fully revealed within a single mirror.
He then resolved to travel extensively to seek instruction from various masters. Later, he arrived at Gusu and met Wanfeng, under whose shout he grasped the essential meaning.
Wanfeng bestowed upon him a verse, which said: "The Linji lineage transmitted through five branches— Upon entering the gate, a single shout reveals its entirety."
Feng. With the earnest compassion of an old wife, he was able to act with ease; behold how the mud snake transforms into a dragon.

Later, while residing at Jiufeng, during the Renxu year of the Hongwu era, when the Empress Xiaoci passed away, the Prince of Chu invited renowned monks from various mountains to assemble at Hongshan.

Upon seeing the Master, they were struck with wonder and treated him with extraordinary respect, providing him with quarters in the royal guest house and requesting instruction on the essentials of the Dharma. The Emperor summoned him to the private hall for an audience and granted him a seat.

His responses were in accord with the imperial will, and he was treated with exceptional courtesy. The Emperor wished to have him remain as the abbot of a capital monastery, but the Master declined resolutely.

An imperial decree was issued to send him back to Jiufeng via an official of the Imperial Household. On the day of Bingzi, the Emperor composed a poem titled "In Commemoration of the Monk Wunian" in one scroll and ordered an official of the Imperial Household to carry it to him.

The imperial consolation reached Mi. The decree stated: "Formerly, the monk Wunian’s observance of the precepts was as pure as the bright moon, and his concentration and wisdom were as stable as a towering mountain.
I came for a brief visit; since then, I have constantly harbored him in my thoughts. As these thoughts did not cease, I dispatched someone to see him.
I have specially provided pine nuts and pine blossoms as offerings, and have also comforted him with poems and prose. The Master also submitted a verse, saying: "Ten thousand..."
In leisure from state affairs, he investigated the profound mystery: "Within the tips of a hundred grasses, there is great Chan; every pore universally contains lands as numerous as motes of dust;

upon the tip of a single hair, the sky of one's nature is revealed. Returning from meditation, he sat watching clouds span the valley; enjoying his stroll, he idly gazed at stones where springs welled forth. How may the monks beneath the forest trees repay [his kindness]?
They offer prayers for the Emperor’s sacred longevity to endure ten thousand years. The eunuch returned and reported this to the Sovereign.
He was greatly pleased. In the year Jia-shen of the Yongle era, one day he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse:
"The World-Honored One lived to seventy-nine; Wunian reached eighty. Having trampled the ocean of the Flower Treasury, the waters once again join the heavens. He then passed away peacefully.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Shizi Rock, and he was posthumously titled Chan Master Qingfu Guanghui.
Chan Master Haizhou Puci of Dongming in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Qian family of Changshu, Suzhou.

He left home at a young age to study at Poshan Monastery and listened to lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "Where there are only words and speech, there is no real meaning," he harbored a doubt.

He went to visit Wanfeng and asked, "Regarding the statement that where there are only words and speech there is no real meaning, what is this 'real meaning'? Wanfeng struck him twice across the head.
[The Master] struck him with his staff, stepped on his chest, and kicked him twice, saying, "This very thing is the true meaning.

The Master rose and said, "It is indeed so, yet it takes too much of your heart-mind, O Abbot. Feng agreed with this and transmitted [the Dharma] to him with a verse, saying: "The tortoise-hair is entrusted to the children and grandchildren;
The hare’s horn is brought forth to question the essential ford. A single shout leaves one deaf for three days— Within this lies the secret message."
"To whom may I entrust this intimacy? He further instructed him, saying, "You must conceal your traces to protect and uphold [the Dharma]. Do not lightly act as a teacher or model for others.
The Master received these instructions and built a hermitage in a valley of Mount Dongting. Twenty-nine years passed. One day, he went to visit Dongming.
Dongming asked, "Master, whom have you encountered? The Master replied, "I have indeed seen one person; were I to speak of it, I fear it would startle people. Dongming said, "Just..."

"What does it matter what is said? the Master replied, "Wanfeng. Ming was overjoyed at this discussion of the school's fundamental tenets and said, "I venture to trouble the Honored Monk to succeed me on the seat of Dongming.
Hui’an will depart before the month is out; I too shall leave on the twenty-eighth.
On the twenty-ninth night, Ming passed away. This was in the sixth month of the *xinyou* year of the Zhengtong era. The Master wished to return to Dongting.
The assembly earnestly requested him to take the seat, whereupon he ascended the hall. He raised the following case:
A monk asked Muzhou, "What is it like when a single word expresses everything? Muzhou said, "The old monk is inside your alms-bag.

The Master said, "This monk was like a tiger emerging from the forest, only to be caught by Muzhou and cast into a deep pit within a heavy net, where he was buried alive. At that time, a monk asked, "I wonder where [the old monk] was?"

"This is the place where the heavy net flows into the pit. The Master said, "Prostrate yourself before me. When the monk rose from his prostration and repeated his previous question, the Master cried out, "My father!
My mother! The monk was at a loss for words, and the Master struck him straight out. Later, he ascended the hall and cited a case: A monk asked Zhimen, "What is the essence of prajñā?
Zhimen said, "An oyster containing the bright moon. [The monk asked,] "What is the essence of prajñā? (The Master continued the citation.)
If used, the Gate says: "A rabbit conceives. The Master said: "When the ancients engaged in such question and answer, even if you were possessed of eyes all over your body, you could not see it;
even if you were possessed of hands all over your body, you could not touch it. Do you understand this thoroughly? [He drew a circle with his whisk and said:
'When a single thought does not arise, the whole body is manifest; as soon as the six sense organs stir, they are obscured by clouds. He raised [the whisk].
When a monk rose from his prostrations, Xuefeng struck him five blows. The monk asked, "What fault have I committed? Xuefeng struck him another five blows.
The Master [Yunmen] commented: "The first was the sword that kills; the second was the sword that gives life. Alas, this monk did not awaken.
Had he awakened, I guarantee that Xuefeng would have had cause to eat a punch. He then cited the case of Huangbo seeing Zhaozhou.

As he came, Baizhang closed the door of the abbot’s quarters. Nanquan entered the Dharma Hall and cried out, “Put out the fire! Put out the fire! Baizhang opened the door, seized him, and said, “Speak! Speak!
Nanquan said, “It is like drawing one's bow after the thief has already fled. The verse says: One captures, one releases; both applications are skillful.
Spear thrusts and lance strikes display great merit. Who can recognize the mechanism of each? To this day, they leave us in doubt.
General Li raised the topic of Ba Ling and addressed the assembly. The Patriarch said, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving.
Since it is neither the wind nor the banner, where does one apply this? If there is someone who can act as the Patriarch’s advocate, let them come forth and meet with Ba Ling.
The verse says: *Lord Shang’s laws were too severe and cruel;* *They terrified the people of neighboring states.* *If so...*

There are those who, whether acting vertically or horizontally, remain free from transgression. Emperor Qin sat with hands folded in leisure while guarding the Pass of Han; Zhaozhou went to visit Zhunyu.
As soon as he stepped onto the Dharma Hall, Zhunyu said, "Look at the arrow! Zhaozhou also said, "Look at the arrow! Zhunyu said, "It has passed. Zhaozhou said, "It has hit."
The verse says: In late spring, the *fúyǐ* grows along the front path; In the third month, peach blossoms flourish in the small garden. A pity that people do not recognize this fragrant springtime;

The hundred-tongued bird atop the tree can speak even more eloquently. Shen Guan asked: "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yuanjue jing) states: 'The teachings of the sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon.
If one sees the moon, one realizes that what the finger points to is ultimately not the moon. What is the meaning of this principle?"
"How is it? the Master asked. He raised his hand and said, "The sutra, the moon, and the finger—Guang could not find a way to penetrate them.
The Master struck the table once and said, "The moon falls into the cold pond. At this, Guang attained realization and said, "The Way of my Master cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments."
The Master’s years of ordination were equally venerable; he had been in the world for barely ten years when he suddenly announced his passing.

At the moment of death, he spoke this verse: "Sixty-nine years spent in the world, Seventy-four years as a monk. How many contradictions and errors lay in between— Today, they are all locked away at once.
From Śākyamuni down to myself, there have been countless elder monks. Then, taking his whisk, he drew a circle and said:
"Everyone should find rest right here! *Pah!* He cast aside his whisk and passed away. In the year Jingtai Kangwu (1450), his disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa to the left of Dongming.
Virtually Bai (Xubai) went to visit Chan Master Guolin Rong of Mount Dengwu in Suzhou Prefecture. The Master threw down his meditation cushion and said, "Try to say something about this.
Bai replied, "This very news is fundamentally beyond words; upon this broken meditation cushion, earth bursts forth and heaven splits asunder.
The Master asked, "Tell me, what is it like after it has split? As Bai hesitated, the Master struck him out.
Chan Master Da’an, a dharma successor of Chan Master Songyinran, has lost his recorded surname and given name.
He was determined in his vows and rigorous in his conduct, possessing the character of his father. He frequently practiced the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (Banzhou Sanmei).
He passed away in the Bingshen year of the Yongle era, leaving behind this verse: "I do not understand digging into the earth to seek heaven; yet I also understand emptiness."
A vain strike at a wooden stake; it startles Mount Sumeru into a wild dance. A frog from the ocean floor swallows the moon; he tramples over the great ocean of birth and death.
What need is there to speak of bubbles arising and bubbles extinguishing? His worldly lifespan was seventy-seven years.

Chan Master Xizhu Benlai of Shouchang in Xincheng, Jianchang Prefecture, was a successor of Chan Master Jinshan Ji. Born into the Pei family of Chongren, he entered the monastic life at the age of seven at Guanyin Temple.
At thirteen, he went to attend upon Yifeng, serving him for seven years. One day, while listening to the recitation of the *Qing*...
In the *Jing jing* (Pure Sutra), there is a concise verse which says: "For how many years have you wandered abroad, losing your true soul?
Today we meet, yet it is utterly different. Your body is accompanied by a golden-haired stone lion; Turning his head, he swallows the Iron Kunlun. Fengji traveled to Mount Jinshan to see Cizhou.
Upon rising from his prostrations, he asked, "I have captured a thief; I beg the Master to pass judgment. Cizhou said:

"Where is the stolen goods? The Master struck the desk once. Zhoubian then shouted. The Master again raised the story of Xiangyan Climbing the Tree, interrogating him repeatedly until he found the correct response;
thereupon, he granted him formal certification (*inka*). He first resided at Shousheng Temple on Sword River.

When the Prince of Ning sent a letter inviting him, he did not go even after three returns, replying only with a letter inquiring about the Way. [The Prince] bestowed upon him the title "Wisdom-Light Universal-Illumination Sudden-Enlightenment Perfect-Penetration."
The Dharma-name [of this master] was [omitted]. In the *Yongle* year of *Yiyou*, he opened the Dharma at Shouchang. Ascending the hall, after finishing the offering of incense, he said:

"The heavens and sun are bright and high, the summer heat gradually intensifies; the pomegranate flowers erupt like fire, shining within the courtyard. Within the eyes of the patch-robed monks, the true mechanism is revealed; the Unranked True Person is encountered face-to-face.
If you know the essential point directly, hesitation creates a thousandfold barrier. If you wish to reach the matter of your own person,"
At the highest peak of Huanglong, he descended from his seat. Later, he went to Shanguan in Min to once again open up fields of merit.
On the eighth day of the tenth month of the Renyin year, he suddenly asked for a brush and wrote this verse: "This old beggar—when will his teaching ever end?
Staggering and stumbling, he merely follows the current; Whether he is a sage or an ordinary person, no one knows. Hah! Come, come, come! Go!"
"Go, go! The sea is profound and the sky is clear; the wind is pure and the moon is bright. Having finished writing, he sat in meditation and passed away.
His secular age was sixty-eight, and his monastic seniority was fifty-five. His entire body was enshrined in the Dharma Hall for offerings.

Chan Master Wujie Mingwu of Dongpu Daolin Monastery in □□ Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Tianjie Jun, was styled San’gu. He was the son of the Mo family from Tongxian Town in An’e County, Shu.
At the age of twenty, he left home to become a monk. Initially, he practiced the methods of Chan meditation; later, he studied under...

Lushan Qing was practicing the "Mu" (No) koan of Zhaozhou. At that moment, the Master attained realization. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he remained constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
One day, while sitting, a brilliant light suddenly illuminated him; there was not a single atom to be grasped. He composed a verse:

There is a saying: "The void cannot contain it; the great earth cannot support it. When the head seat Wuxi of the West River pointed this out to him, Jianwu realized that conceptualization is non-conceptualization (*wunian*).
Upon his realization, he took leave of the world and went to study under Guzhu. During a prostration, Guzhu said to his attendant, "This monk has the marks of great merit.
He set down his staff, leaned back in his chair, and commanded the master to recount his travels. The master related them directly and in detail.
Xuchi said, "You may go for now; I do not recognize such craftsmanship in you. One day he went again to the abbot’s quarters.
Xuchi let out a thunderous shout, took up his staff, and made a gesture as if to strike. The Master stepped forward to meet the blow.
Xuchi said, "My staff has eyes; I will not strike such a dead man. He dragged his staff and went out. The Master stood with palms joined, remaining motionless. Xuchi then—
He returned to his seat. Suddenly, [Zhaozhou] asked: "When the great earth has completely submerged, where are you? The Master said, "The Dharma King’s body is fully revealed.
Zhaozhou said, "All dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master said, "I do not speak."

Chushu said, "Why do you not speak? The Master said, "From antiquity to the present. Chushu said, "Setting aside for a moment 'from antiquity to the present,' while you were in Sichuan, what thing came in such a manner?
The Master remained silent for a long time. Chushu said, "A mute person has a dream; to whom can he tell it?
One day, Chushu changed his dharma-name to Wuji (Boundless). The Master said, "If that is so, then you are Boundless."
Nor is it not so. All the old monks of the world attain the Way here; all the ancestral masters of successive generations attain Buddhahood here.
If anyone comes forward now who speaks of Buddhas or speaks of patriarchs, I will send them all out the door.
"It is not as good as this fellow here, snoring away in his sleep. [The Master] laughed heartily and said, "This fellow shall henceforth no longer be deceived by others.
The verse on the "Lantern of the Galloping Horse" says: Rounding and galloping, it never stays still; There is no clear-sighted person to point out the way.
Extinguish that tiny spark within the mind, And the swords, spears, men, and horses will all cease at once. The Dharma of the Gate.
He had seven successors. There is a verse on the transmission of the Dharma that says: "I have no Dharma to transmit; you have no mind to receive.
With neither a mind to transmit nor a mind to receive, who would not achieve realization?"
Chan Master Wunian Yuanxin of Founu in Henan Prefecture was the son of the Gao family from Jintai. He was born in the Jiyou year of the Xuande era.
He left home to become a monk at the age of nine and received full ordination. He first visited Wuji at Long’en, where he attained a realization.
In the Jimao year, he entered Tianxu; subsequently, he returned to Mount Niu to build a thatched hut. In the Xinsi year, he again traveled to Fanchang to visit Yuehuan. Yuehuan asked, "What..."

Huan said, "Face to face, yet we do not recognize each other; its entire body is revealed, vast and majestic. The Master said, "Even so, alas, its horns are not complete. In his youth, he received instruction from Master Xuanji Tong; he first studied under Master Wujie. One day, upon hearing the sound of the wooden board (for striking the assembly), he attained realization.
He had a realization. He further investigated the phrase, "The thief does not strike a poor house," which concerns the destruction of emptiness and existence.

In the Guihai year of the Zhengtong era, he again visited Wuji. Wuji asked, "In what place have you been residing for the past several years? The Master replied, "Vastly open and without fixed location."
Wu Ji asked, "What have you attained? The Master said, "Originally there has been nothing lost; what is there to attain? Wu Ji said, "Then this must be something acquired through study.
The Master said, "Since not a single dharma exists, from where could study come? Wu Ji asked, "Does this not fall into emptiness?"
The Master said, "I am not even 'I. Who falls and who is empty? Ji said, "Ultimately, what is the matter? The Master said, "When the water recedes, the rocks appear;
when the rain clears, the clouds vanish. Ji said, "Do not speak so carelessly. Even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to come, they would not be permitted.
Even if you were to swallow the ocean of the Tripitaka from side to side, or manifest hundreds of thousands of supernatural powers, here you still would not be permitted. The Master—
[Daowu] said, "Although you, Preceptor, hold fast at the vital ford, how can you avoid such great mental exertion? Daowu patted his knee once. The Master then shouted.
Daowu said, "One who sustains the family must be one who breaks the family; doing so to manage the household affairs is truly effortless.
The Master covered his ears and departed. That evening, he summoned the Master again and questioned him, saying, "Regarding the sequence of your past realizations..."
"Speak it out! The Master answered truthfully and in detail. Linji said, "Bring me back the meaning of the word 'no'.
The Master presented a verse, saying: "This monk’s question was full of complications; How could Old Zhao ever have indulged in thought?

A single word spoken offhand was fully revealed, Yet it has turned into something extraordinary that leaves people in doubt. Linji asked, "What is the place where you have no doubt? The Master said, "Blue."
The mountains are green and the waters clear; swallows chatter and orioles sing. Everything is distinct and vivid—what more could one doubt? Zhiyi said, "Not yet; speak further.
The Master replied, "The head touches the void, while the feet tread upon solid ground. Thereupon, Zhiyi recognized him and conferred his certification.

In the year of Ren-shen, he arrived at Jinling and visited Yuexi Haizhou. Upon leaving, he resided at Houshan, where a monk asked, "What is the realm of Tianzhu? The Master replied, "A mountain stream..."
The vast clouds return at evening; the mountain is high, so the sun rises late. [A monk] asked, "What is it like to be a person within this realm?
The Master said, "The brows beneath the forehead shade the eyes; the ears on the cheeks reach the shoulders. [The monk] asked, "What is the house style of Tianzhu?
The Master said, "Steaming pine powder in a cloud-bowl steamer; boiling moon-discs in an ice cauldron. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said:
The Sea God cast forth a night-bright pearl. [The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Mañjuśrī has lost his crystal cup.
[The monk] asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A cast-iron weight. [The monk] asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said—
"A stone, a clod of earth. A monk asked, "What is the monk? The Master said, "A black-lacquered staff. In the year Yihai of the Jingtai era, he moved to Touzi.

Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked, "Having left Mount Huan far behind, you have come to occupy Touzi. The assembly is gathered before you; we pray that the Master will offer prayers for the Emperor.
The Master said, "The long-life inscription within the cauldron; the ageless pine atop the peak. [The monk] said, "I have already received the blessing for the Emperor."
"What is the meaning of the Master’s intent? What is the 'house style' of Touzi? The Master said, "Carrying a water jar through the marketplace; it is not the oil-seller.
[The monk] asked, "As for what the Patriarch said, 'Do not travel by night; you must arrive at dawn,' is this truly so?
The Master said, "Though there is sinew in his eyes, alas, his tongue has no bone. [The monk] said, "Zhaozhou said, 'I..."

"The early monkey is white; that other one is even blacker. [The monk asked,] "What do you mean by this? The Master said, "If it were not for the exhaustion of arrows and bows, he would not yet be willing to raise the flag of surrender.
[A monk] asked, "Venerable Sir, today you have ascended the seat to preach the Dharma; I wonder what auspicious signs there were? The Master said:
The Qilin strides beyond the vermilion heavens; the *ūpava* flower blooms amidst the fierce flames. [A monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "When the snow melts, the mountain peak is revealed; when the wind passes, the tree tops sway. [Another] asked, "How is it before the precious sword has emerged from its scabbard?
The Master said, "The spirits cry out and the ghosts wail. [He] asked, "How is it after it has emerged from the scabbard? The Master said, "The Buddhas and Patriarchs..."
He suppressed his voice and asked, "How is it when [the sun] has emerged and when it has not yet emerged? The Master said, "A hairless chain rattles at both ends.
The monk lifted up his sitting mat; the Master then shouted. The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him.
He then said, "To scratch an itch on the head of a venomous snake or to cast one's body across the mouth of a fierce tiger—this must be done by such a person as this. That monk just now..."
He resembles a lone warrior who dares to come here to seize the drum and snatch the banner; yet, alas, his head is a dragon’s while his tail is a snake’s, and he dies beneath the staff.

Had he known how to turn back for a path of life, he naturally would not have encountered the sharp edge of the blade. Therefore it is said: "To handle a snake, one must be a master of handling snakes;
if one does not know how to handle them, the snake will bite him to death. Again, when Fadian ascended the hall, he covered...
Regarding the old man Qingliang’s unresolved public case (gong'an):
after the story was finished, the Master said, "In general, when a patriarch appears in the world, he must first set forth his own insight; only then may he adjudicate the cases of past and present.
Observe how Fadelan employed such a strategy—it is indeed admirable, yet it remains unresolved. Today, I, Huanzou, shall also act for the sake of Old Man Cangu."
There is an unresolved *kōan*. Come forth and resolve it for him! If someone asks the Old Man of the Silkworm Bones, "What unresolved *kōan* do you have?
he should immediately shout. If the person’s eyes waver, he should strike them out with his staff. Great assembly!
I, this mountain monk, maintain the Dharma in this manner. Now tell me: is there any difference in quality between this and the way Faideng applied it?
If you can distinguish between black and white, I grant that you are a fellow practitioner. Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "This very thing is a source of confusion.
How many monks, upon reaching this point, find themselves unable to open their mouths or reach a conclusion through thought! Let us bring it forth."
It does not emerge; it has now fallen into the hands of this mountain monk. Whether horizontal or vertical, it is up to me;
lifting or setting down, rolling up or spreading out, killing or giving life—all is entirely up to me.

(Pointing a single dot in the air with his staff) At such a time as this, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past to the old monks of the world, upon reaching here, they can do nothing but beg for their lives.
"Divide! Is there no one among you in this assembly who will speak out on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? After a long silence, he struck his staff once and said:
"I have gouged out the true eye of the Vajra and toppled the precious throne of the Empty King. You people, what kind of bowl are you looking for?"

He then descended from his seat and ascended the hall. When the assembly had gathered, the Master adjusted his robes, took his place, and after a long silence said, "The great assembly, take this clearly to heart.
He then descended from his seat and addressed the assembly: "The field for selecting Buddhas has opened; the ancestral mechanisms are fixed.

To distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, the tongs and hammers are forged. The waves at the Dragon Gate are warm and the wind-thunder roars; this is precisely the time when fish and dragons undergo their transformations. Is there anyone among the assembly who..."
"Is it the surging waves and turbulent billows? After a long silence, he drew a circle with his whisk and said, "A single move before the pivot;
a total presentation face-to-face. He struck the meditation seat once and said, "A word beyond the phrase; revealed along with the sound. No room for lingering thought or hesitation;
no allowance for deliberation or analysis. By the time you blink an eye, the sword has long since departed—even were it a Buddha..."
When the Patriarch arrived, he could do nothing but knit his brows; for what reason? It is because this is not a path accessible through words, nor is it something measurable by the conscious mind.
If one were a truly outstanding monk, upon hearing it before a word was even raised, one should immediately nod in agreement with a smile.
It is still somewhat better than that. In recent times, the human mind has not returned to antiquity. Students do not strive for true inquiry and genuine realization;

they merely echo sounds and transmit empty forms. They take intellectual knowledge and superficial understanding as enlightenment, the forced interpretation of circumstantial encounters as investigation, the violation of monastic discipline as liberation, and the manipulation of circumstances to secure a position as transcendence.
Consequently, the ancestral wind has withered and declined, and demons have proliferated.
To speak of "blazing fire" blocks the level path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and blinds the true eye of Heaven.

It causes the Way of our Patriarch’s “separate transmission outside the teachings” to be cast to the ground here and now. The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, more than two thousand years ago, already recognized the mental illness of sentient beings;
he established many expedient means and graciously bestowed rules accordingly. Thus it is said: "Sentient beings in the末法 (dharma-ending) age rarely..."
One should aspire to achieve the Way and not merely seek awakening for the sake of increasing one's learning, which only serves to grow the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is said:

"Since sentient beings have not yet awakened, by what skillful means can they be universally led to enlightenment? For this reason, the retreat (*varṣā*) and the fixed period of dwelling (*anupraskandana*) are established to realize realization within a set timeframe.

Once the three-month period has passed, one may go wherever one wishes without hindrance; thus we know that there is a specific time for untying the knots. O Great Virtuous Ones, regarding the nine...

Within these ten days, have you ever attained realization? Setting aside for a moment those who have already awakened, as for those who have not yet awakened, this entire period will again be spent in vain.
If one is a true follower of the Way, then throughout the ten directions and the Dharma-realm, [one must act accordingly].

For the purpose of establishing a period for Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue), whether for a hundred days or a thousand days, during both the commencement and conclusion of the retreat, one must simply begin by raising the *huatou*.
If one does not attain enlightenment in one year, one shall practice for another year; if not in ten years, one shall practice for ten years;

even for twenty or thirty years, or until the end of one’s life without attaining enlightenment, one must resolutely never shift this resolve, seeking nothing less than to see that [Ultimate Reality].
From beginning to end, at the point of ultimate reality, only then is it the day of "releasing the session" (*fangcan*). As it is said:
"When the time arrives, the principle reveals itself of its own accord. How could this be mere empty words? [The Master] suddenly raises his whisk and says: "Do you know where it lands?"
Today, this illusory old man will not decline to indulge in further verbosity; he shall provide another commentary for you all:

A golden bullet forged in a fierce fire—when it is crushed at the moment of action, it becomes a perfect sphere. Carelessly cast aside both gain and loss; the wind carries the tide-sound out from the sea gate.
When the Master arrived at the garden, he saw a winter melon and asked the gardener: "This one has no mouth; why [is it here]?"
“Grown this large! The head said, “I have never been idle for a single moment. The Master said, “Does your master lend you some strength?
The head said, “I rely entirely upon his power. The Master said, “Bring him here to meet me, old monk.
The head then prostrated himself. The Master said, “This is still merely a servant or a slave. The head turned away.
The Master picked up a bamboo splint and tied it to a frame; he then let out a great laugh and looked back at his attendant, saying, "There are insects in the vegetable garden.
The Head Seat Xingkong requested instruction on the Three Barriers of Mount Mengshan, asking:

"When the minuscule *jiaoming* insect sucks dry the vast ocean, where do the fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs find a place to dwell and establish their lives? The Master replied: "A golden-haired lion on the road to Chang'an."
[The monk] lay down. [The Master] said, "The water-jelly flies up to the Ultimate Heaven (Akaniṣṭha), enters the eye of Maheśvara, and performs a dance.
Why is it not seen? The Master said, "Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, iron horses neigh. [The monk] asked, "The Lotus Lake Bridge serves all people;

why does one who points directly to the clear-eyed person fall into the well? The Master said, "The bright moon illuminates the traveler at night. [The monk] said, "I request the Master to provide a verse."

[The monk] went out. The Master said, "A good one deserves a severe beating. [The monk] said, "I am willing to accept the beating; I beg the Master not to be sparing with his verse. The Master laughed heartily and spoke this verse:
"When the opportunity arises, he cuts off the passage for both sages and commoners. If you hesitate, you will know that his path is neither bent nor extended.

If you wish to understand the essential meaning of Mount Meng, He lowers his hook, intending to catch the golden-scaled fish. In the *dingchou* year of the Tiānfùn era, [he departed] from Mount Kuānglú.
He returned to Shu. Han Duhou established Yunfeng Temple on Fangshan and invited the Master to serve as its abbot.

In the third month of the *guisi* year of the Chenghua era, he manifested a slight illness. When the assembly requested his final words, the Master extended both hands and asked, "Do you understand? He spoke again:
On this very day of this year, pushing his cart, he struck the wall; striking through the void, a thunderclap in the blue sky.
Aha-ha! The clay ox swallows the old dragon’s pearl; the tranquil ocean of nature’s essence stills its foam-flowers. He passed away in serene stillness. His worldly age was seventy;
his monastic seniority was sixty-one. His stupa was completed at Tiānchéng.
Chan Master Shanjian Guiting of the former Yunnan Prefecture was the son of the Ding family from Kunming in that same prefecture.

At the age of nineteen, he visited Boye (Baiyan). In the gengxu year of the Xuande era, he traveled to Jinling to visit Wuyin Dao. Wuyin gave him the koan: "All dharmas return to One; where does the One return?
He applied himself with great effort to investigate this thoroughly, yet for some time he made no spiritual entry. In the year yimao, he arrived in Yong [Cheng County], Guizhou.

Luoshan entered Shu, where he did not touch his mat for several years before attaining great enlightenment. During the Zhengtong era, he traveled to Long’en with incense in his sleeve to attend upon Wuji.
Wuji asked, “Why is your realization different from that of this old monk? The Master extended both hands and said, “This is nothing other than that.
Wuji nodded in approval. One day, as the Master was taking his leave, Wuji asked, “Where are you going? The Master replied:

At the crossroads, he reviled the Buddhas and cursed the Patriarchs. Ji asked, "Will you return? The Master replied, "I shall not fail to pay my respects to the Honored Countenance of the Abbot," and having prostrated himself, he departed.
Initially, he traveled to Jintai and stayed at Mount Dayong; later, he returned south to reside at Tianjie Monastery in Jinling.
During the Tiānshùn era, he moved to Fushan on Mount Tóng in Wǎn. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Fenyang Wuye said: 'The ancients...'"
After the man of virtue attained his realization, he lived in thatched huts and stone dwellings, cooking his meals over a broken-legged cauldron for more than twenty or thirty years.
Fame and profit did not trouble his mind; wealth and treasure were no concern to him. Having utterly forgotten the ways of the world, he concealed his traces among the mountain crags and thickets.
"When a sovereign summons them, they do not come; when the feudal lords invite them, they do not attend.

How can this be the same as our own pursuit of profit and fame, wallowing in the ways of the world like petty peddlers who, having a small desire, forget the great fruit? Truly, these words are right."
We merely seize upon empty appearances and delusively exalt ourselves. The three poisons of ignorance are secretly bound within our hearts;
when confronted by adverse conditions, we know no way to liberation. To speak according to reality, let us for now set aside whether you are a spiritual friend or not.
Setting aside all conditioned activities—whether movement or stillness, speech or silence, or written characters—when birth and death arrive, how will you ultimately escape them?
You must not mistake a lifeless corpse for the truth and dwell in delusive thoughts within the state of long silence;

nor must you cling to a revolving wheel and wander recklessly within the state of lively liberation. Should there be even a hair’s breadth of discriminatory view or intellectual awakening, it is directly...

Even if your backbone were forged from cast iron and your wit and eloquence flowed like a cascading torrent, you could not avoid being cast by Old Man Yan into the eight cold and eight hot hells, undergoing ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births. It is certain, it is certain.
[He strikes the whisk and says: "Last night a gnat swallowed the six directions; empty space was smashed to pieces and fell before the cliff. Again—
He summoned the great assembly and said, "Take care. Later, he returned to his native village of Guting and established the Guihua Chan Monastery.
He passed away on the twentieth day of the seventh month in the *Guichou* year of the Hongzhi era. Guting and Panlong stand side by side, north and south;
to this day, the flesh bodies of these two Great Beings remain preserved.
Master Zhen, the successor of the Great Being Tian Su’an, of the [Name] Prefecture’s Foji Temple, addressed the assembly: "The green mountains rise in layers; the green waters flow on and on."
Attaining it within this assembly, one walks alone, transcending all. Nevertheless, even so, it is but ordinary tea and rice. An ancient said:

"If you wish to exhaust the view across a thousand li, you must ascend another story. If the function does not leave its station, one falls into a sea of poison; if the words do not startle the multitude, one sinks into vulgar custom.
If you can distinguish the black from the white amidst the sparks struck from flint, and discern the lethal blow within a flash of lightning, then you have it.
Alive! One can thus cut off all manifold differences and stand like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high. Brothers, do you know if there is such a time?
Nowadays, the various quarters are filled with a clamor of "Chan," and everyone claims their heels touch the ground and their nostrils reach the heavens.

Yet, those who ultimately possess the true eye are rarely heard of, appearing as few as scattered stars. Consequently, views of partiality and correctness vary, and each establishes their own divergent path.

Stubbornly clinging to their own interpretations, they fail to penetrate the true principle. As it is said, "When the True Dharma is difficult to uphold, heterodox teachings flourish in competition. An ancient master remarked:
"If there is ten parts of faith, there will be ten parts of doubt; if there is ten parts of doubt, there will be ten parts of awakening."

You should exhaustively pour out everything you have seen with your eyes and heard with your ears throughout your entire life— your false knowledge and misconceptions, your wondrous words and subtle phrases,
your notions of Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma, and all thoughts of arrogance and self-importance— leaving not even a hair’s breadth remaining. Then,
regarding a koan that you have not yet understood or resolved, plant your feet firmly and straighten your spine, practicing without distinction between day and night.

To apply doubt where there is no place for doubt, and to entertain suspicion where there is no cause for suspicion, one reaches a state where east and west cannot be distinguished and north and south cannot be told apart.
One remains in a state of dazed stupor, like a corpse still possessing breath; the mind is transformed by its environment, yet it still retains the capacity to perceive when touched.
Smashing the skull—this is not obtained from another. Is this not a source of lifelong celebration and joy?
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Dongming Xian of the twenty-eighth generation under Da Jian.
Chan Master Yongci of Haizhou at Wushan Yishan in Jiangning Prefecture was the son of the Yu family of Chengdu. He was born in the Jiaxu year of the Hongwu era.
Orphaned in his youth, he felt joy whenever he saw monks. One day, hearing that the matter of birth and death is of great importance, he resolved to leave the household life.
With determined intent, he set out to seek out spiritual teachers. His first encounter was with Taichu, who asked him: "Before your parents were born, who was it?"
"This is your original face. The Master immediately moved from east to west and stood with his hands folded.
The Master said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master replied, "Two eyes facing two eyes. In the Dingwei year of the Xuande era, he left the gorges to travel to the capital, Yanjing.
Continuing his southern inquiries, he arrived at Wulin and visited Dongming, asking: "Who is worthy to wear the formless field-of-merit robe? Dongming then struck him with his palm.
The Master asked, "What is it? Ming struck him again. The Master said, "One blow does not function as a single blow; how about that? Ming struck him once more.
The Master said, "The reputation of this old monk is not transmitted in vain. He then prostrated three times with his ritual implements. Not long after, he traveled to Jinling again.
In the *ding-si* year of the Zhengtong era, the eunuch Yuan Cheng invited the Master to take charge of Yishan Monastery. In the fifth month of the *geng-shen* year—
On the twenty-eighth day, Dongmyeong left behind a verse, saying: "I entrust this to the boat of the compassionate sea; seek me, yet I shall have no recompense.

On the first day of next year, the west wind will smile and nod its head. In the following year, the Xinyou year, Dongmyeong passed away exactly as predicted. In the Bingxu year of the Chenghua era, the Master [Soksan] entered nirvana.
He was seventy-three years of age and had been a monk for over fifty winters. His stupa was erected to the left of the temple.
Chan Master Juejing of Suizhou Shuixin Yuezhang was the son of the Fan family of Gusu. At the age of fifteen, he left home under Gu Shi.
In the *Renyin* year of the Yongle era, he went to study under Xianshan Zong; later, he met Dongming, upon whom he relied most intimately for the longest period.
One day he asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Ming said, "Where have you come from?
The Master stepped forward, bowed, and said, "Where have you come from, Reverend? Ming gave a shout; the Master also shouted. Ming struck him out. Later, he lived in seclusion at Tianmu.
During the Tiānshùn era, he moved to Shuixin in his native village. On the nineteenth day of the first month of the Jǐhài year of the Chénghuá era.
On that day, he exhorted his disciples with solemnity and passed away while reciting a verse. He was seventy-nine years old and fifty-one years since his ordination.
Master Huitong Dachen of Mount Junfeng in Shaowu Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Tianjie Zhong, was the son of the Shao family of Jianning; he received the precepts from Mount Doufeng.
Fahai went to study under Xuegu. One night he attained realization and composed a verse, saying: "Holding the rope of tortoise fur in my hand, I push against the crown of Vairocana’s head.
The Buddhas and patriarchs of the three thousand worlds— I have threaded them all onto a single string. In the morning, he went to the master's quarters to see him.
Xuegu said, "Give me back the *huatou* (the critical phrase). The Master replied spontaneously: "I cut off the sands of the Ganges; The entire mind is but a single object."
"None. The floating clouds have all dispersed; alone shines the solitary orb. This was acceptable to him. Later, he resided at Junfeng for over twenty years.

His style was pure and remote, and many were transformed by his influence. On the seventeenth day of the second month of the Xinyou year of the Hongzhi era, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse:
"In human life, reaching seventy is rare from of old; to add another year is even more extraordinary. If one asks..."
"Where has the old monk gone? The void alone is revealed, smiling broadly. He bathed, changed his robes, sat in the lotus position, and passed away.
Chan Master Jinshan Bao of Zhuozhou in Shuntian Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Touzi Qi. He went to visit Chushan, who asked him: "Facing south, you look at the Big Dipper."
"Tell me, what matter does this clarify? The Master said, "Venerable Sir, you had better keep your mouth shut. Xuefeng said, "Not yet. The Master said, "You may get away with deceiving others.
Xuefeng asked, "What is the eye that penetrates the barrier? The Master let out a loud shout.
Xuefeng asked, "And as for the single pivot beyond—how is that? The Master said, "The sun at high noon in a clear blue sky. Xuefeng said, "I have not even dreamed of it."
[Zhaozhou] was present. The Master said, "The wooden boy holds the jade thread; the stone woman passes the golden needle. Xuefeng said, "Speak quickly, speak quickly—a phrase for turning the body.
The Master said, "The rain makes the mountain colors more exquisite; the wind comes and the shadows of the bamboos shift. Xuefeng took up his staff.
The Master then gave a shout and swept his sleeves, exiting. Mount said, "I grant you thirty blows. The Master turned around, prostrated, and said, "I thank the Master for your compassion.
Mount said, "Though you possess waves that overflow the heavens, you still lack the stillness of deep water."
The Master lowered his head and remained silent. Mount Shan approved of this.
Chan Master Zhan-yuan Yin-chuan of Tang’an relied upon Chushan for the longest period of time. One day, while in the inner quarters for formal instruction:
Shan asked, "What is the single word of ultimate truth? The Master said, "There are those with mouths who cannot speak it.
Shan said, "Why then can the wind through the pines and the flowing water speak it? The Master said, "Because they have no mouths. Shan said, "Tell me, what do they say?
The Master said, "What did you ask just now, Preceptor? Shan said, "As for that place where sound and echo are utterly cut off..."
"Is there anything more to say? The Master said, "There certainly is; it is simply that you have not heard it.
Shanshan said, "Setting aside the hearing for a moment, tell me, what did he say? The Master then raised his fist. Shanshan said, "Is there anyone else who can hear it?
The Master pointed to the incense burner and said, "It is this one that hears. Shanshan said, "Because..."
"Did you hear it? the Master asked. Shan said, "He has ears. The Master said, "You also have two ears;
why can you not hear it? Shan said, "Even though I cannot hear it, I cannot deceive him by even a single point.
The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows. Shan then bowed.
Chan Master Da Yunxing of Xiangyang Prefecture had long served under Chushan. One day, as Chushan was returning from the prefectural seat, the assembly went out on the road to welcome him.
Chushan said, "I have never descended from the mountain, nor have I ever left the prefecture.

Tell me, where have I come from? The Master said, "The assembly has been standing for a long time; please, Reverend, return to the monastery. Chushan asked, "Where is the monastery? The Master replied, "The sound of the bell."

"Excellent," said Shanhé, laughing heartily. The Master then prostrated himself. Later, Shanhé bestowed upon him a verse, saying: "In person you have established the fundamental tenets in the Western Capital;

From Touzi yourself, you have received the *kāṣāya*. In years to come, when you appear in the world to uphold the essential principles, Do not stand alone in precarious isolation—this is the mark of a true master."

While Chan Master Hai Zhu Yizhi was in retreat at the Stone Scriptures of Fangshan in Shuntian Prefecture, one day Chushan arrived before the gate, struck it once, and said, "I request to see the master of the retreat. The Master stood with his hands clasped and his body bowed.
Mount [Wuzu] asked, "What about Zhaozhou’s 'No-Character'? The Master said, "It is precisely because his compassionate heart is so earnest that he pours out his very liver and gall to others.
Mount asked, "How is it when one does not involve oneself with existence or non-existence? The Master said, "At this point, I myself do not understand."
Mountain said, "Wait until you pass through the barrier; I shall give you a blow. The Master said, "I am not even inside the barrier right now.
Mountain pointed to the gate and said, "What can be done about this? The Master then gave a shout. Mountain said, "The weather is sweltering."
"Please protect me well. The Master then prostrated.
[The Record of] Chan Master Changsong Daxin Zhiyuan of Fu Prefecture, a native of the Zhang family of Sanchi, visited Chushan and asked:

"Please, Master, point directly to that place where the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs above have not reached, and where practice has not arrived. Zhaozhou took up his staff and said, "Hmm? The Imperial Preceptor (Zhongguo Shi) Pengxian, named Beici Chongshan Yitianzhi, was a native of Peng County. His physical appearance was extraordinary.

Chushan asked, "What is the meaning of the word 'Mu'? The Master replied, "A drawn sword from its scabbard."
The cold light shoots toward the Dipper and Ox constellations. Mount Shān asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The Master said, "A Persian chewing ice and snow does not realize his teeth are cold.
Mount Shān said, "Having set aside 'is' and 'is not,' how can one find a place to settle?
The Master said, "In the deep of night, who takes my hand to stroll together through the Imperial Street? Mount Shān asked, "What is that most extraordinary phrase beyond this? The Master said:
"The autumn night has the moon in every house; spring comes with flowers everywhere. A pair of 'blue and white eyes'—what need is there to scatter sand and mud?
Shan Yin approved this.
Master Changyun of Xiyinshan in Fu-chou went to visit Chushan. Chushan asked, "What is your name?"
The Master said, “Changyun. Sanshan said, “What is this designation? The Master said, “Yinshan. Sanshan said, “Clouds are hidden within the mountains; why then do they emerge from the mountains?

The Master said, “It is simply because last night a crane carried them across the mountain pass. Sanshan said, “What happens when they transform into drenching rain? The Master said, “They moisten the entire realm.

Chan Master Zutang Zuyu of Fushan Shijing Monastery in Fangshan, Shuntian Prefecture, was the son of the Ju family from Chengdu.
He had long followed Chushan as his teacher. One day, while Chushan was reading a scripture, the Master approached him and asked, "What is it that the Monk is looking at?"
Mountan shouted once and said, "Tell me, what is this? The Master also shouted.
The Mountain held up a scripture and said, "Hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings all flow forth from this single scroll of scripture.

Chan Master Yueguang Changhui of Sanchi in [Name] Prefecture was the son of the Li family of Jianzhou.

Chan Master Juecheng of Gaosuo at Jiangning Fu was a native of Weizhou.

Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed; yet, viewed through the True Eye, both are nothing but fire pits. The Buddhas of the three periods are bound within a simple cloth robe from Qingzhou;

the lamp-stand and the lantern both emit light. On the ninth day of the eighth month of the Gui-si year of the Chenghua era, he gathered the assembly for his final parting and passed away while sitting upright.

When the attendant Zu Jie of Guian was ill, Chushan entered his quarters to visit him personally. At that time, the senior monk Xinxin arrived;
Chushan looked at the Master and asked, "What is mind? The Master replied, "Opening one's mouth admits no sentiment. Chushan said, "Not yet."
Master Shanshan turned his head back and said to Xinxin, "Why do you not pay obeisance to the Master? Xinxin immediately prostrated himself once. Shanshan remained silent.
Later, when his illness became critical and he made sounds of pain, Shanshan asked, "At a time such as this, is the phrase upon which you relied during your daily practice still effective for you?
Master Xinxin replied, "It is. Shanshan said, "If it is still effective, why are you crying out in pain? Master Xinxin said, "It hurts."
When itched, he laughed. The Master said, "Suppose the three-inch breath is severed; where would you establish yourself and find your life?
The Master said, "After the rain has passed and the sky is clear, the green mountains remain as they were. Shan said, "From now on, after we part, will we ever meet again?
The Master said, "Throughout kalpas beyond measure there is no separation; how could there be any interval now? Shan said, "If that is so, then you have never been ill."
"Indeed," the Master said. "Sickness and health are both entirely irrelevant. Shan then grasped the Master’s hand and asked, "What is this?
The Master pressed his palms together and said, "I must depart now," then straightened his body, sat upright, and passed away.
Chan Master Wuyong Wenquan of Huguo Temple on Mount Cha in Fengyang Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Guanshan Tan. He was the son of the Liu family from Shanghe in Jinan.

At the age of nineteen, he went to Lingyan Temple to shave his head. Initially, he had an awakening upon meeting Yue Tian; subsequently, he studied under Biezhuan, through whom he attained further realization. He then entered [the lineage of] Biezhuan.
Question: "When the void is shattered and the great earth sinks flat, where do you establish your body and life?
The Master said: "Last night the earthen ox swallowed the bright moon; this morning the wooden horse breathes forth the clear wind.
Chuan asked: "Where does 'One Return' go, pray? The Master said: "Since the white ox returned to the snowy peaks, its tracks have not been seen until this very day. Chuan nodded in approval.
He went again to Mount Jinshan to visit Wujie. Wujie instructed him to see Bao Yue. Yue asked, "Do you have money for straw sandals? The Master replied, "The green mountain does not reveal its peak.
Yue asked, "What is 'manifesting form in response to things'? The Master said, "The solitary light of the bright moon shines throughout the heavens;

"It is cold, it is cold. The Master then moved the brazier forward. Yunmen asked, "What is the matter by the brazier?

The Master snatched the staff away, threw it to the ground, and stood with his hands clasped behind his back. Yunmen—

Later, he appeared in the world at Chashan. He ascended the hall and said: "Dharma does not arise in isolation; it arises by depending upon conditions. The Way is fundamentally without words."

Words are used to manifest the Way. Now, as dragons and elephants mingle and the various mountains dwell together, we are moved by the Emperor’s great bounty and the protection of worthy scholars and gentlemen.

We have established this period of Chan practice to assist in this sacred transformation, commanding this mountain monk to raise up the eye of the school so that those in the final age may plant roots of goodness.
Nevertheless, even this is not yet the matter beneath the patched robe; for now, let us simply...
"What is the matter beneath the patched robe? A monk asked. "I do not ask about the Three Vehicles;
