Chan Master Yixin Huanyou Zhengchuan of Longchi Monastery in Yixing, Changzhou Prefecture, was the son of the Li family of Linyang.
At the age of twenty-two, he entered the monastic order under Layan at Jingle Monastery in Jingxi. Layan showed him the matter of his own fundamental nature.
The Master then made a solemn vow, saying, "If I do not see my nature and clarify my mind, I shall never lie down to sleep on my back.
One night, hearing the crackling sound of a glass lamp flower, he attained realization. He reported this to Chan Master An, who nodded in approval. Not long after, Master An passed away.
The Master proceeded directly to the Yan capital and visited Xiaoyan at Guanyin Hermitage. Xiaoyan asked, "Where have you come from, Senior? The Master replied, "From the South.
Xiaoyan said, "What do you intend to seek by coming here? The Master said, "I simply beg the Master to certify my progress in the practice of the mind-ground.
Xiaoyan said, "If you truly recognize the mind-ground, what need would there be for certification? The Master said, "Even so, it cannot be obtained..."
He did not repeat it even once. Yankuan said, "Go to the hall. The Master, saying "Take care," then departed. That evening, he entered the room and fully recounted what had happened.
Yankuan suddenly kicked out a single sandal and said, "Speak a word here! Thereupon, he cut off the master's line of inquiry all at once.
The Master left in a state of confusion and went out, unable to sleep the entire night. The following day, Yankuan came out from the abbot’s quarters.

Seeing that the Master was still standing under the eaves, Yankuan suddenly called out, "Upadeśaka! The Master looked back; Yankuan stood on one leg, assuming the posture of an asura obstructing the sun and moon.
At that moment, the Master attained a sudden and thorough realization of the essential meaning. Later, when the Master took his leave, Yankuan wrote down the lineage of Caoxi and entrusted it to him.
He further presented him with a straw hat, saying, "Wear this so as not to expose your sharp edges. Having received these instructions, the Master went directly to Mount Tai and built a hut.

He resided at Miaobiyu Cliff for thirteen years. During this time, Tang Hezheng, Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, came to seek the Way and earnestly requested that the Master return south.
He stayed at Longchi in Jingxi for six years, then traveled to the capital, Yanjing, where he stayed at Puzhao Temple; later, he returned once more to Longchi.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* gate called 'Perfect Enlightenment' (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
[He] suddenly held up his whisk and said: 'The hawk has already flown beyond the heavens; the simpleton still searches beside the moon.
Ascending the hall, [he said]: "All phenomena are not existent; all phenomena are not non-existent. If one can understand it in this way, it is like pressing a gourd onto the water. Buddha.
Dantan ascended the hall and said: "This morning, the eighth day of the fourth month, is the time when our Śākyamuni Tathāgata manifested his birth.

As I suddenly began to reflect, I pondered over the more than two thousand five hundred years since then—how many people have there been who, seeing injustice on the road, felt compelled to seek out another person to act as my Śākyamuni’s [successor]?"
Laozi! You compare victories and defeats and judge superiority and inferiority, yet you do not realize what kind of countenance our Śākyamuni Tathāgata possesses.
Do you all know where the feet of our Śākyamuni Tathāgata stand?
"Have you ever dreamed of the crown-marks of my Śākyamuni Tathāgata? After a long silence, he said:

"Raising his hand to grasp the Southern Dipper, turning his body to lean against the Northern Pole; looking out from beyond the heavens—what person is there like this? He then suddenly held up his whisk and said:

"Master Yunmen arrives! He threw down his whisk and descended from the seat. Entering the hall, he said: "In this place of mine, I ask neither those who have long practiced nor those who are latecomers;
what I value is correct knowledge and correct view. If your knowledge and view are correct, you will understand birth and death as easily as turning over your hand.
You will naturally not fall into the biased views of the two vehicles regarding annihilation, permanence, existence, or non-existence. What further deliberation is there? If..."
A monk asked, "What is right knowledge and right view? The Master replied to him, "I, the old monk, am beneath your feet.
After a long silence, he let out a shout and descended from his seat. Another monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The deer sleeps alone north of the house. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The roosters cry together west of the stream. [The monk] asked, "How is it?"
"This is a most extraordinary thing," [the monk] said. The Master replied, "A toad catching a tiger. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then it is not extraordinary.
The Master said, "A cat catching a mouse. The monk bowed; the Master then gave a shout. [The monk] said, "Old Monk, why do you not let me pass?
The Master said in a stern voice, "I have business here; you may go now. A scholar once raised this case.
A monk asked Yunmen, “What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen said, “On the water above the Eastern Mountain. The monk asked, “What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, “How many can play the holeless flute? The monk asked, “May I, your disciple, do so? The Master said, “You may.
The monk asked, “What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? The Master said, “Sitting in the fire in Xihe.”

Rarely did anyone find these words truly resonant. A verse on dwelling in the mountains says: "At the Five Peaks’ Cloud-Capped Summit dwells Mañjuśrī;
All day long he sits in *kaḍa*-posture, laughing at me in total. Not even a single speck of bitter cold can restrain him; While I hesitate, still not finished, he [has already]..."

[The author] hesitated. The Master’s demeanor was simple and easygoing, yet his spiritual presence was solemn and concentrated. He took the Way of the Dharma as his personal responsibility, and his skillful application of means was so subtle and profound that it far transcended ordinary understanding.
On the twelfth day of the second month in the Jia-yin year of the Wanli era, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
One day prior, a monk arrived from Mount Wutai; the Master conversed with him extensively regarding their past lives. When evening came, he requested a bath. The assembly observed the Master...
[The assembly] entreated him earnestly for his final instructions. The Master raised the hat he was wearing three times; the assembly remained silent. He stroked his knee and passed away suddenly.
His secular age was sixty-six, and his monastic seniority was forty-four. He was cremated, and his sacred relics were enshrined in a stupa to the right of the mountain where he resided.
Chan Master Tanzhi of Linggu Monastery in Jiangning visited Xiaoyan and asked, "The ancients said, 'Break the mirror and we shall meet.
I wonder, having broken the mirror, where do they meet? Xiaoyan replied, "It would put people to shame."

Upon these words, the Master attained sudden and clear realization of the essential meaning; he then forgot to perform his prostrations and departed dancing. He served [his teacher] diligently for several years.
The Master of the Rock (Yan) bestowed upon him this verse: "The first principle of the smile and the plucking of the flower— Transmitted through eight eights, who knows it is not otherwise?
Now, I entrust this non-dharma of the ancestors above To you, O worthy one, to carry back with all your strength."

Chan Master Sanji Guangtong of Ruifeng on Mount Wutai in Taoyuan Prefecture had long served under Xiyuan. When their karmic conditions were met within the master’s quarters, [Xiyuan] bestowed upon him a verse, saying:
"When not a single thought arises, all calculations cease; When myriad functions are brought to rest, the ten directions are empty.

With realms empty and calculations ceased, the bubble clears the sea; Buddhas and sentient beings appear as reflections therein. Later, he resided at Mount Tai. Shouchang... [the text continues with the title of a work].

The Master said, "I told you there is not much; why do you seek further meaning? [The student] said, "Xuansha said, 'I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate.

Zhaozhou said, "The old woman of Mount Tai—she has been thoroughly exposed by me. Now tell me, in what way did Zhaozhou expose her?

Chan Master Tianning Huan’ao Fohui of Jiaxing Prefecture was the son of the Shi family of Kuaiji. His mother dreamed of a monk seeking lodging before she conceived him.
At the age of fourteen, he paid his respects to Songgu at Tiantai to receive full ordination.

One day, during his morning recitations, when he reached the passage on the "five Sumeru mountains encircling the white curl between the Buddha’s brows," he suddenly attained awakening. He presented this realization to Songgu, who struck him with a staff and drove him away. Thereupon, he traveled everywhere...

He traveled to various regions and found his spiritual resonance with Xiao Yan, subsequently becoming a disciple within Xiao Yan’s quarters. He went forth to reside at the Udumbara Garden of Tianning Monastery in Yan-shan.

Later, returning south, he stayed at Tianning Monastery. Ascending the hall, he said: "The flute is blown and the phoenix arrives; the zither is played and the crane comes. The alms bowl is unfurled and the dragon descends;
the staff is carried and the tiger crouches. When causes and conditions meet, the needle and the magnet fit together. At this very moment, do not—"
"Is there anyone who has attained the Way? After a long silence, he said: "The sound of the bell pierces the dawn; the rooster crows at dusk.
If you wish to understand this thoroughly, even the mantra *oṃ muriti svāhā* will not suffice. He addressed the assembly: "The great meaning of the West is a dry piece of dung."
How many have failed to chew it through? At that time, I regretted my tardiness;

I should have given him a shove to the ground, teaching him to eat so much that he could not defecate, sparing his descendants the trouble of their tongues. Heh! The sun rises over a thousand mountains at dawn;
spring returns to the great earth in blossoms. Green willow smoke hangs outside the gate, yet the traveler has not yet returned home. *He!* Addressing the assembly:
Birth is one *qiankun*; death is one *qiankun*. The sage is one *dharmadhātu*; the ordinary person is one *dharmadhātu*. How has it ever deceived anyone?
If it could deceive, where would there be right and wrong, good and evil? Xiansancai is capable; it is truly a matter of some substance.
It cannot be deceived, nor can anything be lacking. You say: what kind of realm is this? Do you understand? Dust fills the eyes.
A monk entered for an interview. The Master asked, "Where is your deity? From which direction do you come, O spirit? The monk said, "Jin-sul (Golden Grain).
The Master asked, "What are you doing there? The monk said, "I am in charge of the gardens.
The Master asked, "When the vegetables are being cut, do they cry out in pain? The monk made a sound of groaning in pain. The Master said, "I have not even laid my blade upon them yet."
[The Master] asked, "Why are you crying out? [The monk] replied, "Today I have personally seen the Master. The Master said, "It is like a blind man feeling an elephant.

Throughout his life, the Master’s quarters were serene and simple; he did not neglect the myriad practices. Regarding matters of benefiting sentient beings, there was nothing he did not delight in doing, yet all such actions arose spontaneously from his own conditions, never through seeking out or soliciting others.
In the third month of the Bingyin year of the Tianqi era, as he was about to pass into nirvana, he consulted the calendar and showed it to [the assembly].

The attendant monk said, "Two days from now would be sufficient. Startled, the attendant asked, "Master, where will you go? The Master replied, "I have somewhere I intend to travel to. The attendant wept and earnestly entreated him to stay.
The Master smiled and consented, saying, "It is also acceptable to stay for three more days. When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, came forth, and changed his robes.

Seated cross-legged upon his couch, he passed away just as word arrived that the construction of his funerary shrine was nearing completion. He was ninety-one years old and had been a monk for seventy-eight years. [The remainder of the inscription is illegible.]
Chan Master Nanyue Huiguang of Xingshan Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture was a dharma heir of Chan Master Chong of Mount Jing. He was the son of the Han family of Haining.

Having left home at his own monastery, he encountered doubts while practicing the "Mu" (No) kōan and sought further instruction from Chexi. Later, he entered Shuangjing, where he picked up a fragment of paper from the ground. Upon it, there was:
"Observing the direction, one knows where he has gone. Regarding the phrase "the one who goes does not arrive at the direction," [Zhaozhou] had an awakening and presented it to Xixian.

The nostrils are not half-present; for years past, both eyes have been unable to function fully. This year, at thirty, my vital bones are offered to the blue sky.
I have finished speaking of Zen; how will you deal with it? Examine! Wengu asked:

[The questioner] said, "Fundamentally empty. [He asked], "What then of the head? The Master said, "Fundamentally empty. [He asked], "Why did one arm of the King fall to the ground?

The Master said, "Fundamentally empty. On the twenty-seventh day of the second winter month in the first year of the Taichang era, having finished instructing his disciples on his final affairs, he passed away suddenly.
His remains were interred in the General Commemorative Stupa at Mount Jing.

In the Wuxu year of the Shunzhi era, his remains were moved to the left of Haihui Monastery in Jingxi. He was sixty-one years of age and thirty-seven years since his ordination.
Chan Master Xueqiao Yuanxin of Yunmen in Shaoxing Prefecture was the son of the Zhu family from Ning County.

At the age of nine, he heard a monk reciting the passage, "The water birds and forest trees all constantly recite the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Thereupon, he gained faith and turned toward the Buddha Vehicle.
At twenty-nine, he left home and visited the mountain master Zhen of Qinwang. Zhen posed the "other-mind" question to him, asking: "Where [is it]?"
A monk came forward and said, "From India. Xuefeng said, "I have heard there are three Indias; from which one have you come? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
The monk was utterly bewildered and had no reply. Upon hearing this, the Master’s doubt was suddenly aroused.

The following day, he took up his staff, ascended the rock, and called out in a loud voice, "From which India have you come? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Suddenly, the boundaries of past and future vanished.
It was severed. It was like the sun’s orb suddenly bursting forth from the sky. He then spoke a verse: "The stone is pressed against the spine;
The body turns, yet the ribs remain. Look closely at this: Though it moves, it cannot move. He then shouted: "Zhang San has committed murder;
Li Si must pay the debt of life! Next, he went to Tiantai. Raising his head, he saw the three characters for "Ancient Yunmen," and he was suddenly enlightened.
He attained enlightenment and composed a verse, saying: "One day ascending Mount Tiantai, the clouds grew deeper; I stepped upon my straw sandals and snapped their cords.
The five hundred bhikṣus left no trace; If I see them again, I shall break their tendons. He then returned to the Double Topknot Peak (Shuangji Feng) to live in thatched huts.
One day he visited Yunqi and presented this verse: "I do not understand the West, nor do I study Chan; Having come by chance into this dusty world, I simply follow along."

Circumstances: He lived by a stream in a three-bay thatched hut. With two bamboo windows closed, he slept as the moon shone through. His patched robe was worn to tatters, yet he had no intention of mending it;

he let his hair grow long until it reached the point of madness. Since he realized the meaning of the Westward Transmission, even in the sixth month of the year, snow falls in profusion from the heavens.
Later, he attended upon Longchi, with whom he attained a karmic resonance within the meditation hall. In the *Yimao* year of the Wanli era (1615), he resided in seclusion at Mount Jing.
Zhian. In the Wuyin year of the Chongzhen era, he opened a Dharma center at Kaixian on Mount Lu. In the Guiwei year, he established a retreat at Dongta in Jiaxing.

"For forty years I have practiced in this way; I have slashed open the azure sky until it reeks with blood. Within it, there is indeed a wondrous occurrence: the lion roams about without fear."

He asked about the journey. He prostrated to the Tathāgata King of Lamps and made a universal vow that the sentient beings of lands as numerous as motes of dust would all enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā.
The assembly, tell me: how does one enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā?
Raising his whisk, he said: "To perceive that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body; to realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion. He then ascended the seat.
To realize that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty—how does such a person differ from a Buddha? Master Xinshang was not like this:
"The eel gathers at the bottom of the water; the hawk soars close to the sky. If you can grasp the meaning within these lines, there will be no further doubt about attaining Buddhahood.

In the *Yihai* year of the Chongzhen era, Yu Dacheng, the Provincial Governor, Huang Duobu, the Judicial Intendant, and others visited the Master and requested that he ascend the hall for a formal discourse at the Great Hall of Mount Jing.
"Du! Du! Du! [The Master] exclaimed. "Mount Jing is the very same Mount Jing as it has been since the Tang and Song dynasties. Striking his whisk, he said:
"Eighty-one people have passed through here; this is not merely the Mount Jing of today, nor is it the Mount Jing of a single day."
Jingshan too. A thousand-year-old monastery has but one morning’s worth of monks. Today, the Patriarchal Command is being put into action;
the ten directions are cut off at once. Now tell me, is there any auspicious omen? The bell tower grows ears; the Buddha Hall conceives a child again.
Huang Gong asked, "What is meant by 'the bell tower grows ears'? The Master picked up the incense and said, "Understand this. He asked, "How about..."
"What is this Buddha Hall, and yet you are pregnant? The Master said, "She has given birth. Huang bowed and said, "It must be the Master himself who can do so.

The Master then said, "Now, relying on the protection of the assembly of Dharma-protectors, I have been commanded to ascend this seat to restore the desolate ancestral hall and to uphold the decaying traditions of the past.
This is what is called 'the dog's tail following the fox fur'—what about the householder?"
"I do not ask about the torches before the family gate, nor about Xie Sanlang on the fishing boat;
I ask you for the saying: 'The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while the mother-in-law leads. Can anyone say it? After a long silence, he said: 'A single sweep opens the moon over the golden hall;
among the ten thousand households, there is none that is not illuminated. That very day, he went to the banquet at Han Cui Lou."
When the meal was finished, the Master said to the assembly, "This mountain monk is sixty-six years old this year. He then counted on his fingers, saying, "Bing, Ding, Wu, Ji, Geng.
After a long pause, he said, "I knew it would be strange that people were being pulled this way and dragged that way; it turns out the water buffalo has entered the palace of my destiny.
It drags through mud and carries along water, bumping into things to the east and to the west. Nevertheless, I am glad that there is plenty of water and plenty of grass. One day—
Manifesting a slight illness, he wrote a series of verses as a final instruction, saying: "Little children, on the road of birth and death, one must be carefree.
Under the bright moon and frosty dew, at dawn, drink a cup of tea and depart while sitting. Having finished writing, he cast aside his brush and passed away.

This was on the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month in the Dinghai year of the Shunzhi era. His worldly age was seventy-eight; his years since ordination were forty-eight. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa.

On the right slope of Yunmen, there was the Chan Master Dalian Jingming Baopu of Huzhou Prefecture, a native of the Luo family of Lin’an. At the age of fifteen, he went to Qingshan Miaoyan to receive the tonsure;
at twenty-two, he received full ordination at Yunqi. After traveling extensively among lecture halls for a long time, one day he himself—
He reflected that although there were points where he could reconcile the intent of the various doctrinal systems, they were entirely useless at the brink of birth and death.
He subsequently entered Mount Jing to practice *zazen*. Within twenty-one days, his realization became vast and penetrating. He composed a verse, saying: "Since childhood, I lost my mother."
He searched everywhere in foreign lands until suddenly they met by chance; he no longer engaged in further deliberation. Upon the conclusion of the retreat, he went to visit Longchi.
Having traveled from afar to catch a glimpse of his reputation, he requested the Master’s instruction. Longchi said, "This old monk’s teeth are sparse and missing. The Master replied:
"Since you have been so kind, please grant me one more word. Daci took his seat. The Master called for an attendant to bring some tea.
Daci said, "The Senior Monk is quite clever. The Master replied, "I am deaf. Daci then withdrew. One day, as he was taking his leave, Daci said:
"The old monk still has words that remain unsaid. The Master said, "Although the Master’s words are not yet finished, I already know their meaning.
Daichi said, "But tell me, what is the old monk’s meaning? The Master gave a shout. Daichi said, "Shout again and see!
The Master turned around and went out. Daichi then bestowed upon him the lineage whisk (fuzi). Later, after taking up residence there, a monk asked: [The Master said: "..."
"What is the meaning of 'Buddha'? The Master said, "The meaning of awakening. [The student] asked, "Does a Buddha still become deluded? The Master said, "He does.

[The student] asked, "Since he has awakened, how can he become deluded again? The Master said, "He does not. [The student] asked again, "How so? The Master said, "You must ask further. The Master then raised his staff and struck him out.
[The student] asked, "What is it to seize the person but not the environment? The Master said, "A swallowtail butterfly pierces through the shadows of flowers. [The student] asked, "If so..."
"What is 'seizing the object but not seizing the person'? The Master said, "Lifting the eyebrows, sweeping away the white clouds.
[The monk] asked, "What is 'seizing both person and object'? The Master said, "Neither has any news. [The monk] asked, "What is 'neither seizing person nor object'?
The Master said, "Pushing open the window to see the bright moon. Xiong Yushan asked, "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return? The Master—
Raising his tea cup, he said, "Please have some tea. He then asked, "I was in Qingzhou; I made a cotton shirt that weighed seven *jin*. What do you make of this?
The Master replied, "A shell-shedding turtle flies up into the sky. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'three *jin* of hemp'?"
The Master said: "The weight and measure are clearly distinguished; they correspond to daily use. A verse says: ◑ Black and white proceed together, yet they share the same year.

At [blank], the Chan Master Yuanhu Miaoyong of Puming Temple in Jianning Prefecture,
a successor of Chan Master Xingshan Guang, was born into the Zheng family of Haian. At the age of twelve, he left home.

Jiahe Xingshan received the dharma-transmission from Nanming Guangshou and maintained the precepts at Yunqi. One day, while reading the *Siyi Fantian Jing* (The Scripture of the Brahma Heaven of Increased Benefit), he attained a realization.
He composed a verse and presented it to Guangshou, who rebuked him. Jiahe served as his attendant for several years, yet he ultimately felt a persistent sense of obstruction.
Later, upon reading the story of the Fifth Patriarch Yanzhao’s "Clear Breeze," he finally attained liberation. One day, Guangshou raised the topic of the incense.

Yan Ji asked the Master. As the Master was about to answer, Guang let out a shout. Just as the Master was about to open his mouth, Guang shouted again. At that moment, the Master suddenly realized the profound essence of the teaching.

Guang bestowed upon him a verse, saying: "A dharma without transmission and without reception; a mind without transmission and without reception. It is entrusted to one who has no hands, who severs the sinews of space.
In the Jīmō year of the Chongzhen era, he entered Fuzhou to rebuild Puming Temple. In the winter of the Xinsi year...
I have now begun to open the Dharma for the assembly. If we were to discuss the Buddha-dharma, this mountain monk would have no place to set his teeth.
Today, however, the new mountain gate has seized my staff and wandered about in play, passing through Guozi Ridge and going straight to Huoshao Bridge.
There he lost his footing and fell into a deep stream. Fortunately, the old Buddha Hall was willing to come to his rescue; not only did it rescue him, but...
"Furthermore, I shall ride back upon his neck. Upon returning, I will cry out at the New Mountain Gate for justice, demanding that the mountain monk pass judgment.
To both the New Mountain Gate and the Old Buddha Hall, I shall grant thirty blows of the staff; the principle shall not be wrongly adjudicated. Does anyone have evidence?
After a long silence, he threw down the staff and said: "Let others at their leisure speak of its length or brevity; let us all return together to the warm room."
The Elder Duanfu resided at Lingfeng. The Master went there to pay his respects. The assembly requested him to ascend the seat. Raising his whisk, he said: "Do you understand?
'This very mind is Buddha'—this is still a point of confusion. 'Neither mind nor Buddha'—this leaves nothing toward which one can turn.
'Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing'—the butterfly piercing through the flowers is seen deep within; it cannot be grasped, nor can it be discarded. It is ineffable."
To attain the Middle Way is simply this: a dragonfly sips the water and flies with slow, deliberate grace.

Does the assembly know how Puming makes such a move, treading upon the very place where Lingfeng’s itch is found? He is able to stride boldly across the great square, trampling the crowns of all the saints.
Steep and towering, solitary and remote, he sometimes holds fast and sometimes lets go; sometimes letting go...
Sometimes one holds fast within the midst; sometimes one lets go while holding fast. In a sandalwood forest, there is nothing but sandalwood;

in a lion’s den, there is nothing but lions. Suddenly, if someone clever among the assembly were to come forth and say, "The hidden depths of Lingfeng have been needlessly laid bare by Puming," I, this mountain monk, would simply reply: "It is only because we once shared a bed."
"Therefore, I know deeply that the soles of my feet have been pierced. He struck his staff and descended from the seat.

While with Yunmen Xian, as they were admiring the new moon, Yunmen pointed at it and asked, "Where has that other half gone? The Master remained silent for a long while and then said, "Do you understand? Yunmen said:
"Even so, one only obtains half. The Master then asked, "Where has that other half gone? Mian remained silent for a long while. The Master said, "Even so, one only obtains half.
Mian then let out a great laugh. Ji'an Jin came for a second interview. As soon as he stepped across the threshold, the Master asked, "What is this?
Before Jin could respond, the Master let out a thunderous shout. Jin covered his ears and departed immediately.

The Master approved of this. One day, manifesting illness, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Generally speaking, among the monastics of Chan, those of the highest caliber study the Way through Zen inquiry.
Those of middling capacity are diligent in both observing the precepts and practicing meditation. Those of the next level are willing to devote their hearts to realizing the Way.

As for the rest, who are merely mediocre, they are not even worth mentioning. I, this decrepit old man, have also come through from that very path. Now, as my life-force and physical elements are about to disperse, I have finally been able to see through one pivotal point. He did not finish speaking.
"Bound by past conditions, tell me: what was that pivotal moment? The clear breeze carries the cry of the wild geese, note after note;
the autumn rain falls upon the *wutong* trees, silent and deep as the mountains. He then took up his brush and composed a verse: "To live is a mistake; to die is a mistake.
The iron ox snaps the golden rope. He threw down his brush and said, "Tsk! Thereupon he passed away peacefully. It was the *Renwu* year of the Chongzhen era, the tenth month...
He passed away on the eleventh day of the month at the hour of the Dragon (辰). His age was fifty-six; his years since ordination were forty-four.
His disciple Jie’an Jin and Yichu Yuan enshrined his remains and erected a stupa for them at Xingshan in Heshan.

Chan Master Ruxue of Wupeng on Mount Gui in Changsha Prefecture was the son of the Ren family from Lintong.

Having lost his father at the age of seven, he shaved his head under Tianqi of Mount Wutai. He received full ordination from Vinaya Master Cheng and subsequently traveled extensively throughout various regions.
While visiting Tiandong at Jinsu, during a conversation one night, Tiandong suddenly extended his leg and asked, "What do you make of this? The Master [responded] with his own leg.
He kicked him. The boy laughed and said, "Not yet. The Master said, "Tell me what the Monk says. The boy lay down on his back. The Master said, "That too is merely being tired.
The boy said, "And so it goes again. The Master bowed. One day, as he was taking his leave, the boy held up his whisk and said:
If you call it a whisk, you are in contact with it (*chu*). If you do not call it a whisk, you turn your back on it (*bei*).
You may not pick it up; you may not put it down. You may not utter words; you may not remain silent. You may not raise it incorrectly.
If you do not raise it incorrectly, I shall entrust it to you. The Master leaped about and said, "No, no! The boy said, "That was still just shouting and leaping about. Try raising it again."
"Look! The Master turned his body and said, "I am going. He then transmitted [the Dharma] to the boy. Later, while in seclusion at Hongji Temple, a monk asked, "What is one drop of water from Wulong?
The Master replied, "It contains all phenomena within its emptiness. As the monk hesitated, the Master drove him away with his staff, saying, "Do not dwell among the dead.
A monk asked, "For what purpose did Śākyamuni appear in the world? The Master replied, "A poor child longs for [his mother]."
"Old debt. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Why do you not ask again? The monk swept away his sitting mat and departed. The Master said, "This fool has gone off in that manner once more.
A monk came for an audience. The Master knocked on the door once. As the monk was about to open his mouth, the Master immediately closed the door.

He asked, "When Mañjuśrī gave rise to the view of Buddha and the view of Dharma... Before he had finished speaking, the Master said, "You, *ācārya*, shall receive [the karmic retribution] from this mountain monk."
Homage! When the monk was about to open his mouth, the Master covered it with his hand. The Master left the monastery gate leading the assembly to Wulongtan (Black Dragon Pond).
Probing the water with his staff, he asked, "Why does the dragon not appear? A servant stepped forward and prostrated; the Master struck him immediately.
The other shouted. The Master covered his ears with both hands. The other performed a somersault and stood up. The Master smiled at him.

Later, when the Master was seated at the ancestral pagoda of Daopei Tongqing Temple, Vinaya Master Ming came to pay respects at the pagoda. The Master said, "Those who prostrate are but dry bones. What are you doing?
Ming replied, "I thought I had forgotten," and he immediately prostrated. The Master then rose and departed. One day, during a communal work session (*pǔqǐng*), the Master...
While selecting vegetables, Ming Weina said, "I am going to retreat into stillness. The Master said, "Where is it not still?
Ming struck the Master with his palm. The Master asked, "What is this? Ming replied, "Where is it not still? The Master laughed heartily.

In the spring of the Guiyou year, he left the mountain and arrived at Jinling. The Grand Councilor Yu Jisheng invited him to reside at Jetavana Forest, where both monastics and laypeople listened to the Dharma.

He had ten thousand followers. Before long, he contracted a slight illness. On the twenty-second day of the seventh month at the hour of the horse (noon), he wrote a verse, cast aside his brush, and passed away.
His dharma heir, Yangzhuo Ming, escorted his remains back and erected a stūpa at the foot of Mount Dawai.
Chan Master Hanyue Fazang of Mount Dengwu in Suzhou Prefecture was born into the Su clan of Liangxi. From childhood, he received the tonsure at Deqing Temple in his native district.
Upon reaching adulthood, he read the *Record of Gaofeng* and harbored doubts; after more than ten years had passed, he reached Sanfeng, where the master had closed his death-dwelling gate (mushin).
Hearing the sound of a bamboo being snapped, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. At that time, Tiantong was flourishing his teachings at Jinsu.
The Master went to visit him. It happened that the boy was ascending to the hall. [The Master] raised a case: A monk asked an ancient worthy, "When the bright moon is suspended in the sky, what then?
The worthy said, "It is still a person standing on the steps below. The monk said, "I pray the Master will lead me up the steps. The worthy said, "We shall meet after the moon has fallen.
The boy then looked at the Master and said, "Tell me, how do you meet after the moon has fallen? The Master shook out his sitting mat and departed.
He went out, opened the furnace, and immediately commanded the head of the assembly to ascend the hall for the formal discourse. A monk asked, "What is the first mystery?
The Master said, "It is not the mind of Nirvana. The monk asked, "What is the second mystery? The Master said, "Nor is it the Eye of the True Dharma."
"What is the third mystery? The Master said, "The Buddhas of the three periods know it only for themselves; the six generations of patriarchs find it difficult to proclaim with their mouths.

Chan Master Tongqi of Linye at Tongxuan Temple in Taizhou Prefecture had, since childhood, exhaustively studied the scriptural teachings. Later, he left Sichuan to travel south for inquiry and shut himself within a meditation cell at Danghu.
Suddenly, he received a gatha on Zen practice from Tiantong that read: "Try to look at its form before the single thought has yet arisen. A state of doubt (*yiqing*) arose within him all at once.
One day, while losing his footing and falling from a building, he attained realization. He then broke through his confinement and went to visit [the master].

Tiantong resided at Qingliang in Wumen; subsequently, he lived at Yuyang with Dong. When Dong ascended the hall, he raised the case of the World-Honored One who, immediately upon descending from his mother’s womb, knew how to point to heaven and point to earth.
[Dong said: "As for you all, what kind of bowl do you still intend to beg from this old monk?
He then dragged his staff down from the seat and dispersed the assembly. From that time on, the Master was completely liberated. One day, he took up a broken...
The bowl was brought into the storehouse to fetch oil. A temple attendant asked, "Why have you broken the monastery’s bowl?
The Master said, "It was not I who broke it. The attendant said, "Then why is it in your hands? The Master said, "When the city gate catches fire, the disaster reaches even the fish in the pond.
The attendant said, "You must pay for the bowl. The Master then opened both his hands. The attendant desisted. In the *guwei* year of the Chongzhen era, he resided [there].
Tongxuan. He subsequently resided at Qizhen in the Eastern Pagoda, later moving to Tiantong. Entering the hall, he said: "This morning, our Buddha was born;
he immediately turned toward the golden basin to bathe, then pointed to heaven and pointed to earth—acting as if he were utterly shameless.
He further declared, 'I alone am honored. I, this mountain monk, do not yet dare grant him such approval. But tell me, what longings does this mountain monk possess? [He] then..."
He then opened his mouth wide and struck the ground with his staff, saying: "One need not plant thorns at the gate;
otherwise, future descendants will find them clinging to their robes. Ascending the hall, he cited the public case of Danxia visiting National Teacher Zhong, who happened to be asleep.

The attendant stared with wide eyes while speaking in his sleep, causing the National Teacher distress that unsettled him from both sleeping and eating. Although Danxia understood how to bury [the matter] on the spot...
People fail to observe that bystanders have seen through this. Is there anyone who knows the attendant who was struck with a staff and Danxia who was startled?
I shall not refuse to offer a verse on this: Sitting upright in his chamber, he sleeps alone; Unexpectedly, spring flowers fall before the railing.
"How vexing it is that the wandering bee haphazardly gathers pollen; even now it pursues [the fragrance] toward the grassy embankment. Ascending the hall, he said:

"Before you had reached Tiantong Monastery, you thought Tiantong was something extraordinary beyond this world. But once you have arrived and witnessed it with your own eyes, it remains as it was: pines and bamboos leaning against the green mountains.
Clearly, clearly—the pines and bamboos; clearly, clearly—the meaning of the Patriarchs. If you should, for even a moment, harbor a conceptualizing mind..."
Once born, one cannot avoid encountering obstacles wherever one goes. Now tell me: how can that single phrase which does not involve the journey be manifested?
[He suddenly strikes the meditation staff and says: "Returning home is entirely the business of the descendants; the patriarch has never gone out from his door. [Ascending the hall:
In the past, beneath the previous Master, ten thousand fingers surrounded him, and those who tasted the Dharma-flavor were numerous. I now seek that milk of the Dharma.
[The character] "zhě" (者) is pronounced with the *shuī* (誰) and *qiè* (切) finals. This mountain monk proclaims the Prajñāpāramitā to repay the immense kindness of my late master.
One might say: "An offense has its source; a debt has its owner. That single phrase from which one gained strength in the past transcends both past and present.

But tell me, what phrase is it? Suddenly he grasps his staff, strikes the ground, and says: "No one recognizes the horse that sweated [in battle]; let us once more discuss this epoch-making merit. He strikes again.
Descending from his seat, the Master ascended the hall and said, "This mountain monk’s four elements are not strong; I am unable to preach the Dharma for the assembly.
He then took up his staff and said, "Only this wooden elder, though entirely without apertures, is able to skillfully preach the essentials of the Dharma.
Striking the incense table, he said, "Do not follow him into delusion. While the Master was ill, the Head Seat asked, "When the ancients faced their final moments..."
At the tip of the branch, he leaves behind a word or two to serve as eyes for the future. What instruction do you have for us now?
The Master said, "To move is to invite calamity. [The monk] said, "The official does not allow even a needle, yet in private one passes carts and horses. The Master said, "Why such excessive talk?"
[Zhaozhou] said, "It is not beyond my capacity. The Master struck him a blow across the face with his fist. The monk bowed in prostration.
As the Master was about to pass away, he sent Xuanze from Tiantai to visit him. The Master hurriedly asked, "Have you arrived? Xuanze replied, "I have just now arrived.
The Master asked, "What time is it now? Xuanze replied, "Noon. The Master stared at him with wide-open eyes. Xuanze said, "Previously, I received the favor of the Master..."

Shang remembered his prediction. He now requested that the Abbot further bestow upon him a dharma name. The Master said, "The fruition of practice is perfectly accomplished. Shang then performed a ritual of thanks and departed.
The Master passed away with serene composure.

The layman Huang Jiazi, whose courtesy name was Yuti, was a renowned figure from Chengjiang in Pilin. Having inherited his enlightened vocation from an early age, he extensively mastered both Buddhist and secular classics.
He had long been a disciple under the guidance of Tiantong and Qingshan, attaining a profound realization.
He once composed a preface to a *yulu* (recorded sayings), stating: "The sound of the stone chime is so resonant that even the deaf can hear it; these words do not deceive me. Long ago...
Emperor Wu of Han taught Qi Jing-bing the art of war. Bing said, "It does not lie in studying antiquity; rather, it depends on what one's strategic plans are like.
Emperor Ming showed Han Gan a painting from the imperial collection. Gan said, "I do not wish to look at it. Qi Bing had the living method within his breast.
Han Gan had living horses within his breast; Qingshan has the living essence of the profound and essential within his breast.

He gathers [the prey] from the mouth of the fierce tiger and places it upon the head of the venomous snake. To extract the nails and pull out the wedges for all people under heaven—how could this be transmitted through mere words or ears?
I have recorded this here to catch a glimpse of a single speck of its brilliance. Later, when Tiantong was about to pass away, he...
He presented him with a *nà* robe. In the year Jiǎshēn, when the dynasty was overthrown, the Master encountered hardship while imprisoned in the Southern Capital.
One day, he wrote a verse on the handle of a fan and sent it to his fellow practitioner, Chan Master Mùyún, saying: "Through the sword-trees and knife-mountains, I pass with arms swinging free;
Stretching out my two legs, I rub them myself. The thirty thousand Sugatas were never Buddhas; The million Bāxiūns—how could they be demons? I am but a weary old man..."
"It does not hinder Heaven from being drunk as well; let the waters rise in waves as they are tossed about. Last night I dreamed of the hands of an Asura;
what can be done when the two orbs suddenly leap? Thereupon he cast aside his brush and passed away.

Zen Master Lin’gao Benyu of Zhulin Monastery in Jiangning Prefecture was the son of the Chen family of Kunshan.

At the age of seven, he paid respects to the elder master Zhanchuan of Yao Peak and left the household life. After receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively throughout various regions and visited Boshan.
Boshan said, "Before entering the golden cage, whose wild sparrow are you? The Master replied, "The crane soars through the azure heavens from the nine peaks; the horse has no... [text fragment].
"Chasing the wind for a thousand *li* is in vain. Mount Shan said, "To wield an adze when there is no Yings city is unavoidable; it will leave its scars.

The Master said, "When those in all quarters brandish mallets and raise fly-whisks, what kind of business is that? Mount Shan said, "A single cloud spans the seas and mountains; woodcutters are utterly lost on their way home.
The Master said, "No wonder the tiger beneath the crags suddenly startles people in the dark," and he then departed. The Master arrived at Jingu Temple, where he encountered...
It was late in the day. [Zhaozhou] then asked, "When one comes to seek lodging for the night, how should one proceed? Miyan said, "One cannot rest here. The Master said, "Is there no expedient means?
Miyan raised his staff as if to strike him. The Master caught it and gave him a shove, saying, "I have seen through you!"
He then departed. Later, he went to visit Qingshan. Qingshan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Wulin.
Qingshan said, "How do you know about this place of mine? The Master said, "A foul reputation is hard to hide. Qingshan said, "It only defiles your ears. The Master then gave a shout.
Qingshan said, "After the shout, what is it like? The Master said, "Still, it is not known. Qingshan said, "I, the old monk, do not know; what is it that you know? The Master—

[The Master] raised his hand as if to strike him. Xuefeng said, "Do not plunder the void. One day, while attending him, Xuefeng said, "Students of the present day are unwilling to engage in true inquiry and genuine realization;
for this reason, the Dharma-gate has fallen into decline. The Master replied, "Even so, it also depends on the teacher.
If Huanglong had not received a severe beating from Ciming, how would he have known that the Way transcends ordinary circumstances? Xuefeng said in a stern voice, "Is it merely a matter of words?"
"Is it something transmitted through the ears? From this point on, the Master [Zhaozhou] took up the teachings with devotion, serving his teacher intimately for three years.
Later, while presiding over the assembly in the Dharma Hall, a monk asked: "How was it before you met Qingshan? The Master said: "The mouth of the alms bowl faces the sky.

The monk asked: "How is it after you met him? The Master said: "The tip of the staff strikes the ground. The monk asked: "What about both having seen him and not having seen him? The Master said: "Fine."
The waist-drum is struck at both ends. [A monk] asked, "Today the Master resides at Jingyun;
how will you respond? The Master said, "Come with another question. He then said, "The entire Tripitaka is nothing but useless old paper;
the seventeen hundred cases of the Patriarchs' intent are all but trailing vines and entangling branches. A clever fellow does not set foot here, but goes straight—"
A pure breeze sweeps through; a gentle rain falls in mist. He blows the great void into a single bubble and squeezes the sand-grain worlds into a single eye.
What are you all doing within that? He lets out a shout and says: "Śūnyatā-jātīya did not understand how to sit in the mountain cave."
It rouses the heavenly flowers to fall and the earth to tremble. Entering the hall, [the Master] said: "Before Mount Xiong’er, one constantly faces the wall;
the True Man of No Rank is a dried piece of dung. Deshan and Linji were far too reckless; yet within the blow of the staff, there is an eye as clear as the sun.
He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Look! Look! Linji and Deshan are coming! He struck the ground with the staff and said, "Linji and Deshan have been..."
Jingyun struck his staff once, whereupon Malar immediately withdrew. Master Bodhidharma, from behind him, said gently, "In official matters, even a needle cannot pass;
in private, one may pass carriages and horses—how is this? He then struck his staff once more and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The willow eyes open and the peach cheeks smile; the spring breeze blows, scattering how many fallen flowers?

If you are one who knows the sound, then turn around at once—the Yunmen fan suddenly leaps up! It startles the hundred-tongued bird on the branch, whose every cry proclaims: (He then struck the gavel.)
"It is better to go back. He threw down his staff. On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, he ascended the hall, struck the ground with his staff, and said:

"The past Buddha Dīpaṃkara—his original radiance and auspiciousness were like this. Again, striking once more, he said: "The future Buddha Dīpaṃkara—his original radiance and auspiciousness were like this.
Once again, striking once more, he said: "The present Buddha Dīpaṃkara—his original radiance and auspiciousness are like this. After a long silence, he looked around.
The attendants said, "One must not speak of dreams in the presence of a fool. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
"One person, atop the summit of a thousand peaks, is struck and bumped with no place to hide.
Another person, at the crossroads, lies prostrate and sprawled, with no way out. If you recognize the whereabouts of these two, you will understand the question Pánggōng asked Mázǔ."

He asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as companions? The Patriarch said, "Wait until you can swallow up all the waters of the West River with a single draught, and then I will tell you.
The official then attained realization. This too was like pouring foul water over one's head.
Here, what need is there to speak of bodhi, nirvana, true thusness, liberation, the twenty-five states of existence, or the eighteen realms? All are utterly cleansed away.
Washing away [delusions]. If you understand, the golden-maned lion transforms into a dog; if you do not understand, he kicks out Yangqi’s three-legged donkey.
*Chán*. Entering the hall, he said: "If you see that all forms are no-form, then you see the Tathāgata.
He held up his whisk and said: "This is 'all forms. What is 'no-form'? Again, he made a fist and said: "This is 'no-form. What is..."
The Tathāgata struck his meditation seat and said: "Though acquaintances fill the world, how many can truly know one's heart? Ascending the hall, he said: "The three realms offer no peace;
they are like a burning house, filled with manifold sufferings and most terrifying.
Guizong chopped down a live snake; Danxia burned a wooden Buddha; Puhua kicked over a rice table; An-guo smashed a cooking stove. And yet—"
The Way. There is no fear. A yellow oriole perches upon a tree with a single branch; a white egret descends into the field like a thousand dots of snow.
[He] strikes the whisk and descends from his seat. Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Before the Many-Sons Stupa, what did they discuss together?
The Master said: "Six ears do not share a secret. He then said: "A stone tiger roars at the mountain peak; a clay ox walks on the ocean floor. One knows not where it is."
[He] took up his staff and said, "When people contend over it, I strike my staff and say: 'It can bestow and it can take away; it can kill and it can bring to life.

He struck the staff repeatedly and descended from the seat. He ascended the hall and raised the example of Qianfeng, who said: "If you raise one, you must not raise two. To let pass one move is to fall into the second.
Yunmen stepped out from the assembly and said: "Yesterday someone came from Tiantai and went back to..."
On his way to Jingshan, Qianfeng summoned the *vinaya* master (Rector) and said: "Tomorrow there shall be no communal labor (*pǔqǐng*).
Qianfeng’s path is lofty and those who can harmonize with it are few; had it not been for Yunmen, things would have nearly come to ruin.

Ascending the hall: The fragrant breeze blows as the summer heat steams; the bowl-bag hangs high against the jagged blue peaks. The Buddhas of the three periods cannot find them by groping;
the patriarchs of successive generations have lost their eyes. The person of no station cannot restrain his impatience;
he claps his hands and laughs aloud. But tell me, what is it that he laughs at? After a long silence, he said: "A broken wooden ladle. Ascending the hall, he took up his staff.
The Staff said: "In the kingdom of Magadha, he personally issued this decree; for many years, who has paid the price for these stagnant goods?
Before the Bear Ear Peak, he holds aloft [the Dharma] alone—this is much like selling a dog while hanging up a sheep's head. And when has he ever actually raised up this one crucial point?

"Today, the life of Yao Peak rests in the hands of you all. The lives of you all rest in the hands of Yao Peak."

He asked, "What is 'The great earth has no grass'? The Master said, "It is one zhang deep before the Dharma Hall.

"Before the moonlit hall, flowers bloom on a withered tree—is this a guest's phrase or a host's phrase? The Master said, "The stone woman weeps for the blue sky. Question: "What is the Secret Demon’s Fork?
The Master held up his rosary and said, "This is a foreign *bodhi*. The questioner said, "Before I have even asked, please [explain] to me, Master..."
The Master replied with a harmonious voice and struck him. A monk asked, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? The Master said, "A blazing fire of three feet.
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A cool heap of ashes. One day, the Master was slightly ill;

at that time, the monastery was undergoing extensive construction and repairs. He went everywhere to inspect them and then returned to the Dharma Hall, where the drums were sounded to assemble the community.

The assembly recounted the circumstances of his departure from the world and, as he was about to enter into stillness, they were all filled with grief and longing. The administrator said, "The mountain master has gone away and has not yet returned;
we pray that you, O Venerable One, will delay for one more day. The Master bowed his head and returned to his quarters. On the following day, the mountain master arrived.
The Master ascended the seat once more to express his gratitude, and after concluding the arrangements for his final affairs, he spoke a verse while remaining upon the seat.
End. His disciples constructed a stūpa on the ridge behind the ancient Bamboo Grove.
Chan Master Tongxiu of Yulin at Mount Tianmu in Hangzhou Prefecture was exceptionally gifted from birth. As a youth, his speech was extraordinary.

At the age of nineteen, he entered the monastic order under Qingshan, where he received full ordination. He served as an attendant, tending to the master’s water vessel and handkerchief, and by night, he joined the assembly.

The Master said, "I knew well that the Venerable One would not dare to speak. Shàn said, "Why would you not dare to speak of the *Recorded Sayings of Shíwū*? The Master said, "To follow him."
