Chan Master Zuan Shi Jian of Xuedou in Ningbo Prefecture was the son of the Wu family of Quanpao in Chuzhou.
As a child, he delighted in reading Buddhist scriptures. One day, while his mother was washing a sore on his hand, he asked in jest, "What is this? The master replied, "It is a Buddha’s hand.

Upon seeing his mother laugh heartily, he suddenly lost both parents and went to Zhenzhou, where he relied upon Master Liao of Changlu to receive the tonsure and precepts. He then went to study under [Master] Chan.

He applied himself with such rigorous diligence that his ribs did not touch his mat for several years. At that time, Da Xiu Jue served as the First Seat (Diyizuo) and regarded the Master as a vessel of the Dharma.
After receiving full ordination, the Master entered Mount Zhengxingshan on Elephant Mountain (Xiangshan) and dwelt in a thatched hut he had bound together.

As the mountain fronted the sea, it was frequented by many malevolent spirits; a giant python once entered the hut, raising its head and glaring at him with rage. After several days, it returned and coiled itself around [the hut].

The snake coiled around the master’s bed. The master did not look back; the serpent led him away. A hundred strange transformations ensued, yet none could distract him. Gradually, they subsided into stillness.
One night, while in deep meditative concentration, he thought to himself, "Is this truly an external object? Thereupon, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
His body, mind, and the world became as transparent as lapis lazuli. He then descended the mountain to see Yan-shou Ran and said, "Lately my belly has grown large, yet there is nothing [to fill it]."
Ran was staying in a small hermitage where there was no bed to lie upon. He said, "If you can provide me with food, I will stay here by spreading out my mat; otherwise, I shall depart.
He continued, "Where did this fellow see ghosts or spirits that he has come here to suffer defeat? The Master then shouted at him.
Ran attempted to cross-examine and challenge the Master repeatedly, but he could not overcome him. Ran then said, "Master Jian is a man of thorough realization," and went again to see Daixiu.

Yuelin’s eloquence and discernment were exceptionally outstanding. Xiu said, "From now on, neither Buddhas nor patriarchs will be able to withstand you. Consequently, he ordered the Master to go begging for the assembly.
Carrying two bags, the Master accepted whatever was obtained immediately; thus he underwent many hardships and labors until his hair turned white at Mount Cui.
He said to the Master, "You exert yourself to the utmost for the sake of the assembly; are you not weary? The Master said, "You must know that there is one who does not grow weary.
The monk asked, "When one cannot be contained within the station of honor and nobility, what then? The Master said, "Meeting him everywhere, yet not being recognized.
The monk asked, "That is still the guest and host on the road. What is the host within the host? The Master said, "A flame is extinguished by the element of fire itself."
Xuedou Zong covered the Master’s mouth with his hand. The Master shook out his sleeves and withdrew. Later, when Zong moved to Xuedou, he invited the Master to go with him.

At that time, the Dharma Hall had been newly renovated, and the Master was ordered to deliver a general discourse. Zong listened in secret and sighed, saying, "I have had ears since birth, yet I have never heard such a thing.
He subsequently succeeded the Master on the seat. Entering the hall, he said: "The World-Honored One has a secret word; Kāśyapa did not conceal it."
One night, falling flowers rained down; throughout the city, the flowing waters were fragrant. He presided over six monasteries, all through the recommendation of princes, dukes, and great officials.
In the *Xinhai* year of the Shaoxi era, he retired from his duties and dwelt in the Eastern Hermitage of Xuedou.

In the seventh month of the following year, he manifested illness and instructed the assembly, saying, "I am going. For my funeral rites, you must strive for simplicity; do not wear white robes or wail in grief. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
He passed away at the age of eighty-eight, having lived for fifty-three summers. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the left of his native mountain.

Those who preserved his hair and beard found relics (śarīra) within every single strand. His reputation resounded throughout the land, yet his physical traces never ventured beyond the Four Ming Mountains;
thus, he styled himself "Zu'ān" (The Satisfied Hermitage).

Chan Master Weigan Daqin of Guangfu Monastery in Taizhou, Yangzhou Prefecture, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xuedou Zong. He was the son of the Yu family of that same prefecture. One day he ascended the hall and, citing a case, said:
"A monk asked Tong’an, ‘What is the house style of the Master? Tong’an replied, ‘The golden rooster carries its chicks back home.’"
In the Milky Way, the Jade Hare conceives and enters the Purple Microcosm. [A guest] asks: "If a visitor suddenly arrives, how will you receive them? Tong'an says:
"The golden fruit was plucked by the monkey at early court; the jade blossom was carried back by the phoenix at evening.
The Master said: "Guangfu would not do so. If someone asks, 'What is the master’s house style? I would simply say to him: 'Singing beside the clusters of emerald bamboos.'"
*Kuannai*: Lying amidst the mist and vines deep within the emerald cliffs, what will you use to receive a guest who suddenly arrives?
An unfathomable basket holds the bright moon; a mindless bowl stores the pure breeze.

Chan Master Zao of Chao-hua in Shaoxing Prefecture, successor to Chan Master Shanquan Zhi, ascends the hall for the opening of the furnace: "Snow fills the cold window; the wooden Buddha of Danxia is burned to ashes.
Ice meets at the wild crossing; the iron ox of Shanfu is frozen to death. Truly, the cold embers flare into flame, and a single snowflake—"
Without lingering, moving freely and spontaneously, it is realized as immediate enjoyment. Do you all Zen masters understand this essential point?
Wrapping one’s head in a patched robe, one is utterly unaware of cold or warmth.
The Late Evening Assembly of Chan Master Mingji Huizu of Huazang Monastery in Changzhou Prefecture, Dharma Heir of Chan Master Jingci Hui. [The Master] raised the following case:
On the night of the winter solstice, Dongshan invited Head Seat Tai to eat some pastries. Dongshan said: "There is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth, black as lacquer."
It is always present within movement and activity, yet it cannot be grasped within movement and activity. Tell me, where does the fault lie? Tai said, "The fault lies within movement and activity.
Deshan called to his attendant and had him remove the fruit table. The Master then offered this verse: "Dongshan’s fruit—whom does it not belong to?
Removing the tray is a wondrous turning of the pivot. Tonight I shall lightly break it open for you: The peony flower."
Sleeping Cat Below.
The seventeenth-generation successor in the lineage of Chan Master Xuedou Jian of Dajian.
Chan Master Chang’eng Ru Jing of Tiantong in Ningbo Prefecture was born with extraordinary intelligence, unlike ordinary children.
As he grew up, he studied the world-transcending Dharma and went to Xuedou to attend upon Zu’an. Zu’an instructed him to contemplate the kōan of “the cypress tree in the courtyard.

He attained realization and presented this verse: “The ancestral meaning from the West is the cypress tree in the courtyard; The nostrils are vast and empty, facing the eyes. Falling to the ground...”
The withered branch just leaps; the pine and ivy laugh aloud as they soar upward. Anhan accepted this. Later, he appeared in the world and moved through several famous monasteries.
While residing at Jingci, he was granted an imperial edict to ascend to Tiantong. Holding up the imperial yellow document, he showed it to the assembly and said:
"The clouds part in the nine heavens. He held it up and said: "Behold! A multicolored phoenix brings it forth. Now tell me, how do you understand this? 'Swift as the command of the law.'"
The Imperial Decree: Opening the Stove for the Hall Discourse. He summoned the assembly and drew a circle, saying: "This is the Tiantong stove. Approach it and you will be burned to death;
retreat and you will freeze to death. Suddenly, if a man were to come forth and ask, "What should be done? [He would say: "Hmph! (𠰢).
The hearth-fire stirs. Ascending the hall, he said: "The frosty wind howls with a chilling severity; the leaves of the trees fall in a desolate rustle. Raising his whisk, he said: "Look!
Only Linglong Rock remains, its towering peaks rising ever higher. This so-called 'Tiantong’s滞貨' (stale goods)—today I shall make one short sale of it.
Is there anyone who can offer the price? He descended from the seat and inspected the hall. Ascending the hall again, he said: "Outwardly, do not let [it] escape..."
Entering, he does not let anything go out from within. With one blow of the hammer, all matters are brought to completion.
But tell me, how is it? Before the Peak of Great White, the command is renewed; the internal and external regulations are both fully understood. He offers thanks to the new and old two assemblies.
Entering the hall, he opens the Avīci Hell, manifests King Yama, gathers a host of yakṣas, and arranges the ox-head demons in two rows. Together with...
Those who advance are driven upward by fierce fires upon sword-trees; those who retreat are forced to hide away amidst freezing ice within mountain-blades.
Tell me, what matter are you trying to understand? It is intolerable to fiddle with chopsticks when one’s belly is full, or to urinate on one’s bed when the arrow is already at the bowstring.
If you have not yet realized this, the spring breeze of the willow and peach trees enters the theater. [Ascending the hall: "The stinking iron fist of Tiantong!"
I have slaughtered the water-buffalo of the rivers and lakes. In the depths of night, suddenly an egg was born; at daybreak, the great sun was pushed forth.
Tell me, how is this? I smile at all you people in your damp places, so that you may avoid having your steps slip as if on oil.
Wanqiao ascended the hall and said: "Go there; come here. Between them lies an abyss and a precipice. Tell me, how will you manage it?
He made the gesture of a curved bridge with his whisk and said: "Look! Vague and wide is the golden stairway; faintly curved like a rainbow.
When a person passes over the bridge, what then? Within the shadows of pine and ivy, heaven’s artistry unfolds. (Han)
Enter the painting within the luster of the ink and look. He ascended the hall and said: "Where Lingyun saw it, the peach blossoms were in bloom;
where Tiantong sees it, the peach blossoms have fallen. When the peach blossoms bloom, the spring wind urges them on; when the peach blossoms fall, the spring wind is harsh.
Setting aside Lingyun for a moment—does anyone here meet with Tiantong? When the spring wind is harsh upon the peach blossoms, they leap over the waves and manifest their horns. New.
The Hall of Wondrous Adornment has been erected; for the celebration of the repentance ceremony, I ascend the seat.

I have toppled the rat’s nest of many years and swept the ground clean until it is level, smiling broadly. The rafters and beams stand tall, piercing the clouds; for ten billion years, they shall provide ample shelter. Does the assembly see?
This morning we have accomplished a great cause; for a thousand ages, the Great Matter has been brought forth. But tell me, how so? He planted his staff upright and said:
"With brows furrowed, I leave it to the guests outside the gate; having arrived home, I return it to those within. He then cited:
Manjusri asked Wuzhuo, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "The South. Manjusri asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the South? He replied, "At the end..."
Fahui asked Zhishu, "How many followers do you have? Zhishu replied, "Sometimes three hundred, sometimes five hundred.
Fahui said, "The spring breeze beckons the partridges to sing. Zhishu asked, "How do you maintain the Buddha-dharma here? Zhishu replied, "Ordinary people and sages dwell together;
dragons and snakes are intermingled. Fahui asked, "How many followers do you have? Zhishu replied, "Three times three before, and three times three after. Master [Fahui]—[nodded].

It is said: "On level ground, amidst waves and mountain torrents, one drives an iron boat. These two turns of phrase by the Celestial Youth barely cause his eyebrows to knit with those of the various quarters.
There are two further turns of phrase intended to open the eyes of the various quarters:
three hundred or five hundred copper coins and iron coins, with the count complete and the value full. Three before and three after; radishes and taros, shallowly stored yet full.
Carrying [this burden], suddenly the eyes open in all directions; one will certainly clap hands and laugh loudly. But tell me, what is there to laugh at?
It is not a laugh at a "bācha" (a foolish person); it is a laugh at a fabrication. Nevertheless, those who laugh are still rare.

If someone were to ask me how many people are in the assembly at Tiantong, I would simply say: "The newly built Miaoyan is praised as number one; they are all gathered together within the painted circle."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Lu Xiujing, Tao Yuanming, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra—[they] draw a perfect circle and say, 'Ei!
Herein lies the full confession. Now tell me, by whose authority is this judged? If it were Confucius, he would have said: 'I have nothing hidden from you.
[The Master] then cited the koan of the World-Honored One’s birth and offered this verse: Bathing the infant beneath the Ashoka tree, At the clear dawn, the rosebushes bear dew.
Open! Turning over the place where monks meet one another, the donkeys and horses of the back stable emerge from the womb.
He cites the story of the First Patriarch facing Emperor Wu, who did not recognize him. The verse says: The golden crow flies up onto the jade balustrade;
A black-lacquered Kunlun faces you face-to-face. In the end, these few things cannot be transmitted; Falling flowers and flowing water are utterly groundless. He cites Yangqi Lianhua.

Regarding the "Briar Hedge" and "Vajra Circle" koans, the verse says: *Suddenly a casual, dangling cord appears behind the elbow; / Abruptly before the wind, a chaotic crossbar is set up. / Nalaka, with his eight arms, is left in vain despair;
/ At the third watch of midnight, one walks in broad daylight.* The Master sat in the seat of enlightenment six times and twice received imperial edicts.
The flourishing of his Dharma path can be imagined from this. When he was about to pass away, he spoke this verse: *Six...*
In the sixteenth year, his transgressions filled the heavens; with a single leap, he fell alive into the Yellow Springs. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa at his home mountain.
Chan Master Donggu Guang of Ningbo Prefecture, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Huazang Zu, cited the World-Honored One’s response to King Prasenajit regarding the dialogue:
"Is there conventional truth within ultimate truth? He offered this verse: "No hearing, no speaking—the meaning is inexhaustible; Iron walls and silver mountains."
A single thread connects all. Where, then, lies his true Holy Truth? Last night, the autumn wind reached the wutong trees.
[The Master] raised the story of Yaoshan pointing to the two trees—one flourishing and one withered—on Mount Rong. The verse says: Three by three and two by two, they are not the same;
Hand in hand, they walk together into the weeds. Turning the heels around, they step in embroidered shoes; What prevents the spring breeze from blowing in the month of December?
Regarding the story of how Shipman (Chuanzi) received Jia Shan and passed away at Fushan, the verse says:
Where the body is hidden, there is no trace; The numinous bird dwells atop the shadowless tree. Where there is no trace, do not hide the body; On the sproutless branch, the spring flowers bloom.
With origins as they are, who can discern them? At dawn, the west wind blows gently; A single path of pine-needles is cast about in competition.
*Zhì*. A monk asked Caoshan, "What is it like when the funeral shroud is not yet hung? Caoshan said, "Today is the completion of the mourning period for Caoshan.
The monk asked, "After the mourning period is complete, what then? Caoshan said, "Caoshan enjoys talking while drunk. The verse says: Who understands Caoshan’s drunken talk?
In his intoxicated words and wild speech, he feels no shame. At midnight, the sun shines directly overhead; He rides [the ox]...
Wearing a robe and boots with his back half-turned, he raised up the story of National Teacher Yao asking Longya: "Heaven cannot cover it; earth cannot support it. What is the principle of this?
Longya said, "A practitioner should speak in such a manner. He then offered this verse: An iron ship floats upon the heart of the great ocean;
Following the waves, the surging billows flood the heavens. Reaching the shore with a favorable wind, no one recognizes him; From the north of the river...
The envoy brought iron coins, as detailed in the *Lianzhu ji* (String of Pearls Collection).
[He was] a dharma successor of Chan Master Tiandong Jing,
the eighteenth generation under Dajian [Huaihai].
Chan Master Jue of Lumen in Xiangzhou went to visit Chang’ung. He happened upon the Master ascending the hall, who said: “A single black plum is like its original form;
A spider weaves a web to catch a dragonfly. The dragonfly loses both wings; Laughable indeed, the black plum bites an iron nail.
While among the assembly, the Master could not help but let out a laugh and said: “Had I known earlier that the lamp was fire, how long would it take for the rice to cook?”
After a long time, he later received formal authorization (*kanna*). He went forth to reside at Rokumon (Deer Gate) and addressed the assembly, saying:
"The entire earth is the student’s single volume of scripture; the entire universe is the student’s single eye. With this eye, read such a scripture."

For billions of kalpas, it has been constant and uninterrupted. (Master Baoyun Shou remarked: "This is not easy to read. The Master once composed the *Wuwei Song* (*Verses on the Five Ranks*), which says:
"Center within Deviation: The moon is hidden by black clouds at midnight; Buddhas and patriarchs leave no trace, ordinary and holy beings alike vanish.
Who within this can discern the source from whence they come? Deviation within Center: The golden well and jade basin hold autumn waters cold; The red sun has already risen over the sea and heavens."
From the East: the lingering rays do not illuminate the crown of Vairocana. Coming from the Center: wearing horns and clad in fur, how many times has he known this?

Turning his body to respond to things, he attains the full wondrousness; when the clouds have cleared, the towering peak is never revealed. Arriving from the Partial: facing him directly, who can allow for deliberation?
Holding the wondrous seal in hand, he does not face the wind; as great functions proliferate, how could there be any stagnation? Reaching through the Simultaneous: there is none.
Only children with tongues can understand the Way; where can one find the source by brushing away the dust? Casting off the hand and returning to the path, one again attains the wondrous.

This is Chan Master Zhiguang of Donggu, successor to Chan Master Yiju "Zhigong" of Tiantong in Ningbo Prefecture (the recorded sayings are contained in the twenty-seventh sheet of the first volume of the *Zengji Xu Chuandeng Lu*; the woodblocks were lost, so this portion is missing).
[Record. To be supplemented once retrieved from further research].
Dajian’s nineteenth-generation successor, Chan Master Jue of Lumen.

Chan Master Puzhao Yibian of Qingzhou had thoroughly investigated the essential meaning and intent of the scriptural teachings. Later, he abandoned them and went to visit Lumen, where he attained the meaning beyond words.
He emerged into the world at Wanshou Monastery in Zhongdu. In his quarters, he would often set forth one hundred questions to test practitioners from all quarters.
The first was: "If you realize it before the sound, you fall into the present moment; if you take it up after the phrase, you lose your head and mistake it for a reflection."
"What is one's own nature prior to the empty kalpa? He said again: "Do not establish the two extremes; there is no need to settle upon the Middle Way.
Tell me, where can you encounter the true point? He said again: "Returning to the path and shifting the position—must one truly wear horns and fur?
Can one call such a person a beast? He said again: "In every thought-moment, Śākyamuni appears in the world; at every step..."

When Maitreya descends to be born, why is it that directing the mind toward him is already an error, and stirring a thought is already a deviation? It is further said: "With a mouth, one could not praise him enough;
without words, the mind is naturally clear. To say this is to tear asunder empty space; to say it is not so is the livelihood of ghosts.

"Where is the ultimate point of the Superior Man? Bring forth a single phrase! Thus it was that those who frequented his quarters were many, yet few were those who could accord with his spiritual mechanism.
The Master once composed the "Verses on the Four Guests and Hosts": Guest within Guest:

Wandering across the world for many springs, Carrying one's studies, merit grows ever poorer. The ocean of practice is deep and vast, requiring full immersion; The sky of meaning is boundless, admitting no dust.

The Host within the Guest: His robes are tattered, his emaciated bones exposed with nothing left; alone he presides over the realm, radiating the Great Beginning. Within the three-foot case lies the sword that slays the sycophants;
within the hundred-fold pouch is the letter recommending the worthy. The Guest within the Host: On the vermilion steps, the whip is still as the Nine Palaces open;

ten thousand miles of rivers and mountains are utterly free of a speck of dust. Casting off the official robe and donning the scholar’s cap, every sound proclaims only this: [That] "Who? (Nà) — *Nà* (那).

Coming from the edge, the Lord of Lords: Deep and secluded, heavy cliffs lock in the misty peaks; in ancient caves, dragons roar as the fog thickens. The Stone Woman sings her return within the red flames;
the Wooden Man sets his steps to seek a kindred spirit. Furthermore, he offered verses on the sixteen topics shown by Fushan to Touzi.
First, "Recognizing One’s Own Lineage": In questions and answers, do not repay with phrases or gāthās; in the end, Buddhas and Patriarchs are all one.
Withdrawn. After nine years facing the wall, many complications arose; standing in the snow seeking the divine light was also a forced pursuit.

To live amidst two deaths—now that time has reached its end, what further intimacy remains? Clouds lock the secluded crags, ice locks the ferry crossings. How admirable is the one atop the ridge, his spirit swelling with vigor!
A single branch of spring blooms alone amidst the snow. Life within death among the three modes of life—how fitting that they resemble one another, pleasing the hearts of men.

The moon in water, flowers in the void, reflections in a mirror; glory is but a phantom. On a desolate path, travelers are lost; across fragrant grasses, they cross the ford. One intends to take a spark from a flint to illuminate the heavens.

In the four ways of non-falling, whether in life or death, reaching the ultimate end, drawing water and gathering wood are never in vain. Carrying water and moving firewood naturally accord with the proper time. The swallows chirp.
The curtains remain still as he has not yet returned; where the dawn oriole sings, green willows hang down. V. Five Non-Relinquishments:

The Three Peaks and Mount Hua are all leveled and cleared. Snow presses upon the cold forest, breaking the frozen branches. When not a single thought arises, the entire body is revealed; the moment the slightest movement stirs, one falls back to the steps.
VI. Six Relinquishments: The road is broad and the cliffs high, with azure streams flowing. Mountain flowers bloom everywhere, reaching up to meet the clouds.
The pavilion. After the rain, where does the oriole’s song warble? Disregarding the waning spring, its cries do not cease. The Seven Life-Giving Swords:

listening with the ears is not as intimate as listening with the eyes. Rain falls on the Southern Mountain, clouds gather over the Northern Mountain; every movement and gesture differs in its squareness or roundness.

The Great General does not speak of his meritorious deeds. The Eight Killing Swords: A chilling frost wind arises, scraping the earth; A thousand mountains of ice and snow make the path difficult to traverse.
Before a sprout has even emerged, it has already fallen away at the limit of Voice-Sound (Vigana); As soon as one attempts to conceive of the profound and subtle, one falls into a pit.
Nine: Ordinary and Natural. Spring comes, and the waters in the secluded valley glisten and flow; Leaning on a staff, he strolls leisurely along the fishing banks. What a fine state of Great Peace!

The Guest of Nothingness: At the Muddy Waters of Luo, one is not necessarily the only one who is wide awake. The Way of the Ten Benefits uproots birth; the matters of Shaoshi and Ling Shan remain vividly present.
Never did they discuss doctrine nor dwell in dhyāna; a single phrase of returning the light transcends past and present.
Among great men, who is first and who is last? The eleven words are free from error: when silent, it seems as if speaking; when speaking, there is nothing. Delusion and awakening are made distinct.

One becomes distant from the Way. Do not say that human faculties have their sharpness and dullness; coarse words and subtle speech have nothing to do with it. **Verse 12:** After the snow, the wind is mild and the dawn sky is clear.
The oriole sings, the flowers smile, and the willows hold the mist. The traveler from Peach Blossom Spring does not lodge in the Phoenix Tower.
At midnight, he puts on his shoes and enters the marketplace. **Verse 13:** Whether one penetrates or does not penetrate—this is a lightning-fast, arrow-sharp pivot.
Look with fixed eyes. When facing the sun, pursue the subtle smile; look on from the side. Clouds span the mouth of the valley, and birds lose their nests;

snow encircles the gate of the brushwood cottage, making the path ahead difficult to traverse. (Verse 14) Praise: The cold pool does not set a date for the moon; the sound of ten-thousand-year-old pines never shifts its rhythm.
If you can understand this through seeing with the ears and listening with the eyes, only then will you know the secret transmission held by the Buddhas and Patriarchs. (Verse 15) Descending phrase:

When the bright mirror on the stand reflects, shadows cannot be hidden; the incense burner pillar and the lantern proclaim themselves spontaneously. Not a single sage has ever left behind even half a verse;
Shaolin was already a mismatch from the start. When the sixteen [disciples] enter the circle, the jade maiden carries her lute as she returns at night.

The phoenix turns through the crimson heavens into the Purple Microcosm; fragrant mists spray forth as the floral vapors thicken. On the islets, the fisherman’s oars are silhouetted against the dim moonlight.

Furthermore, the Verses on the Five Positions state: "Centered within the Deviant: The handle of the Dipper first crosses before the midnight hour. In the secret chamber, no dragon-phoenix candles burn;
In the Hall of Broad Cold, the moon hangs in the sky. "Deviant centered within the Centered: A wooden woman holds a seal of no-words in her hand."
Dawn has passed and Mount Kunlun frowns in darkness; naturally one is ashamed before the mirror of the Qin era. Coming from the Center:
even the trees of swords and mountains of knives collapse of their own accord. The jade horse neighs as it leaves the Moon Palace; the ninefold gates remain locked with moss. Arriving from the Bias:
great function manifests freely without artifice or cleverness. Fishermen’s songs and woodcutters’ chants pay homage at the Golden Gate; peace and prosperity are not brought by force.
The army arrives; he reaches the center simultaneously. His horns are complete and without distinction; casting off the precious to don the tattered, he enters the marketplace.
Transversely and longitudinally, he tramples through the path of the present age.
Chan Master Yunwai Xiu of Tiantong in Ningbo Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Tian Tongju. He was a native of Changguo Garrison in the commandery; his family name is lost to history.

Having received ordination under Zhigong, he clarified the fundamental principles of the ancestral teachings and subsequently inherited his lineage. He first resided at Shimen in Cixi, and then... [continued].
At Tianning Monastery in Zhimen County of Xiangshan, [Zhaozhou] succeeded Xizhu in presiding over the seat. Later, he moved to Tiantong. Upon ascending the hall, he said:

"Within the bustling markets and the red dust, there is the Buddha-dharma within the bustling markets and the red dust. Amidst the deep mountains and rocky cliffs, there is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs.
Yesterday, when this mountain monk went out through the city gate, [I encountered] the Buddha within the bustling markets and the red dust."
The Dharma—suddenly, it was all forgotten. Traveling twenty *li*, with pine trees and clouds filling his vision, he beheld the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs.
The assembly, tell me: what is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs?
After a long silence, he said: "Pale white clouds drift indistinctly, appearing and disappearing within the vast void; green creepers wind their way, climbing straight up the cold pines."
[He] ascended to the seat. Upon reaching the top, he descended from the platform and entered the hall. Holding his whisk, he drew a circle in the air and said:
"The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations. He drew another circle and said: "In the application of ritual, harmony is the highest value;
this is what makes the Way of the former kings so beautiful. He drew yet another circle and said: "The mani-jewel people do not recognize; it is within the Tathāgatagarbha."
"I personally received it. Do you all see it? What you perceive differs; some have gains and others losses.
Here at Tiantong, there is no rigidity and no insistence. One day he asked the assembly, "Today Tiantong has died a great death.
How will you save him? Wuyin stepped forward and said, "Please, Master, eat your meal. The Master said, "Today at Tiantong..."
"Daita has died a great death. You need not try to save him. Zenjō said, "Why are you speaking in your sleep?
The Master said, "Tientong has died a great death today. Who will go with me? Zenjō said, "The Master goes first;
Dazheng shall follow behind. The Master laughed heartily and then passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at his home mountain.
The twenty-first generation descendant of Dajian (Baizhang),
Chan Master Wuyin Dazheng of Xuedou in Ningbo Prefecture,
was a son of the Shi family from Poyang in Raoyang. From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant.
He was different. He received the tonsure at Changguo Temple in Chuzhou under Master Zhijie. Initially, he visited Jingshi Yan at Yuan Tong, but they did not reach a mutual accord.
At that time, Sian Rui was residing in a secluded room; the Master devoted himself to him daily, undergoing rigorous training.

Later, hearing that Yunwai was preaching the Way at Tiantong, he went to rely upon him and gained entry into his inner circle. The exchange between master and disciple was like that of Dayi and Daoci at Dayue.

In the year of Jizhi (the tenth year of the Zhi-zhi era), he responded to an imperial decree to transcribe the Great Canon in gold ink. Emperor Yingzong bestowed upon him *quxian* (linen) garments embroidered with gold.
Upon returning south to Jiangzhe, Chancellor Tughan invited the Master to preside over Nanquan in Quzhou, followed by his leadership of Guangxiao.

He was subsequently transferred to Xiangfu in Xin and Dingshui in Ming, and later led Xuedou. Ascending the hall, he said: "A thousand explanations, ten thousand explanations, are not equal to seeing [it] directly."
A single glance at the face. Yesterday was the twenty-ninth; this morning is the first day of the seventh month.
I inform you, you practitioners of Zen: herein lies a profound mystery. Your mother gave birth to two eyes, each as black as lacquer. Hurry! Hurry! Turn your head and see through to the True Buddha.
After a long silence, he said, "Tell me, what kind of face is this? He then descended from his seat, toured the hall, and partook of tea. Up.
The Hall. Wondrous, wondrous, wondrous! The nostrils of a patch-robed monk have no more than two holes. Mysterious, mysterious, mysterious! Upon the top of the banner pole hangs the blue sky.
A man of wisdom need not fold his hands; a fine steed does not wait for the whip. Completely transcending staff and shout, it falls neither into the trap nor the net.
When the hundred birds do not come and spring has passed, one wins the right to sleep late before the cliff. [The Master] raised [his whisk]. Just—
Ascending the seat, Mañjuśrī suddenly struck the wooden gavel and said: "Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King.
Thereupon the World-Honored One descended from the seat and spoke in verse: "The spring breeze has just begun to fan the world's edge, And everywhere roots and stems compete to sprout."
"Why must the cuckoo speak so much more? It causes its blood to flow once again, staining the mountain flowers.

The student’s deluded mind was layered upon layers and would not subside; he requested the Master for a skillful means. The Master said, “For how long has this deluded mind of yours been coming?
I wonder, does it have a beginning from which it arose? As for this deluded mind, how do you sever it? The student replied, “To sever this very deluded mind is itself non-severing;
it is true hearing. He then prostrated himself with a vast sense of clarity and departed. In his later years, he lived in seclusion.

He had much leisure. He once compiled the *Congrong-an Lu* (Record of Leisurely Dwelling) based on Hongzhi’s *Baishou* (One Hundred Verses), and also authored the *Qingyi Lu* (Record of Seeking Instruction).

Following in the footsteps of the *Biyan Lu* (Blue Cliff Record), he polished the heavy tarnish from the ancient mirror, providing great benefit to the Chan school. By nature, the Master was exceptionally quick-witted and sharp.
He was thoroughly versed in the teachings of the hundred schools of thought. Having read the Tripitaka three times, he had mastered it from beginning to end.

He compiled the *Zu deng lu* (Record of the Patriarchal Lamp) in sixty-two fascicles, as well as several volumes of the *Shi shi xin wen*, *Ming dao ji*, *Bian zong shuo xin jing*, and *Feng ming chan yue fa xi ji*.
He also produced records for the four monasteries of Jingtu, Yangshan, Hongji, and Wanshou, all of which are currently in circulation.
In the first year of Yuanding (1096), on the fifth day of the fourth month in the year of Bingwu, he manifested illness. On the seventh day, he wrote a verse, saying:
"Eighty-one years—just these words. Take care, all you people; do not fail to grasp them correctly. Thereupon, he passed away.

He lived for eighty-one years. In the second year of the Qiandao era of the Song dynasty, the year Bingxu, at sixty years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*), he was cremated outside the Tongxuan Gate.
His *śarīra* relics were innumerable; disciples from all quarters divided them and enshrined them in stupas.
Chan Master Juchuan Haichuan of Zhulin in □□ Prefecture had a verse on wind bells that said: "Copper lips and iron tongues, so sharp and new;
Hung from the corner of the tower, they have forgotten spring. The hundreds of thousands of samādhi-dharmas beyond words— Through the wind, they are spoken to those who are ready.
Once, the scholar Chen Xiuwang asked: "Why did Wansong [call him] Maitreya Bodhisattva?"
"I do not cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), nor do I sever afflictions (*kleśa*. Song said, "Because the true mind is fundamentally pure, one does not cultivate meditation;

because delusive thoughts are fundamentally empty, one does not sever afflictions. He asked again, "What about Xiangshan Da-run? Run said, "The mind of meditation is already settled, so there is no need for further cultivation;
the afflictions are already exhausted, so there is no need for further severing. Later, he took this to ask his teacher. The teacher said, "Fundamentally..."
"There is no affliction regarding meditative concentration. The Master said, "Only this is what brings true joy.

Chan Master Xueting Fuyou of Wanshou Monastery in Shuntianfu was a dharma successor of Chan Master Bao’en Xiu. His courtesy name was Haowen. He was the son of the Zhang family of Wen-shui in Taiyuan.

He was born in the year Guihai of the Jia-tai era during the reign of Emperor Ningzong of the Song dynasty. At the age of nine, he could recite a thousand words daily. In his village, there was a "Holy Child" (Shengxiao).
The boy, named Cheng, was soon caught up in the upheavals of the times and lost contact with his siblings.

Left all alone and without support, he encountered an elderly bhikṣu on the road who urged him to study Buddhism, saying, "It will suffice for you to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The master asked, "Is this all there is to studying Buddhism?
The bhikṣu marveled at his insight and accompanied him to Xianyan to pay respects to the ancient Buddha Xiulin. The ancient Buddha accepted him and offered prayers for his well-being.
He received full ordination in the Jiading Jia-shen year. He served alongside Shuangxi Guang for seven years, after which he went to Bao’en Monastery in Yanjing to study under Wansong.
Upon first seeing him, Wansong granted him entry into the inner circle and asked, "From where did you receive this news that you have come here with such an air?
The Master replied, "Old and decrepit as I am, I have been defeated by the hands of students. Wansong said, "Old man..."
"Where does the fault of the monk lie? The Master replied, "The student was merely paying homage; let me temporarily cover it up for you, O Abbot. Song was struck with wonder by this.
He then attended the Master personally for ten years. During the upheaval of the Renchen era, the ancestral monastery fell into ruin.

Subsequently, he received an invitation from Mansong Haeyun, who appointed him to the Shaolin Monastery. From that time on, his Way flourished further and his reputation grew increasingly prominent. His students...
His followers increased daily. While Emperor Yuan Shizu was still in his private residence, he commanded the Master to perform the *Zijie* (Precepts for Rebirth) ceremony.

In the year Wushen of the Yuan Dynasty’s Dingzong era, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at Helin. In the Xinhai year of the Xingguo era, Emperor Xuanzong summoned him to the temporary capital at Beiting; there, his concise discourse on the Way pleased the Emperor’s mind.
In the year Gengshen, when Yuan Shizu ascended the throne, he appointed the Master as the General Overseer of Buddhist Teachings and restored the monastic community of monks and nuns.
He acquired two hundred and thirty-six abandoned temples, which he subsequently bestowed upon the Chan Master Guangzong Zhengbian.

He constructed a monastery for his master in his native village called Ba’en (Repaying Kindness), providing fields for the sustenance of the assembly; the imperial favors granted to him were most profound.

At that time, the seat at Wanshou Monastery was vacant, and the community requested the Master to preside over it. Subsequently, he established branch monasteries in Helin, Yanji, Chang’an, Taiyuan, and Luoyang.
Throughout the various lands of the realm. In the spring of the Xinwei year of the Yuan era, an imperial decree was issued summoning all Buddhist monks to the capital;

the Master’s followers constituted one-third of the assembly, appearing in such grand numbers that they were a magnificent sight to behold. The Emperor was pleased with this. The Master possessed an extraordinary intelligence and had read through the Tripitaka three times.

He completed his recitations before finally resting. He guided and assisted later students without ever showing a sign of weariness. He was well-versed in various classics, skilled in calligraphy and poetry, and when ascending the hall for a general discourse (*pǔshuō*), he delivered several hundred thousand words.
When his disciples requested that these be carved into woodblocks for publication, the Master rebuked them, saying, "This was merely what emerged from my temporary playfulness.
How can the wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs be reduced to mere physical traces? He ultimately forbade it. Thus, he remained so even in his old age.

"A monk asked Dalong, 'The physical body decays; what is the indestructible Dharma-body? Long replied, 'Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; the mountain stream is as clear as a mirror.'"
Lan asked, "Master, when the Great Dragon speaks thus, I, this mountain monk, do not agree. If someone were to ask, 'The physical body perishes;
what is the firm Dharma-body? I would tell them: 'Mountain flowers blind the eyes; stream water poisons the ears.'"
The crane does not pine for its secluded nest; the dragon does not hide in stagnant water.
Chan Master Changqing Degao of Shuntian Prefecture ascended the hall. A monk asked the Master, "Whose song do you sing? Whose ancestral style do you inherit?
The Master said, "Riding an ox while wearing a bamboo hat, arriving unexpectedly in Luoyang. The monk said, "If that is so, then [it is like] milk..."
The Peak’s direct lineage: the waters of the cave flow upstream. The Master said: "When the herdsman’s flute is blown, heaven and earth are stilled;
before the rustic old man’s gate, no signboard stands.
One day, Zen Master Huiyuan of Pingshui in □□ Prefecture said to his disciples: "In my own youth, I was..."
People called him a "rice-wine dregs eater," which filled him with indignation and resentment. He traveled until he had worn out several pairs of straw sandals, yet he could find no point of entry.
Later, he asked Wanshou, “What is Chan? Wanshou replied, “A monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing behind.”
"If you do not understand, we shall again set a fierce fire and fry you in oil. Only then will you attain a sense of joy and liberation.
By this, one knows that a person must inevitably encounter provocation. Nevertheless, it must be that there is still blood beneath your skin for this to happen.
A monk then asked, "What if one insults another without piercing to the bone? The Master said, "You are a scoundrel without skin."
There is nothing to say regarding his bones.
Chan Master Tongxin of Yuequan at Anshan,
Shuntian Prefecture— a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Boren Lun— whose courtesy name was Zhongyi, was born into the Guo family of Fangshan, Yanjing.
Disciple, you followed Shan Jian at Anshan to receive the tonsure. You were able to serve the assembly through arduous practices, yet one day your intelligence suddenly blossomed.
When you shared your realization with your fellow practitioners, Xusuo and the others mocked you. The Master was deeply indignant; he wrote a verse on the wall and departed. The verse said:
"A great man whose spirit pierces the clouds—how could ordinary ditches and channels ever restrain him? In hand he holds a three-foot blade..."
Maojian went directly for the pearl from the jaws of the black dragon. He went to visit Qing’an Fang. Fang asked, “If you wish to travel a thousand li, the first step is the beginning.
What is this very first step? The Master stepped forward, stood with his hands crossed, and remained there.
Fang said, “What can you do about your heels not touching the ground? The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Next, he saw Daming Gao, who brandished his staff and whisk.

Below, he was greatly inspired and stimulated; yet, in the end, he felt a sense of insufficiency because his realization was not yet complete. He returned once more to Qing’an, and after another three years, he finally attained a state of great, expansive clarity.
Subsequently, he visited Linquan, whereupon he received the seal of certification (*mudrā*). Soon thereafter, he accepted an invitation to serve as the *yinzuo* (introducer) at Lingyan Temple.
As soon as the Master uttered a single word, the multitude cheered with joy; many were able to grasp the essential meaning beneath his words. Not long after, Yuan...
The Imperial Founder (Shizu) issued an edict appointing him as the abbot of Lingyan. Later, he retired to Anshan.

One day, while traveling to Jinan to enter the summer retreat at Guanyuan Temple, he suddenly fell ill and spoke this verse: "Coming, there is no place from which it comes; going, there is no direction to which it goes.
He suddenly raised his fist and said, "Tell me, is there still any obstruction here? He released his fist and said, "With hands cast loose, one moves freely through the clouds and sky."
Azure and vast. With eyes closed, he passed away. His age was sixty-six; his years since ordination were forty-five.
Regarding the Dharma successor of Chan Master Fuchaan Zhao, Chan Master Bin of Xian Prefecture—when a monk asked, "What is the 'partiality within the center'? the Master said, "A wooden man."
At midnight, he was swinging on a swing. [The Master] asked, "What is 'correctness within partiality'? The Master said, "The various officials fear seeing the mirror of the Qin Terrace.
He asked, "What is 'coming from the center'? The Master said, "The wooden child and the earthen figurine laugh heartily.
He asked, "What is 'arriving through both'? The Master said, "The wrathful Nala raises his eight arms. He asked, "What is 'reaching through both'? The Master said, [silently].
The Master said: "The staff leans against itself before the wind.
This is the lineage of Chan Master Taishan Tai, the twenty-sixth generation descendant of Dajian.
Chan Master Huan-yuan Fuyu of Baoying Temple in Henan Prefecture was a native of the Wang family in Lingshi, Huozhou.

He received the tonsure at Doushuai Monastery in his home district and subsequently traveled extensively throughout various regions. His eloquence was so formidable that none dared to rival him; he looked up to Lingyin Tai as his model.
His Dharma-eye was sharp and clear; thus, he knelt and requested instruction. Taishan once said to the Master, "When I raise my whisk, you immediately understand it on the whisk.
As soon as I remain silent for a long while, you immediately understand it in that silence. Is this how it is?"
"How can one penetrate the matter of one's own fundamental share? The Master’s face flushed with heat and sweat poured down; he was unable to respond.

One day, hearing Taishan ascend the hall and cite the words, "One must by all means avoid seeking from others; to seek from others is to distance oneself from me," the Master attained great enlightenment on the spot.

Two years later, he received formal certification (*inka*). In the *Bingxu* year of the Yuan *Zhizheng* era (1296), he began teaching at Yongqing. In the *Jichou* year (1300), he successively presided over Baoying.
In the *yǐwèi* year of the Yuánzhēn era of Emperor Chéngzōng, he received imperial edict to reside at Shàoshì. In the *xīnhài* year of the Zhìdà era of Emperor Wǔzōng, he retired to Băimǎ.
A monk asked, "What is the essential meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The wind carries the sound of the spring to the side of my pillow;
the moon shifts the shadows of the flowers to the front of my window. The monk asked, "What is the Prince at Birth?"

The Master said, "Though one possesses the lot of nobility, one is not yet a noble person. [The student] asked, "What is a prince born at dawn? The Master said, "He does not rank as high as those on the golden register; in the end, he remains but an old court official. [The student] asked, "What is a prince born at dusk? The Master said, "He is already a prince; though he has not yet ascended the throne, his status is fixed. The student asked, "What is a prince born at midnight? The Master said, "He is neither a prince nor a commoner; he is simply a man of the Way. The student asked, "What is a prince born at daybreak? The Master said, "He is a prince who has ascended the throne; he is truly a noble person. The student asked, "How is it that one possesses the lot of nobility yet is not a noble person? The Master said, "It is because one has not yet attained the Way. The student asked, "How is it that one is a prince who has ascended the throne and is truly a noble person? The Master said, "It is because one has attained the Way. The student asked, "What is the meaning of 'the Way'? The Master said, "The Way is not something you can grasp with your mind or conceive with your intellect. It is simply the realization of the self-nature. The student asked, "How does one realize the self-nature? The Master said, "If you wish to realize the self-nature, you must first sever the root of delusion. Once the root of delusion is severed, the self-nature will manifest spontaneously. The student asked, "What is the root of delusion? The Master said, "The root of delusion is nothing other than the mind’s grasping at phenomena. If you can cease this grasping, the root of delusion will naturally vanish. The student asked, "How does one cease grasping? The Master said, "Ceasing grasping means not seeking anything outside of yourself. Do not seek the Buddha, do not seek the Dharma, and do not seek the Sangha. Just let go of all seeking, and the self-nature will be revealed. The student asked, "Once the self-nature is revealed, what is there to do? The Master said, "When the self-nature is revealed, there is nothing more to be done. You have simply returned to your original state. The student asked, "What is the original state? The Master said, "The original state is the state of non-arising and non-ceasing. It is beyond words and concepts, and cannot be described by any name. The student asked, "If it cannot be described by any name, how can we speak of it? The Master said, "Speaking of it is precisely not speaking of it. To speak of it is to miss it entirely. The student asked, "If speaking of it misses it, how can we attain it? The Master said, "Attaining it is not a matter of attainment. If you think you have attained it, you have missed it. If you do not think you have attained it, you have attained it. The student asked, "If I do not think I have attained it, how do I know I have attained it? The Master said, "If you do not think you have attained it, you will act without artifice. Your every movement and every word will be spontaneous and free from calculation. This is the mark of having attained the Way. The student asked, "If my every movement and every word are spontaneous and free from calculation, am I still subject to the laws of karma? The Master said, "Karma arises from the mind's grasping. If there is no grasping, there is no karma. If you act without grasping, you are free from the cycle of birth and death. The student asked, "If I am free from the cycle of birth and death, where will I go after this life ends? The Master said, "Where will you go? There is nowhere to go. You have simply returned to the source. This is called 'the great liberation. The student asked, "What is the great liberation? The Master said, "The great liberation is to be without fear, without attachment, and without seeking. It is to dwell in the present moment, free from all conceptualization. The student asked, "If I dwell in the present moment, free from conceptualization, how can I benefit others? The Master said, "Benefiting others is not something you can plan. When your own mind is liberated, its radiance will naturally shine upon others. This is called 'great compassion. The student asked, "What is great compassion? The Master said, "Great compassion is to see all sentient beings as oneself. To treat others as you would treat yourself is the essence of great compassion. The student asked, "If I treat others as I treat myself, will I still encounter suffering and joy? The Master said, "Suffering and joy are like dreams and illusions. If you understand their nature, they cannot disturb you. Even when encountering suffering or joy, remain equanimous and unmoved. This is the practice of a bodhisattva. The student asked, "If I remain equanimous and unmoved, will I still be affected by external conditions? The Master said, "External conditions are like the wind and the clouds. They come and go without staying. If you do not grasp at them, they cannot affect you. This is called 'mastery over circumstances. The student asked, "If I have mastery over circumstances, am I still subject to the constraints of time and space? The Master said, "Time and space are manifestations of the mind. If the mind is liberated, time and space are also liberated. There is no longer any distinction between past, present, and future, nor any separation between here and there. This is called 'transcending the three realms. The student asked, "If I transcend the three realms, what is the ultimate goal? The Master said, "The ultimate goal is to return to the source of all things. This is called 'enlightenment. Enlightenment is not something to be sought; it is simply the realization of your own true nature. The student asked, "If enlightenment is the realization of my own true nature, why did the Buddhas of the past undergo such hardships to seek it? The Master said, "The Buddhas of the past did not seek enlightenment; they simply realized it. Their hardships were merely the removal of their own delusions. You should not look for enlightenment elsewhere; it is right within yourself. The student asked, "If it is right within myself, why do I not perceive it now? The Master said, "Because you are looking for it with your dualistic mind. Cease this seeking, and it will be revealed. It is like the sun rising in the sky: once the clouds part, its light shines forth naturally. The student asked, "Once the clouds have parted and the light shines forth, what should I do? The Master said, "Do nothing. Simply abide in the light of the sun, which is the light of wisdom. This is called 'dwelling in the dharma-realm. The student asked, "What is the dharma-realm? The Master said, "The dharma-realm is boundless and all-pervading. It encompasses heaven and earth and contains the ten thousand phenomena. It is not a place you can enter or leave; it is simply the reality of all things. The student asked, "If it is the reality of all things, how can I distinguish between right and wrong? The Master said, "Right and wrong are relative concepts. In the dharma-realm, there is no right or wrong, only the manifestation of suchness. If you act in accordance with suchness, you will naturally accord with the Way. The student asked, "If I act in accordance with suchness, will I still be subject to the retribution of good and evil? The Master said, "Good and evil are like shadows following forms. If you do not create forms, there will be no shadows. If you do not create good or evil, there will be no retribution. This is called 'freedom from karmic obstacles. The student asked, "If I am free from karmic obstacles, will I still be reborn in the world? The Master said, "Rebirth is a delusion. If you are free from delusion, there is no rebirth. You will simply return to the source and dwell in eternal peace. This is called 'nirvana. The student asked, "What is nirvana? The Master said, "Nirvana is the extinction of all suffering and the cessation of all delusion. It is the ultimate state of peace and bliss. It is the destination of all Bodhisattvas and Buddhas. The student asked, "If I attain nirvana, will I still exist? The Master said, "Existence and non-existence are both extremes. In nirvana, there is neither existence nor non-existence. It is beyond all conceptualization. This is called 'the inconceivable dharma. The student asked, "If it is inconceivable, how can I understand it? The Master said, "Understanding is not through the intellect. It is through direct experience. You must let go of all thoughts and views, and then you will see it for yourself. This is called 'awakening. The student asked, "If I awaken, what is the next step? The Master said, "There is no next step. Awakening is the final stage. Once you have awakened, there is nothing more to be done
The Master said, "Having exhausted all hardships and labors, one finally attains an audience with the sky of Yao. [The student] asked, "What is the 'transformed-born prince'?
The Master said, "His essence is no different from his father's; he temporarily wields the authority beyond the palace gates. [The student] asked, "What is the 'internally-born prince'?"
The Master said, "I have long remained within the deep palace, but even at a distance of a few inches, I beheld the Dragon’s Countenance. He asked, "As for the path that leads upward, how is it?
The Master replied, "The lute without strings has its own resonance; how could humans or devas hear it? In the tenth month of the Gui-chou year of the Renzong Huangqing era, he passed away.
He was sixty-nine years of age and had been a monk for forty-nine years.
When Chan Master Qiu Jiangjie of Lingyan in Jinan Prefecture was visited by the monk Xuexuan Cheng, the Master asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From Qingzhou. The Master said, "Did you bring the Qingzhou cotton robe with you? He replied, "I have already presented it to the Master."
The Master said, "Wait for another time for those thirty blows.

Chan Master Lingyan Su was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yueyan Yongda of Baoying Temple in Henan Prefecture. He was a native of the Liu clan of Fenzhou and received the tonsure in that same prefecture.
At Tianning Temple, he constantly kept in mind that the matter of birth and death is of the utmost importance. He traveled south to seek instruction and inquiry.
Hearing that Master Lingyan Su’s dharma resonance was resonant and majestic, he went to visit him with blistered feet. Upon seeing him, Master Su immediately regarded him as one of great capacity;

after some time, he became his入室 (入室) disciple—that is, a disciple who had entered the inner chamber. The Master suddenly said to himself: "Awakening is derived from the teacher, but its practice rests with oneself."
"How can one know this and yet not practice it? Thereupon, he closed his door in Taian Prefecture.
Later, as the seat at Baoying Monastery was vacant, he acceded to the request of the assembly and accepted the position. Upon ascending the hall, the Elder of Lumeng said:
"The entire great earth is this person’s single scroll of scripture; the entire universe is this person’s single eye. With such an eye, look upon such [reality]."

This sutra has continued for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas without interruption. Even the Elder Wansong, his calculations exhausted and his strength spent, could only say that reading and reciting it is no easy matter.
Can you all read and recite it? You must know that as for this one volume of sutra, who does not possess this single eye?
Who is not complete in it? If you wish to extend it, it would be difficult to exhaust even in thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
If one wishes for brevity, it is completed in a single kṣaṇa. Today, Baoying does not spare his eyebrows to point this out for you all.
He snaps his fingers once and says: "Look! You have finished reading. Everyone, do not let this slip away. After a long silence, he strikes the whisk and says:
"From now on, when one returns, one shall surely find it; who can vie with the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?"
Chan Master Pujou of the Ancient Cliff on Mount Fenglong in Zhending Prefecture was the son of the Liu family of Huyang. From childhood, he abstained from meat and strong flavors.

At fifteen, he paid his respects to Chan Master Cheng at Mount Fenglong and received ordination through the celebration of the *pravarana* ceremony. In the year Yichou of the Zhiyuan era, at the age of nineteen, he received full ordination and immediately began traveling to consult various masters.
He first visited Chengchong and Anxiao of the Pure Land school; although he was recognized by both, he ultimately did not [remain with them].

He did not dare to consider himself satisfied. In the year *Xinsi*, he joined Chan Master Paramu at Wanshou Monastery. Paramu, recognizing him as a vessel for the Dharma, subjected him daily to the forging of his fundamental nature.
One day, there was a sudden explosion of realization. He soon received formal certification (*kaji*).
Later, he took leave of Paramu and lived in seclusion at Baoji for ten years. In the year *Guisi*, when Chan Master Guitang resided at Lingyan, he invited the Master to serve as the First Seat.
Virtuous One, in the ninth month of the Year of the Tiger (1362), Yue-an Haeng-hae retired from his temple, requesting the Master to succeed him on the seat and open the hall.
In the Year of the Sheep (1367), King Seongjong specially conferred upon him the title of State Preceptor Myo-yeom Hong-bul. Subsequently, he moved to Bongnong.

In the Year of the Ox (1313) of the Huangqing era, he resided at Seorim, causing the ancestral temple to flourish greatly. A monk asked, "What is 'falling into the category'? The Master replied, "It is not."
[The student] said, "One who wears skin and has horns—what is 'falling into accordance'? The Master said, "It is not one who hears sounds or sees forms.
[The student] asked, "What is 'falling into nobility'? The Master said, "It is not one who sits upright in the hall. [The student] asked, "If it is like this, how can there be a name for 'falling'?
The Master said, "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water. [The student] said, "An ancient said, 'Three...'"
This is the sickness of one who has "finished the business. Since he is one who has finished the business, how can he have a sickness?

The Master said, "Precisely because he has finished the business, the sickness arises. [The monk] asked, "When will this sickness be cured? The Master said, "Only when there is no body will this sickness finally be cured.
Thereupon, he presented a verse: "The heavy golden locks have long since been flung open; Tranquil and at ease, he goes forth alone in the three realms."
"Come! A wild goose passes through the vast sky, unattached; its shadow sinks into the cold water, leaving others to their conjectures. Master Jian was dignified and possessed few worldly adornments;
his conduct in advancing and retreating was marked by propriety. He lived seventy-two years in the secular world and fifty-eight years as a monk.
The Chan Master Xiangyan Chunhui Wencai of Nanyang Prefecture, Dengzhou,
a successor in the twenty-seventh generation under Dajian, was the son of the Yao family of Pingyang Linfen.
From birth he was extraordinary; his parents, who delighted in seeing the Sangha, observed that in every movement and stillness he was unlike ordinary children.

When he grew older, he requested to study Buddhism. His parents, recognizing his resolve, granted him permission. He went forth as a monk under Fuyuan at Fuyan Monastery in Jizhou. There he read the *Song of Realizing the Way*.
Upon reaching the state where the illusory and transformed body is the very Dharma-body, he attained a joyful realization. He went to visit Huayan to present his understanding.
Huayan interrogated him, saying, "As for the saying, 'The Lord does not see,' to whom is this pointing? The Master replied, "Presented face-to-face, there is no evasion.
Huayan said, "You pit-fall-dweller, you speak such words! The Master said, "And what about you, Preceptor?"
"How is it? Yuan said, "I will block your mouth. The Master said, "You have been seen through. Yuan approved of this.
He subsequently spent three years at Longmen Mountain perusing the Tripitaka. In the year of Tai Ding Jiazi, he presided over Shaoshi. Entering the hall, he said:
"Having calculated the entire board, there is only this one move that is most advantageous. I dare ask you all: tell me, which one is it?"
He stood up, leaned on his staff, and said, "Above all, do not engage in speculative calculation. A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Not even a needle or an awl can pass through.
The monk asked, "What is Chan? The Master said, "Wheels and horses have their paths. The monk asked, "Why does the Master overturn the public cases of the ancients?
The Master said, "Promote the upright and set aside the crooked. In his later years, he lived in seclusion at Xiangyan and composed commentaries on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
Regarding the *Sūtras* and the *Huayan fajie guan*, a monk asked: "What is the Dharma-realm of Principle (*li-fajie*)? The Master said:
"When empty space falls to the ground, it shatters into pieces that form no pattern. The monk asked: "What is the Dharma-realm of Phenomena (*shi-fajie*)?

The Master said: "When you arrive, the house is utterly emptied; one need not be a fool within the dwelling. The monk asked: "What is the Dharma-realm of the Non-obstruction of Principle and Phenomena (*li-shi wuai fajie*)? The Master said: "The three winters..."
The withered tree flourishes; in the ninth month of summer, snowflakes fly. [A questioner] asked, "What is the Dharma-realm where all things are unimpeded?
The Master replied, "The clear breeze accompanies the bright moon; the rustic elder smiles as they draw near.

On the seventeenth day of the fifth month of the *wuchen* year of the Zhizheng era of Emperor Shun, he bathed, changed his robes, and called his disciples to give them final instructions. The following day, he passed away in auspicious peace. His remains were interred whole.
At the age of eighty, while at the Xueting Pagoda, Chan Master Kongxiang Gui of Xiong’er Mountain in Henan Prefecture addressed the assembly: "If I shout, you immediately take it as a shout;
wherever you go, you will shout recklessly and at random. If I strike with a staff, you immediately take it as a staff; wherever you go, you will strike with your hands at whim."
"Random blows with a staff, random shouts! If I were to remove these staffs and shouts and teach him toward his own fundamental nature—that single phrase of the Middle Way—he would not be struck;
nor would he circumambulate and perform a woman’s bow, which is nothing but the fabrication of two phrases and the emergence of ghostly talk."
They are just like mute sheep. Such as these are all mad dogs; they chase clods of earth—when have they ever dreamed of seeing a lion’s swift fangs and claws?
[The Master] suddenly called out, "Is there a lion here? Try showing off your fangs and claws!
A monk stepped forward, and the Master struck him, saying, "Chasing clods and sniffing scents is not the mark of a good dog. The monk...
The Master struck him again, saying, "The staff is broken, yet I will not let you go. The monk said, "If that is so, then the path to Yunyan is cut off.
The Master said, "When you have no way to ascend to heaven, how can you blame me for cutting off the path to Yunyan?
He then drove him out with a continuous stream of blows, saying, "I entrust this to the chaotic fellows of the world!"

Chan Master Longtan Shen of Mount Song in Henan Prefecture addressed the assembly: "In my youth, I attained ultimate *nirvāṇa* at the point in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* concerning 'inverted dreams and delusions.
Later, I realized that all the sages and worthies have, by means of ultimate *nirvāṇa*, actually accomplished nothing but inverted dreams and delusions.
It was only upon meeting my late teacher, the Old Monk Huan-yuan, that I understood this."
The questioner asked, "Others say that ancient tombs do not serve as one's home; what is Chan? The Old Monk replied, "These are dead words.
The mountain monk said, "What are living words? The Old Man struck him a blow across the face and said, "How can you be so lethargically dead?
As the mountain monk was about to respond, the Old Man struck him again. At that moment, the mountain monk was suddenly awakened, as if emerging from darkness into light.
Deng then proclaimed loudly: "This time it was no dream; it was truly Mount Lu. Today, this mountain monk dares not deceive you;
I have come from afar specifically to point this out to all of you. You must see it for yourself in this way before you will finally attain it.
He then struck the table once and said: "Alas! Today this mountain monk has been far too indiscreet."

Chan Master Xuexuan Daocheng of Tianjie Monastery in Jiangning Prefecture was a dharma heir of Chan Master Lingyan Jie. His single-character pen-name was Jiufeng. He was a distant descendant of the Great King Zhao of Yunzhou.
When his father moved to Baoding, he settled there. At the age of fifteen, he left home to become a monk at Xingguo Temple in his native prefecture. He served as the abbot of that monastery.
He had a broad forehead and a flat brow; he was majestic and possessed great resolve. After receiving the precepts, he formed a group of three as companions and dwelt in an earthen cave in Qingzhou.
He engaged in secret investigation and intensive meditation for many years. Suddenly, an old man said to them, "You three shall one day become the pillars of the Dharma-gate.
The Master rebuked him, whereupon the old man vanished. Thereupon, the Master applied himself with even greater vigor and refinement.

Having heard that Qiujiang was greatly propagating the fundamental tenets, he went to attend upon him. An account of their conversation appears in the chapter on Qiujiang. Qiujiang remained silent and directed him to attend the hall.

After a long period of refinement, he realized for himself that there was no longer any doubt. One day, he hurried to the master’s quarters, where Qiujiang said, "The golden lock and the mysterious gate."
"Have you ever opened it up completely? The Master said, "Within a peach pit a thousand years old, what do you seek?—the kernel of the past.

Jiang nodded in agreement. The Master then instructed him, saying, "This is that which you inherently possess; guard and maintain it well yourself. Later, he returned to Qingshe, where the assembly requested him to reside at Puzhao.
Subsequently, he moved to Dazeshan in Donglai. In the Renxu year of the Hongwu era, he was selected by imperial decree for the Prince's spiritual affinity.

His Highness’s wise favor was especially profound. In the year Dingchou, an imperial decree arrived at the palace, commanding him to reside as abbot of Tianjie Monastery. The Master submitted that he did not understand the Buddha-dharma;
the Emperor then composed a poem and engraved it upon a golden plaque, ordering it to be hung in the Dharma Hall. His respect was thus extreme. [The Master] ascended the hall.
Ten thousand acres of white clouds roll and unroll, revealing the true mechanism beyond kalpas; a thousand peaks of crimson leaves blaze forth, manifesting the wondrous principle within.
Unfailing throughout antiquity and the present, it remains ever-present through the dust of kalpas—a bird-path, empty and penetrating, upon which one moves.

The threshold is dense and subtle; the lion strings are interlaced. As the fingers press, ancient resonance rings out with a clear, piercing clangor. The stone woman nods her head; the wooden man claps his hands.
Grasping the golden needle, the jade thread passes through. Cut off before the mechanism moves—this is the hare’s horn and the tortoise’s hair.
Revealing the upward direction, the orthodox and the deviant are laid bare; the hidden and the manifest are fully encompassed.

Thus, in every object and every instance, in every speck of dust and every world-system, there is not even a single hair’s breadth lacking. Do you all understand? Last night, a wooden horse galloped through the clouds.
Startled, the Southern Dipper and Northern Dipper vanish. Entering the Hall: When yin reaches its limit and yang returns, the days of transformation grow long;
plum blossoms everywhere emit their fragrant scent. Within this, there is not much of a message to be found—how could it ever be concealed throughout the entire realm?
Thus, it is luminously clear, encompassing the hundred grasses; meeting at the very head, it is secretly proclaimed within the light of the ten thousand phenomena. Alone...
Lù: On the field of fame and profit, he is recommended for selection; the True Person of No Rank reveals his original face amidst the mountains of self and other.
The shadow contains the mirror of the school: when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the body is the realm of the Way and the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
The barren woman holds high the precious seal, its patterns fully manifest; the wooden man silently passes through with the golden shuttle, the thread [unfolding].
