A monk asked Chan Master Fu of Zhengzhou, "How does the pear of Zhengzhou compare to the jujube of Qingzhou? The Master said, "Too many bundles;
you monks are accustomed to such carelessness. The monk said, "The Master must also extend another hand. The Master said, "Where would one find the leisure funds to reward falling petals?"
Chan Master Gutan Benshen of Fengxue in Ruizhou was the son of the Zhang family from Jangzhou in Shanxi.

While he was in the womb, his mother repeatedly dreamed that a strange light entered her mouth. His father marveled at this. When he reached the age of seven, he left home to become a monk under Master Hong of Dajue in Jintai Village.
At twenty-five, he visited Nengran at Shaoshi Mountain, where he served him for twelve years and received the transmission of the robe and the final injunctions. He resided at Yongle.
In the year Jiawu, he received an imperial decree to collate and verify the Tripitaka. In the Dingwei year of the Xuande era, he presided over Fengxue.

On the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the Gengxu year, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell and depart this world, reciting a verse: "The clouds come and the clouds go; the primordial heaven is pure.

The bubbles vanish and the bubbles arise; their essence is inherently the same. If you ask for the essential meaning within this, A single bright moon accompanies the clear breeze. Thereupon, he passed away. His disciples...
A person erected a stupa to the west of the tomb of Master Jiao (Zhao Gong) at the founding site.
He was the dharma successor of Chan Master Bing of Mount Song, who belonged to the thirty-first generation under National Teacher Dajian (Mazu).
The Chan Master Wufang Cong of Dingguo Monastery in Henan Prefecture was the son of the Xu family of Luoyang.
He left the household life under Fuxian Pifeng. Initially, he visited Longtan Shun of Songyang and Chaozhua Zong of Mili County to seek instruction and enter their chambers for formal inquiry.

He entered [the lineage] together with Qi. Later, he went to Mount Song to study under Chanjun. There, the Master subjected him to further refinement through the dense and profound mysteries of the gate.

One day, when Chanjun raised the case concerning the "Five Phases" and summoned the Venerable Shi, the Master immediately attained personal realization of the profound principles of the Five Ranks (*wuwei*).
Having received the transmission without omission, he later lived in seclusion at Dingguo Temple in Guandu.
In the year of Kaiming (1613), he sought and realized the Bodhi of the Dharma. In the year of Huacheng (1653), he presided over the Dharma at Shaoshi. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"The ultimate vehicle of the ancestral school is fundamentally beyond words and speech. For the person of realization, this single point does not require external seeking;

it must simply burst forth from within one's own breast. It is biased against clinging to things and correct in not establishing mysteries. Only when one does not traverse the paths of practice will one arrive home and find stability."
“Sit! Although you know this, do you still accept that Jiufeng refused to acknowledge the Head Seat? Did Baizhang fall into the den of foxes for five hundred lifetimes?
When the golden awl scrapes away the film, if you attempt to grasp it, you will become perverse; those with true resolve must be most careful in this school. Be heedful!
In the Renyin year of the Chenghua era, he was invited by the Prince of Wei of the Ming court to reside at Guanyin Temple in Junzhou. On the sixth month, he passed away. His age...
He lived to the age of sixty-four and had forty years of ordination seniority. His entire body was enshrined at the ancestral tomb on Mount Shaoshi.
He was the Dharma successor of Chan Master Cong of Dingguo, the thirty-second generation under Dajian (Huineng).

Chan Master Wencai of Yuezhou from Mount Song in Henan Prefecture was also known by the sobriquet Xubai (Empty White). He was a native of Tongzhou in the north, born into the Wang family of Guangning in Weizhou.

His grandfather, Cai Yong, served Emperor Chengzu of the Ming dynasty and participated in the suppression of the internal rebellion; he was subsequently posthumously granted the title of General of Martial Virtue and settled in Tongzhou.
The Master was born there in the Jiaxu year of the Jingtai era (1454). At that time, his father dreamed of a monk seeking lodging.
The following day, he received the tonsure from Master Dan. In the *Bingxu* year of the Chenghua era, he left the household life at Wannan Temple in his native province under Master Baian Kong.
In the *Guisi* year, he went to Hangzhou to receive full ordination. In the *Bingshen* year, he returned north and shut himself within his quarters.

He read through the *Wansong Nianti*, which contains the recorded encounters and kōans of ancient worthies, yet he remained as if facing a blank wall. One day, he suddenly attained realization, exclaiming: "This school is not one that perishes once and never revives."
One who lets go from a precipice must still expect another’s needle and thread; they move with subtle intricacy and circulate through mutual interplay without contact.
It is like a rabbit facing a person trying to milk it—it can by no means be obtained. Eventually, he turned back and left the monastery, seeking out Master Wufang to inquire further.
He received the Master’s words: "The one pivotal point for a person does not depend on seeking externally; you must simply turn directly toward your own breast."

He burst forth from within and only then reached his home. Suppose, however, a person comes who fundamentally has no self and whose very being is entirely empty—how would you respond to such a person’s words?
Before the question had even ended, [the Master] struck him across the face with his palm and said, "How can you be like that? At this, the teacher attained great enlightenment.
He presented a verse, saying: "Splitting the face, blocking the cheeks; lightning and sparks from flint. To establish life and settle the body, all traces vanish;
In the twelfth month, lotus flowers bloom one by one. One day, Cong asked: "When the Second Patriarch made three prostrations and returned to his place, what was the meaning of that?

The Master said: "A tattered shirt and a worn monk’s robe. Cong said: "That is not it; speak further. The Master said: "Wearing straw sandals and leather boots. Cong said: "Not yet; speak further. The Master said: "Straw sandals and leather boots. (Cong remained silent.)

He exclaimed, "A strange matter! The Master shook his sleeves and departed. [The Emperor] patted him on the back and certified him, saying, "In days to come, you shall uphold our school and spread it widely throughout the world.
Be cautious; do not be negligent. In the *Renxu* year of the Hongzhi era, he began his dharma ministry at Huayan Monastery in Dengfeng.
In the first year of the *Zhengde* era, the *Bingyin* year, by imperial decree, he was transferred to Shaolin. Disciples gathered like clouds, and the drum was struck without end.
On a day of emptying the mind, he ascended the hall and raised this case:

Once, when a monk came to pay his respects, Jinfeng seized him and said, "Do not tell anyone on my behalf that I have a karmic occasion (nidāna) to relate. As the monk made a gesture of listening, Jinfeng gave him a slap.
The monk asked, "Why did you strike me? Feng said, "I want this story to circulate. The Master remarked, "An owl pecks at rotten rats;
a hawk carries off a dead snake. This is because their kind is base and lowly; they possess only such wiles.
It brings shame upon Jingu Peak and turns him into a mere subject of gossip. At that time, if Huayan had seen him say this, he would have immediately told people, 'I..."
I shall cite an anecdote for you to consider: as soon as it is mentioned, you should cover your ears and leave.
Why? Because it is said: "Where the lion turns its body, the adamantine true eye opens. [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "Where worldly people dwell, I do not dwell;

where worldly people travel, I do not travel. This is not because I find it difficult to live together with others; rather, it is because, in general, the monastic and the lay must be clearly distinguished."
The ancients were thus: cautious and vigilant, renewing themselves day by day. They only knew how to climb high, yet could not let go;

it was much like bathing while clutching the bridge pillar. If I, this mountain monk, were to do so, it would not be like that: I would cast my body across the sea of right and wrong, walking with natural ease through the field of sound and form.
When the blazing flames reach the heavens, there is no need to seek fire—who would instruct one to strike at noon?
The Third Watch. [The Master] raised the case: A monk asked Shimen, "What is it like when the year ends and the age is exhausted?

Shimen said, "The story of Old Wang from the eastern village burning paper money at night. The verse says: Old Wang from the eastern village burns paper money at night; He calls out to ghosts and spirits, who arrive before his eyes.
A black-lacquered giant wears a paper hat; He swings on a swing outside the curtain of luminous night. [The Master] raised the case of the Woman Emerging.
A Discourse on Meditation. The verse says: "A three-bay thatched hut, Six great plumes of smoke; Suddenly, a mind of anger arises, And the entire world is steaming hot.
Addressing the assembly: "When Bodhidharma came from the West, he used the Dharma of the One Vehicle to point directly and transmit alone, enabling people to see their nature and become Buddhas.
Yet when it reached my Shaoshi [Mount Song]—like nine tripods suspended by a single thread—it is enough to make one’s soul tremble with fear."
"You all must pursue it with vigor and strength; you must settle this matter. You must strive urgently and not let the days pass in idleness.
O assembly, what do you call it? Do you call it the One Vehicle Dharma? After a long silence, he said: 'Above all, do not mistake a jar for a bell.'"
The three governors—Yi, Zheng, and Hui—were drawn by the Master’s virtuous influence and diligently followed him to inquire about the Way;
thus, the Master’s flourishing of the Dharma and the Way can be readily imagined. In the Jiaping year of Jia-shen, at the age of seventy-one, weary of receiving visitors, he charged his disciples.
Among the mists and clouds of the thirty-six peaks, he built a hermitage to spend his final years.
He was the dharma successor of Chan Master Sōngshan Zài of the thirty-third generation under Dajian (Huìnéng).
Chan Master Dazhang Zongshu of Zongjing Monastery in Shuntian Prefecture was also known by the sobriquet Xiaoshan.

He was the son of the Li family of Nanhe in Shunde and was born during the Gengshen year of the Hongzhi era of the Ming Emperor Xiaozong. While playing with other children, he delighted in performing Buddhist rites.

At the age of ten, he was able to master the general principles of the Classics and Histories. One day, he suddenly set aside his scrolls and sighed, saying, "These are matters for governing the world;

they are not the Dharma for transcending the world, understanding life, and escaping death. He then informed his father and went to the Kaiyuan Monastery in the prefecture to receive the tonsure and become a monk.

Hearing that the Master Yuezhou possessed a refined and penetrating spiritual eye, he went to attend upon him. Entering the inner chamber, he requested instruction, secretly delving into and closely practicing the teachings.
In the eighth year [of his training], one day while reading *Zhuzhou’s Recorded Sayings*, he had an awakening upon seeing the account of Dingguo’s sudden realization of the Way.
He thought to himself, "This is simply a red eye bumping into a firebrand. He immediately entered the room and asked, "I shall not ask about the nine years of facing the wall;
but as for the matter of severing the arm to find peace of mind, what is it? Zhuzhou replied, "It was precisely because I harbored poison at the beginning that I harmed you, my son."
Sūn washed the soil, yet it would not turn to mud. The Master said, "If it were not for the Venerable’s mention of it, how could one see the people of Shaolin?
Zhòu then gave two puffs of breath. The Master said, "When you can do nothing with the boat, break it! Guǔdǒu then went out. On another day, he entered the room for private instruction.
Zhaozhou asked, "One must have words upon entering the gate; do not bring a question to ask. The Master said, "Sun-face Buddha, Moon-face Buddha.

Zhaozhou said, "I see his jowls from behind his head. The Master said, "The Abbot must also be careful. Zhaozhou drew back his body and said, "This mountain monk’s year is in the hexagram Kan (the abyss).
The Master prostrated and said, "I, this humble one, am at fault. Thereupon, Zhaozhou entrusted him with the Great Dharma.

In the *Renchen* year, he opened the Dharma at Xingde; next, he presided over Tianqing and Wutai. In the *Dingsi* year of Shizong’s Jiaping era, Shaoshi repeatedly submitted petitions [requesting his presence].
The Master then sighed, saying: "Thirty years have passed since the passing of my late teacher. The spirit of our school has reached its decline, and the elders of former generations are exhausted.
It is said that the Zen groves are in decay; those who propagate the Dharma are many, yet they merely feign me to live in ease. We must not fail to support it with urgency."
He leaned upon it; its collapse was imminent. Although I felt ashamed of being entrusted with such a task, what could I do about the entrustment?

Thus, he joyfully took charge of it. In the year of Bingyin, he went to the capital. He presided over the Zongjing (Mirror of the Source) at Longqing Monastery. When the reign title was changed to Dingmao, he traveled to the Western Mountains, reaching Sanxue Cave on Guji Mountain.
The Master delighted in its seclusion and tranquility, and thus entered the summer retreat there. By winter, his illness flared up. In the twelfth month...
On the sixteenth day of the month, he took up his brush and wrote a verse. He sat upright and passed away. His secular age was sixty-eight, and his monastic seniority was thirty-six.
His remains were cremated and divided into three portions: one was kept at Zongjing, one was sent to the ancestral cemetery in Shunde, and [the third was] [implied].
He returned once more to Shaoshi. Previously, this was the site of Xieyuan; every day the Dharma drum fell to the ground, and illness broke out daily.

When the locust branches withered after the Master’s passing, the trees eventually collapsed. Thus, the decline of the Dharma at this site corresponded exactly to the Master’s departure from the world.
Chan Master Wuyin of Xianqing Shu’an at Yansheng in Kaifeng Prefecture took the tonsure in his youth and received the precepts, taking Monk Kebiao as his teacher.
He attained realization under Yuezhou, who entrusted him with a verse of instruction. In the Jiajing year of Jichou (1529), he resided at Bailiang.
At the request of Minister Liu Ren, the Master ascended the seat and said: "The moon has set and the stars are sparse; the night is deep. The radiance of the sun rises high, revealing the Emperor..."

Jingdong. Translating scriptures, I cherish the whiteness of the empty window; entering samādhi, I watch the red glow of the flickering wax candle sway. Upon the meditation couch, the bundled *bō* grass is lush and green;

before the morning mountains by the water, the jade-green waves are vast and shimmering. When guests arrive, the stone cauldron is fit for composing verses in unison; as the curtain rolls up, the clear mists fill the hall. Then he descended from his seat.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the year of Bingchen, having finished expressing his thanks to the assembly, he spoke this verse:
He passed away peacefully.
Chan Master Jinshan Debao of Baoshan (Jinshan) at the Neiqiu Biaoshan Guanyin Monastery in Shunde Prefecture was a native of the Liu family of Yangjin in Shandong.
In his youth, he left home for ordination under Weian at Haiyan Temple in Beijing; after studying there for three years, he then went to seek instruction from [the Master].

Wunian resided at Yuci County in Shanxi for seven years, during which he achieved great enlightenment. Subsequently, he visited Yuezhou at Shaoshi Mountain, where he attained the Dharma after another nine years.
Later, when Zhao Yan heard of the Master’s Way, he came to welcome him; there was not a single day that the Master did not preside over the opening of a hall.
He occupied the seat of the Dharma for more than twenty years, finally retiring at Guanyin Temple. One day, suddenly—
He entrusted all his ritual implements to his disciples. Master Tong continued to propagate the Dharma and its transformation; he then spoke a verse to bid farewell to this world, saying:
"When coming, there was no shadow; when departing, there is no trace. The cycle of birth and death—emptiness is best explained. Today I turn my body upon the path beyond the clouds."
Like a single bright moon, he was free to drift west or east. Suddenly, he closed his eyes and passed away.

His disciples enshrined him in a stupa to the south of his former hermitage, north of the Li River. On the fourth day of the third month in the Gengwu year of the Longqing era, his age was eighty-five.
The thirty-fourth generation descendant of Dajian [Huineng] was Chan Master Shao-shi Huanxiu Changrun of Mount Song at Dengfeng in Henan Province;
his courtesy name was Dayuan (Dàqiān). He was a native of Nanchang.

He was the son of Huang of Jinxian. Having lost both parents in his youth, he followed his paternal uncle in traveling about. Once, while observing a troupe of performers, he felt a sudden clarity as if struck by a profound realization:
"All illusions are but limited constructs; what then of impermanence? He subsequently entered Mount Funiu to pay homage to Tantan, where he received the tonsure.

After three years, he first attempted to restrain his mind, which was like a floating gourd tossed upon the waves—arising and ceasing in rapid succession, leaving him utterly at a loss for how to apply himself.
At first, Nan went to Wansong Lin at Mount Jing to resolve his doubts. Lin questioned him, saying, "Who is it that doubts? What is the thing upon which doubt is cast? The Master could not explain.
He then traveled to Jiuhua, where one night he realized his body was identical to empty space. He went to a guest to verify this realization.

The guest considered this to be an obstruction to the principle. Upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained an awakening at the passage concerning "perfect and luminous knowing that does not depend on mental ideation.
It was vast and clear, like an image in a mirror, not falling into illusory emptiness. He then realized that the external objects before him were merely a single breath of worldly toil.
Next, he visited Daifang Lian. He asked, "When an elephant appears in a mirror, what then? Lian said, "You must simply smash it to pieces. The Master asked, "After it has been smashed, what then?
Lian said, "It still does not transcend the realm of mind and objects (*cittaviṣaya*). The Master remained undecided.

Having heard that Xiaoshan’s method of teaching the Way was different from that of other regions, he went there to visit him. He brought up the previous dialogue. Xiaoshan said, "Why must you smash it? The Master said, "..."
"What about the reflection in the mirror? Fushan asked. "Where is the reflection? the Master replied silently.
One day, Fushan asked whether his former doubts had been resolved. The Master held up his palm. Fushan said, "Are you not asking for a phantom to catch a shadow?
The Master said, "What else could there be beyond this? Fushan said, "Try turning your robe inside out and looking. Thereupon, the Master applied himself with even greater diligence.
Lijiou practiced for two years. One day, while reading, he came across a verse by Dongshan. He asked, "If it is certainly not that person, then who exactly is he?
The Master attained sudden enlightenment and presented this verse: "If you wish to recognize this person, there is a true message:
Formless, he fills the void; with form, he leaves no trace. He has been the teacher of Buddhas and patriarchs; He constantly acts as heaven and earth."
Then, from a whisk made of tortoise hair, a pure breeze arose; with a staff made of rabbit horns, he picked out the bright moon.

The Master again seized him, saying, "Do not merely repeat the words of others; you must further enter the gate of awakening yourself. The Teacher replied, "Since I do not even rely on conditions, from what gate could I enter?"
Shushan wrote: "Since you do not rely on conditions, why have you come here? The Master said: "Precisely because I do not rely on conditions, I have come here. Shushan said:
"Regarding the single phrase 'not relying on conditions,' speak for me. The Master said: "The colored phoenix soars with body at ease;
the iron ox gallops with mind ever free. Shushan then transmitted the Great Dharma to him, saying: "There will surely be one who acts as a Lord of Men and Gods."
One should reflect upon the verse concerning the autumn at Shaoshi. Later, the Master traveled to Huagai in response to an imperial decree and stayed at a monastery.

The monks there prepared with exceptional reverence. When the Master inquired about the reason for this, the monks said, "Yesterday we dreamed that the deity of the monastery swept the gate, saying, 'On the morrow, a Patriarch will pass through here.
The Master replied, "The Patriarchs passed away long ago. Upon the arrival of the written report of his passing, public opinion [converged].

The successor to the seat was not yet appointed; the Master would not accept. The assembly requested a second time, and the Master declined a second time. Thereupon, someone presented a written petition expressing the intent of the formal entrustment (*parindanā*);
only then did the Master grant his consent. In the autumn of the Wuli Jiaxu year (1614), he entered the monastery, where he took up the *dharma-staff* and delivered discourses on the Dharma.

All marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. His presence before the assembly was solemn and majestic, possessing the style of ancient times. The Imperial Censor Wang Dakun remarked that the Master’s appearance was truly eminent.
Yet his deportment was refined and dignified; his resonance was like that of a great bell; his universal salvation was like a broad raft;
he steadied the turbulent currents as immovably as a mountain; and his manifestations according to the capacities of beings were like a pearl rolling upon a tray.

When it came to upholding great enlightenment and awakening the masses from their delusions day after day, he applied himself with tireless diligence, taking the Way upon himself as his own responsibility. (And so forth. This is indeed a factual record. Year of the Yiyou cycle.

On the seventh day of the fourth month, he spoke a verse to announce his passing; this is recorded in full in the complete biography. The Minister of Rites, Lu Shusheng, composed the inscription for the stele.
The stupa was built at Mount Ben on Mount Linshan in Jianchang Prefecture. Chan Master Changzhong, whose secular surname was □ of the same prefecture, followed the Elder of Heilin.
Having shaved his head the night before, on the day of Jiǎzǐ (the first day of the sexagenary cycle), he went to Mount Shàolín. He encountered the Master [Shénxiū] coming out from the mountain.

The Master stepped forward and asked, "Where is the stone where Bodhidharma sat facing the wall? The Master pointed toward a dark, verdant spot. The Master said, "Why do you point east when speaking of the west?
The Master replied, "There are as many contrived Chan practitioners as there are hemp or millet seeds. The Master said, "This old fellow is right here; he is a demon!"

When Meiren asked this, Shanshan struck him. Later, when Shanshan was succeeded by Master Jingzong, the latter served him diligently for three years. Having received his instructions, he returned to Xujiang and lived in seclusion at Conggu.
Shanshan spent his days sitting only in *dhyāna* (meditative posture). Whenever someone questioned him, the Master would merely wave his hand and say, "You do not understand my words.
When the questioner pressed, "Try saying something," the Master replied, "The waters outside the city walls of Nancheng flow steadily toward the north. The questioner— [remained silent].

His eyes were fixed in a stare. The Master said, "I told you before that you do not understand my words. Later, he lived for twenty years in a thatched hut on Mount Lin, never associating with the world.

When officials and scholars came to visit him, he would simply sit in silence. When Luo Jinxi and others discussed Neo-Confucian learning with him, the Master would directly sweep away their arguments with talk of the "Ultimate" (shangxiang).
When a monk attempted to challenge him with the essential points of the sutras and treatises, the Master likewise dismissed them.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "If the eye of the school is not clear, it is not ultimate. The monk then asked, "What is the eye of the school? The Master shook his robe and rose.
Wuming presented what he had attained, and the Master said, "To realize it is not nothing;
you must further attain its functional application. Only then will you succeed. Otherwise, it is merely 'mercury-silver Chan. He then cited Nanquan’s story of breaking the cauldron.
Regarding the causes and conditions: A question was asked, "Where did the ancients intend their meaning to be clear? He replied, "Sweeping the sleeves and walking away;
the hook has bait. The cauldron is broken, yet the jade is flawless. The Master said, "Go to the cow-pasture; I have been waiting for you for a long time.
In the Wuli Wuzi year, one day he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "I have a great matter that must be settled; you all must know this."
The assembly was bewildered. The Master raised his fist and asked, "Do you understand? The assembly had no reply. He then struck the desk once and said, "Hūṃ!
Hūṃ! I have finished for you. Thereupon, he passed away. His stupa was enshrined at the foot of his home mountain. He was seventy-five years old and fifty years since his ordination.
Throughout his life, his conduct and speech were meticulous. He would never casually reveal [the Dharma] unless one possessed a sincere heart for the sake of the Teaching.
Chan Master Tianran Yuanzuo of Shiheshan Monastery on Mount Pengque in Shunde Prefecture, whose courtesy name was Shaoxi, was the son of the Fan family from Xianren Village in that same prefecture.
In his youth, he followed Master Ying of Puli Monastery to receive the tonsure. By nature, he was fond of learning and accompanied great masters to various places.
He visited Xiaoshan at Shaoshi Mountain, where their spiritual faculties were in accord and he was entrusted with the great Dharma.

Upon returning to his hometown, he lived in seclusion on Mount Pengque, firmly refusing all invitations. Although the Palace Secretary of Mount Pengyan, Mr. Wu, exhorted him repeatedly and four times over, he only then arose and followed him.
Entering the hall, he said: "In years past, Zhuge Liang was called a recluse; yet at the thatched cottage, he was firmly invited to leave the mountains. If even the pine blossoms are moistened..."
The power of spring lies in the deep crags; when it manifests, how could I dare to resist? This has been so since antiquity.
Now that I have no choice but to yield, I can do nothing but entwine my eyebrows with you all. (With the whisk, he draws a circle and says: Do you understand?
The single path beyond—where the sages of a thousand ages have not transmitted it—is such that students exhaust their bodies, like a monkey trying to catch its own reflection. Unless one forgets...
When form departs, wisdom perishes; when the pair of opposites cease, the mechanism reaches its end. This state of empty lucidity, never obscured, is the field of constant, clear knowing.

To truly pass through this, one must see the meaning of the "Plucking the Flower" and the essence of the "Facing the Wall. It is much like counting another's peaches and plums outside the palace walls;
in the end, they do not belong to oneself. Do you all still wish to know the direct pointing message of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Thereupon, [he] said:
He struck the desk with his whisk and said, "Just now, this mountain monk has already made my announcement. He then descended from the seat.
A monk asked, "Pounding the mallet and raising the whisk, citing the ancients to clarify the present—all these are merely ways to stop a child's crying.

What are the golden coins? The Master said, "One sees only the thunder and lightning issuing their commands; who knows that the stars and constellations manifest their literary brilliance? The monk said, "The Master holds them in his hand."
Huixing asked, "What about those who are still training? The Master said, "Closing one's eyes and sitting in mid-autumn, yet resenting the moon for having no light.
Wu Pengyan asked, "What is the essence of *prajñā*? The Master said, "Quiescent and unmoving. He asked, "What is the function of *prajñā*?
The Master said, "Responding and thereby penetrating all things. He asked, "Where is the place where one gains strength when applying oneself? The Master said:
When Wangxiang arrived, the light was brilliant and dazzling. [Wangxiang] asked, "What is it that does not gain strength? The Master said, "Where Li Lou walks, the waves overflow the heavens.
[Wangxiang] said, "If that is so, then Confucianism and Buddhism have never been different from the beginning. The Master pointed to the void and said, "Is this Confucianism or Buddhism?
Are they the same or different? Yan bowed and said, "Thank you for your instruction. From then on, [the Dharma spread through] the south of the capital and the Yellow River.
To the north, there were none who did not submit upon hearing his reputation. In the tenth month of the year Wuyou (1605) of the Wanli era, he passed away while seated at Ben’an.
His disciples erected a stupa at the site of his former hermitage, where he had received his formal ordination.
Chan Master Rujin of Xingguo Temple on Mount Dakei in Dafeng Commandery was the son of the Chen family of Yongnian in Guangping.

At the age of seventeen, he went to Dongshan Xiao to receive the tonsure and the full precepts. He traveled to the capital to frequent lecture halls, but realized that such pursuits were not the ultimate goal.
Thereupon, he withdrew from his post and traveled south. Joining a companion, they crossed the river and visited Xiaoshan at Shaoshi Mountain. After a long time, he attained some realization.

When Xiaoshan questioned and cross-examined him within the hall, [Dongshan] was always ready to act without yielding, as if competing for mastery. Fearing that the Master’s disposition was too rigid and lacked emotional flexibility, Xiaoshan once cautioned him, saying:
"Our school has gradually become distinct from the world. The life-force of wisdom is like a single thread suspending nine tripods; it is vital to possess true power."
Descendants, protect this with deep sincerity. Since you already know that the stone tortoise walks at night, you may act like the wooden horse roaming in spring.
You must forget all artifice in every place before you can see the truth revealed in every instance. Yet, there remains the path beyond this; you should still examine it thoroughly.
He then offered this verse of entrustment: The long-winged stone tortoise walks beneath the moon; He now reveals himself face-to-face, clearly and distinctly.

He then sought seclusion in his old village, keeping his shadow from leaving the mountains and taking no pleasure in seeing visitors from within. After a long time, he began to teach the Dharma; his spiritual mechanism was like rolling pearls, and the number of monastic disciples increased daily.

His austere integrity and solitary style are truly sufficient to inspire those of the degenerate age; this is indeed a factual record.

Chan Master Zhànrán Yuánchéng of Yúnmén Xiǎnshèng in Shàoxīng Prefecture was also known by the sobriquet Sànmù (Scattered Wood).
He was the son of the Xià family of Huìkěi and was born in the eighth month of the *xiānyǒu* year of the Jiājìng era of the Míng dynasty. His grandfather, Qiāntú, was renowned for his filial piety.

From birth, the Master was exceptionally intelligent and possessed eloquence; he understood things upon encountering them and had a free-spirited nature. Although there were matters that others found difficult, lowly, or trivial, he invariably...

He personally undertook [his practice] without any sense of avoidance or dread. After his father passed away, he went to seek out Yinfeng, knowing that there was the matter of Zen meditation (*chán*).

He investigated the koan "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? for three days and three nights until he had an awakening. He rushed to see Yinfeng, who rebuked him. Upon withdrawing, he felt as though something were obstructing his chest.
At the age of twenty-four, he went to Tianhuang and received the tonsure under Miaofeng; he did not lay his side upon a mat for three years. (Section B)
In the year Wuyou, he heard a monk reciting a verse by the Great Master Fu. That which had long been a "lump obstructing his chest" was suddenly cast off;
he was then able to memorize it and comprehend its profound meaning. He took charge at Yunqi Monastery and subsequently returned to seclude himself in retreat at Baolin.

Thereupon, he recalled the dialogue between Qianfeng regarding "raising one and not being able to raise two," and attained a sudden, great enlightenment. He expressed this in a verse, saying: "Raising one, raising two—distinct ends."

Ni! Originally, herein there is neither right nor wrong. The tune of the "Snow Song" is sublime; those who understand it are few. Only Shaoyang was granted permission to harmonize it in perfect accord.
How could these two elders have ever moved their tongues? Yet in all quarters, people vainly knit their brows in conjecture—like a hawk flying past New罗 (Luo).
The story of "Carving a Mark on the Boat to Seek the Sword" was fundamentally delusive. He also offered a verse on Yunmen’s dialogue regarding the fifteenth day.

From that time on, his speech was always able to break free from conventional molds. While at Yunqi, he encountered the return from the cremation of a deceased monk. Yunqi asked, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go?
The Master stepped forward and said, "Thank you, Great Master, for your concern. Yunqi nodded in approval. Later, when visiting You at Bantang, [he...]
"Wu-nian (No-Thought). He asked, "The ancients said it is like a flake of snow flying onto a red-hot furnace; tell me, does it possess the eye that penetrates the barrier or not?
Wu-nian replied, "I do not see any such thing as 'ancient worthies. The Master hurriedly pointed behind him and said, "What about the one behind you? Wu-nian then desisted.
In the *Xinmao* year of the Wanli era of Emperor Shenzong, Master Cizhou arrived from the capital and preached the Dharma.

When the boatman arrived at the "Wind-Stopping" landing on Mount Kuaiji, he presented what he had attained to the Master. The boatman asked: "The Wind-Stopping Landing faces the Green Mountains nearby;
the city of the King of Yue lies by the vast blue sea in the distance—what is it like there? The Master replied: "The moon pierces through the blue sea; the Persian does not raise his eyebrows.
The boatman further interrogated the Master regarding the sequence of the school’s fundamental principles. The Master responded with a verse concerning the Five Ranks: The Five Ranks.
Ruler and minister, you must know this with urgency: within this, why wait for thought? A stone woman is adept at playing with no thread;
a wooden puppet can raise the mechanism beyond transformation. Red dust billows and swirls from the bottom of the well; white waves roll and fly over the mountain peaks.
"Birth itself is originally effortless; unaware, one naturally attains the imperial foundation.

Zhou said, "My son, in the future you will open two flaps of skin and have the capacity to cut off the tongues of all people under heaven. He then ordered him to enter the room and sealed it with a verse:
"A single drop of water from the Cao source, The Buddhas and Patriarchs have transmitted it to one another. Now, at the time of my transmission and reception, The great earth becomes sweet."
Lù said: "Alas! From the peak of Wǔrǔ, an unbarbed arrow shoots down, striking half a child from the South.

Tàoshì Táo Jūn and Zhāngxùn Yuán of the Imperial Academy requested that he restore the Xian-shèng Monastery. He served as abbot for thirty years, dedicating himself solely to the propagation of the Way.
While in Yuezhou, the ancestral temple was first praised for its grandeur. In the year Jiǎyīn, he presided over Guǎngxiào; in Yǐmǎo, he presided over Jìng.
At Mount [Name], on the Bingchen day, the Master presided over the East Pagoda and ascended the hall. A crow cawed on the front mountain peak; a magpie chirped on the back mountain peak.
This is simply this ○○. To contemplate it deeply is not subtle. Whether subtle or not, it is like a mute eating yellow myrobalan: having a mouth, one cannot explain it.
Ascending the hall, he encountered the sound of a stream and said: "Golden Cock, for your sakes, first turn the first..."
The single ultimate truth is the realization of the fundamental wheel of Dharma. What more do you seek? Do you understand?
If not, I, this mountain monk, shall speak it once more for you all. (He strikes the ground with his staff. "Those who have ears are certainly not deaf."

He held up [the staff] and said: "One who has eyes is certainly not a blind man. Do you understand? 'Calling for Xiu-yu again and again was originally no matter; it was only that the patron wished to recognize the sound.
He then struck the ground once with his staff. Ascending the hall, he said: "To call two three, and to point to seven as eight.
Grasping the Great Axe upside down, Buddhas and demons are all slain. Yet I recall Old Lady Wang of the Eastern Village, who turned her clothes inside out."
"Li Gongwa of Xicun—those who see him and hear of him all laugh themselves to death. They clap their hands and say: 'Ai xi xu a la la. When entering the hall [the Master said]:
'If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of land in the great earth.
One might think that even the Goddess Nüwa had to smelt stones to patch the breach in heaven; yet what is the purpose of this mountain monk ascending this seat today? After a long silence..."
He said: "Raising the intention shatters the iron bowl; without a thought, one shoots the stone tiger. He ascended the hall and said: "This old fellow does not know characters;
he has misread 'yi-si-yi' (the character for 'self'). I went to ask the Great Great Man, and his answer was: 'It is truly Ni. Now tell me: who is it that knows the characters?"
The illiterate one was right. After a long silence, he said: "If one is a lion, one never chases after clods of earth.
He ascended the hall and said: "First, pulling stones; second, pushing millstones. In your daily conduct and actions, take care not to let them slip away. Xuansha was originally Xie Sanlang."
"Do not go to the neighboring village to seek Li Da. "Great assembly, what is the matter that is not missed?

One sees only the six dragons contending in their dance; who knows that the vermilion phoenix has entered the azure heights? Entering the hall, [he said]: "The western wind is truly fierce and cruel."
The myriad sounds are all withered and desolate; branches and leaves have all fallen away. That which remains exposed—tell me, O assembly, what is this one thing?
After a long silence, he said: "Last night, where was the fire that burned out the ancient tomb?"
Ascending the hall: "Silent, silent!"—I say directly: silent. "Awake, awake!"—I say directly: awake. A clay ox performs somersaults in the void;
a wooden woman eats a great fright before the cliff. Tell me, what is the meaning? The jade hare conceives her fetus and shines at noon;
the golden rooster embraces its chick and crows at the fifth watch. Small Assembly: Mist and rain steal away the mountain colors; the stream wind...
"Sending forth the sound of water; fundamentally, every dharma is fully manifest. Do not allow the mind-consciousness to forcefully arrange it. "O Great Assembly!
If you understand this as an external object, I grant you one eye. If you understand this as the Buddha-dharma, I shall shatter your skulls!
The staff has not yet ceased its work. Why? 'In the treasury of my King, there is no such sword. (He brandishes the staff.)
"Assembly! If one discusses this matter, it is enough to make the Triple Vehicle lose heart and the Ten Stages tremble in their souls.

Even a Great Being at the stage of Equal Enlightenment, upon reaching this point, can only gaze at the moon through a gauze screen. Tell me, assembly: what extraordinary quality do the patch-robed monks possess that they dare speak such bold words?
Have you not heard it said: 'To bestow the rank of Brahmā directly upon the ordinary and mundane'—this is truly extraordinary."
This is the essential meaning. How can people conceal it? To the assembly: The Confucian scholar burns torches to read in the bitter cold;
the farmer plows and weeds amidst the rain. Although their toil and ease differ, they are nonetheless engaged in the same practice.
As for those of us who are śramaṇas, we eat without farming and wear clothes without sericulture—after all, what kind of work have we accomplished? (He strikes the ground with his staff. Rain.

The three types of grass flourish and grow tall; in this place, the song of Yao is sung. To the assembly: "At the tip of a hair, a world-system appears; within a speck of dust, the Wheel of Dharma turns.
A mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru; a grain of millet hides a world. Looking at this with cold eyes, such things are not yet our own fundamental business.
Tell me, what then is the fundamental business? It is simply to be clear and aware by oneself alone, something that others do not see. To the assembly:
One who contains a pearl to repay a kindness is merely deluded; one who presents a raw jade to the ruler and has his feet cut off is unwise.
Is there anyone among you who feels gratitude and seeks to repay such kindness? If there is, do not fail this old monk. To the assembly:
As long as one has not realized that objects are but mind, various kinds of discrimination arise. Once one has realized that objects are but mind, discrimination no longer arises. Manifestation—
The mountains ahead are bright and the waters are exquisite; magpies screech and crows caw—is this discrimination or non-discrimination?
Try to decide! Addressing the assembly: "If you do not look back, you are already mistaken; if you attempt to deliberate, when will you ever awaken?

Setting aside for a moment Master Yunmen’s act of taking the mountain gate and placing it inside the Buddha hall, tell me: what about moving Mount Sumeru and putting it into the eye of a mustard seed—what is that?
[The Master] addressed the assembly, raising his whisk and saying: "Master Yunmen is coming! He says:
'Last night, this whisk transformed into a dragon and swallowed up ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, and ten billion fragrant seas.
How can you all know of this? Today, I shall speak at length once more to deliver this news to you."
He tossed his whisk and said, "A lotus leaf moves though there is no wind; it is certain that a fish is swimming beneath. He addressed the assembly:
"The solitary wanderer outside the gate—what purpose does he have for roaming at leisure? With no family wealth to entrust, the elder’s sorrow increases day by day.

Alas! How can this compare to listening to a singing girl in a wine tavern? If you have no heart [for me], then I shall simply leave. When the Master was first at Jiashixi Temple, he was together with...
The masters Zibai Yuechuan, Taoshiku, and Huang Shenxuan were enjoying the moon together.
Shenxuan asked, "I beg the Master for a word regarding the karmic conditions of Mazu, Nanquan, Xitang, and Baizhang as they enjoyed the moon. The Master said, "You sit; I stand."
He was not permitted to speak of it. Xuan rose immediately to apologize for his transgression. Shuanchuan said, "The Academician has missed the point.
Baizhang said, "My phrasing could not match that of this old man. Xueqiao Xin asked, "What are you doing here, Master? The Master replied:
[The Master] killed someone. Xìn said, "There is a certain method for this. The Master said, "I have not seen you for five years;
I simply thought your nostrils had turned upward. One day, while sitting around a brazier with Shíkùi Jīlóng, Jìlóng said, "Master Wúniàn is here.
I beg you to cite for me the phrase by which you attained realization. The Master said, "Facing the fire, my back is still cold. [He then] went on his rounds.
Su Yunpu asked, "The embroidered mandarin ducks are for you to behold; the golden needle is not passed on to others. What is this golden needle?
The Master said, "I traveled all over the capital, yet I did not meet a single person [who knew it]. As Yunpu was about to offer a word, the Master said, "The golden needle is lost.
A monk came to pay his respects. The Master asked him, "What is the matter with your traveling? The monk—
The Master drew a circle. The monk struck the table three times. The Master then drew another circle.
The monk struck the table three times again. The Master then drew three more circles. The monk wiped them away. The Master said, "Apart from this."
He uttered a separate phrase. As the monk hesitated, the Master shouted him out. The Master asked: "When the myriad dharmas return to the One, where does the One return?
He held up his sash and showed it to him, saying, "This was bought with six-tael silver from Hangzhou.
He asked: "Regarding Nanquan’s killing of the cat—what was his meaning? The Master said, "Do not slander him. The monk asked, "How can one avoid slandering him?"
[The monk] departs. The Master says, "Heaven! Heaven! [The monk] asks, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?
The Master says, "A single bright moon shines upon Gusu. [The monk] asks, "When Magu visited Zhangjing and Zhangjing said 'That is so,' what was the underlying intent?
The Master says, "Picking up one and putting down another—this is not the hand of a master. [The monk] asks, "'Originally pure and still, how did it suddenly..."* *Note: The text cuts off here.*
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise. The Master said, "It is because you have this one question. [The monk] asked, "The Master often teaches people to 'let go.
I wonder, what is it that they let go of? The Master said, "The *utpala* flower blooms once every three thousand years.
In the evening session, he cited the anecdote concerning Gushan’s response to the invitation of the King of Min, saying, "One person has attained life from within death."
A master’s hand presents itself within the master’s grasp. One person withdraws from the path midway; where one gains advantage, there one loses it.
Xuefeng said, "What a fine sacred arrow! It has shot into the nine-layered city. This was already like casting a hook and throwing a line.
Fú the Elder said, "I will wait until I have finished my examination before I grant it; the blind turtle and the lame tortoise have already been caught in their own defeat.
Fú pursued them halfway back and reported this to Xuefeng. [Xuefeng] remarked, "It is very much like clutching one's hair and heading to the yamen.
Xuefeng said, "He still has words; you must know that he did not mean well. Fú said, "That old frozen lump still retains a trace of local sentiment; he only knows..."
Hastily rushing forward, one does not realize they have taken the wrong path. Xuefeng then stopped. A toothless tiger harms people without knowing pain.
"Great assembly," said Jingshan, "if you are long-standing practitioners of high caliber, you will certainly understand Xuefeng’s way of acting. But as for beginners..."
By no means may you set foot upon the ground of those three people; you must have your own living path yourself before it will do.
Throughout his life, the Master was not bound by the Vinaya; he cast aside formal protocols, his intestines were as straight as a string, and his tongue was as swift as an arrow.
Whether encountering people of high or low station, old acquaintances or newcomers, he treated them all with the same fundamental methods of guidance and discipline.

When the Prince of De in Shandong drew blood to write a letter inviting him to his residence to inquire about the Way and receive the precepts, the Master accepted. Indeed, there was nothing beneficial to others that he would not undertake.
On the first day of the twelfth month of the Bingyin year of the Xizong era, he composed several sheets of words of entrustment. On the fourth day, he traveled to Tianhua.
Having finished his address to the assembly, a monk requested leave. The Master said, "I, the old monk, also wish to set out on my journey today.

In the evening, he again offered words of instruction to the assembly, speaking with earnest persistence until midnight. At the hour of the Ox (2–4 a.m.), he passed away while lying on his right side.
His disciples enshrined his entire body in a pagoda on the southern mountain of Xiansheng. He was sixty-six years of age and had forty-three years of monastic seniority.
Chan Master Xinyue Huixi of Shaoshi on Mount Song at Dengfeng in Henan Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Daoshao of Shaoshi. His courtesy name was Hanhui.

He was the son of the Liu family of Mancheng in Jintai. He received the tonsure under Pujiseng and, at the age of sixteen, requested instruction from Panshan; his investigation into the Way was diligent.
Now, one who is resolute and untiring in their vow may even forget to sleep or eat. One day, while reading the *Lamp Records*, he encountered a monk asking Xuan Sha, "What is the seamless stupa?
Xuan Sha replied, "This single seam—how large or small is it? At these words, the Master attained a sudden realization.
Thereafter, he visited various eminent monks, including Ciyun, Songgu, and Jingyuan. When Wuyan came to preside over the Dharma at Shaolin, the Master went to study under him.
There was a covenant. After a long time as the *karmadāna* (Vina), he spoke in verse to entrust [the dharma], saying: "The Esoteric Dharma has no dharma to be transmitted;
how can it be transmitted? There is no place of transmission or entrustment; luminosity and darkness interpenetrate wondrously. He subsequently lived in seclusion in the wilds for many years.

When his words fell silent and he passed away at Dengfeng, an imperial edict requested the Master to succeed him on the seat. The Master entered the monastery in the *jiǎzǐ* year of Emperor Míng Xīzōng. The monks...
Question: "What is the ruler? The Master said: "A son of a thousand pieces of gold does not sit with his back to the eaves. Question: "What is the minister? The Master said:
"When a person is exiled from their country, their thoughts turn deep as they travel far away. Question: "What is the union of the way of ruler and minister? The Master said: [The text ends here].

Within the realm, the Son of Heaven has bestowed his imperial edicts; beyond the passes, the General returns with reports of victory. In the *Guīyǒu* year of the Chóngzhēn era (1633), the Prince of Zhōu invited [the Master] to enter Bìndǔ, where he resided at Xānglín in the Imperial Garden.

Day after day, officials and scholars came to inquire about the Way. Cáo Yìngqiū, the Military Commissioner, asked: "Your Reverence, you have reached seventy years of age, yet your complexion is like that of a youth; you may truly be said to possess virtue. The Master replied: "Layman," [and continued:

"The body is like a withered tree, the mind is like dead ashes. When the wind blows through the trees, there is no sound; when the ashes are extinguished, there is no heat. This is what is called 'having virtue.'"
"How can one use virtue to praise longevity? Cao said, "One who possesses virtue possesses longevity.
The Master asked, "Does Yan Yuan not possess virtue? Cao replied, "Yanzi certainly possesses virtue; it is simply because he was excessively clever that he lacked longevity.
The Master asked, "In that case, was the cleverness of Confucius not superior to that of Yanzi? Cao was unable to respond. The Master thus discerned [his deficiency].

His intellectual agility was of this sort. In the winter of the Jia-mao year, he took his leave to return to Shaoshi Mountain. Manifesting a slight illness, the assembly gathered around him to inquire after his health.
The Master counted on his fingers and said, "On the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month, I shall recover. When that time arrived, he ordered a bath, sat upright, and passed away.
He lived to the age of seventy-six. His disciples, including Hai-kuan and others, erected a stupa for him to the west of the temple.

Chan Master Wuyi Yuanlai of Boshan in Guangxin Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jing of Shouchang; he was the son of the Sha family of Shucheng, Luzhou, and was born in the Ming dynasty.
In the year Wuli Yihai (1615), he was born wearing white robes and wrapped in heavy layers. At sixteen, he frequented lecture halls and gained a reputation for his learning.

Suddenly, he sighed and said, "The pursuit lies within myself; how could it be merely a matter of literary phrases? He then went to Mount Wutai and entered the Jing-an Monastery to receive the tonsure. For five years, he practiced the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Realizing this was not yet the ultimate truth, he went to visit Shouchang, where he contemplated the koan: "Where did the boatman hide his body so that no trace remained?"
Jiexia. One day, at Mount Baimu in Min, while reading the kōan concerning Zhaozhou’s “Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell,” he had an awakening.
He returned to see Changqing, who asked: “The ant knows how to seek out the place of the stench; the blue fly tends to fly toward the side of the foul odor.
Is this on your side or on the subject’s side? Jiexia replied, “On the subject’s side. Changqing rebuked him. Jiexia was displeased and subsequently...
Dwelling in a single room, he redoubled his efforts at the work of death. One day, hearing that the Dharma-protecting deity had fallen to the ground, he suddenly attained a state of vast clarity.

He presented a verse to Chang, saying: "Yushan offered me a single word; my mind was extinguished and the path of speech cut off. How many profound interpretations and understandings there may be—they are like pouring boiling water on snow.
There is no handle to grasp, yet the golden needle is excellent. Through the conditions of time and season, the plum buds burst forth; from withered branches, the peach blossoms bloom."
"Flowers bloom in the ninth month; when they meet the eye, there is no need for further discrimination. Casting a probe-rod at a rapids on a swift current, countless noble seekers are drowned.
Chang laughed and said to him, "Once you have entered one gate, you enter another.

The Master replied, "This is unnecessary," yet he still could not bring himself to accept it. One day, while using the toilet, he saw a man climbing a tree and was suddenly greatly enlightened. He hurried—
He hurried to see Chang. Chang asked, "How have you been doing lately? The Master said, "There is a way of life, but it simply cannot be known by others.
Chang said, "Since it is a way of life, why not allow others to know it? The Master said, "Not knowing, not knowing.
Chang suddenly said, "What kind of skill and vision does this old woman possess, that she burns down the hermitage and drives away the monks? The Master said, "Only..."
Yao Huanjin asked for a verse on the case where Chang said, "When a monk questioned Xuantze, the dragon roared and mist arose;

the tiger sighed and the wind sprang up. The Master stood and offered this verse: "Killing and bringing life to, each vies for mastery with its own marvels; How could the dim-sighted eyes perceive them?
Though it emits light, it does not follow the whims of the age; As before, the spring breeze pursues the horse's hooves. Chang laughed and said, "You..."
"Today I finally believe that I have not deceived you," [the Master] said. The Teacher asked, "Will there be anything further hereafter?
Chang replied, "This old monk knows only the morning and evening meals; after this, it will suffice for me to sit and don my robes, as I lack any other schemes."
In the year Renyin, at the age of twenty-eight, the Master left to reside at Boshan. Subsequently, he presided over Dongyan, Dayang, and Gushan in Min.
In the Jisi year of the Chongzhen era, he accepted an invitation to Tianjie Monastery in Jinling; his dharma assembly was renowned for its great prosperity. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition. It cannot be depicted even upon several rolls of plain silk. Boshan appears in the world..."

This is also for the sake of the one great matter of causal conditions. A single length of white silk passes straight through the head. The old fellow with the broken smile has already entrusted this to you;
how many among gods and humans have been deceived by its heat? Brothers, you must know that this matter is not attained through effort or practice.
It is not attained through cultivation or realization; it is not attained through contemplation; it is not attained through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Even if you were to refine your own body and mind until they were like withered wood or cold ashes, remaining in samādhi for a hundred years, in the end you would still be but a dead man.

This has absolutely no connection to the matter of one's fundamental nature. Therefore it is said: "Even if you reach the moon’s reflection in a clear pool, or the sound of a bell in a quiet night..."
Sound follows the striking without fail; it encounters waves and ripples without dispersing. Yet, this remains a matter of the shore of birth and death.
Brothers, you must directly seize the spring colors of the nine avenues before the flower-and-willow streets, and [grasp them] upon the lotus bank.
Bringing forth the autumn winds from the eight directions, one finally attains a state where application is without deficiency—a time of sovereign freedom according to conditions.
Brothers, do you know where Boshan stands today? After a long silence, he said: "I have a pair of hands for the destitute;
I have never lightly bowed to those who take things for granted. He then ascended the hall and said: "He who does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion..."

Who is this person? Within the heap of red dust, they reveal their entire body. Having realized that the myriad phenomena are empty and without substance, how could mountains and rivers obstruct the eyes?
A three-year-old child with hair like snow; his divine light extends ten thousand miles as a single iron bar.
To tell this matter clearly to one who knows: the continuous mountains facing the gate are truly marvelous. Furthermore, he has personally burst forth from within the ranks.
Before the cliff, the stone tiger gives birth to a cub at night. Setting aside for now the matter of giving birth to a cub, tell me:
at what time does this occur? Zi, Chou, Yin, Mao, Chen, Si, Wu, Wei, Shen, You, Xu, Hai? Three unbroken lines for Qian; six broken lines for Kun; the center of Li is empty; the center of Kan is full.
Counting them backward on one's fingers, they remain as ever: an inch long and a foot short. Entering the hall: "The Real does not conceal itself."
Falsehood! When a crooked thing does not conceal the straight, the great chiliocosm becomes as black as lacquer. When the clouds and mist are lifted, the blue sky is revealed.
If a man is willing to seek it there, within a single word are contained the Three Mysteries: "The bride rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads.
Within one mystery are contained the Three Essentials: "A lame monkey leaps about profusely. Having both illumination and function, he strikes the sand basin.
The very bottom is frozen solid. Establishing host and guest, they walk hand in hand across Western Qin. Only Wang Taiyi of the Eastern Village—every time he raises his brush, it is ever more new.
He ascended the hall and said: "Today, Boshan does not speak of the existence of dharmas; nor does he speak of the non-existence of dharmas;
nor does he speak of both existence and non-existence; nor does he speak of neither existence nor non-existence. He transcends the four propositions."

Severing all hundred negations: the stone man nods his head; the green mountains knit their brows. Having won the warmth of spring through deep winter’s chill, one pierces the mist and rends the clouds to enter the emerald heights.
Entering the hall, he said: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad dharmas are of one body with me."
Master Zhao only knew how to withdraw his body and force his way in; he simply did not understand how to shift positions and turn the pivot of the mechanism.
Little did he realize that by speaking of "one essence," it has already become two separate pieces. Have you not seen it said: "To call it 'Suchness' is already to have altered it"?
Brothers, you must know that before the hall of the ancient Buddhas there was never any divergent teaching; beyond the curtain of the night-bright moon, there is a distinct family transmission.
The moon shines clearly upon the golden sand; joyfully one beholds auspicious grass sprouting in the courtyard. Let the family tradition unfold as it will; at the wild crossing there is no one.
When the wind clears through the jeweled trees, one must believe that the white clouds have a master.
Herein lies a distinct way of life; one may then walk hand-in-hand with the ancients. If this is not yet so, Boshan has a skillful means. (He plants his staff upright and says: "Hurry!"
A Small Sermon for the Assembly: The matter of the ancestral school is difficult to express with words or exhaust with effort.
When there is a phrase that cannot be spoken, how can one open one’s mouth? Someone has already explained the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings;
someone has already explained "this very mind is Buddha"; someone has already explained "neither mind nor Buddha. It is not...
"The mind is neither Buddha nor an object. Someone says, "It has departed. But tell me, what exactly are you analyzing for your fellow practitioners?
After a long silence, he said: "Gold has its own price; who would be willing to sell it to others mixed with sand?"珍重 (Be careful).
Small Assembly (Xiao-chan): Changqing said, "Within the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed," for the sake of people.

Only through self-acceptance do we become intimate with one another. Right now, the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the pavilions, terraces, ponds, and galleries—all these myriad phenomena filling the eyes in their greens and yellows—what do you call this "unconcealed body"?
[The Master] picks up his staff and says, "Do you understand? Do not merely seek the beauty of the mountain scenery;
