Every winter, when it was time to conclude [the retreat], he would invariably resolve [the matter] on the final day of the first month of the New Year. On the third day of the first month in the year Wuzi, he beat the drum and ascended the hall, saying:
"Everyone wears a rattan straw hat; each carries a traveling pack for the waters and clouds. Stepping out the door, they tread upon the grass; the road ahead grows ever more remote.
Arriving here, if you do not achieve a decisive severance once and for all—then even if you speak of 'attaining the wondrous through returning' or 'finding the path along the way'—"
To return home is already to travel ten thousand *li*. This is simply because you are unable to act among the "different species.
But tell me, how does one act among the different species? Then, counting on his fingers, he said: "First, the chicken; second, the dog; third, the pig; fourth, the sheep."

Five oxen. Six horses. Why does he not speak of seven? *Chan*. In the evening, he addressed the assembly with repeated and earnest instructions. The following morning, he took leave of the assembly and departed from the mountain.

The Head Seat asked, "When will the Master return? The Master said, "The first, eighth, or ninth. On the sixth, he arrived at Baoshou Temple and gave instructions regarding the affairs of the monastery.
On the seventh, he went up to Longmen. In the evening, he manifested a slight illness and made his final, earnest entrustments. The following morning, he commanded...

After finishing his bath, he sat upright and remained silent. A disciple asked, "Is there anything further to be entrusted? The Master replied, "I have just something to entrust," and then passed away while seated.
This was on the eighth day at the hour of Shen (3–5 PM). His body was cremated, and a stupa was erected at the base of Geumgwisan Rock in Longmen.
He was fifty-six years old and had been a monk for thirty-five years. The Master had practiced the Way for eighteen years and served as the abbot of famous monasteries.

There were more than ten such individuals in total. His intelligence and insight were of an extraordinary caliber, and his spiritual transformations were innate. Thus, his strategic applications—whether to kill or to give life—could not be fathomed.

His love for talent and his dedication to nurturing others arose from his very nature; though his methods of training were severe and rigorous, everyone regarded him as affectionately as their own parents.
"Embracing the vast wilderness and crossing the river—this is what he prizes. Thus, all quarters acclaimed him as "the banner of coolness amidst the heat and afflictions.
Chan Master San’i Mingyu of Yúan in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Ding family of Qiantang. From birth, he possessed extraordinary qualities.

At eight years of age, he played with a group of children and delighted in chanting Buddhist hymns (*brahman*). At fourteen, he abandoned worldly distractions and took pleasure in practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

A practitioner of Chan reprimanded him for his errors and instructed him to contemplate the "Patriarch of the High Peak" koan. One day, upon encountering the words of Master Pang, he composed a verse, saying:
"The iron ox knows how to bellow; The wooden man is skilled at running. As for the mind and its objects— I perform a somersault. He simply focused on this...

Baochan had doubts regarding the story of the "Difficult Birth. At the age of twenty-three, he went to Zhenji to receive the tonsure under Master Yin. He delighted in extensive learning, yet Yin would often suppress and humble him.
One night, while walking in meditation, Baochan recalled the karmic conditions of the Old Lady who turned the Tripitaka; upon touching a fragrant table, he attained awakening.
He presented this to Yinzhu. Yinzhu asked, "Have you realized the Way? The Master replied, "As for the Way, I have not realized it;
I have simply caught Zhaozhou red-handed. Yinzhu asked, "Where did you see Zhaozhou? The Master then recounted what he had attained. Yinzhu said, "What is that 'half-treasury'?

The Master replied, "This is the matter of penetrating the Dharmakāya. Yinzhu suddenly struck him across the face with his palm. The Master withdrew. Subsequently, he went to study under Yunmen. He entered [the assembly].
In the Dharma Hall, while Mañjuśrī was strictly observing the precept of silence, he suddenly entered the hall and called out in a loud voice, "Put it down!
The Master involuntarily raised his eyebrows and smiled. Mañjuśrī asked, "When the ox in Huaizhou eats grain, why does the horse in Yizhou get a bloated belly?"
The Master said, "Go ask the pillar. Mendun asked, "If the tree falls and the vines wither, where does the ultimate phrase finally return?
The Master said, "The long river tosses white waves. Mendun asked, "What is the phrase that cannot be exhausted by a single utterance?
The Master said, "A small moon sets behind a solitary peak. Mendun said, "I still have my doubts about you. The Master then composed a verse, which begins: "The Stone Umbrella Peak..."
Before the Jade One, there is a single stream. When one encounters its source, how can one speak of the boat being lost?

As the spring mountains close with boundless falling flowers, one finds the path home and listens to the birds’ cries. Master Men [Zhaozhou] shook his sleeves and departed. One day, he entered the inner quarters, and Men asked, "The dog has no Buddha-nature—what do you make of this?
The Master responded with a verse: Buddha-nature, no Buddha-nature, no Buddha-nature. A scale... [weighs it].
A weight dropped into a well can float. Having once defeated Zhaozhou, he clapped his hands all day long and sang the *zhègū* (partridge) song.

Menke received him and subsequently entrusted him with the lineage. Thereafter, he traveled extensively to visit various masters. Arriving at Huangma, he went to call upon Wunian You. Upon seeing him, You scolded and reviled him incessantly.
The Master asked, "What is the meaning of Nanquan’s beheading of the cat? You, responding with arrogance, said, "I..."
"Can you not kill me, sir? The Master said, "If you must kill, then kill. [The monk asked: "What was the intent behind killing the cat? Ultimately, how is it?
Another said, "Wait for Zhaozhou to come, and I will tell you. The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Upon hearing the news of Yunmen’s passing, he returned to wail in the portrait hall.
The assembly requested him to give a small lecture (xiaocan). He raised the kōan concerning Shishuang’s "The entire world has never been hidden," and having finished, he said: "The assembly..."
Zengzang said: "The eastern breeze sways the willow filaments long; the red is plump, the green is slender. Fluttering butterflies cross the precarious wall;
pairs of swallows circle the painted beams. Making the gesture of playing the lute, he said: "In vain you trim the silver lamp;
deep in the night, you alone tune the *gong* and *shang* notes. He then gave a shout and descended from his seat. In the year Yihai, he resided at Longmen, and subsequently at Huashan. [Chong...]

In the *zhēng* year of the *guīwèi* (57th) cycle, he succeeded to the seat at Xianxing Temple. In the *wùzǐ* year, he established the retreat at Zonghui Temple. In the *jǐchǒu* year, he preached the precepts at Zhenji Temple.
Subsequently, he built a hermitage by Lake Hu to care for his mother. In the *gēngyǐn* year, he presided over Fanguan Temple. In the *bǐngshēn* year, he presided over Zhuming Temple.
When ascending the hall, he said: "The seamless stupa covers the imperial palace; eating oil-cakes does not deceive the local deity. The Buddhas of the three periods possess wisdom."
Sunk into lowly ranks—white oxen and stray cats. To occupy a high position without virtue is to be base; yet to be base is not truly base, and to be noble is not truly noble.

In every case, they are no match for the lamp-post or the lantern, which excel at harmonizing all things. (He held up his staff and said: "This is the Samādhi of Non-contention. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Having lit a lamp without oil, I have cleared open the aperture at the crown of my head and entered the bustling marketplace."
In the midst, one encounters the source on all sides and attains the wondrous. How is it that Hanshanzi forgot the path he came by?
Ruan Ji was unrestrained and wild; Sun Deng let out long, piercing cries. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "At the tips of the hundred grasses, recognize the Patriarch.
The grasses have withered away. In the bustling marketplace, recognize the Son of Heaven. The market has dispersed. Where do you all meet one another? After a long silence, he...
He beckoned with his hand, saying, "Singing Apes, we have met at last. He ascended the hall and said: "The sun rises over the eastern sea gates;
clouds shroud the mountains of Yue. Countless villages ahead, where red trees seem to vie with the apricot blossoms. A bridge spans across the wild waters."
Walking slowly with a staff, it is just as when Master Liu visited before. "The wisdom of all-knowledge is pure; it is non-dual and not divided;
it is without distinction and without interruption. [He] ascended the hall and said to the assembly: "After the World-Honored One held up the flower, has anyone yet brought up this matter?
After a long silence, he said: "If you wish to know the price of rice next year, go ask Wang Da of the eastern village."
Ascending the hall: It is well to rest, yet one does not rest. With white hair, one has passed the examinations, yet still clings to the black robe.
The yellow chrysanthemums vainly boast of their color after the frost; white clouds and red trees fill the desolate mounds. Śāriputra’s disappearance leaves no trace;

the sword is gone, so laboring to carve a boat upon the water is in vain. Truly, even a son of the Golden Wheel is burdened by worldly ties; how could he be willing to seek the merit of a fief of ten thousand households? Small Assembly for Private Inquiry.
A single phrase from Xinfeng was exposed on the spot by Dangyang; without touching the lips, it has already become a public proclamation.
Fine rain drizzles, yellow chrysanthemums fill the path, striking away the nostrils of the śramaṇa and causing him to forget his former steps at Handan. Before the ancient mirror stand—
How many errors there are! Looking toward the assembly, he said: "Exposed. A brief sermon: After the rain, the distant mountains possess a beautiful air;

before the window, one gazes upon the blossoms of the red trees. From atop the tower at this clear night comes the sound of the *dòngxiāo* flute; beneath the moon, we shall walk together through the misty waters."
Whether you understand it or not, you must by all means avoid missing the puppet on the stage. A small instruction:

Before Ox-head saw the Fourth Patriarch, the hundred birds brought him flowers; after he saw him, wild ghosts flew sand. It is laughable that Changting’s Cloth Bag Man made his living in the bustling marketplace.
"Great assembly, return to the hall for tea. A monk asked: "Dongshan said, 'I have always...'"
"Regarding this point, what is your intention? The Master said, "I too have harbored doubts about this for twenty years.
Today, because of your single question, I am left speechless. Question: "What is the phrase that penetrates the dharma-body?
The Master said: "A young boy playing on a green lotus leaf. Question: "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return? The Master said: "I am clear."
"Early they harvest the vegetables; at night they carry water. Where is there any leisure energy to dally with you? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Bodhi svāhā.
The monk visited for an audience. The Master asked, "Do you understand thoroughly? The monk replied, "What does the incense smoke have to do with what the Master says?
The Master said, "Three thousand blows in the morning, eight hundred blows in the evening. The ladle handle of the eastern neighbor is long."
"The handle of the ladle in the western house is short. "Is there anything more to say? A monk hesitated, and the Master struck him.
He asked another monk, "What are you doing here? The monk replied, "I am practicing Zen (sitting with the master). The Master struck him. He sneezed once; the monk was at a loss.
The Master said, "Who was it that spoke of me there? The monk prostrated himself, and the Master said, "This old monk is going to hell."
The Master’s teaching was adapted to the capacity of his audience; he did not follow conventional paths, and thus those who could truly grasp his meaning were few.
When he retired to seclusion at Yuyan Hermitage, he once addressed the assembly, saying: “Distant mountains are like dark eyebrows; the wild waters are a shimmering expanse of clear blue waves.

From the winding bridge, one faintly hears the crowing of roosters. In the village dwellings, thatched fences line the lanes. Egrets preen their feathers on the reed flats; the migratory geese form a few scattered rows.”
The sound is clear and resonant; amidst the wind, the flutes and pipes produce notes both long and short. The moon has naturally withered away since last night.

Upon the paulownia tree sits the Yellow Ox itself. Tangerine-peel soup quenches thirst. The Master Lan-can’s taro is fragrant and unharmed. With hair grown long, he sits upon the grass under the southern breeze.
With eyes turned upward, he regards princes, dukes, and high ministers. The old monk Yufan and the Venerable Shipman—how laughable is this lack of spirit!
Han was expelled from the monastery and further punished with a meal of coarse rice. After a long while, he said: "The spring has ended on the Ten Islands and the flowers have withered;
the red sun rises upon the coral branches. The Master [Zongze] felt ashamed that Zen practitioners were empty-minded and haughty, failing to understand even a single scripture.

Therefore, he frequently gave lectures. In responding to circumstances and engaging with people, he possessed the style of the ancient Yunmen; he would immediately employ witty banter, all of which was subtle and profound.
Master Yi passed away on the eleventh day of the tenth month in the year of Yisi (1705) of the Kangxi era. He was sixty-seven years of age and had forty-five years of monastic seniority.
His entire body was interred in a stupa on the northern slope of the mountain in front of Xiansheng Temple.
Chan Master Ermi Mingfu of Mount Dongshan in Shaoxing Prefecture was also known by the sobriquet San'i. He was the son of the Wang family of Kuaiji. From birth he was robust and imposing;
his strength was such that he could knock over an ox. By nature he was frank and upright, and whenever he perceived righteousness, he dared to act upon it. At the age of twenty-two, he...

He visited Zhenbai Shan at Daci Temple and resolved to practice with vigor, to the point that he almost forgot to sleep or eat. While on a boat with Deqing, he suddenly heard the sound of a gong and had an awakening.
He composed a verse, saying: "The gong resounds through the void of body and world; Avalokiteśvara reveals her solitary form.

The clay ox chews the moon as it runs; The wooden horse heralds the New Year. At the age of twenty-seven, he went secretly to Kaiyuan Temple to shave his head and once again relied upon [his teacher].
Shan was at Guangming Temple. When Shan passed away, he visited Jinrong. Rong recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and sent him to study under Yunmen.
Shan presented his realization upon hearing the sound of a gong. Yunmen said, "This is merely the result of past roots; you must still know that there is a further point beyond this.
The Master responded with respectful assent. One day, when Yunmen ascended the hall, he said, "Let go! At these words, the Master suddenly experienced total liberation.
Luo entered [the hall] and presented a verse, saying: "Midnight frost is cold and the moon suddenly lowers; All travelers reaching this point are filled with hesitation.
Turning back, they tread upon the path from whence they came; Starlight glimmers as the handle of the Dipper hangs low. Mendi approved it. Two years later, he entrusted him with a verse, saying:
"The gong rings and the drum resounds; Guanyin blocks the ears at the gate. Truly grasping the meaning of perfect penetration, One rides the moon..."
He ascended Mount Kunlun on the day of the Buddha’s enlightenment in the *guihai* year of the Tianqi era.

Because the gravity of his lineage transmission was paramount, the Master withdrew from view at Xiangxuewu on Mount Dongshan, where he manifested the style of Daopei. Not long after, the Gatekeeper (his teacher) passed away. The Master traveled to Jinling on account of affairs regarding the Yuyang Monastery.
It happened that Boshan came and was preaching the Dharma at Tianjie Temple; the Master went to visit him and engaged in detailed discussions on the Dharma-gate.
He engaged in a debate on the principle that "the great and material things do not transmigrate," arguing until the end of the day without yielding even slightly.
Master Shan remarked, "The Buddha-dharma in Jiangnan truly has its men. In the *wuchen* year of the Chongzhen era, Dongshan Guoqing Temple invited him to lead its restoration;

within a few years, its regulations and structures were fully established. In the winter of the *bingzi* year, he began his dharma teaching at Meishu Mito. The following year, he took charge of the affairs of Xiansheng Monastery.
In the Gengchen year, he returned once more to Mount Dongshan. There were those who requested him to take charge of Jingshan and Xuedou, but he declined both with firm resolve.

Only regarding Xiansheng did he feel it could not be without a master for even a single day; thus, he resumed his duties there. He ascended the hall and said: "The Nine Years at Shaolin facing the wall—his words filled the world.
Śākyamuni’s forty-nine years of preaching the Dharma—there was originally not a single word. For the most part, it is not in [the words]."
It is added, yet it does not decrease when diminished. Today at Dongshan, we overturn the old molds with him.
There is no carving of ornate patterns, nor the writing of Sanskrit or seal script; it is simply a seal without characters. Ordinarily, when encountering adversity, he reviles, scorns, and rages;
when meeting with favor, the four seas are filled with spring breezes. Brothers, even this fellow’s face still has a bit of yellow and black upon it, yet—
Thus, ultimately, adding more is precisely it; reducing is precisely it. If there are those among the clergy and laity who can discern this, I grant them one eye.
Even if they cannot discern it, I still grant them one eye. Why? It is simply because I must ensure that rewards and punishments are clear.
[The Master] ascended the hall and cited the story of Langye asking Elder Ju: "Where have you recently come from? The circumstances of the encounter were concluded.
The Master said: "Brothers, you must swing upon the tongues of these two venerable elders before you can know that which transcends ordinary circumstances.
Not only will you then not be ensnared by right and wrong, but you will be able to take right and wrong itself and perform the work of a Buddha.
If this is not yet so, you go to West Qin while I go to East Lu. (Shaocan) Xinghua.

The Vinaya Master was expelled because he sought to manifest that my Way is of one thread. Great Head Dadian struck the Head Seat, and only then did people believe in the "Special Transmission Outside the Teachings.
Within my sanctuary, there are times when cotton wraps a whetstone, squeezing the myriad phenomena until they go mad;

at such times, every star in heaven bows toward the North. There are times when iron encases a hūcōng onion, pressing the thousand forests until they all wither; at such times, there is no water in the human world.
He did not face east. Striking the whisk upright, he said, "There is still this one more; I have not revealed it to you all. Why? [Because] he threw down the whisk and said:
'The sea deity knows its preciousness but does not know its price; it remains for the world to illuminate the night.'"

Small Assembly Sermon: To establish merit and preserve the function of illumination is much like climbing a tree to seek fish. To withdraw the senses of sight and hearing and cast aside cleverness and intelligence—how is this any different from a cow taking milk?
It is also said: "The Way is not seen, heard, sensed, or known; yet it is not separate from sound, form, voice, or language."

According to what has been said above, tell me: how must one ultimately practice so as to attain the perfect state? After a long silence, he said: "When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it;
carry it home in a bottomless basket. This was the Small Assembly for the Eve of the New Year.

Throughout the thirty-six decans, there is entirely present good fortune, misfortune, regret, and caution; throughout the seventy-two seasonal signs, there is nothing that is not addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division. You must know this.
Within the clouds, a thousand peaks reveal their natural splendor; before the kalpa, the myriad phenomena are ever new. The cold pines, bearing dew, stand tall and solitary atop the crags;
the cultivated bamboos, defying the frost, are majestic and utterly transcend the mundane world.
If you people can here reach a decisive resolution once and for all, every year will be a good year and every day a good day. Should this not yet be so, there is more to come tomorrow.
The new shoots remain; the spring wind’s vexations have not yet ceased. A monk asked Fengxue, "When deer in the dust gather in herds, how does one shoot the 'dust within the dust'?
Fengxue said, "The fishing boat is carried to the banks of the Xiao and Xiang rivers; breath choked and despondent, one asks the white gulls. The verse says:
The Emperor is distant, the heavens high—how can one revile the Most Honored One? By chance meeting a man of state, the silken decree descends. The Imperial Edict.
Proclaiming throughout the land that all have returned to the Imperial Transformation: the feathered tribes carry reeds as they pass through Yanmen Pass.

A monk asked Touzi, "Among the three bodies, which one preaches the Dharma? Touzi snapped his fingers once. He offered this verse: "Birds sing and flowers fall, yet the person within remains obscured;
In preaching the Dharma, how could one ever rely on multiple bodies? Picking up a broken chopstick and turning it toward the North Sea, Only then do fish and dragons recognize the water."
As for "To Be Intimate": Qinglin Gyan was once asked by a monk, "When a student has finally reached [the ultimate], what is it like?
The Master added the comment: "Above all, do not linger until you forget your way home. Qinglin said, "A dead snake lies across the main road; I urge you, do not step on its head.
[The monk] said, "If one steps on its head, how is it? [Qinglin replied,] "Risking one's life to eat pufferfish. Qinglin said, "You have lost your child."
"Life-faculty. Today, in this hall, how many have lost their bodies and forfeited their lives? The monk said, "When it is not yet upon one's head, how can it be said they have been burned away?
Lin said, "There is likewise no place to evade it; it fills the eyes and fills the ears, leaving no trace. The monk said, "..."
"At such a time as this, how can one avoid being stuck to the skin and bones? Lin said, "It has already been lost. "A boat that does not leak even a needle's point.
The monk asked, "Ultimately, where does it go? "Indeed, indeed. Lin said, "The grass is deep;
there is no place to find it. "He has struck you, but do you see it yet? The monk said, "The Master must also be on guard; he has drawn me in."
"The child knows how to strike his father. Master Lin clapped his hands and said, "In one sense, they are equally a poisonous vapor. It is easy to kill oneself with heroic resolve;
it is difficult to meet righteousness with composure. He spoke again, "When I, this mountain monk, deliver such a critique, how do you all understand it?"
After a long silence, he said: "I ask you, where has the fishing boat gone? At nightfall, it still rests within the reeds. The Master practiced the Way for fifteen years;
he regarded people without distinction of high or low and was skillful and adaptable in his dealings with others. In presiding over his monastery and leading the assembly, he acted with great wisdom.
He was majestic yet not fierce; broad-minded yet possessed of restraint. He held the Great Dharma in profound secrecy, never lightly casting a *maṇiratna* pearl from Mount Sui to strike at a sparrow.

Whether whipping dragons or striking elephants, he shattered their sharp points and broke through their fortifications, all emerging with effortless composure amidst a mere glance or gesture. His words reached their fulfillment in his deeds;

his realization of the essence (*zongtong*) and his mastery of the teachings (*shuotong*) truly did not belie the prescient recognition of Bozan. In the summer of the Renwu year of the Chongzhen era, he manifested a slight illness.
He fasted for over ten days, yet he continued to instruct others with conversation and laughter, no different from his usual manner. At the hour of the Tiger (3–5 a.m.

on the sixteenth day of the sixth month, he recited a verse and passed away. He was fifty-two years of age and twenty-five years since his ordination. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the southern mountain of Xiansheng.
Chan Master Mingyou of Xiangxue Monastery in Shaoxing was the son of the Yang family of Kuaiji. From his youth, he served his parents with supreme filial piety;
when his father fell ill, he once cut flesh from his own thigh to save him. At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life and investigated the koan, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"

Having heard that Yunmen’s lineage was uniquely distinct from all other quarters, he went there to study under him. When he heard a monk cite the koan, "The Northern Dipper faces south," his state of doubt was suddenly ignited.
One day, while walking in the meditation hall, he looked up at the mountains before him and attained a sudden, great awakening.
He composed a verse to present to Yunmen, which said: "The void is shattered, with neither partiality nor correctness; The great earth sinks level—what is this?"
"Father and Mother, from this day forth I shall settle the debt of longing. The stone tiger and clay ox laugh ever more freshly. He sealed the door with a verse, saying:
"Filial piety is the foremost of the supreme Way; who can achieve both at once? If one maintains mindfulness in the midst of time in this manner, the wisdom-life of all Buddhas may be preserved.
This was in the year of the Heavenly Stem *Yi* and Branch *Chou*. Later, he went to reside at Xiangxue in Shangyu, where he broke his staff and retired.

The old man asked, "An ancient said, 'He is worthy to be a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs. I wonder, what do the Buddhas and Patriarchs learn from him? The Master said, "Buddhas and Patriarchs? Listen!
Fubi said, "To be a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Listen! The Master said, "Huang Shanggu plants vegetables in his back garden.
Fubi said, "I ask not of the Buddha, nor of the Patriarch; I care nothing for your Buddha, nor for your Patriarch. Speak quickly!"

"Quick path! Quick path! The Master said, "The peach tree in the eastern village; the plum blossoms on the western ridge. A monk asked, "What is it like when one remains long stuck and cannot penetrate?
The Master said, "The prayer beads are in your hand. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when sounds have not yet ceased? The Master said, "Cockscomb seeds.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like when the six sense-gates are not yet purified? The Master said, "We have already met. On the day he passed into *nirvāṇa*:
Xiangtian asked, "The ancients said, 'Among the sick, there is one who is not sick. What is this one who is not sick?
The Master remained silent. Xiangtian said, "Is it not so? The Master said, "Receive thirty blows; I shall go out and strike you myself.
Xiangtian asked, "What about that final word at the very end? The Master gave a shout. Xiangtian said, "How about after this? The Master said: [silence].

"Clouds over the Southern Mountain, rain upon the Northern Mountain. At that time, as he had no heir to continue his lineage, he entrusted his *ruyi* (wish-fulfilling) dharma robe and dharma scrolls to the Elder Duanfu, providing a verse to seek a worthy vessel for the Dharma:
"The fragrant cypress branches divide into fine shoots; Following conditions, I pluck one branch.
When the flowers bloom, their fragrant snow spreads afar; Why must it be from a different seedling? He passed away and was interred in a stupa on the Southern Mountain of Xiansheng.
Chan Master Rui Bai Ming Xue of Bian Mountain in Huzhou Prefecture was also known by his pen-name Ru Jiu. He was the son of the Yang family of Tongcheng.
He was born on the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month of the Jiashen year of the Wanli era. While still in his childhood, he prematurely lost his left front tooth.

He served his mother with exemplary filial piety, earning widespread renown for his devotion. At the age of twenty, he received the tonsure under Zhu Long at Mount Jiuhua. From Zibo Zhenke, he was granted the name Pishamon.

He was instructed to maintain the *Buddhāvatamsaka-gāthā*. In the year Wushen (1608), he received the full precepts at Yunqi. In the year Gengxu (1610), he visited Yunmen. Yunmen asked, "What have you been doing lately?
The Master replied that he had been maintaining the *Vaiśya-gāthā*. Yunmen said, "The four elements are provisional; the deluded mind is empty."
"Who dragged this corpse here? The Master remained silent. Doubt reached its peak, and he wept bitterly until death.
One day, hearing Master Nanquan’s story about the beheading of the cat, he suddenly realized the truth. He then threw his meditation cushion out [of the room]. Master Nanquan said:
One day, while traveling through Xuzhou, Huì was among the assembly attending at Menqiao. Men said, "The mountain stream flows with a murmuring sound;
each of you, try to express a single phrase. The Master said, "Striking the void produces resonance; striking wood yields no sound. Men laughed at this.

Six days later, upon hearing the sound of a bell, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment. From then on, his spiritual discernment was preeminent among the assembly. In the year Bingchen, he was bound...
In the year Jiwu (1619), he visited the venerable masters of Bei and Boshan in succession; his realization and their words were in perfect accord.
In Gengshen (1620), he returned to visit his family at Yunmen. The following year, he lived in seclusion on Mount Tianzhu. In Guihai (1623), the Master appointed him as the Second Seat.
He succeeded to the abbacy at Jing Tiebiju (Iron Wall Hermitage). A monk requested instruction on the "Patriarch" (Zhugong) koan of High Peak (Gao Feng).
The Master showed him this verse: "Shattered the azure lapis lazuli; Cast off the precious imperial robes. The pillow opens its mouth and laughs; The double-tufted one scolds Tianmu.

Regarding the meaning of "nature" (*dharmatā*): one must observe the conditions of time and season. Tonight is the eve of the new year; tomorrow morning is the first day of the New Year—this is the season.

After twenty years, when it is cold he knows the cold; when it is hot he knows the heat. He welcomes the New Year by pasting up the talisman on his door; he sees off the waning winter by returning the firewood to the hearth.

If you say they are known, you are called an ordinary person of the "hair-path" (mārga); it is like saying that while the flowering branches are uniquely colored, the oriole’s song is but a weary labor for whom?
If you say they are not known, you remain stuck in the trap of pure whiteness;
it is as if the ice is so hard that the carp cannot leap, or because the water is too shallow that the dragon cannot hide. Departing from these two paths, how can one ultimately act? [Thrust!]
Holding up his staff, he said: "The stinking falcon’s robe has been cast off entirely; one dons the nun’s cassock and bows for the New Year. Entering the hall, he said:
"I, this mountain monk, have opened a shop where I am accustomed to exchanging goods;

"If someone were to bring me a cold heart and liver, I would exchange it for a hot one. Why?
Because that which is hot is too excessively hot, and that which is cold is too excessively cold; because the cold and heat are uneven, they cause illness.
Suppose someone were to come forth who is neither cold nor hot—tell me, what would I, this mountain monk, exchange it for? Thereupon, he gave a shout.
