I now universally see that all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata. It is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments [that they do not realize it]."
Yet they are unable to realize it. This is because people, being deluded regarding the essence of this mind, do not know how to seek it within themselves;

they are externally distracted by the six sense-objects and internally afflicted by the two maladies of sinking and agitation. Consequently, they remain cramped and ignorant, harboring biased and heterodox views.

Only the Buddha-Tathāgata turned his gaze back toward this mind, suddenly awakening to its original nature and attaining Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. Therefore, amidst the immeasurable [phenomena] of the world...

Regarding the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates, and the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of supramundane Dharma gates, there is none that he does not penetrate with clarity and unimpededness, nor any that he does not comprehend thoroughly and without contradiction;
therefore, he is titled the Great Teacher of the Three Realms and the Compassionate Father of the Ten Directions.

Now, even the Confucian scholars do not recognize their own fundamental mind; how then could they observe external objects with the mind? Furthermore, it is said: "If one does not recognize one's own mind, then the root itself [is lost]."

How could one who has lost [this mind] be able to contemplate things and clarify principles? Furthermore, he said: "The *Yushu* (Book of Yu) states: 'The human mind is perilous; the Dao-mind is subtle.
Only through refinement and singleness may one truly hold fast to the Mean. This is the source of the study of the mind. The human mind consists of deluded thoughts;
it is perilous because of attachment and inversion. The Dao-mind is the principle of Heaven; it is beyond the reach of discursive thought."
Therefore, it is subtle. That which is refined is not obscure; that which is one is not mixed. Because there is no discursive thought, it is not obscure;

because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not mixed. Thus, one can exhaustively fulfill ultimate sincerity and firmly maintain this Middle Way. "Middle" refers precisely to the "middle" of the *Zhongyong* (Doctrine of the Mean).
"It resides in the mind and not in external things; it dwells within and not without. This is what Mencius meant by "the state where joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused.
Mencius simply held that when emotional consciousness has not yet moved, this is the meaning of the "Centrality" (*zhong*).
This is close to our Buddha’s principle of the "single thought-moment of non-arising"; it merely lacks awakening. The Confucian explanation of Centrality says: "It is neither biased nor..."

To say that "leaning" (*yi*) refers to being neither excessive nor deficient, and that this constitutes the harmony of the emotions already having been aroused, would contradict the intention of Zisi.
For when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused, there are no visible forms or characteristics;
how, then, could there be matters of partiality, excess, or deficiency? Furthermore, he said: "Since he does not know the subtlety of observing the mind, he merely wishes to [use] pervasiveness..."

To calculate with the deluded mind and observe external objects to exhaustively seek principle is like trying to use a dusty mirror that has not been polished or water in which a whirlpool has not yet ceased;
to hope to reflect objects therein is impossible. Failing to realize that this principle resides within oneself, one strives only to seek it externally;

thus, as one's scholarly understanding increases, one moves further and further away from the Way. It is also said: "If one observes the mind for a single day and realizes the principle, then [one understands] the myriad things under heaven..."

The principles of all things and all affairs are thoroughly permeated [by this]. The Master also said, "If for one day you can master yourself and return to the ritual propriety (li), the whole world will acknowledge your benevolence.
This, too, is a matter of seeking that which lies within. A brief distinction between the Inner Teaching and the Outer Teachings states:
Because the teachings differ as Inner and Outer, there is a difference in the depth of their realization of principle. One seeks it within the mind.
The nature is this very thing. To seek it externally is to rely on intellectual understanding. Therefore, when the mind is penetrated, the myriad dharmas are all harmonized;
when one clings to appearances, one is naturally obscured even before one's eyes. Alas! The error of seeking externally is extreme indeed.

Today, the corruption of Confucian learning is such that those who are superficial and flowery take literary composition as their primary task, while even those who are sincere and substantial do no more than focus on textual exegesis.
As for our school, when it comes to the study of the mind, we are all equally ignorant. The great Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty deeply understood this malady;

they also knew that the work upon our own minds has its fundamental source. It would have been appropriate for them to emphasize the root and suppress the branches, thereby refuting the errors of mere words and texts.
Why, then, do you contradict yourself? Furthermore, you say: "In the past, the sages all [focused] on the internal..."

Learning is the foundation, from which its application is extended outward. In later generations, literary scholars focused on external matters and consequently failed to recognize the source of learning within the mind;

they instead made intellectual interpretation their primary task. Only with the school of Henan in the Song dynasty did there first emerge discourse on human nature and principle (*xingli*) accompanied by traces of practical cultivation.
Nevertheless, they understood only the function of the mind (*xin*) without investigating its substance (*ti*), and thus remained ignorant of [the ultimate reality].
They cultivate the "centrality" (*zhong*) that has not yet been aroused, yet they remain ignorant of the principle of the "Supreme Ultimate" (*taiji*).

Because they take the principles of physical phenomena (*wuli*) to be the principles of human nature (*xingli*) prior to the differentiation of the two polarities (*liangyi*), the relationship between the fundamental and the derivative, and between essence and function, consequently remains obscure;

thus, the Way of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius has become faint. Furthermore, it is said: "To awaken is called 'internal,' while to understand is called 'external'—this refers to the internal teaching and the external."
This is why their teachings differ. Confucianists apply their efforts exclusively to the external;

because they do not further investigate what lies beyond the reach of intellectual understanding, they do not know the Way of "faithfully upholding the Mean" (yǔnzhí juézhōng) nor the place where the principles of Heaven (tiānlǐ) flow forth.

All these exist when thought does not arise and when material desires are completely purified. Although one may practice with single-minded devotion, one will ultimately fail to enter the realm of the Sage.
Regarding the principle that "activity is the functioning of nature," it is briefly explained as follows: Great Enlightenment is without thought, yet it possesses universal knowledge of the world;
consciousness and emotion involve attachment, leading only to the vain arising of worldly toil. Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally one.
The essence is one, yet because of delusion and awakening, there appear divergent paths. Buddha-nature resides precisely within the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue;

its wondrous function is never apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. It is simply this: not accepting a single speck of dust, not abandoning a single dharma—this is called "directly reaching the site of enlightenment" and suddenly beholding one's original face.
Furthermore, it is said: The Sūtra states, "It is as if I were pressing down my finger... [and so forth].

Yin Fanguang, as soon as you raise your mind, the dust of affliction arises first. If you can realize it through non-mind, then the myriad phenomena of the universe will be clearly manifest in a single mirror.
This is the "fingertip emitting light," which refers to the total manifestation of the body when not a single thought arises.

If one speaks of this "nature," it is merely to cling to a shadow. Should even a hair’s breadth of thought be attached, or a fleeting emotion arise, the marks of karma will be manifest once more, and one remains as before in delusion and inversion.
This is what is meant by "when the mind stirs, the dust arises"; as soon as the six sense organs move, one is obscured by clouds.
Reaching this point, there is no room for effort. It is also said: "In the generations prior to the Three Dynasties, there was no 'Buddha' to be named; only..."
The Sage Emperor, succeeding Heaven and establishing the Ultimate, traced the origin back to Heaven. He spoke of how humans obtain this luminous awareness and know the principle through Heaven;
therefore, he said, "That which Heaven mandates is called nature (*xing*). "Nature" means that all people take this luminous awareness as their essence.
To follow and rely upon this awakened nature, remaining constantly unclouded, is called the Way (*dao*). "Cultivation" refers to nourishing one's joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure.

It is the state of centrality before any movement has arisen. This "centrality" refers to the time when private desires have not yet emerged; it is that which is purely the principle of Heaven (*tianli*).
When private desires have not yet arisen, there is no thinking and no acting; it is tranquil and unmoving. This "tranquility" is sincerity (*cheng*). Supreme sincerity is without thought.

Therefore it is said: "The Way cannot be departed from for even a moment. This is followed by the injunctions to be "cautious and fearful" at the juncture where one neither sees nor hears, so as not to allow even the most hidden and subtle movements to arise.
All of this is to nourish this "centrality" (*zhong*) that has not yet been manifested;

because one is constantly aware and never deluded, when it is manifested, it becomes the harmony of being "moderate" (*he*). Thus, benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom will hit the mark without the need for deliberate thought. This—
Therefore, in the subsequent chapters of this teaching, it is said: "Sincerity" (*cheng*) is quiescence; "clarity" (*ming*) is awakening.
Quiescence yet awakening is called the Way of Heaven; awakening yet quiescence is called the Way of Humanity. Both are principles for cultivating the Way. Furthermore, it is said:
"The Sage, having attained this principle, established the laws of worldly governance and instruction. Our Buddha, having attained this principle, established the world-transcending [teachings]."
Regarding the Dharma of liberation in the world: the Confucian school clarifies only the Way of Heaven and Man, whereas our Buddha clarifies the Way of the Four Sages and the Six Realms of Beings.
If one exhaustively masters the Way of Heaven and Man, one can then advance toward the Buddhist Way.

However, if one does not clarify the principles of human nature (xingli), then the principles of Heaven and Man will remain obscure; and if those are obscure, how can one possibly fathom the principles of the Buddha?
Ah! This scholar possesses far-reaching insight and complete talent; he has profoundly mastered the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). His discourse is纵横 (zōnghéng) and unimpeded;
he exposes hidden mysteries and directly clarifies the essence of the mind (*cittatattva*). Furthermore, his phrasing and purport are exceptionally skillful and exquisite.
That he says, "Continuing the Original Teaching," may indeed be called one who is truly able to carry on the legacy of Tiantan.
The hairpin-maker Zhang, whose given name was De, was a native of Xiashui in Ningbo. For generations his family had served as attendants at the Great Compassion Hall (Daci Gongtang).
While listening to the Dharma with the assembly, he attained a realization. Once, during a heavy snowfall, he took a ball of snow and fashioned it into the form of a Buddha.

As everyone else recited verses, Zhang also composed one on the spot, saying: "A single flower supports the emergence of a Tathāgata; Six petals unfold in a circle, revealing a smiling face. If you can recognize this..."
The skull is originally water; within the Maṇi palace, one does not undergo rebirth.
*Continuation of the Lamp, Orthodox Lineage*, Scroll Forty-two (End).
